Ukraine Reveals Secretly Delivered Skyranger 35—and the Footage Suggests There’s More Than One
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:24:54 UTC
23:24:54 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Reveals Secretly Delivered Skyranger 35—and the Footage Suggests There’s More Than One
Ukraine has finally shown Rheinmetall’s cutting-edge Skyranger 35 in action—but the biggest surprise is not that the system has arrived. Footage released by the Ukrainian military suggests the powerful 35mm drone killer may have been quietly defending Ukrainian skies for months before its existence was publicly acknowledged.
Ukraine has publicly revealed its Rheinmetall Skyranger 35 air defense system for the first time, confirming that the latest German-built anti-aircraft gun is already operational and may have been serving with Ukrainian forces for considerably longer than previously believed.
The 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile and Artillery Regiment released the footage on September 3, showing the Leopard 1-based system and a brief sequence in which it engages an aerial target.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The appearance is significant because no delivery of the systems had previously been publicly confirmed. Defense Express assessed that at least some Skyranger 35s therefore appear to have reached Ukraine without a public announcement.
Even more intriguingly, the footage itself may be months old.
Ukraine may have had Skyranger 35 since winter
Although the video was released in September, Defense Express noted several visual clues suggesting it was recorded no later than around March 2026.
Trees visible in the footage are still bare, while Ukrainian air defense personnel are wearing cold-weather uniforms.
If that assessment is correct, Skyranger 35 systems were already operating in Ukraine months before their first public appearance.
The commander of one system, identified by the call sign Timati, offered another clue when describing his experience with the new weapon.
He said operating the Skyranger 35 feels like working aboard a “spaceship” because of the number of modern technologies incorporated into the system.
More importantly, Timati said his unit was “among the first” to receive the Skyranger 35.
That wording suggests the vehicle shown in the footage was not necessarily Ukraine’s only example even at the time the video was recorded.
The revelation also challenges earlier assessments by some defense-aid trackers that Ukraine had still not received the Skyranger 35 by summer 2026.
Leopard 1 turned into a modern drone killer
For Ukraine, Rheinmetall paired the Skyranger 35 turret with the tracked chassis of the Leopard 1 tank.
The older tank platform provides mobility and protection, while the turret transforms it into a highly modern short-range air defense vehicle.
The Leopard chassis used for the Ukrainian systems has been refurbished and modernized. Footage from inside the vehicle also appears to show updated electronics available to the driver.
The centerpiece, however, is Rheinmetall’s KDG 35/1000 revolver cannon.
The 35mm weapon can fire at rates of up to 1,000 rounds per minute and effectively engage aerial targets at ranges of up to approximately 4 kilometers.
Against targets such as drones and cruise missiles, the system can use programmable 35×228mm airburst ammunition.
Rather than requiring a direct impact, these rounds can be programmed to detonate at a calculated point near the target, releasing a cloud of projectiles into its flight path.
That capability is particularly valuable against relatively small and fast-moving aerial targets.
The newly released Ukrainian footage also provides a brief view from inside the combat compartment during an engagement. Even in the short sequence, the Skyranger’s rapid rate of fire and digitally controlled automatic target tracking are visible.
First public look at a system already fighting
The most important revelation is therefore not simply that Ukraine has acquired another Western air defense system.
It is that Skyranger 35 appears to have moved beyond promised aid and into operational service without a public rollout, while Ukrainian crews were already learning to use it against real aerial threats.
Exactly how many systems Ukraine currently operates remains undisclosed.
But the commander’s statement that his crew was “among the first” to receive one suggests Ukraine’s Skyranger presence could extend beyond the single vehicle finally shown on camera.
Previously, a Ukrainian Skynex air defense artillery system destroyed 12 Russian aerial targets in a single battle, including one cruise missile and 11 Shahed-type drones, according to Ukraine’s Western Air Command.

Fuel Costs and Corporate Pushback Stall US “Sanctions From Hell”

Fuel Costs and Corporate Pushback Stall US “Sanctions From Hell”
A Russia sanctions bill that overwhelmingly passed the Senate last month faces mounting opposition in the US House and is likely to stall until after the November elections over concerns regarding expanded tariff powers and rising oil prices, Bloomberg reported on September 3.
The growing resistance is a major victory for corporate lobbying groups, including the Retail Industry Leaders Association (RILA) and the US Chamber of Commerce, Bloomberg wrote.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The “Sanctions from Hell” package, formally known as the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act, had cleared the US Senate with an overwhelming 86–11 bipartisan majority. Designed to choke off Moscow’s energy revenues, the legislation secured broad support in the upper chamber following more than two years of development before encountering its current impasse in the House.
Corporate giants such as ExxonMobil, General Electric, Ford, and Pfizer sent a joint letter to Congress expressing concerns that the measure could trigger severe unintended economic consequences for American consumers by imposing broad tariffs on key trading partners.
Bloomberg noted that the bill, authored by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, would authorize 100% tariffs on the top five buyers of Russian crude and natural gas—directly targeting major purchasing nations like China, India, and Turkey—as well as countries assisting in Russian energy sanctions evasion.
House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast confirmed to Bloomberg that lawmakers are evaluating the bill’s potential impact on global fuel costs.
Mast warned that forcing massive buyers like India out of the Russian crude market would compel them to compete for other international oil supplies, driving up global prices at a time when domestic gasoline costs are already elevated due to war in the Middle East.
Bloomberg highlighted that Speaker Mike Johnson cast significant doubt on bringing the measure to a floor vote before the November congressional elections, citing both Democratic resistance and opposition from GOP factions.
House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Gregory Meeks told Bloomberg he cannot support granting any president additional tariff authority, while also criticizing a built-in waiver provision that allows the administration to unilaterally bypass sanctions, fundamentally weakening the legislation.
Prior to the bill passing the Senate, US Senator Rick Scott urged Congress to immediately enact the Sanctioning Russia Act to cripple Moscow’s war economy.
In his push for the legislation, the Florida Republican framed the defense of Ukraine as essential to confronting an authoritarian coalition of Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea, emphasizing that secondary sanctions must target any nation enabling the invasion.

Czechia issues warning over Russia-linked attempts to access Signal accounts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:24:42 UTC
23:24:42 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
The Czech Republic’s cybersecurity watchdog has warned of attempts by actors primarily linked to Russia to gain access to accounts on the encrypted messaging application Signal, local media reported on Friday.
The National Cyber and Information Security Agency said the attacks mainly target politicians, government officials and security experts, though any user could fall victim, Radio Prague International reported.
According to the agency, the attackers do not seek to breach Signal’s encryption. Instead, they use social engineering techniques to persuade users to connect an unknown device to their account or disclose their personal identification number.
The methods include fraudulent messages purporting to come from Signal’s support service, malicious links and fake QR codes disguised as invitations to join groups, it added.
By convincing users to link another device to their accounts, attackers can gain unauthorized access without directly compromising the application’s encryption.
The agency urged users to remain cautious when receiving unsolicited messages, links or QR codes and to verify requests before linking new devices to their accounts.
The warning follows similar campaigns reported earlier this year in the Netherlands, Germany, Ukraine and other European countries.
In March, the Netherlands’ AIVD and MIVD intelligence services warned of what they described as a large-scale global campaign by Russian state actors targeting government employees, military personnel, civil servants and journalists.
In April, German authorities also warned of attacks targeting senior politicians, lawmakers, diplomats, military officers and journalists. Berlin later said it believed Russia was behind the campaign, while federal prosecutors opened an espionage investigation.

Russian Conscripts Increasingly Blocked From Leaving the Country, Rights Group Reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:24:02 UTC
23:24:02 KST

- Category
- World
Russian Conscripts Increasingly Blocked From Leaving the Country, Rights Group Reports
Russian conscripts are increasingly being blocked from leaving the country, with some learning of exit bans only at border control or watching the restriction surface in the state registry minutes later.
The pattern was documented by the human rights project Idite Lesom, which reviewed appeals from conscripts attempting to cross the border between August 18 and 31.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Of 73 conscripts who contacted the project while trying to leave Russia directly, 50 managed to cross, and 23 were turned back, the group reported. Attempts through Belarus fared worse: of 11 who sought help on that route, four succeeded, and seven were stopped, including one man who turned around in Minsk.
The project emphasized that its 73 cases are not a representative sample of all Russian conscripts, but rather a self-selected group who wrote in precisely because they had already received a summons, faced a restriction, or doubted whether they would be let through. It noted that trouble-free departures are likely more common but simply go unreported.
Several accounts described bans materializing without warning. One conscript who had lived in Indonesia for years on a residence permit returned to Russia for two weeks and found he could not leave, a departure ban already logged against him. Another was stopped at a Moscow airport despite stating he had never received a summons, learning of the restriction only at the border.
One man checked the registry before a Moscow–Yerevan flight and found no ban, yet was told at passport control that his exit was restricted; when he reopened the registry minutes later, the ban had appeared there too. A conscript from Novosibirsk discovered his summons only after being blocked at an airport, and although his enlistment office lifted the restriction, he was stopped again two days later because border guards still saw the ban.
Not every case ended in a refusal. One conscript holding a summons for a medical assessment and a valid deferment reached Yerevan with no ban in the registry, while another left on a paper summons. A third crossed the land border into Kazakhstan despite a departure ban and other temporary measures imposed against him. Reservists, the project added, face no such travel restriction tied to the electronic summons.
Complaints about blocked exits began surging in March, after Russia fully launched its registry of electronic summonses. In April, a conscript from St. Petersburg was prevented from leaving through Belarus, which the Movement of Conscientious Objectors described as evidence that border services in the two countries had begun exchanging data from the electronic military registration and summons systems.
The tightening of exit controls coincides with persistent rumors of a fresh wave of mobilization after the September State Duma elections. Analysts at the Washington-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) have written about preparations for a new call-up, a possibility not excluded by Western intelligence or by European officials who spoke to The Washington Post. Those sources indicated that the Kremlin could take the step due to heavy front-line losses.
The Center for Strategic and International Studies estimates Russian forces have lost at least 1.4 million people in Ukraine, counting the seriously wounded unable to return to duty. Against that backdrop, the outflow of Russians has spiked: between August 15 and 18, more than 19,000 to 20,000 people a day crossed into Sakartvelo through the Verkhny Lars checkpoint, far above comparable periods in previous years, according to the Federal Customs Service.
The move toward registry-enforced bans follows an earlier, informal phase of the same effort. In August, border and airport staff in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and Yekaterinburg were reported to be quietly screening men of mobilization age, holding some travelers aside under the pretext of database checks until their flights had closed and then sending them home without any documented restriction.

Rubio to visit Colombia, Ecuador, Peru to strengthen US partnerships

14:22:21 UTC
23:22:21 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will travel to Colombia, Ecuador and Peru from Sept. 8-10 to strengthen key US partnerships in the Western Hemisphere, the State Department said Friday.
Rubio will meet with Colombia’s new government, led by President Abelardo De La Espriella, Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa and Peru’s new government, led by President Keiko Fujimori, according to a statement by State Department spokesman Thomas Pigott.
The talks will focus on US support for Colombia’s earthquake response, enhanced cooperation in the fight against narcoterrorism and the benefits of deeper commercial ties between the three countries and the US.
The visit comes as Washington seeks to expand cooperation with Latin American governments on security and trade, with combating drug trafficking and organized crime becoming a growing focus of US regional policy.
The State Department said the secretary’s trip will reaffirm the Trump administration’s commitment to a “secure, prosperous, and democratic Western Hemisphere.”
Colombia recently joined the Coalition Against Cartels of the Americas (A3C), a Trump administration-backed alliance to combat drug trafficking and organized crime in the region. US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said De La Espriella authorized joint US-Colombian counter-narcotics operations on Colombian soil.
 
Colombia, Ecuador and Peru are considered key partners in Washington’s efforts to address illicit drug networks and other security threats across the region, with the Trump administration seeking closer coordination with governments that share its priorities on regional security.
Rubio is also expected to discuss security cooperation with Noboa, as Washington and Quito have carried out joint counter-narcotics operations in Ecuador over the past year.

Russia is shutting down the Goethe-Institut. For many Russians, it was their gateway to Germany.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:20:53 UTC
23:20:53 KST

Russia is shutting down the Goethe-Institut. For many Russians, it was their gateway to Germany.
What is the Goethe-Institut
The Goethe-Institut was founded in West Germany in 1951 to train foreign teachers of German. The institute later expanded into a broader language and cultural exchange, teaching German to other students and immersing them in the country’s culture. Goethe-Institut centers now operate in 100 countries.
The institute opened its first Russian branch in Moscow in 1992, followed by others in St. Petersburg and Novosibirsk. Russia is now home to four Russian-German cultural associations, 16 reading rooms, 18 German language centers, and 60 educational literature centers affiliated with the Goethe-Institut.
The German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD), a partner of the institute, provided scholarships to students seeking bachelor’s or master’s degrees in Germany. Russian authorities designated the organization “undesirable” in February 2026, and DAAD subsequently closed its Moscow office and ended its scholarship selection process in Russia. Russians must now apply from third countries.
What former and current Goethe-Institut students say about its closure
Alina (name changed)
took online German courses at the Goethe-Institut and later got into a master’s program in Germany; now lives in Berlin
I started learning German at the Goethe-Institut in the fall of 2023. At the time, I was in my third year at university, though I had been studying German since my first year. I had decided to pursue a master’s degree in Germany, which meant passing a C1-level exam at the start of my fourth year. My university’s program wasn’t going to get me there in time, so about a year before the exam, I enrolled at the Goethe-Institut.
I think it was the best-known option for learning German, and it was fairly cheap. I studied online, first at the Moscow center and then at the one in St. Petersburg. Goethe-Institut centers outside the capital charged noticeably less.
Cost was exactly why I didn’t choose a private language school or tutor. A 78-academic-hour course at the St. Petersburg Goethe-Institut cost 27,000 rubles with a student discount in the fall of 2022. That’s about 346 rubles per academic hour, far less than an hour with a private tutor.
The main problem for me was that people within the same group weren’t always at the same skill level. To get placed at a particular level, you had to take an online test and were asked not to use outside resources — though of course people could still peek at something.
Unfortunately, some people didn’t take the test entirely honestly, or they had attended previous courses [after which you don’t need to retake the test] without really applying themselves. As a result, they ended up at a level clearly above their actual language ability.
After my first online course at the Moscow center, I asked for a recommendation to move straight up to a higher level. There, I felt my language skills were genuinely progressing and developing. It was a good course, and the young female teacher was pleasant.
But there was another problem: everything moved too fast, and there wasn’t always enough time to practice the material. That actually worked in my favor, though, since I needed to prepare for the exam as quickly as possible.
Unfortunately, the course didn’t last long. At the end of May [2023], we got a letter saying it was closing and the Goethe-Institut was going on an early summer break. I remember it came as a response to sanctions against the “Russian House” in Berlin. It was all quite unexpected. At the time, I didn’t even know what the “Russian House” in Berlin was or why it had anything to do with the institute shutting down. Now I live in Berlin, and I know.
They wrote that we could request a refund for the remaining part of the course if we wanted.
They also wrote that the institute’s partner centers would keep operating in Russia. As I understand it, these are the same language centers, just without the Goethe-Institut name: they started calling themselves German language study centers, and they existed in cities across Russia. The library also kept operating.
Besides the courses, I also used materials from the Goethe-Institut’s website. They have sample exams that I now use myself when teaching German, since I work as a tutor, along with good prep textbooks and sample tests — all of it really helps.
When I saw recently that Germany had refused to renew its agreement with the “Russian House” in Berlin, it became clear to me that the Goethe-Institut would be closed too. The two organizations go together.
It’s very sad, of course, because for many people in Russia, the Goethe-Institut is the main, best-known, and most accessible source of information about Germany, educational courses, events, and everything connected to the German language.
I think it’s great that this system was spread across the whole country. It’s wonderful that courses in the regions cost less than in the capital, which meant people living there could take part. There was a chance to take the exams and then use that certificate to study abroad.
Now all of that is becoming much more complicated. There are online courses and online schools, but nothing comparable to the Goethe-Institut in terms of name recognition and accessibility. There’s surely some alternative out there, but you would already need to know where to look.
I hope that people who stay in Russia will get the chance to take Goethe-Institut online courses through other countries.
Oleg
tutor who prepares students for the German language exam at the Goethe Center and for DAAD scholarship applications; currently pursuing a master’s degree in Germany
I chose Germany for my master’s degree primarily because of free education. I already knew the language and was familiar with the system, and I had several acquaintances and friends who had already been studying and living there for years. I knew I’d have someone to turn to if I needed anything.
What appealed to me most was how well everything was set up, along with the free education and its overall quality. The education in my field is probably better in the U.K., but it’s much harder to get admitted there, and tuition is far more expensive.
I decided to apply at the end of my third year, which is also when I started preparing — about a year before classes were set to begin. I already knew German from studying it in school, and by that point I was teaching it myself, so my level was fairly good. I just needed to get more familiar with the exam format.
I had already taken the Goethe-Institut exam back in school, at the A2 level. Our school had a partnership with the institute, and its staff and my teachers knew each other. In Samara, there weren’t really any other options [to confirm your German level].
I took the exam I needed for admission in Moscow in the fall of 2023. The main difficulty was payment: it was only accepted in euros, to a German account. I didn’t have a foreign card or any close friends living abroad, so I had to ask friends of friends.
The Goethe-Institut matters for more than just exams. It’s also a place to learn about admissions and the education system itself, and to get advice.
I applied for a German master’s program, but a much more common path is going straight into a bachelor’s program after finishing school. That’s harder, since schooling in Germany lasts 12 years versus 11 in Russia, so there’s a special program set up for foreigners.
The Goethe-Institut was where you could learn more about what options exist, how to apply, and what documents to prepare — probably one of its main roles, besides teaching the language and administering exams.
These days, it’s mostly people planning to move to Germany or other German-speaking countries who study the language.
I see interest in moving and applying among my acquaintances, though my sample is obviously skewed — mostly people who graduated from good Moscow universities, mainly in the humanities. They’re finding it hard to find a place for themselves in Russia right now, so they’re more often interested in moving abroad.
Because of the Goethe-Institut’s closure and problems with scholarships, studying in Germany is becoming significantly less accessible. There are now major difficulties with taking the exam and securing funding.
I suspect interest in German among Russians has declined since the [full-scale] war in Ukraine began, because there are fewer opportunities to use it in Russia. Before the war, there were German companies and joint projects. Now, if you study German, it’s already quite hard to find work in business in Russia — unlike in the cultural sphere.
Olga
has taken the German language exam several times and frequently visited the library and events at the Goethe-Institut; lives in Russia and plans to apply to study in Germany
I decided to apply for a master’s program in Germany back when I was still in my second year [of a bachelor’s degree]. The decision was fairly simple: Germany is one of the developed European countries where you can get [financial] support and study more or less for free, which greatly expands opportunities for people from CIS countries.
I looked into which universities offered a good level of education and liked that they aren’t concentrated in Berlin. Every field has its own strong programs in different cities, and the humanities are well developed throughout Germany.
At the time I didn’t know the language. I only started learning it in my second year. There aren’t many options in Russia for taking a German exam if you need an officially recognized certificate; really, there’s only the Goethe Center. There’s also the TELC (The European Language Certificates) exam, but taking it means traveling to another country.
There’s also TestDaF, which can be taken remotely, but it’s held roughly once every three months, and you have to pay for it with a foreign card. There are also problems with proctoring: the internet can drop, or the microphone or screen sharing can fail. I know someone who had to retake the exam because of a technical issue.
In Russia, taking the German exam at the Goethe Center was the most convenient option. For those who had already studied there, it worked even better, since the teachers know the exam format well and can prepare students specifically for it.
I didn’t end up studying the language at the Goethe Center: by the time I started learning German, enrollment for the academic year had already closed. I found a tutor and later didn’t want to leave him, but I’d originally considered the Goethe Center my main option. It’s a respected institution, and when you’re just starting to learn a language, it seems like the logical place to go.
I also used the Goethe Center’s library, which is very large. I haven’t seen another place in Moscow where you can borrow that many books and educational materials in German in such quantity. Even buying the textbooks you need can be difficult, since Russia simply doesn’t have that kind of selection. In that sense, the Goethe Center was a pretty unique resource.
Besides the library, they also have film screenings, exhibitions, and lectures devoted to German culture. There are quite a lot of opportunities. But for me, the library was the main thing, and I was very upset about losing it.
There are quite a lot of Goethe Centers in Russia, and I’m not sure whether they’ll all actually close. When I was still planning to take the B2 exam and looking at options [in 2025], it was even possible to take the exam in Sergiev Posad [outside Moscow]. I’m curious whether they’ll really close every location.
The atmosphere at the Goethe Center is very friendly. [While taking the B2 test] I was late for the exam, and by the rules I shouldn’t have been allowed to take it at all, but I was able to take it anyway: no one humiliated me [for being late], no one gave me a hard time, no one added unnecessary stress. The same thing happened with the C1 exam. The examiners are kind and, as much as they can, try to help you, or at least stay out of your way.
At the end of September, I was planning to retake the listening and reading portions [of the C1 exam]. Because of the news about the institute’s closure, it’s still unclear whether the exam will even take place. I was very upset. My first thought was almost panicked, because it’s unclear what to do.
I have an exam scheduled in two weeks that I’ve been preparing for all summer, and they’re holding my certificates. The exam consists of four parts, and if you fail one, you can retake it separately. The Goethe Center keeps certificates for each part, and once you’ve passed all four, they’re combined into one overall certificate — the one you can then submit to a university or anywhere else that requires proof of your language level.
If they suddenly shut down now, what happens to those papers? Will I have time to pick them up? And what am I supposed to do with them afterward if I don’t have a complete certificate? For now, I don’t have a clear idea of how this is going to work.
I think it’ll make sense to write or call them to figure out what to do about my situation once the Goethe Center puts out an official announcement. For now, the plan is to wait for the exam date and not panic. In the worst case, I could go take the exam in another country. If I have to, I have to.
The Goethe-Institut was also closed in Belarus [in 2021], and quite suddenly. I can’t say that significantly reduced students’ or schoolchildren’s interest in German or in studying in Germany. At least, the people I know just go to Russia to take their exams. But of course it’s more convenient when you can not only take the exam but also be integrated into the culture [by attending a center like that].
Even at the closed Goethe Center in Belarus, where exams and classes no longer take place, there are still occasional film screenings in German and lectures. It has remained more of a cultural space. It would be great if it survived in Russia in at least that kind of format.
It seems to me that, over the years, studying in Germany is becoming less accessible for people who don’t have a financial cushion or who haven’t started preparing for it well in advance.
It used to be possible to get into a DAAD program in Germany without knowing the language at all, because there were separate competitions for Russians and Belarusians. People were admitted primarily based on their academic achievements and dealt with the language afterward. Now there are fewer of these opportunities.
If you apply to DAAD now, you [as a citizen of Russia or Belarus] have to compete in the general global pool. On top of that, the choice of universities is shrinking, especially if you need funding. Getting into a program in Germany is turning into a long game.
For me, the Goethe Center was primarily a place to take the exam. But for many people, it’s also a way to sustain their interest in Germany: going to exhibitions, conversation clubs, film screenings, and lectures. We’re probably losing not so much the ability to take the exam as, more broadly, an opportunity for globalization.

Zelensky Orders ‘Tangible Response’ Against Russia After Drone Strikes SBU HQ in Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:20:32 UTC
23:20:32 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he has ordered the head of Ukraine’s SBU security service to carry out an “appropriate and tangible” response to a Russian drone strike against the agency’s headquarters in central Kyiv on Friday afternoon.
In a post on X, Zelensky wrote that a Russian drone took direct aim at the office of SBU chief Oleksandr Poklad.
Ukrainian media reported that Poklad was not in his office at the time of the attack, which took place at around 3:30 p.m. local time.
Heavy black smoke was seen rising in central Kyiv following the strike, which Ukraine’s foreign minister described as a major escalation of the war.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least seven people were injured in the attack.
Zelensky said he spoke with Poklad and instructed him to prepare a response that “mirrors” the Russian strike. “Our military will support this response,” the Ukrainian president wrote.
The Kremlin did not immediately comment on the attack.
Ukraine’s SBU is a vast and secretive agency responsible for ambitious operations deep inside Russia.
It is also widely seen as a leading player in a campaign of covert assassinations of senior Russian military officials and other figures blamed by Ukraine for carrying out war crimes.
Reuters contributed reporting.

Reform UK, France's National Rally agree plan to stop small boat crossings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:16:29 UTC
23:16:29 KST

Reform UK, France's National Rally agree plan to stop small boat crossings
BIRMINGHAM, Sept 4 - The leaders of Britain's populist Reform UK party and France's National Rally announced a pact on Friday that they said would enable Britain to return asylum seekers arriving in small boats to France if their parties win power.
For the past decade, both countries have struggled to curb the flow of asylum seekers travelling from France to Britain, often in overcrowded, inflatable boats.
Speaking at Reform's annual conference in the central English city of Birmingham, Bardella said a National Rally government would tighten border controls, return migrants to their home countries and stop boats crossing to Britain.
"I make you this promise, if the French people (give us the presidency) our government will do everything in its power to make sure that France is no longer the gateway for illegal migration into Britain," he said to a standing ovation.
Farage and Bardella later appeared on stage together where they signed a memorandum of understanding.
The agreement said asylum seekers arriving in Britain from France would be detained and returned to France, which would repatriate them to their countries of origin.
The pact said both countries would establish a mechanism for sharing border security costs.
Opinion polls predict that National Rally's Marine Le Pen will win the first round of the next presidential elections next April by a large margin, and will also be well-placed to win the run-off in May.
Reform, which topped polls for almost 16 consecutive months until the summer, is neck-and-neck with the governing Labour Party. The next national election in Britain must be held by 2029 at the latest.
Last month, Reform said that if it got elected, it would stop asylum seekers in what it described as the largest military operation in the Channel since World War Two, including plans to return asylum seekers to France even without permission. The French government rejected the plans saying it would be a violation of its sovereignty.
More than 16,000 people have been detected arriving in Britain in small boats since the start of the year, a decline of more than 40%. But the number of asylum seekers arriving on each boat was increasing as people smugglers change their tactics.
Earlier this week, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron announced that extra police would be deployed on beaches to deter small boat crossings. REUTERS

French government promises €1B for drought-stricken farmers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:15:39 UTC
23:15:39 KST

France's Agriculture Minister Annie Genevard gives a press conference at the Agriculture Ministry in Paris on September 4, 2026. | Lou Benoist/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — France will spend more than €1 billion to help its farmers cope with a summer of devastating heat and drought, French Agriculture Minister Annie Genevard said on Friday.
The package aims to compensate farmers for their losses, prevent bankruptcies and ensure that agricultural production gets back on track, in particular to enable the purchase of seeds and fodder, the minister said.
Between 30,000 and 35,000 farms, or about 10 per cent of French farms, “are in a precarious situation or at risk of becoming so,” Genevard warned.
Advertisement
Three schemes account for the bulk of the government’s spending under the new plan.
France will speed up payments under its “national solidarity” scheme designed to compensate for crop losses. It will be topped up to a total of €520 million, provided the country's 2027 budget is duly adopted.
An “agricultural recovery fund” of €235 million aims to provide targeted support for the hardest-hit and most vulnerable farms across the produce, cereal and livestock sectors.
Finally, a targeted tax relief scheme on unbuilt land will cut €330 million in tax revenue for the state. The government is also considering extending a program helping farmers to purchase fertilizer and non-road agricultural diesel.
Genevard also suggested that the retail sector could "play its part" by keeping price rises in check.
Part of her plan is already funded for this year, but more cash will need to be allocated in next year's budget, which is set to be presented by Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu at the end of September.
Advertisement
“This is new money,” Genevard said.
The government is also expected to set out the details of a broader “recovery plan” for farmers, with key measures to be included in the 2027 budget.
Lecornu recently promised a tax depreciation scheme for “projects aimed at the future of agriculture,” alongside other measures to “continue adapting agriculture to climate change.”

Kovr Studio rethinks the look of the conventional light switch
Small details can influence the overall coherence of an interior, including elements such as light switches that are often overlooked. Standard white switch plates can contrast with painted or wallpapered walls, introducing a visual interruption within otherwise carefully coordinated surfaces. Kovr Studio addresses this detail with modular switch covers designed to alter the appearance of existing switches without tools or adhesive. The covers can be installed and removed within seconds, providing a simple way to integrate the switch into the surrounding interior.
bio-based PLA+ derived from corn starch shapes the Kovr covers
Each cover is handmade in Kovr Studio’s workshop in Lille using precision digital fabrication tools. The production process combines digital fabrication with individual finishing, allowing each piece to be produced and refined separately. The covers are made from PLA+, a bio-based plastic derived from corn starch. The material was selected for its strength and flexibility, allowing the covers to withstand repeated installation and removal while maintaining their structural integrity.

Five EU countries aim to send migrants to return hubs by 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:14:23 UTC
23:14:23 KST

Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece have agreed on a common model for deportation centres, to be negotiated with non-EU governments. The first agreement is expected around the New Year, but the partner countries have not been disclosed.
Five EU countries say they expect to be ready to send irregular migrants to deportation centres built outside the European Union by 2027. The announcement came after a meeting in Copenhagen on Friday attended by the interior ministers of Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece.
The ministers agreed on a common model for "return hubs" — facilities set to host asylum seekers whose applications have been rejected by the five countries and who cannot be returned to their countries of origin.
The five-state group is currently negotiating the creation of the hubs on the territory of one or more partner countries, which have not yet been disclosed. Uganda and Rwanda are seen as the most likely possibilities, according to several press reports.
"Today's guiding principle forms the basis for the way forward [...] to be ready to transfer the first irregular migrants to a partner country outside of the EU in 2027," said Danish Migration Minister Morten Bødskov.
He claimed that the hubs are not "a prison" or "a detention camp", but facilities where "partner countries give irregular migrants a new chance".
The five countries are expected to fully finance the hubs and may also provide additional funding, commercial partnerships or other incentives to partner countries. "A return centre scheme will be established through equal and mutually beneficial partnerships with countries outside the EU," reads the guiding principles document.
The new model should also lead to a noticeable reduction in the number of people migrating illegally to the EU. "Our common goal is pushing illegal migration towards zero," said Austrian Minister Gerhard Karner.
In the meantime, meetings with potential partners are continuing and the discussions are "becoming deeper and more fruitful," said Greek Minister Thanos Plevris, who hopes to announce an agreement in the near future.
The five ministers are set to meet again in Munich at the end of September.
The agreements with the non-EU countries will define the procedures applicable to migrants in the return hubs, the conditions of their stay and the responsibilities of the EU states involved.
The ministers said the project will be carried out in partnership with international organisations, such as the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and the International Organization for Migration, and in full accordance with EU law and international obligations.
In June, the European Parliament approved the 'strictest-ever' migration law, granting member states the right to set up return hubs by reaching agreements with non-EU countries. The adoption of the "return regulation" is likely to take place in the autumn, with final approval by EU countries, an EU official told Euronews.
The majority of EU countries seem interested in setting up return hubs, while Italy already has a similar project in place with Albania.
Nineteen EU governments are convinced that this is an "innovative solution" to pursue for migration management, as made clear in a joint letter sent to EU leaders last June, suggesting that the centres could become a reality sooner rather than later.
Return hubs have raised concerns in Europe over their compatibility with EU law and the protection of human rights. The idea has been harshly criticised by European civil society and non-governmental organisations.
"Sending people to deportation centres outside the EU means uprooting children, adults and families from the lives they’ve built in Europe and subjecting them to prolonged detention in places they don’t even know," said Michele LeVoy, Director of Picum, a Brussels-based NGO promoting the human rights of undocumented migrants.
So far, attempts to transfer migrants to non-EU countries have not been particularly successful.
The United Kingdom abandoned a scheme to deport asylum seekers to Rwanda, where their applications would have been examined. Denmark ditched a similar plan in 2023, changing its strategy from a national approach to a European one.
Italy initially projected housing around 3,000 migrants a month in its Albanian centres; the actual figure has reportedly been just 500 in total since the facilities were converted into deportation centres in March 2025.
The entire bill amounts to over €670 million, and, according to a recent study by an Italian university, detaining migrants in these centres has proven to be much more expensive for Italy than hosting them on its own territory.

====================================================================================================

‘It Still Causes Severe Stress’: Fear of Expulsion Upends Life for Some Russian Asylum Seekers in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:09:49 UTC
23:09:49 KST

Between learning a notoriously difficult local language, studying for a professional certification in economics and volunteering to help Ukrainian refugees, Nikita Belov might seem like the exact kind of Russian asylum seeker who would be welcomed in Europe.
But that didn’t stop authorities in Finland from nearly deporting him and his mother, Olga, last month. After being denied asylum and told that they faced little risk back home, the pair were “on the brink of deportation,” Belov, 25, said, before a court stepped in and ordered their case to be reconsidered.
Hundreds of Russians have landed in a similar situation in recent years. After fleeing to Europe to escape state repression, many of them manage to find a legal path to permanent residency — but others face a harsh reality when their asylum applications are rejected at their host country’s discretion.
In 2025, the EU reported that more than 10,000 Russians were ordered to leave the bloc’s member states. Advocates argue that high-profile cases like the Belovs’ show that some of the most vulnerable among them are slipping through the cracks.
Experts who spoke with The Moscow Times attributed the trend in rejected asylum applications to rising anti-immigration sentiment across Europe, which is pressuring governments to curb pathways to settlement.
“There is a strong wave of fighting illegal migration,” said Artyom Klyga, a lawyer based in Germany who works on cases of conscientious objectors and army deserters, some of the most at-risk asylum seekers from Russia. “It’s become a very popular topic for the political agenda, not only in Germany but in all of Europe.”
In the Belovs’ case, it’s unclear to what extent broader political trends were a factor. The evidence is largely circumstantial: In Finland, a right-wing government that came to power in 2023 has taken steps to curb illegal immigration and accelerated deportations, coinciding with sweeping new EU-wide migration rules designed to expedite the processing of asylum applications.
The Belovs’ lawyer told The Guardian that those changes in particular have created headaches since they came into effect this summer, adding that it’s now “even more difficult to get refugee status, even with clear political opinion showing.” Back in Russia, they face likely persecution for speaking out against the war in Ukraine. Their case was only reconsidered after a large public outcry.
“It certainly left a deep mark,” Belov said in a phone interview with The Moscow Times, reflecting on his and his mother’s ordeal, which saw them detained briefly this spring. “It still causes severe stress, sometimes even panic attacks.”
“I don’t know how long it will take to recover from this considering the process is not yet over and a positive decision is not guaranteed,” he added.
Elsewhere, the stories of Russians facing asylum denials and expulsions cut across demographics and geography. Last year, Austria deported two men from the North Caucasus republic of Chechnya who were at risk of being conscripted back home. A few months later, Latvia ordered 841 Russian citizens to leave after they failed to undergo background checks and prove their proficiency in the local language.
One of the countries that has attracted the most attention is Germany, whose historically liberal immigration policies have made it one of the top destinations for migrants in recent decades.
During the initial months of Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine, German officials signaled that their country could serve as a safe haven for Russians fleeing conscription. The reality, however, has fallen far short of the rhetoric: a report by German media last year revealed that 95% of asylum applications from draft-eligible Russian men had been rejected since the war began.
In fact, Germany’s so-called “total protection rate” — the number of all positive decisions — for asylum seekers from Russia declined each year between 2022 and 2025, from 11.5% to 4.8%, according to government tallies shared with The Moscow Times. As of June, this year’s was only slightly higher at 5.1%.
Edith Avram, a spokesperson for Germany’s Federal Office for Migration and Refugees, said in an email that the asylum process is “conducted on an individual case-by-case basis.”
“The applicant’s country of origin and the reasons on which the application is based are important factors in the examination of an asylum application,” Avram said. “However, neither factor alone determines whether protection is granted or the application is rejected.”
Advocates complain that the system is mercurial, producing judgments that ignore the facts — and risks — of individual cases.
In one recent example, German immigration authorities came under scrutiny for denying an asylum request from Georgy Avaliani, a pacifist who reportedly fled the front line in Ukraine, underwent torture after being recaptured and then escaped again.
Media reported that the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees believed there was little risk of him being persecuted in Russia. In reality, deserters can face a harsh punishment of up to 10 years in prison. Klyga, who is advising Avaliani and his German lawyer, said that an appeal against the denial of his asylum request has been filed in a Berlin court.
Similarly, Said Abuyev, a 53-year-old Chechen man facing deportation from Germany, told The Moscow Times that he fears imprisonment or worse back home. He is a regime opponent who previously served four-and-a-half years in a brutal detention facility on charges of weapons possession and being part of an illegal armed group that he claims were fabricated.
When asked what awaits him in Russia, he replied: “I can’t say for sure, but it won’t end well.”
The Chechen government is notoriously repressive and operates with near impunity, meting out severe punishments to critics and regularly drawing accusations of human rights abuses. Abuyev’s case is one of many that have caught the attention of advocates who say Europe isn’t doing enough to shelter asylum seekers from the broader North Caucasus region.
The prevalence of extraditions and deportations to the North Caucasus grew so alarming that in 2024 human rights watchdog Amnesty International published a report on the issue, calling on EU members to immediately halt the expulsions. But according to Rosa Dunaeva, a Chechen activist based in Austria, little has changed.
“It’s double standards,” Dunaeva said. “They hand over Chechens to Russia without a full risk assessment.”
Across Europe, scores of similar cases are likely playing out far from public view. The asylum process is inherently sensitive — especially when a person faces criminal charges at home — and many applicants avoid media attention to keep from drawing further scrutiny from the Russian authorities.
Klyga said that he is aware of a particularly troubling case from this summer in which a Russian man fleeing conscription was deported from Lithuania to Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave between the Baltic country and Poland. The man has been outspoken about his opposition to the war and could face prison time. Klyga requested not to publish the man’s name because it could interfere with efforts to provide support to him.
Much of Europe’s hesitation in granting asylum to Russians stems from fears that migration could be used as a backdoor for covert Russian operations, analysts say. With Moscow increasingly accused of orchestrating acts of sabotage across the continent, restricting entry to Russians is seen by some governments as an easy political fix.
“There is this rising pressure on European policymakers to react to this and to do something about this, and one dimension of this debate is about what can be done with migration,” said Simon Papuashvili, program director for Eastern Europe and the Caucasus at the International Partnership for Human Rights, a Brussels-based NGO.
For now, Brussels looks poised to increase restrictions rather than ease them.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas just this week announced that the bloc is considering cutting off visas for former Russian combatants and tightening entry restrictions for tourists.
Her comments came shortly after Germany said Russia was behind an attempted drone attack at an airport last month. One of the suspects in that incident allegedly holds a Russian passport and obtained an Italian tourist visa, German media reported.
“If it is true,” Kallas said of the allegations, “it shows very clearly that visas are a tool of these people who are meaning harm to the European Union.”

Customs officials found a loaded military-grade weapon on a young man travelling into Brussels from France
A man carrying a loaded Kalashnikov rifle was arrested yesterday morning at Brussels-South station in Brussels. The man was traveling by train to Brussels from France, and the weapon was discovered during a customs check.
The customs officer noticed that the man seemed nervous and that he was carrying a heavy bag. The weapon was found in the bag hidden among baby clothes. The rail police arrested the man, and the case is being investigated by the public prosecutor’s office.
“This shows that the reinforcement of patrols in railway stations with the assistance of our military personnel is necessary and must continue, or even be expanded,” said interior minister Bernard Quintin in response to the incident.
No other details have been released about the man or his motives. While it is unnerving that someone can walk around Brussels-South with a loaded military-grade weapon, police have said that they have no evidence that he meant to use the weapon himself. Such weapons can make their way into Brussels to be sold to criminals, particularly to drug traffickers.

IVF clinic’s embryo specimen mix-up linked to ‘intentional unlawful conduct’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:08:36 UTC
23:08:36 KST

IVF clinic’s embryo specimen mix-up linked to ‘intentional unlawful conduct’
Watchdog says it has ordered Heal Fertility to comply with law and code of practice to prevent recurrence of similar incidents
A mix-up of embryo biopsy specimens may have been caused by “intentional unlawful conduct” at a private fertility clinic, which breached the code of practice for reproductive technology by lacking sufficient protective measures, a Hong Kong regulator has found.
The Council on Human Reproductive Technology said on Friday that, following an investigation into the incident, it had ordered service provider Heal Fertility to comply with the Human Reproductive Technology Ordinance and the code to prevent any recurrence of similar incidents.
“The council confirmed that no embryos were mixed up or wrongly implanted into the human body in the incident,” it said.
The council also put the clinic’s licence under review.
It concluded that “intentional unlawful conduct by an individual” was the main cause of the embryo biopsy specimen mix-up at Heal Fertility’s clinic in Central.
The council said it would continue to provide professional support to police in an ongoing criminal investigation into the case.

Germany aims to finalize 'return hubs' by year's end
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:08:00 UTC
23:08:00 KST

Germany, partners aim to finalize 'return hubs' by year end
September 4, 2026
Germany and other European Union countries are aiming to finalize so-called "return hubs," detention centers outside the bloc where they wish to send migrants whose asylum requests have been rejected, by the end of the year.
The European Parliament in June approved tougher migration rules that paved the way for the creation of "return hubs."
"We want to reach an agreement with third countries this year," which would then enable the establishment of so-called "return hubs," said German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt after a meeting with his counterparts from Denmark, Greece, Austria and the Netherlands in Copenhagen on Friday.
He added that "technical discussions" were currently underway with countries outside the EU, but did not name such countries.
The highly controversial plan has been met with wide rejection from rights groups.
What did the EU ministers say on 'return hubs?'
The five EU countries whose ministers attended the Copenhagen meeting are seeking a deal with an undisclosed non-EU country to host the "return hubs." Uganda and Rwanda in particular are seen as possibilities.
"Around New Year, we expect to have a common understanding with a partner country outside of the European Union," said Danish Migrations Minister Morten Bodskov.
Both the Greek and Danish migration ministers said they wished for the "return hubs" to become operational by 2027.
"We do not accept that foreigners staying illegally in Denmark should be rewarded because of our difficulties in returning them," Bodskov said in an earlier statement.
The controversial scheme had already been briefly adopted by the United Kingdom under the former conservative government, but has since been scrapped after the social democratic Labour Party came to power.
In Italy, the right-wing government of Giorgia Meloni reached a similar deal with Albania which currently faces legal challenges.
Are EU 'return hubs' legal?
The legality of the plans for the so-called "return hubs" remains unclear under EU law.
A legal appraisal issued by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) in April concluded that the controversial Italian deportation centers in Albania do not violate European law.
EU law does not in principle prohibit member states from establishing such centers outside their own territory.
However, it stipulates that deportees continue to receive legal counsel and linguistic support, and are able to maintain contact with their families and the relevant authorities.
Edited by: Zac Crellin

Opposition by US and Russia raises doubts over autonomous weapons talks outcome, diplomats say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:06:26 UTC
23:06:26 KST

Opposition by US and Russia raises doubts over autonomous weapons talks outcome, diplomats say
GENEVA, Sept 4 - Opposition from the United States and Russia has raised doubts that countries meeting in Geneva will on Friday agree on a document that could pave the way to international rules on the use of autonomous weapons, three diplomats said.
The 128 states that are party to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW), an international framework hosted under the United Nations in Geneva that regulates or bans specific types of weapons considered excessively injurious or indiscriminate, have been meeting this week in the Swiss city.
They are set to decide whether consensus can be reached on a non-binding text that may usher in negotiations on prohibitions and regulations for Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS).
Concerns have been mounting about the role of semi-autonomous weapons that can identify and engage targets with varying degrees of autonomy in conflict zones such as Ukraine, Sudan and the Middle East.
Human Rights Watch and the Stop Killer Robots campaign group have warned that weapons systems, some of which are assisted by artificial intelligence, may behave unpredictably, raising the risk of fatal errors.
States agree that international humanitarian law applies to LAWS, but specifically binding international standards for such systems remain virtually non-existent.
A majority of countries at the meeting have expressed support for a draft text, but the U.S. and Russia have proposed late changes and deletions to it, two diplomatic sources said.
The Russian mission in Geneva did not comment. The U.S. mission did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"The window is getting smaller to getting an agreement," one of the diplomatic sources told Reuters.
Diplomats may run out of time and key provisions discussed over several years could be dropped, running the risk of no deal emerging, a second diplomatic source said.
DIFFERENCES OVER LANGUAGE
The U.S. position has hardened over the past six months, a senior diplomat said, with Washington favouring something more akin to guidelines than a legally binding international treaty as it says international humanitarian law already provides a framework to govern the conduct of warfare.
This position is supported by states including Russia, India and Turkey.
At least six countries received formal diplomatic approaches from Washington to back its position concerning the draft text, two diplomats said. This showed U.S. engagement to try to reach consensus on the issue, one of them said.
But differences remain over language, with the use of words such as "lethality" and a section related to exercising human judgment and control being debated, one of the sources said.
Backers of a legally binding treaty, including Brazil, Ireland and several African states, say safeguards are needed to ensure meaningful human control over the weapons systems in question. Opponents favour greater flexibility.
In August U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and Red Cross President Mirjana Spoljaric warned the world was nearing a moral red line where autonomous weapons could kill without human involvement. REUTERS

Free to Be Experimental Philosophy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:06:21 UTC
23:06:21 KST

Free to Be Experimental Philosophy
“But is this actually philosophy?”
Ethan Landes (Eindhoven University of Technology) is tired of experimental philosophers being asked The Question.
And he’s tired of experimental philosophers “appeasing” those who ask it by “dressing up experimental scholarship up as relevant to armchair analytic philosophy.”
He writes:
Every experimental philosopher has tons of practice doing this. It is how we answer The Question in Q&As. It is how we write grant applications. It is how we pitch ourselves in cover letters for jobs: “Oh sure, if you hire me, I will be conducting empirical research, but actually this is super important to existing debates in philosophy because x, y, and z”. This is the strategy experimental philosophers advise each other to use. It is the strategy I advise others to use.
This sort of appeasement is, by and large, what we see in the academic literature on experimental philosophy. Arguments for experimental philosophy, whether friendly or unfriendly for the armchair, have, in one way or another, positioned themselves as being in service of academic philosophy’s status quo. The stated goal is always improvement upon existing questions and not the creation of something fundamentally new.
He thinks it’s time for a change. His preferred answer to The Question is: “Of course we are doing philosophy. We are just not doing philosophy in their way. Not in the analytic way.”
What if we as experimental philosophers stopped playing this game? What if we pitched experimental philosophy as something historically connected with analytic philosophy but not metaphilosophically connected to it? As its own philosophy with its own methods and its own questions? As a tradition of philosophy as legitimate of an heir to Aristotle, Leibniz, Hume, and Quine as analytic philosophy?
For a lot of us, this would certainly be more truthful than how we currently pitch our work. Experimental philosophy is by no means a unified field, but a lot of its members, myself among them, just do not care about or believe in the specific problems and specific questions analytic philosophy is working on. Sure, we can pitch our research as applying to those debates. God knows I could monologue off the cuff for an hour about why my experimental research actually matters to ongoing debates in analytic philosophy. Nonetheless, if we are being honest with ourselves, those problems aren’t what motivates us. They are little more than a gateway drug introducing us to other puzzles about, e.g., knowledge, morality, or the mind. We are now interested in our own things, and they are philosophy because they are deep, deep questions about ourselves and our reality…
As experimental philosophy matures and diverges from the sorts of debates it first emerged to address, we are seeing experimental philosophy becoming an independent philosophical tradition in its own right. A tradition interested in its own set of philosophical questions with its own view of how best to approach them. Consequently, experimental philosophers should celebrate and defend this against analytic philosophy’s more chauvinistic tendencies. We should be (and largely already are) proud that we are pushing the limits of what philosophy can be, shaking up stale literatures and challenging stale methodological assumptions. Why not take the extra step and openly embrace experimental philosophy [as] its own independent tradition?
You can read Landes’ whole post here.* His is one view about the reception of experimental philosophy in the profession today, and I’m wondering if it is shared, both by those who do experimental philosophy and those who do not. We can also take up the question of whether we should, as he suggests, “embrace experimental philosophy [as] its own independent tradition,” what that would mean, and how it fits with the continued broadening of what counts as “respectable” mainstream academic philosophy since the 1970s.
* I’m not crazy about its treatment of “analytic philosophy”, but let’s leave that aside.

Türkiye, AIIB sign multi-million dollar environment deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:06:00 UTC
23:06:00 KST

Türkiye has signed a cooperation agreement with the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) that will support environmental investments, urban infrastructure and climate crisis efforts, the Turkish environment minister said.
Murat Kurum said on Friday that the first phase of the agreement would focus on environmental projects in the Marmara region through an investment package worth around $465 million.
"We aim to provide significant support for the cleaning of the Marmara Sea and our fight against sea snot through an investment package worth approximately €400 million, primarily for advanced biological wastewater treatment facilities," Kurum said.
He did not give details of any further phases of the cooperation agreement, nor how much the total investment could amount to.
Türkiye in the past faced a plague of "sea snot," a thick, slimy layer of organic matter known as marine mucilage, in the Sea of Marmara, posing a threat to marine life and the fishing industry.
The inner Sea of Marmara, which connects the Black Sea through the Istanbul Strait to the Aegean Sea through the Canakkale Strait, lies in the middle of the most industrialised region of Türkiye.
Kurum said increasing wastewater treatment capacity, expanding advanced biological treatment facilities and strengthening environmental infrastructure were among the main efforts of Türkiye's attempts to address pollution in the sea.
Kurum and AIIB Vice President Ajay Bhushan Pandey signed the cooperation agreement on the sidelines of the Climate Finance Summit in Istanbul organised ahead of the COP31 UN climate conference in November.
Türkiye is one of the AIIB's largest investment destinations, Pandey noted.

Russia: ECtHR decision to strike out more than 800 complaints denies victims truth, justice and reparation and should be reversed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:05:39 UTC
23:05:39 KST

Reacting to the decision by the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) to strike 879 applications against Russia from its list of cases on grounds of their lesser importance to case law and a lack of resources for their examination, Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Director, said:
“The European Court of Human Rights’ decision is deeply disappointing. It deprives hundreds of individuals of what for many of them is their last hope of seeing justice for the violations they have suffered.
“The decision to deny these victims their day in court cannot be justified by Russia’s refusal to execute Court judgments, or the fact that the remaining applications raise no novel questions of law, or restraints on resources. This decision should be reversed and the cases brought back on the Court’s docket.
“Council of Europe member states must meanwhile ensure that the ECtHR has the financial and human resources required to fulfil its fundamental role. In addition, they should exhaust all available means to ensure that Russia is held accountable for its violations under the European Convention on Human Rights and that its obligations to implement the judgments through individual measures, including the payment of compensations to victims, are fulfilled.”
The European Court of Human Rights’ decision is deeply disappointing. It deprives hundreds of individuals of what for many of them is their last hope of seeing justice for the violations they have suffered.
Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Director
Background
On 3 September 2026, the European Court of Human Rights announced its decision to strike 879 applications against Russia from its list, the earliest pending since 2007, despite acknowledging that they contained potentially well-founded allegations of violations of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court said the cases did not raise issues of marked importance for Russia’s responsibility under the Convention or require further development of its case law.
The applications concerned, among other issues, fair-trial rights, freedom of expression, conditions of detention, property rights and freedom of movement as listed in the Lebedeva and Others v. Russia decision. The applications also included cases brought by former prisoners of conscience, human rights defender Oyub Titiev and opposition activist Andrei Borovikov, the Russian-Chechen Friendship Society and Stanislav Dmitrievsky, and politician and prisoner of conscience Lev Shlosberg.
Russia was expelled from the Council of Europe on 16 March 2022 for starting its war of aggression against Ukraine and ceased to be a party to the Convention on 16 September 2022, but the ECtHR retains jurisdiction over violations committed before that date.

South Africa recovers over $500 million in corruption proceeds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:03:38 UTC
23:03:38 KST

South Africa recovers over $500 million in corruption proceeds
South Africa’s Asset Forfeiture Unit (AFU) has recovered 8.3 billion rand ($519 million) in assets and funds linked to corruption, Justice Minister Mmamoloko Kubayi has said, while calling for those who enable graft to face prosecution.
Speaking at the University of Johannesburg’s Combating Corruption Summit on Wednesday, Kubayi said the AFU’s recoveries had increased from about R6 billion reported at last year’s summit.
“These successes are in part because of AFU strengthened collaboration work with anti-corruption task teams, inter-agency working group on illicit financial flows. These are systems that we’ve worked or we are working on, but also these are some of the work that we are doing in partnership, not only with government but also with private sector,” the minister stressed.
But she made it clear that recovering money could not be the end of the country’s anti-corruption efforts. Kubayi challenged professional bodies, particularly those representing accountants and lawyers, to show what action they had taken against members implicated in corruption.
The warning comes as state agencies intensify efforts to recover money and assets linked to corruption. Kubayi said the Special Investigating Unit (SIU) had recovered assets and cash worth R936 million, against a target of R1 billion, over the past year.
”I need to highlight what is important about the work that is being done by SIU. SIU just doesn’t recover, but also, it’s able to stop contracts so that we don’t have to come back and recover,” Kubayi added.
The Tembisa Hospital corruption case is one example of the state’s efforts to recover the proceeds of corruption. The AFU secured a final forfeiture order for about R326 million in assets linked to businessman Hangwani Maumela, including luxury properties and vehicles. The SIU helped trace the assets.
OUTA Chief Executive Officer Wayne Duvenage said the recovery of stolen money was important but should not be mistaken for victory against corruption.
”The recovery of billions of rand is certainly a success and we should acknowledge the work of the SIU, Asset Forfeiture Unit, and other institutions responsible for recovering stolen public money. But recovery cannot be the ultimate measure of success,” Duvenage said.
He added those involved needed to face consequences beyond losing the proceeds of their crimes. Duvenage said major corruption rarely happens in isolation, often involving officials, business people, and professionals who help structure deals, move money or disguise corrupt transactions.
“If those enablers believe that the worst that will happen is that some of the money may eventually be recovered, while they remain free to continue doing business, then the system isn’t creating sufficient deterrence,” he said.
Accountability Now Director Paul Hoffman SC believes the problem is even more fundamental, arguing that South Africa lacks an anti-corruption institution sufficiently independent from the executive.
”The problem at the moment is that South Africa does not have the necessary machinery of state to deal with corruption effectively and efficiently,” Hoffman noted. He also called for legislation creating an independent, stand-alone body to deal with corruption outside Cabinet control, arguing that the Hawks and National Prosecuting Authority remain under political executive structures.
The question of what constitutes real accountability was taken further by AfriForum Private Prosecution Unit head Advocate Gerrie Nel, who was speaking at the three-day summit on Thursday. Nel said South Africa’s failure to act against corruption was partly rooted in what he described as a “willful disregard” of the accepted definition of corruption.
”Nothing is happening if there’s an arrest. Absolutely nothing. It only happens when there’s a prosecution and a conviction. Then something is happening,” Nel said. He added that the failure to prosecute was particularly concerning when politically connected individuals were involved and questioned why there were no consequences for prosecutors responsible for decisions not to prosecute.
