Study: Estonia's climate warming 1.5 times faster than global average
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:02:00 UTC
23:02:00 KST

Study: Estonia's climate warming 1.5 times faster than global average
Estonia's average air temperature is set to rise by 1.5 degrees Celsius for every 1 degree Celsius of global warming, University of Tartu researchers found.
When forecasting climate change, scientists usually opt to determine what the climate will look like at a specific point in time, for example in 2050, or in 2100. In a new study, however, researchers linked local changes directly to the prevalence of global warming. "It does not matter whether two degrees gets reached in 2040, according to a more pessimistic projection, or in 2070, or in 2090 according to a more optimistic projection. What counts is what happens to Estonia's climate once that level is reached," explained the study's lead author, Erko Jakobson, associate professor of atmospheric remote sensing at the university.
The principal finding is that Estonia's annual mean temperature has been going up by about one-and-a-half degrees for every one degree rise in mean temperatures globally. At the same time, periods of very cold weather will become increasingly rare, while hot days, tropical nights and heatwaves are to get more frequent. In other words, during the warmer part of the year, climate change can already be observed with your own eyes, not to mention felt firsthand in Estonia alone.
Observable climate change
In order to create a picture of the future, the researchers ran 31 global climate models. Jakobson noted the public's expectations regarding the accuracy of climate forecasts are unfortunately often far in advance of what current science is capable of delivering. "Some local governments want us to tell them, right down to the village level, how the climate will change in this or that location. We cannot do that – even if it were mathematically viable to do it at the county level, it would not be meaningful, and we would essentially be telling lies," Jakobson explained.
The analysis revealed also that Estonia's winters are warming several times faster than its summers. For every additional degree of global warming, Estonia's average winter temperature rises by 1.9 degrees Celsius, while its summer temperature rises by 1.3 degrees Celsius. The number of freezing days falls by 13 percent for every degree of warming. While milder winters help save on heating costs, they may bring issues of their own, not least to winter sports enthusiasts – though currently active skiers are not likely to see completely snowless winters as a rule, in their lifetimes.
"We forecast a decline in the number of cold days, and we do not actually know whether snow will fall during those cold days. In any case, even under the most pessimistic forecasts, Estonia should continue to see snow until the end of the century. But the fact that we used to have long periods without thaws will be but a fond memory for skiers," Jakobson noted. Even more convoluted challenges await farmers, as the milder conditions actually threaten winter crops: The insulating layer of snow will be replaced by more damaging freeze-thaw action.
A warming climate more generally and globally brings intensified precipitation too. For every additional degree of global warming, precipitation in Estonia rises by an average of approximately 31 millimeters, or 4.6 percent.
This precipitation falls mainly in winter and the fall, but the models remained unclear about summer projections. Estonia's location plays a key role here. "We looked at the bigger picture, meaning the entire Baltic Sea region and points south. It clearly emerged that the dividing line runs more or less through our area: In summer, it becomes drier to the south and wetter to the north," the scientist said.
In any case, Estonia's summer hydrological picture is set to become more contrasting. Short, heavy downpours wash soil and nutrients off fields while failing to alleviate drought stress in plants.
"Instead of periods of steady rain, half of the precipitation will often fall within a few hours. That water does not have time to soak into the ground but immediately runs into ditches and rivers, doing more harm than good to fields. The drought problem therefore actually increases," Jakobson warned. The stronger evaporation characteristic of a warmer climate may cause problems for farmers especially in spring and summer.
The dynamics of air masses, however, continue to pose a considerable challenge for climatologists. Estonia's weather is shaped simultaneously by strong Atlantic cyclones and high-pressure systems to the east. Precise changes in atmospheric circulation and wind behavior are therefore difficult to capture with physical models.
"There is a great deal of uncertainty regarding changes in circulation, and I do not see a good prospect of the forecasts becoming much more certain. Our latitude means that our weather is not made here but comes from elsewhere. Everything depends on whether weather coming from the north or the south gains the upper hand," the researcher added.
Because of the uncertainty, it cannot currently be said that Estonia will experience stronger winds and storms in the future. In summer and autumn, average wind speeds may even decrease slightly. "One very widespread belief is that it will become windier in the future. In some ways, that is logical: there is more heat and energy. In our work, we saw that some models show wind speeds increasing, while others show them actually decreasing. We therefore cannot confirm that winds in Estonia will indeed become stronger and storminess will increase," Jakobson said.
Bigger questions
Jakobson stressed the projections in the models are based on continuous trends, but the climate system contains a number of tipping points. "If the Antarctic ice sheet or Siberian permafrost melts significantly, or the Gulf Stream changes substantially, enormous quantities of greenhouse gases could be released. Current climate models have not accounted for such abrupt changes, so there may still be surprises," the associate professor warned.
Jakobson noted that scientific facts and the future scenarios presented by climate models unfortunately tend to become mixed up with day-to-day politics in public debate. Instead of assessing physical reality, people argue over the economic consequences of the green transition.
Scientists' task, however, is to measure the causes and pace of warming, while finding solutions and allocating resources remain the responsibility of society and politicians. "When large sums of money are involved in politics, fraudsters sometimes get involved and things go wrong. But the fact that something goes wrong in politics unfortunately does not mean that climate change does not exist," the scientist said.
The study was first published in the journal Boreal Environment Research.

Gentle rocking beds could offer a new way to treat insomnia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:00:40 UTC
23:00:40 KST

For adults who struggle to stay asleep, a bed that sways back and forth gently throughout the night might offer a path to a better night of rest. A small study reveals that continuous, slow rocking reduces nighttime awakenings and improves overall sleep quality in people with insomnia symptoms. The research was published in the Journal of Sleep Research.
Insomnia is a common sleep disorder defined by a persistent difficulty falling asleep or returning to sleep after waking up in the middle of the night. These disruptions lead to daytime fatigue, mood changes, and trouble concentrating. The standard clinical treatment is cognitive behavioral therapy, a psychological intervention that targets anxiety around sleep and helps correct unhelpful bedtime habits. While this therapy helps many people feel better about their sleep, it does not always resolve the physiological disruptions that show up on brain monitors.
Normal sleep progresses through a highly structured series of stages, moving from light sleep to deep sleep, and finally to rapid eye movement sleep. Deep sleep is characterized by specific patterns of electrical activity in the brain, notably slow oscillations and sleep spindles. Slow oscillations are large, rolling brain waves, while sleep spindles are brief, rapid bursts of electrical activity. These distinct rhythms help the brain block out environmental noise and process the events of the previous day.
Researchers Aurore A. Perrault, Sophie Schwartz, and Laurence Bayer from the University of Geneva and their colleagues wanted to see if physical motion could directly influence these brain rhythms in a clinical population. Prior experiments by the team showed that healthy sleepers spent more time in deep sleep and had enhanced memory recall after sleeping on a gently rocking bed. Studies in mice indicate that this effect is driven by the vestibular system, a sensory network in the inner ear that detects movement and balance. When a person rocks, the vestibular system sends a rhythmic physical signal to the thalamus, a brain region central to generating sleep spindles and slow waves.
Because the rocking motion directly stimulates the neural circuits involved in stabilizing sleep, the researchers hypothesized that it might provide a unique benefit to individuals who suffer from chronic sleep disruptions. The team suspected that a moving bed could act as a physiological complement to traditional psychological therapies. To test this idea, they recruited 16 young adults who reported mild to moderate difficulties falling or staying asleep.
The team first verified the participants’ sleep troubles to ensure they exhibited objectively poor sleep. For three weeks, the participants wore movement-tracking wristbands at home to log their natural rest patterns. They then spent a baseline habituation night in a sleep laboratory wired to diagnostic equipment to rule out other medical issues, such as sleep apnea or cardiac arrhythmias.
Following the screening period, each participant spent two separate experimental nights in the sleep laboratory. During one visit, the participants slept on a completely stationary bed. During the other visit, they slept on a bed that moved laterally from side to side in a slow, continuous rocking motion. The bed shifted a few inches in each direction, completing a full sweep every four seconds for the entire night.
Throughout both nights, the researchers recorded the participants’ brain waves, muscle activity, and eye movements to precisely track their progression through the various stages of sleep. The participants also completed questionnaires about their subjective sleep experience upon waking. Additionally, the researchers administered a memory test involving pairs of unrelated words before bed and again the next morning to assess whether the rocking motion affected memory retention.
The continuous rocking motion produced measurable improvements in how well the participants maintained their sleep. Compared to the stationary night, the participants spent 34 percent less time awake in the middle of the night. They also spent about 15 percent less time in the lightest and most easily interrupted stage of sleep.
This reduction in wakefulness led to an overall increase in sleep efficiency, a metric that calculates the percentage of time in bed that a person is actually asleep. The monitoring equipment also recorded a lower rate of sleep fragmentation during the rocking night. This indicates that the sleepers transitioned much less frequently from deeper sleep states back into light sleep or full wakefulness.
These physiological improvements aligned with the participants’ own perceptions of their rest. On mornings following the rocking night, participants rated their sleep quality about 25 percent higher on average than they did after the stationary night. They generally found the rocking motion pleasant and relaxing, and the participants who experienced the largest drop in sleep fragmentation reported the highest subjective improvements in their rest.
The team also looked closely at the electrical activity in the brain to understand how the physical movement altered the sleep cycle. They observed that the side-to-side motion actively synchronized with the brain’s natural rhythms. Bursts of sleep spindles and the lowest points of slow wave activity clustered at specific moments that matched the physical turning points of the moving bed.
During the deepest stages of rest, this synchronization appeared to boost brain activity. The rocking motion generated a higher density of fast sleep spindles compared to the stationary night. This suggests that the continuous stimulation of the inner ear effectively prompted the brain’s thalamus to generate the electrical rhythms necessary to keep the brain asleep.
However, the rocking bed did not improve every aspect of the participants’ insomnia symptoms. The gentle motion did not reduce the amount of time it took the participants to initially fall asleep. While some individuals drifted off much faster on the moving bed, others took longer, resulting in wide variations across the test group.
Despite the changes in brain wave activity, the enhanced rest also did not translate into better cognitive performance. The participants performed equally well on the morning word-pair memory test regardless of which bed they slept in. The researchers suspect this might be due to the fact that the rocking bed had a variable effect on the exact amount of deep sleep each person received, unlike healthy sleepers who tend to experience a more uniform boost in deep sleep.
As a small study focused exclusively on young adults, the results do not necessarily reflect how older populations or individuals with more severe health conditions might respond to the motion. Insomnia encompasses a wide variety of symptoms and underlying causes, and people with high sensory sensitivity might find a moving bed distracting rather than relaxing. The experiment also evaluated only a single night of rocking per participant.
It remains unknown whether the observed sleep improvements would persist over several nights of use or if the benefits might fade as the nervous system becomes accustomed to the movement. Further testing over longer periods will be required to determine if rocking beds could become a practical, long-term intervention for chronic insomnia. If the results hold up in larger trials, rhythmic sensory stimulation could eventually be paired with behavioral therapies to help patients find more stable rest.
The study, “Whole-Night Gentle Rocking Improves Sleep in Poor Sleepers With Insomnia Complaints,” was authored by Aurore A. Perrault, Nathan E. Cross, Thien Thanh Dang Vu, Sophie Schwartz, and Laurence Bayer.

From Kylian Mbappé’s World Cup style to Erling Haaland’s hair tie, football has had many viral fashion moments in 2026.

As a producer played Baggy Trousers, by Madness, Neville’s chino-style, wider-legged black slacks were mocked by fellow pundit Jamie Carragher, who compared Neville to Frank Worthington, the forward from West Yorkshire whose dandyish off-pitch style raised eyebrows in the 1970s.
“I went shopping in London,” Neville explained as Carragher jogged along to the Nutty Boys’ hit. “This guy styled me. I think they’re pretty cool, you know.” He predicted that Carragher would be wearing a pair soon.
Neville seems to be on to something. Because as far as the cut of your trousers goes, girth is greater.
Nick Pope, the site director at Esquire, said: “In terms of what people are actually wearing on the street, it is the wider silhouette.” Retailers from Cos to Next and Marks and Spencer are going great guns selling wider-fitting trousers in the menswear aisle.
The width currently in style can’t quite be described as “baggy trousers”, however. Pope said what Neville wore was a relaxed 90s fit for today, like the trousers seen on A$AP Rocky at the Tribeca festival in New York City in June.
The silhouette dominated men’s fashion week for autumn/winter 2026-27 among designers including Dior, Prada and Saint Laurent. On the red carpet, the style has been seen on fashion magnets such as Connor Storrie (at the Golden Globes) and Joe Alwyn (at the Baftas).
The classic football pundit dress code grew out of newsreader style: a suit and tie. It was a safe option for the footballer turned television presenter who could not show up wearing their home kit. But Neville and fellow presenter Jamie Redknapp donning a wider leg on Sky Sports speaks to a moment where TV dress codes are morphing.
James Andrew, the editor of FourFourTwo, a football magazine, said: “It’s more relaxed now.”
Pope added: “I think punditry is becoming more fashion forward in the sense that they’re wearing knitted polos and chinos. But it’s still very tonal and sensible.”
Paul Monks, who dresses the pundits for Sky Sports, including Monday Night Football, said he believed the clothes should echo the easygoing feel of the show and its audience.
“We want what we do on screen to feel relevant to the viewer,” he said. “The way people dress generally has become more relaxed. You see far fewer men wearing suits day to day now, so it wouldn’t make sense for television to become more stiff or overly formal.”
The wardrobes of pundits, as well as the England star Jude Bellingham and managers such as Pep Guardiola, have started to have an impact on everyday style.
Pope said: “They’ve become these unlikely style influencers for middle-aged men. Someone like Gary Neville is probably quite aware of that.”
The viral incident illustrated Neville’s growing interest in fashion: he has a clothing collection with Hawes & Curtis.
Corina Gaffey, a stylist, said: “Gary seems receptive to switching up his on screen style, trying different brands, silhouettes and cuts. He’s obviously in tune with fashion and interested in it.”
Pope predicted there would be more collaborations between footballing and fashion. “I think we’re going to see more pundits with their own lines,” he said.
One-nil to wider leg trousers, then.

The team from the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Qingdao did this using a material they developed called PhosCage – a sponge-like molecular structure filled with phosphate groups that act as chemical traps.

Can the Green Party’s Polanski take on Labour and win Starmer’s old seat?
Analysts say although Polanski and the Greens have performed well this year, toppling Labour in its traditional stronghold could prove a much harder task.
When Britain’s former Prime Minister Keir Starmer stood down as the member of parliament for Holborn and St Pancras this week, he ended more than a decade representing a seat that has never elected anyone but a Labour MP since it was established in 1983.
The by-election it triggered which is expected later this year would ordinarily be a formality, but instead, it has become the most closely watched contest of the parliamentary term.

That is because Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader, the self-styled “eco-populist”, who has taken his party from the margins to double-digit polling in a year, announced on Thursday that he will seek nomination for the seat. He now needs to be chosen by local party members as the Green candidate for the seat.
Voting records offer him both encouragement and a warning.
Starmer won 48.9 per cent of the vote in 2024; the Greens finished third on 10.4 per cent, behind a pro-Palestinian independent, Andrew Feinstein.
But in the Camden council elections in May, the borough the constituency is in, the Greens won 28.8 percent across its wards to Labour’s 38.8, taking seats in Starmer’s own patch for the first time.
Al Jazeera spoke to political scientists and election analysts about whether Polanski has a realistic path to Westminster.
A Green win would be a ‘surprise’
Since Polanski became Green Party leader a year ago, it has achieved some success in taking support from Labour’s left.
That includes a surprise by-election victory in Greater Manchester, while the party is currently polling as high as 20 percent nationally.
Despite the Green Party’s recent results in Camden, experts say that Holborn and St Pancras is a strong Labour seat.
“A Green win would be a surprise,” Jonathan Tonge, professor of politics at the University of Liverpool, told Al Jazeera.
For that to change, he said, the current prime minister and Labour leader, Andy Burnham, would have to see his “honeymoon period” end quickly. A “disastrous budget” on October 28 could do just that, he added.
He also said the timing of the by-election is key.
“If Burnham has a good party conference in Liverpool (in late September), the honeymoon should continue until that budget at least; the later the by-election, the trickier for Labour. They will want a quick contest.”
Burnham came to power after nine years as mayor of Greater Manchester and arrived untainted by scandals.
To many Britons, it felt refreshing, after Starmer’s appointment of Peter Mandelson as ambassador to Washington – despite his ties to Jeffrey Epstein.
In an August YouGov survey, 46 percent of Britons had a favourable opinion of Burnham.
In contrast to Starmer’s lawyerly caution, Burnham brings a more down-to-earth, outsider style that seeks to cut through Westminster politics, an approach that Polanski has echoed.
Polanski’s history at play
Polanski’s critics have said he would look parachuted in, while he says he has lived and worked in the area for years.
Polanski told Camden New Journal, “I have lived and worked in this community over many years. I know it well, and I love it”.
“It represents so many of the things that make London so special. I am so excited by the prospect of representing this place in Parliament,” he is quoted as saying.
But Tonge said Polanski is seen “as too left-wing by some voters who prefer the safer Labour option”.
The so-called “Burnham bounce” Labour is revelling in may also hamper Polanski’s chances, he said.
The Green leader’s political history may also stand in his way, John McTernan, political secretary to former Prime Minister Tony Blair, told Al Jazeera, pointing out that Polanski first stood in the constituency in 2015 as a Liberal Democrat, winning 96 votes in a Camden council by-election.
He also had to apologise earlier this year over a council tax issue on his houseboat, with a Green Party spokesperson saying: “Zack apologises sincerely for the unintentional mistake”.
He later admitted he had not voted in May’s local election, saying he had been moving and “fell short of time” to register at his new address.
Greens may have ‘peaked’: Expert
The Greens have never been here before. From 2010 to 2024, they had just one MP.
That changed in February when the Greens won the Gorton and Denton by-election. Hannah Spencer, a local plumber and Green councillor, won 40.7 per cent of the vote in an area Labour had represented since 1931.
It marked the Greens’ first-ever parliamentary by-election win, their highest by-election vote share by a margin of 30 points. The win ushered in their first MP in the north of England.
In May, across London, they went from 18 council seats to 279, taking six boroughs and winning their first directly elected mayors in Hackney and Lewisham, while Labour recorded its worst London local result since 1968. Nationally, the party won 587 seats, its highest ever.
The Greens have momentum on their side but may have “peaked”, said Tonge.
McTernan said Polanski should be wary of conflating this year’s successes with evidence of his own popularity. He should instead see them as dissatisfaction with Starmer and a “message sent by progressive voters” that they didn’t want him.
The August YouGov survey also shows that just 19 percent of Britons now have a favourable opinion of Polanski, down seven points from his peak in April.
McTernan said putting Polanski forward may hamper the Greens as “by-elections often punish candidates perceived as focused on their own self-importance”.
He pointed to Clacton, where Nigel Farage, leader of the far-right, anti-immigration party Reform UK, resigned his seat in July amid scrutiny of his finances and then recontested it.
With the main parties boycotting that election, the satirical candidate Count Binface, a comedian who campaigns wearing a bin on his head, took 26.7 percent of the vote, the highest share ever won by a novelty candidate in a British parliamentary election.

Nepal flood disaster puts climate justice under spotlight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:59:00 UTC
22:59:00 KST

Nepal flood disaster puts climate justice under spotlight
September 4, 2026
Days after devastating floods swept through Nepal's Bhotekoshi-Trisuli river basin, the true scale of the disaster is still emerging.
More than 1,250 people have been confirmed dead and almost 4,000 are still missing.
Buildings, bridges, roads and over a dozen hydropower facilities have been destroyed, causing an estimated $2.6 billion (€2.24 billion) in damage to public and private infrastructure, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).
Search and rescue operations for missing people remain underway, with families still hoping for their safe return.
The exact cause of the glacial collapse remains unclear, but experts say climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.
A global responsibility?
For Nepal, the disaster has raised a question that goes beyond rescue and reconstruction.
It's about climate justice and who should bear the costs and responsibility for such environmental disasters when the Himalayan nation contributes only a tiny fraction of global greenhouse gas emissions yet faces increasingly severe climate-related risks.
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said responding to the catastrophe is a "global responsibility."
"As we work tirelessly to address the damage caused by this sudden and massive disaster, a deeper question has also emerged: How did this destruction happen to us?" Shah asked while addressing Parliament this week.
"Mitigating and managing its impacts is regarded as a shared responsibility of the international community," he stressed.
Kathmandu is planning to raise climate justice issues in the upcoming United Nations General Assembly session in New York, where Prime Minister Shah himself is likely to lead the Nepali delegation.
"We will make our case about the impact of climate change and seek global support and moral obligation to tackle it," Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told DW. "We will also take the initiative of building a coalition of climate-vulnerable countries to raise our collective concerns."
Highly vulnerable to climate impacts
Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people, has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming.
The country accounts for just 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions and emits about 0.5 tons of CO₂ per person each year, making it a "negligible contributor to climate change," according to the World Bank.
But the landlocked Himalayan nation is highly vulnerable to the effects of climate change, with flooding, landslides, glacier-related hazards and other environmental risks threatening lives and livelihoods.
Nepal's leaders say the country needs long-term international support to adapt to a rapidly changing mountain environment.
The country's government estimates that implementing adaptation priorities between 2025 and 2035 could require as much as $18 billion to $20 billion. And Kathmandu wants international climate finance to provide most of these funds.
Nepal has spent years arguing in global climate forums that vulnerable mountain countries need greater support for adaptation and resilience.
In December 2009, Nepal held a historic Cabinet meeting at Kala Patthar, near Mount Everest base camp, at an altitude of 17,192 feet, to highlight the threats that climate change and glacial melting pose to Nepal and other mountainous nations.
Bimala Rai Paudyal, a former Nepali foreign minister, said the latest disaster meant "this is an opportune time for us to highlight glacier melting and climate justice issues in international climate forums."
"Earlier, we were advocating only about climate impacts. Now, we are heavily suffering from it," she told DW.
Paudyal believes Nepal is well positioned to lead an alliance of vulnerable countries, given its exposure to climate risk as well as its expertise and contribution to the climate justice efforts.
An opportunity for global climate action?
Kathmandu has formally approached the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)-backed "Loss and Damage Fund" for assistance over the latest floods.
But the fund, set up by the UN in 2025 to aid the impacts of climate change, has not yet begun distributing its limited cash.
The fund also relies on voluntary contributions and lacks legally binding commitments under current international climate agreements, leaving major emitters such as China, India and the US under no direct obligation to compensate for climate change impacts.
Still, some observers and climate advocates believe Nepal can present a strong case for urgent global climate action.
"Nepal can turn this tragedy into an opportunity for global climate action," Dinesh Paudel, professor of sustainable development at Appalachian State University in North Carolina, told DW. "For which, Nepal needs to build a consensus among national stakeholders and maneuver cautiously, considering geopolitical factors."
According to him, Kathmandu can create an ethical movement for climate justice by highlighting the recent flood. This could then lead to creating an effective and legally binding mechanism to deal with climate impacts in the future.
Ashok Swain, professor of peace and conflict research at Uppsala University and also UNESCO Chair on International Water Cooperation, shares a similar view.
"Nepal should not be left to pay for a climate crisis it did little to create or for regional non-cooperation over which it has limited influence," he said. "This is not a question of charity. It is fundamentally a question of climate justice and a fair distribution of responsibility."
Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

Thailand sets data center policy direction to create added value
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
21:56:24 CST
22:56:24 KST

BANGKOK, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said on Friday that Thailand must not settle for being merely a location for data centers but should extract added value from the investment, as his government moves to draft rules for a fast-growing sector.
Opening the first meeting of the National Data Center Business Policy Committee, Anutin emphasized that Thailand continues to draw interest from domestic and foreign investors thanks to its location, infrastructure readiness, and role as one of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) economic hubs.
However, that opportunity carries challenges, including heavy consumption of electricity, water, land, and utilities, along with environmental, security, and cybersecurity impacts, which require oversight consistent with the law, applicable standards, and the national interest, he said.
Anutin asked the committee to consider the legal definition and status of data centers, green data center standards, promotion of renewable energy, data protection and cybersecurity, and support for the country's artificial intelligence and cloud ecosystem.
The prime minister stressed that the investment must create added value for the kingdom, saying Thailand should attract related industries, promote technology transfer, develop Thai personnel, build a digital ecosystem, and raise long-term competitiveness.
Deputy Prime Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas, who chairs the committee, said Thailand is not closing the door to data center investment but will shift from approving projects agency by agency to setting strategy and screening criteria at the national level.
The committee agreed to integrate scattered licensing data into a single dataset, set minimum standards on an area-by-area basis to limit economic, social, and environmental impacts, and draw up assessment criteria to select projects that benefit the national economy and society, Ekniti told a press briefing. ■

China ready to advance all-round energy cooperation with Russia: vice premier
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
21:56:18 CST
22:56:18 KST

VLADIVOSTOK, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- China is ready to work with Russia to advance all-round energy cooperation and maintain the long-term sustainable development of oil and gas trade, Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang said on Friday.
Ding, also a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, made the remarks when co-chairing the 23rd meeting of the China-Russia Energy Cooperation Committee with Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak in Russia's Far Eastern city of Vladivostok.
China will work with Russia to implement the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, give full play to the role of the China-Russia Energy Cooperation Committee mechanism, and promote China-Russia all-round energy cooperation to a higher level, Ding said.
Ding called on both sides to continue to consolidate the achievements of existing energy cooperation, actively and properly address various concerns of enterprises, maintain the long-term sustainable development of oil and gas trade, and facilitate the orderly construction and stable operation of energy projects.
He suggested that both countries actively explore new areas and new directions for energy cooperation, tap cooperation potential in cutting-edge fields, explore the mutual empowerment of artificial intelligence and energy, and continuously expand the breadth and depth of energy cooperation.
He said China and Russia should jointly promote the reform of the global energy governance system, and make greater contributions to safeguarding the energy security and sustainable development of the two countries and the world at large.
For his part, Novak said that under the strategic guidance of the two heads of state, the Russia-China energy cooperation has continuously achieved new results, playing an important role in promoting the rapid growth of bilateral trade and maintaining the stability of the two countries' energy supply chains.
Russia is willing to work with China to optimize existing cooperation projects, expand and plan new areas of cooperation, and make new contributions to deepening China-Russia practical cooperation, Novak said.
During the meeting, both sides took stock of cooperation in oil, natural gas, coal, electricity, renewable energy and nuclear energy, exchanged views on future cooperation, and reached broad consensus. ■

SINGAPORE, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Singapore and Laos signed an implementation agreement to collaborate on carbon credits under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement on Friday.
The agreement establishes a legally binding framework for the generation and transfer of carbon credits, Singapore's Ministry of Trade and Industry said in a statement.

The collaboration is expected to advance both countries' climate goals by directing financing towards unlocking additional emissions reduction opportunities in Laos, the statement said. ■

Woman, 45, killed in Florence in seventh alleged femicide in Italy since mid-August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:56:14 UTC
22:56:14 KST

A 45-year-old woman abducted and thrown off a motorway bridge near Florence has become the seventh alleged femicide in Italy since mid-August.
Lorena Isceri was abducted on Thursday afternoon, allegedly by her ex-boyfriend, Federico Vella, in the Rifredi area of Florence, before being forced into the boot of his car and driven towards a bridge on the A1 motorway.
Isceri, who worked in the veterinary sector, still had her phone and managed to call an emergency helpline, telling operators she had been abducted.
Vella, 38, stopped the car, snatched the phone and allegedly threw her off the bridge, before jumping off himself.
After Isceri’s call to the helpline, police traced her phone signal but arrived too late to prevent her murder. Officers are establishing whether Isceri was killed before she was thrown off the bridge.
Isceri’s mother told SkyTg24 that she had last heard from her daughter on Thursday morning, and said she sounded fine. When asked about the relationship with Vella, she said Isceri had spoken to her about it and was “very afraid”.
Italian interior ministry data had indicated a downward trend in femicides during the first six months of 2026.
Figures compiled by the feminist alliance Non Una di Meno showed that as of 8 August, 40 women had been killed so far this year.
But numbers have risen since 15 August, Italy’s Ferragosto national holiday, with seven women, including Isceri, killed by a current or former partner.
Giorgia Meloni’s ruling coalition, which on Friday celebrated becoming the longest-serving government in the history of the Italian republic, had pledged to crack down on gender-based violence after the strong public reaction to the killing of Giulia Cecchetin, a 22-year-old medical student, by her former boyfriend, in November 2023.
Two years later, the government approved a law that for the first time introduced a legal definition of femicide in criminal law, punishing it with life in prison, while increasing sentences for crimes including stalking, sexual violence and the sharing of intimate images without consent.
However, a campaign to educate schoolboys about healthy relationships was thwarted after the government made it conditional on parental approval.
Luisa Rizzitelli, the Italy coordinator of One Billion Rising, which campaigns to end violence against women, said: “Perhaps Meloni is right to celebrate her government’s longevity, because there is precious little to celebrate in terms of concrete results.
“The approach to the tragic issue of male violence against women has been based on security policies while completely lacking strategic, structural programmes for training and prevention. The stubborn refusal to implement sex and relationship education in schools is a major factor fuelling the epidemic of femicides in Italy.”
- 
  In the UK, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123 and the domestic abuse helpline is 0808 2000 247. In the US, the suicide prevention lifeline is 988 and the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is on 13 11 14 and the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines can be found via www.befrienders.org

Launched on Sept. 4, 1956, Xiaolaba is the first radio program in the People's Republic of China dedicated to preschool children. It has since grown into a flagship program spanning radio, television, new media and in-school broadcasting. ■

New direct air route links China, Romania and Croatia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
21:55:56 CST
22:55:56 KST

BUCHAREST, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Air China operated its maiden flight on the new route connecting China's Beijing with Bucharest of Romania, and Zagreb of Croatia, on Friday, restoring direct flights between China and Romania after years of suspension and opening the first direct connection with Croatia.
Operating under flight numbers CA913 and CA914, the route departs from Beijing Capital International Airport with a stopover in Bucharest before arriving in Zagreb. Services run three times a week on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, with Airbus A330 aircraft deployed during the initial phase.
Bucharest is among the most populous inland city in the Balkans and Romania's political, economic and cultural center. Zagreb, whose history dates back to the 11th century, is a major cultural, tourism and economic hub in Croatia.
Calin Mitri, director-general for Global Affairs at the Romanian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said in his speech at the launch event held Friday afternoon that in today's world of deeply intertwined economies, direct air connectivity is not merely an improvement in transportation convenience, but also a strong support for international cooperation.
He added that the launch of the new route also provides a valuable platform for both sides to exchange experience in airport development, digital transformation, talent cultivation and the application of new technologies.
Chen Feng, China's Ambassador to Romania, said that the resumption of regular direct passenger flights between China and Romania is a shared aspiration of the Chinese and Romanian peoples and the result of long-term joint efforts by both sides.
"It is expected to help further strengthen bilateral economic and trade cooperation, deepen cultural and people-to-people exchanges, promote mutual understanding, and inject fresh momentum into the sustained and healthy development of China-Romania relations," Chen added. ■

Spain equals national September temperature record at 45.7 degrees Celsius
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
21:55:46 CST
22:55:46 KST

MADRID, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Spain recorded a temperature of 45.7 degrees Celsius on Thursday, matching the highest temperature ever registered in the country in September, the State Meteorological Agency (AEMET) said Friday on social media platform X.
The reading was recorded in El Granado, in the southwestern province of Huelva. It was also the highest temperature measured anywhere in Spain so far this year, according to AEMET. The figure equaled the previous national record for September, set in Montoro in the southern province of Cordoba on Sept. 6, 2016.
The record came amid an episode of unusually intense heat across much of the Iberian Peninsula and the Balearic Islands. AEMET attributed the conditions to a mass of hot, dry air entering Spain under the combined influence of a low-pressure system southwest of the peninsula and high pressure over North Africa and the Alboran Sea. Temperatures exceeded 40 degrees Celsius in several parts of the country, prompting heat warnings in multiple regions.
Spain has endured repeated periods of extreme heat this year. July was the joint-hottest July in the country's recorded history, while June was the second-hottest since records began, according to AEMET.
The January-August period was also the hottest on record in mainland Spain, clearly surpassing the corresponding periods of the previous four years. AEMET described the figures as "an unmistakable sign that warming is accelerating in Spain."
The extreme heat has also posed growing risks to public health. Spain's daily mortality monitoring system, MoMo, estimated that 2,149 deaths in August were attributable to high temperatures, the second-highest August figure since records began in 2015. ■

China, Laos set to hold medical drill to boost disaster relief capacity
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
21:55:44 CST
22:55:44 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- China and Laos will hold a joint humanitarian medical rescue exercise in Laos this September, which is part of bilateral efforts to boost disaster relief capacity, a Chinese defense ministry spokesperson said Friday.
The exercise, which marks the sixth iteration of the "Peace Train" series, will simulate an international humanitarian medical response to a super typhoon disaster, focusing on joint on-site search and rescue, casualty evacuation, health and epidemic prevention, and psychological rescue, Jiang Bin, a spokesperson for the Ministry of National Defense, told a media briefing.
As of Sept. 1 this year, 24 typhoons had formed over the northwestern Pacific and the South China Sea, 10.4 more than the historical average for the same period.
First held in 2017, the "Peace Train" series is a flagship project under the China-Laos military health cooperation framework, with previous exercises covering disaster scenarios such as floods, mudslides and earthquakes.
During the 2026 event, the Chinese side will also offer medical services for Lao military personnel and civilians, Jiang added.
The exercise, Jiang said, will deepen and expand practical cooperation in disaster medical rescue, tropical disease control and epidemic prevention, and "better provide quality public security goods for regional countries and peoples."
It is part of China's expanding efforts to boost cooperation with neighboring countries to better cope with natural disasters.
After a severe mudslide struck the Gyirong-Rasuwa border crossing between China and Nepal last week, China has provided meteorological support, including weather monitoring, forecasting, early warning and impact services, for Nepal's rescue and relief.
The country is also providing Nepal with daily updates on the development of a barrier lake above the Gyirong Port, cascading risks associated with the Cuojian River impact crater in Nepal, glacial lake risks in the Gyirong Zangbo River basin, the development and risk forecasts of new barrier lakes, and emergency hydrological monitoring. ■

Meloni government becomes Italy's longest-serving since establishment of republic
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
21:55:41 CST
22:55:41 KST

ROME, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- The government led by Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Friday became the longest-serving government in the history of the Italian Republic, reaching 1,413 days in office and surpassing the previous record held by former Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi's second government.
"Today, our government becomes the longest-serving in the history of the Italian Republic," Meloni said on social media, calling the milestone a responsibility and saying political stability enables a country to plan, make decisions and fulfill its commitments.
Meloni, Italy's first woman prime minister, has highlighted employment growth, tax cuts, fiscal discipline and the country's increased international standing as key achievements. The ruling Brothers of Italy (FdI) party said, citing Italian National Institute of Statistics data, that over 1.3 million permanent jobs had been added since her government took office. The Meloni government was sworn in on Oct. 22, 2022, comprising Brothers of Italy, the League and Forza Italia.
Italy has had 68 governments led by 31 prime ministers since the establishment of the republic in 1946, with governments lasting an average of about 14 months. Analysts have attributed the longevity of Meloni's government partly to the cohesion of the ruling coalition and fragmentation of the opposition.
The next parliamentary election due in 2027, Meloni's government will face an electoral test over whether its political stability can translate into tangible economic and social gains and continued voter support. ■

Turkish YouTuber’s Hasidic documentary draws US attention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:54:54 UTC
22:54:54 KST

Turkish YouTuber and documentary filmmaker Ruhi Çenet’s latest film examining life in New York’s Hasidic Jewish communities has drawn attention in the United States after being reviewed by prominent streamer Asmongold.
Released on Aug. 26, “The World’s Most Secretive Jewish Community: Hasidic Jews (48 Hours Inside)” follows Çenet during two days in Hasidic neighborhoods.
The roughly 40-minute documentary examines religious observance, education, family life and the restrictions some community members observe on smartphones, television and internet use.
It includes interviews with members of the community as well as a woman who left it.
The film reached a wider U.S. audience after Asmongold reviewed it during a broadcast.
He praised Çenet’s production and access, calling the filmmaker “a total legend.”
His commentary also fed an online debate over the participation of some large Hasidic households in public assistance programs.
Claims circulated on social media that families could receive between $75,000 and $100,000 in annual government support.
The figures do not represent a fixed or religion-specific payment and have not been established as an average for Hasidic households.
In a separate development, President Donald Trump received a delegation of leading Hasidic rabbis in the Oval Office on Sept. 3 ahead of Rosh Hashanah.
A White House official described it as the first comparable gathering since 1979.
Discussions included housing, religious education, prison reform and tax credits for large families.
The delegation included the leaders of the two principal branches of the Satmar movement.
Their inclusion drew criticism from some pro-Israel conservative figures, including Trump ally Laura Loomer, because of Satmar’s religious opposition to Zionism.
The meeting had been planned for months and there was no indication that it was connected to Çenet’s documentary.

OPINION - Can an alliance be priced? Trump's South Korea gambit and Asia's shifting future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:52:36 UTC
22:52:36 KST

Belirsiz Kişi
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
- Prof. Dr. Giwoong Jung is a faculty member in the Center for International Area Studies of Hankuk University of Foreign Studies and a Vice Head of the HK+ National Strategies Research Project Agency.
ISTANBUL (AA) - In August 2026, US President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to "substantially reduce" the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises with South Korea (ROK)—halving an 11-day drill involving 18,000 troops without prior notice to Seoul—and offered two revealing justifications. He said the exercises were too expensive and that they sent "a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile" to North Korea, which had been "unthreatening and respectful." Days later, he confirmed he hopes to meet Kim Jong Un this year, reportedly on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Pyongyang's response was contemptuous: Kim Yo Jong said the gesture changed nothing, and a salvo of ballistic missiles followed. Washington paid with alliance credibility for a concession it did not receive.
When 'ironclad' gets a price tag
This episode captures the shifting foundations of the US alliance system in Asia. For seven decades, that system rested on a shared threat perception and an implicit bargain: allies hosted US power, and it treated their security as inseparable from its own. What is changing is not burden-sharing arithmetic—every US administration since Eisenhower has pressed allies to do more—but the nature of the commitment. Security guarantees are repriced as negotiable services, contingent on payment, trade concessions, and willingness to join US wars elsewhere: Seoul declined to help with the "denuclearization" of Iran, and the drills were accordingly cut. An alliance once called "ironclad" now carries a price tag.
How much of this is Trump, and how much is structural? Both. Structural pressures are real: relative US decline, the prioritization of China, crises from Ukraine to the Middle East, and a war-weary electorate. The 2026 National Defense Strategy document institutionalizes this logic, assigning the ROK "primary responsibility" for deterring the North while repositioning United States Forces Korea as a flexible regional asset aimed at China. But the form the adjustment takes—impulsive, personalized, publicly humiliating to allies—is distinctly Trump's. Recall that he suspended "war games" in 2018 after Singapore and, in his first term, demanded a fivefold increase in Seoul's alliance burden-sharing. What was then improvisation is now doctrine. A future president could restore the tone, but allies have learned that the underlying conditionality can return with any election. That knowledge is itself a structural change.
Disciplined calm and quiet hedging
Seoul and Tokyo are reading the moment with disciplined calm and quiet hedging. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung's office publicly welcomed the prospect of a Trump-Kim dialogue, even as his ministers conceded in parliament that they had not been informed in advance. Beneath the courtesy, Seoul is accelerating the transfer of wartime operational control, pursuing nuclear-powered submarines and a revised nuclear cooperation agreement granting enrichment and reprocessing rights—a "nuclear latency" functioning as insurance against abandonment. Support for nuclear armament is no longer confined to some policymakers; it now extends to the general public. Tokyo, having heard Trump call arms sales to Taiwan "a very good negotiating chip" with Xi Jinping, is pursuing its largest defense buildup in generations while deepening energy and supply-chain cooperation with Seoul. Both are paying unprecedented sums—$350 billion and $550 billion in pledged investments to the US, respectively—that officials privately describe as protection money: the price of keeping the US engaged while preparing for the day it may not be.
The strategic irony is that this undermines the US strategy toward China. Deterrence along the first island chain depends on allied bases, allied industrial capacity, and the credibility of US resolve. Deterrence is capability multiplied by will; Trump has made will the variable under negotiation. When exercises shrink to punish an ally, and tariffs batter the partners meant to anchor the anti-China coalition, Beijing needs only to wait. It has already weathered the Iran war's energy shock better than Japan or Korea.
A self-reliant Asia
Where, then, is Asia heading? Not, in my judgment, toward accommodation with Beijing—the memories of coercion are too fresh, and the hedging underway points the other way. The most probable destination is a more self-reliant Asia: wealthier, more heavily armed, more internally coordinated, and psychologically decoupled from Washington even where formally allied. That outcome is not necessarily tragic; a mature alliance of capable partners is what US strategists long claimed to want. The danger lies in the transition. If repricing proceeds erratically—exercises cut on a whim, summits dangled without consultation—the region may drift toward Beijing not by choice but by default. In its relationship with the US, the ROK has long been plagued by a cycle of alliance entrapment and the threat of abandonment. While Trump's threats are nothing new, from the ROK's perspective (and Japan's as well)—which, despite its absolute power, is treated as a relatively weak nation because of its geopolitical location—it might conclude that an unpredictable patron is worse than a demanding neighbor.
Foundations, once repriced, are rarely restored to par. Trust denominated in dollars can always be devalued again. That is the lesson of this strange August on the Korean Peninsula—and it will outlast any summit.
*Opinions expressed in this article are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Anadolu.

Dog bite ordeal doesn’t end with rabies prophylaxis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:51:37 UTC
22:51:37 KST

NEW DELHI: For a 21-year-old Delhi resident bitten by a stray dog, the ordeal did not end after he received rabies post-exposure prophylaxis. Within seven days, he developed a skin rash that progressed to severe hives (urticaria) and angioedema, causing sudden swelling of the face, lips and throat. His condition later worsened with breathing difficulty, requiring specialist dermatological intervention.The case comes against the backdrop of the Supreme Court’s May 2026 directions on the stray-dog menace, which stressed the need to protect people from dog attacks and strengthen measures for sterilisation, vaccination and dog-bite management.The young man was bitten over two weeks ago and was initially taken to a Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) centre, where he received equine immunoglobulin (IgG) and a rabies vaccine.He was later taken to Ram Manohar Lohia (RML) Hospital. After two days of treatment, when he developed difficulty breathing, he was evaluated by the dermatology department.Doctors advised a single injection of omalizumab to control the severe allergic reaction. The medicine cost around Rs 16,000-17,000. The family was advised to explore obtaining it through the Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS), but the patient’s mother, Rama (name changed), bought it herself, worried about her son’s condition.
The patient improved within 24 hours of receiving omalizumab and remains under treatment at RML Hospital.Dr Kabir Sardana, who treated the patient in the dermatology department, said he sees around one such case a week and believes this could be the first reported use of omalizumab for this type of reaction following rabies prophylaxis. The treatment was given after the option was discussed with the family and with their concurrence.Sardana said it can sometimes be difficult to distinguish whether a rash is due to the vaccine or immunoglobulin, as both early and delayed reactions can occur. “The aim is to maximise treatment, minimise discomfort and, of course, see the financial aspects of the patient,” he said.The episode also highlighted the financial burden of managing severe reactions. “Every patient cannot afford Rs 17,000. What can poor people do? They are suffering so much,” Rama said.More broadly, he said, adverse reactions following rabies post-exposure prophylaxis can be difficult to predict and may be under-reported, particularly skin reactions. Doctors are concerned that severe reactions could create fear of rabies injections and prompt some people to delay or avoid prophylaxis.
Doctors stress, however, that people bitten or scratched by a potentially rabid animal should not avoid recommended post-exposure prophylaxis. Patients should instead be counselled about possible reactions and have timely access to medical care if serious symptoms develop.The concern is greater in rural and poorly resourced areas, where access to specialist and emergency care may be limited. Doctors say the case underlines the need for better reporting of adverse reactions and timely access to treatment when complications occur.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Russia and Ukraine exchanged large-scale drone attacks overnight and into Friday, with strikes hitting areas far from the front lines and causing casualties, damage and fires on both sides.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian drone struck the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service, the SBU, on Volodymyrska Street in central Kiev, directly targeting the office of the agency’s chief.
Kiev Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people were injured, while heavy black smoke rose from the area near St. Sophia Cathedral. Recent reports confirmed the strike as part of an intensified series of Russian attacks on the Ukrainian capital.
In the southern Odessa region, one person was killed and five others were injured in overnight Russian strikes, regional Gov. Oleh Kiper said.
The attacks damaged civilian infrastructure, including administrative buildings and private and official vehicles, he said.
Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia launched 121 drones and one missile, claiming 103 aerial targets were suppressed across the country.
Ukraine strikes Russian energy infrastructure
Meanwhile, Russian authorities reported a major Ukrainian drone assault on the Black Sea resort city of Sochi and the nearby Sirius federal territory.
Falling drone debris sparked a fire at an oil depot, according to the Krasnodar regional operational headquarters.
No casualties were reported initially, while authorities said residential buildings and other structures were damaged.
The Russian defence ministry said its air defences destroyed 490 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory, Moscow-annexed Crimea and the Black Sea during the overnight attack.
Russia also claimed its forces struck what it described as Ukrainian military logistics and energy facilities, including a logistics centre in the Kiev region, vessels allegedly carrying military supplies at the Yuzhny port, and a fuel terminal at Chornomorsk.
The claims could not be independently verified.

Nigel Farage meeting a 'shadowy foreign donor'? It can only be another establishment stitch-up | Marina Hyde

How many sarcastic air quotes is too many for quoting Nigel Farage’s suggestion that Reform have been ““““““““hoaxed”””””””” by some undercover investigators into appearing to seek to get round electoral law to bag a £500k donation from a foreigner, as well as commissioning off-the-books polling and failing to identify it to newspapers? I don’t feel eight was too many. I could run to nine. Amazing, really, that it’s been as long as a few weeks since Farage had a crash-out and forced a byelection. All any of us wants is for Nigel to once again resign after a staged shitfit and ask a few thousand members of the public to judge him.
For whatever reason, though, the law of our country does not amount to an “ONLY THE PEOPLE OF CLACTON CAN JUDGE ME” tattoo, and so it is that as Reform’s conference gets under way today, the party has been reported to the police for allegedly using foreign money to fund its activities. It’s all based on a covert sting carried out by Verbatim – an investigative group founded by journalists from the non-profit Centre for Climate Reporting – and broadcast last night on Channel 4 News.
Though Farage has some very significant walk-on parts in this secretly filmed footage, the chief protagonists in the hokey cokey are James Orr, the party’s director of policy, and Nigel’s right-hand man Dan Jukes. Jukes is one of the many Farage aides to physically resemble an Apprentice candidate who crashes out in week four after miscalculating quantities in the sweetshop task. Still, he’d make a lovely Rolf in a regional production of The Sound of Music. And, happily, would now have the time to really commit to the role.
“If Nigel makes it to No 10,” he honks at one point during filming carried out by an undercover “donor”, “you’re having a pint with who’s effectively going to be his chief of staff in No 10. If that isn’t a business interest, I don’t know what is.” As it turns out, the guy is effectively having a pint with someone the party chair, Lee Anderson, this morning said was “gone” with “no chance of them coming back”. Slightly less definitively, the official party statement said that Jukes and Orr had stepped down pending an internal investigation. Can’t imagine what form that will take. I always picture Reform’s internal affairs department as a toy phone ringing out in an abandoned wendy house.
But perhaps this sort of thing is the job of flailing enforcer/terminal shitposter Zia Yusuf, who this week could be found branding a possible Labour byelection candidate for Keir Starmer’s vacated Holborn and St Pancras seat as something other than the tireless community servant her career has thus far marked her out as. Or as Zia put it: “The front runner being foisted on the people of Holborn by Labour to replace the former Prime Minister Keir Starmer in our Parliament was born in Somalia. Do you understand what is happening?” If not, certainly one to discuss with that much-vaunted recent defector to Reform, the Iraq-born Nadhim Zahawi. Still, the episode does at least confirm Yusuf as the biggest Pick-Me in British politics. He’s really not like the other children of immigrants, you see – he actually enjoys being racist for approval.
Back to the undercover investigation, though, which a highly defensive Reform statement whinges was “perpetuated by foreign-funded climate-change activists posing as would-be party donors”. Foreign-funded! That’s a bit rich in the circumstances. But the real standout bit of footage for many will be the moment when Orr laments: “We just don’t have British resident donors, British entities, that would support us. That’s the grim reality.” From the horse’s mouth, then, comes apparent confirmation that Reform is funded by foreign-based money for reasons on which we can only speculate.
It’s often the incidental details that seem most weirdly illuminating. Take the scene when the fake American donor finally journeys to some sort of Clacton beer garden, where he and Farage and co seem to have settled themselves in one of a row of cursed teak gazebos. Here, Nigel chortles about “Guinness with a champagne top”, confirming his undying addiction to an even more annoying brand of alcohol-based identity politics than a Gin O’Clock poster.
He’ll no doubt be butching it out with a drink at the Reform conference this weekend. The rest of the country might do well to once again ponder the 64,000-of-indeterminately-sourced-dollars question: why does this sort of thing keep happening to Farage and his party? Is it because of a byzantine conspiracy involving climate activists, “the establishment”, the deep state and Big gazebo? Or is it because they are just endlessly, repeatedly and ineptly dodgy? Watching the footage, it’s fairly difficult to conclude anything other than that we are dealing with a bunch of preposterously self-regarding amateurs.
We’ll have to see if this latest exposure further fans the anger that has been radiating off Farage all summer, ever since his undeclared £5m gift from a Thai-based crypto billionaire was revealed. As discussed here before, I am ever-more convinced that Farage is too mentally fragile for the highest office – indeed, leading anything other than an insurgent party seems to be either spinning him out or finding him out. Today’s attempt to shift focus saw him promise to declare a “national emergency” in the event he becomes prime minister. On the basis of all we keep discovering about him, you can’t argue with that.

Ladies Only: Afghan pop star Aryana Sayeed takes on Taliban with European tour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:50:31 UTC
22:50:31 KST

Aryana Sayeed, one of Afghanistan’s biggest pop stars, is kicking off a women-only European tour, using her platform to bring Afghan women together and speak out for women’s rights.
She was one of Afghanistan’s biggest stars. Then the Taliban returned to power and she fled the country. Now, Aryana Sayeed is taking her music and message across Europe - with one key difference: the audiences will be women only.
Sayeed remains one of the most recognisable faces in Afghanistan, building a huge following as a singer, an outspoken advocate for women's rights, and from her time as a judge on The Voice Afghanistan and other major talent shows in the country.
But when the Taliban retook control of Afghanistan in 2021, her life and career changed dramatically. Unable to return home or perform there, Sayeed has continued her work from abroad, using her platform and her organisation DEFAW (Defenders of Equality, Freedom, and Advancement for Women) to speak out for Afghan women and girls living under what she calls "dark days."
Five years on, she is taking her message of hope across Europe with her "Ladies Only_"_ tour, a series of concerts exclusively for women. The tour begins this Friday in Rotterdam, where Sayeed will perform at the Laurenskerk. She will then head to Stockholm on 5 September, followed by Hamburg on 26 September and Wiesbaden, near Frankfurt, on 3 October.
Ahead of the shows, Euronews Culture spoke to her about what sparked the idea behind her Ladies Only concerts, the current situation facing women and girls in Afghanistan, and the message she hopes to share through her music and activism.
When did you come up with the idea for a ladies-only tour?
Aryana Sayeed: Well, I have been planning to do this Ladies-Only tour for the past three or four years. Since the Taliban took over the power in Afghanistan, you know, they literally banned women from most things. Like, they have banned schools for girls past grade six, and women are not allowed to work anymore.They are not even allowed to go to the park. You know, like some simple things in life. They're not allowed to do it anymore.
So when all of this happened, obviously, besides my singing career, I am also an activist for women's rights in Afghanistan. And I thought, you know what? We need to stand against this injustice, against the Taliban and what they're doing. And so I thought initially it would be a great idea to do this Ladies-Only concert where we show the power of women, where we stand together as women, and raise our voice and raise awareness against the injustices that are going on in Afghanistan and stand up for the millions of voiceless women in Afghanistan.
Many people around the world will know you from The Voice of Afghanistan. How influential has your voice been in Afghanistan, and how big are you there?
Well, it's really hard to talk about yourself and say how big you are, but I know that the things that I have been doing in Afghanistan for the past, I would say, 15 years have been quite effective. It has had major effects on the society. It has been able to give so much hope to the hopeless women of Afghanistan.
Empowering them in a way to think differently, to know their rights and to stand up for their rights and things like that. As much as I've been focused on my singing career, as much I've been focused on my activist side as well, trying to give voice to the voiceless women of Afghanistan.
I used to be a judge on these talent shows, and I used to be present there during all of these problems and issues as well. Even before the Taliban came, Afghan women did not have their full rights at all. Before the Taliban came, things were getting along really well, and the things that we were doing in Afghanistan, the effect it had on society, was going really well.
Since the Taliban returned to power five years ago, do you feel more free and more heard outside Afghanistan, as a performer and as someone delivering a message of hope?
Even when I was in Afghanistan, I still had my concerts outside of Afghanistan. I still was touring all this time. For me, there's no major difference in that field. But I do feel that we are very isolated now. I do feel like there's so much that I could do in my country. There's so much more that I could. But right now, I am unable to do that because of the fact that I'm not allowed to go back to Afghanistan. I'm not allowed to physically be there, be on the screen of the TV, give out my messages, be that support and that hope for the Afghan women.
But the one thing that I'm grateful for is the fact that we were able to establish the organisation outside Afghanistan. I have this organisation called DEFAW, which stands for Defenders of Equality, Freedom and Advancement for Women. And through the organisation, I've been trying to be active and do my activism through that and raise awareness and try to be the support for the voiceless women of Afghanistan, do interviews all around the world and try to be, you know, as helpful as I can.
And the great thing is that in Afghanistan, we still have YouTube, we still have all these platforms where women can be connected with me, so they can still hear me, they can still see my videos.
You can’t completely silence voices like yours, particularly when young girls can still access your work online. What message would you give to those girls who look up to you?
The one advice that I constantly keep giving them is not to give up hope because honestly, they are living in the dark, dark, dark ages right now. I speak to around 100 Afghan women or girls inside Afghanistan on a monthly basis through my organisation, through Zoom. And I actually get to speak to them, ask them questions, hear their stories. And what they tell me is heartbreaking, quite sad.
They literally talk without crying because of the fact that they've been abandoned from school and from work, and they feel so hopeless and they feel so useless as humans. Most of them have to just go ahead and get married, you know, at a young age because they don't see a future and they don't have another choice.
Let's say a woman who doesn't have a husband and doesn't have somebody to support the family with the income, with the food, with the money and everything. What is she going to do? And she's not allowed to go to work. So the only choice left for her is just go to bed. That's it. And so it's really sad to hear all these stories.
Because I honestly, I do feel from the bottom of my heart that these dark days will pass. They will not exist forever. This is, at least as a human, what I think, because what they have brought upon women in Afghanistan is ridiculous and inhumane, and this kind of a life, I don't think it's going to last forever.
People will eventually raise their voices. People will eventually stand up against them, and justice will prevail. Maybe it will. I don't know when. Maybe it will last another two, three, four or five years. But it cannot be forever. I don't believe that.
Men will obviously have a crucial role in making that change happen. What is your message to Afghan men, both inside Afghanistan and those living in exile?
I have literally made videos on social media and asked the Afghan men all around the world, and particularly in Afghanistan, to stand up for the rights of their women, for their mothers, for sisters, and for the women in general. And that's my message to them. I have a strong feeling that unless Afghan men come together and stand up for the women, women alone cannot do much for themselves.
And in order for this change to come, or for the women to have their full rights, men need to start supporting them. And I have seen a glimpse of, you know, their support here and there. Of course, not inside Afghanistan yet, but I have seen Afghan men getting together for protests outside the country, like, for example, in Germany and the U.S. and other countries like this, which is a good sign, which is a good thing to happen.
And hopefully, there will be more of that in the future.
How would you describe your music?
Well, I mostly sing pop. My songs are pop. That's how I started. I started with R&B and then pop music, but then I also have a lot of traditional songs. Funny enough, when I went to Afghanistan for the first time in 2011, I mixed a few songs of, like, old 40, 50-year-old songs and I made them with new music, and I presented them on the stage to people and people just loved those songs.
For me, that gave me kind of this indication that people still love the traditional music. So I do traditional music, but also a big portion of my songs are dedicated to the rights of Afghan women. And those are the ones that are the most effective in the society, I would say. And I actually performed some of them at the European Parliament, at UNICEF and all these big government gatherings that take place.
And it's been amazing. And this is the part of my career I love and enjoy the most. The songs actually, you know, give me something that is very fulfilling as a human being and that performing well.
You mentioned what music means to you as a human being, so I can’t let you go without asking about artificial intelligence. A significant proportion of music streamed these days is either created or influenced by AI. Are you open to using AI in your music?
I find it scary. I honestly am not for AI at all. I don't like it. It scares me and it makes me worried of where are heading. I know in a way it's - it can be really good. It can be fantastic. But in a way we are losing that human touch. For example, nowadays they can even create the sound of the singers, they can create my sound, they can create my videos when I'm not even there.
And that scares me. That's not nice. I feel like the human touch should exist, and it should be there. And you cannot even compare it with AI at all. And I don't like AI, and I don't use it, and I'm not for it. I don't support it at all.

ST. PETERSBURG, September 4. /TASS/. The resolution of the Caribbean Crisis is a successful example of diplomacy winning out over escalation, one that would be worth emulating today, Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) Director Sergey Naryshkin stated.
He noted that the propaganda mechanisms set in motion by politicians create such a rigid worldview that they become hostages to it and fall into their own traps. "Diplomacy no longer works in this situation, and the major powers are literally plunging into total war, often with devastating consequences for all," he said at the 22nd meeting of the Conference of Heads of Security Agencies and Intelligence Services of the CIS member states.
"We must prevent such a turn of events," the SVR chief noted. "Thankfully, history offers a few examples of a successful way out of the spiral of escalation. One of the most striking examples is the Cuban Missile Crisis, when the Soviet Union and the United States made mutual concessions and averted nuclear war," he recalled.
"We have good reason to doubt that there are still statesmen in the modern West, and especially in Europe, capable of taking such decisive and responsible steps," Naryshkin pointed out. "Therefore, without waiting for the escalation in Eurasia to reach its peak, our task is to strengthen our collective security system and develop dialogue and cooperation mechanisms without interference from external forces or the imposition of foreign development models and values that are alien to us," he stressed.
Naryshkin pointed out that the Commonwealth of Independent States will celebrate its 35th anniversary this December. "The cooperation between our countries, our peoples, and our intelligence services has stood the test of time. It is a crucial element of stability across Greater Eurasia," the SVR chief concluded.
