Iraq emerges as Iran’s economic lifeline amid tighter US sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:28:01 UTC
22:28:01 KST

Iraq remains one of Iran’s most important regional economic and financial links as Washington expands pressure on Tehran and entities accused of supporting it. Iraq’s close political and commercial ties with Iran, along with the influence of Iran-backed armed groups in parts of the economy, give Tehran access to trade routes, currency markets, and commercial networks that are difficult for US authorities to monitor.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The issue has gained urgency as Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has pledged to bring the weapons of Iran-backed armed groups under state control by a Sept. 30 deadline. Iraqi officials and analysts have said progress has been slow, while Washington has continued pressing Baghdad to strengthen oversight of dollar transactions and the banking system.
Iraq and Iran share a roughly 1,600-kilometer border, with multiple formal crossings as well as longstanding informal trade routes. US authorities have documented the use of Iraqi banks and currency-exchange mechanisms to move dollars to Iran and Iran-aligned armed groups.
In December 2023, the US Treasury said Al-Huda Bank had used access to US dollars to support the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force and Iran-aligned Iraqi armed groups, including Kata’ib Hizballah and Asa’ib Ahl al-Haq. Treasury also accused the bank’s owner of using front companies and forged documents to circumvent restrictions on currency purchases and international transfers.
US restrictions on dollar transactions have narrowed the formal channels available to some Iraqi banks since 2023. The measures have reduced access to dollars for institutions targeted by the restrictions, though they have not eliminated incentives for illicit currency trading.
The Central Bank of Iraq has set the official exchange rate at 1,300 Iraqi dinars per dollar. The parallel-market rate has remained higher, reflecting continued demand for hard currency outside formal channels.
Dollar smuggling routes remain difficult to track
Ali Hamza, a former Iraqi banker, told The Media Line that the volume of money smuggled from Iraq to Iran is difficult to establish. “Daily shipments of dollars go to Iran through several border crossings, most notably the Shalamcheh border crossing between Basra and Iran, which is clearly controlled by Shia militias,” he said.
Hamza said the funds being moved had declined following US restrictions on Iraqi banks but had not stopped. “There is still a network of smuggled funds whose amounts are unknown,” he said.
He said one method involved accounts opened at Iraqi, Lebanese, and other banks in the names of Iranian nationals or figures whose beneficial ownership was difficult to trace. “These accounts are used by the Iranian Revolutionary Guard, or even some agencies of the Iranian regime, and it is impossible to trace who benefits from these accounts,” he said.
Iraqi markets carry a wide range of Iranian products, including agricultural goods, dairy products, iron and steel, household goods, ceramics, and other consumer and industrial items. Iranian customs data put Iran’s non-oil trade with Iraq at more than $7 billion in the first seven months of 2024, while Iraqi official statistics recorded about $3.1 billion in non-oil imports from Iran for all of 2024. The differing figures reflect the use of separate national reporting systems and trade classifications.
Sanjabi Shirazi, secretary general of the Iran-Iraq Joint Chamber of Commerce, told Iraqi and Iranian media outlets that “despite the decrease in the value of exports between Iraq and Iran, trade in non-energy goods is growing and active.”
Iraq exported goods worth approximately $2.2 billion annually to Iran, according to Trade Map.
“Trade between the two countries cannot be stopped for several reasons, most notably that the current government is loyal to Iran, and there are militias working for Iran as well,” Abdulrahman al-Sheikh, an Iraqi economist, told The Media Line.
“Furthermore, some families living near the border between the two countries have shared ancestry and work together for each other’s benefit.”
Al-Sheikh said Iraqi exports to Iran could increase and that Iraq could be used to obtain goods restricted by US sanctions. “Iran will obtain all the goods it lacks through the Iraqi market, especially since transporting them is easy through several border crossings between the two countries, most notably the Shalamcheh crossing in Basra,” he said.
Local currency deals reduce Iran’s reliance on dollars
The economist also said Iran pays for some goods in Iraqi dinars and that the Iranian toman is used in some southern Iraqi provinces with Shia-majority populations. He argued that these arrangements reduce Iran’s need for dollars in bilateral trade while increasing the economic burden on Iraq.
He said Iranian goods retain a strong market in Iraq because of their price and established distribution networks. Al-Sheikh alleged that Iran-backed armed groups use their political and economic influence to favor Iranian goods.
A source familiar with the matter at the Iraqi Ministry of Industry and Minerals said repackaging operations had increased in industrial areas of Karbala and Najaf. The source, who requested anonymity because he was not authorized to speak publicly for the ministry, said some facilities might be repackaging Iranian goods for export under Iraqi labels.
Ali al-Badri, an Iraqi businessman, told The Media Line that Iranian goods could increasingly be sold with “Made in Iraq” labels to facilitate exports to other countries. He said armed groups with economic interests in manufacturing could exploit factories to repackage and relabel goods, harming Iraqi producers.
Al-Badri also said access to several industrial areas in Iraqi governorates had been restricted, though he could not identify the authority imposing those restrictions. He said he believed Iran-backed armed groups were responsible.
Iraq has also faced allegations that its oil-export system has been used to help disguise Iranian oil or fuel-oil sales and circumvent US sanctions. A source familiar with oil export operations at the Iraqi Ministry of Oil told The Media Line that “the mixing of Iraqi oil exported by the government with Iranian oil exported by other parties outside Iraq” made it difficult to determine the full volume of Iraqi oil shipped abroad.
The Ministry of Oil did not respond to a request for comment.
That allegation is consistent with a May 2026 US Treasury action against Deputy Oil Minister Ali Maarij al-Bahadly. Treasury accused al-Bahadly of facilitating the diversion of Iraqi oil products and the blending of Iranian and Iraqi oil to disguise its origin before export. The deputy minister’s designation, along with sanctions against Iran-aligned armed-group figures, pointed to the continuing risk that official and informal networks could be used to evade sanctions.
Iranian businesses continue to operate in Iraq
Iranian business activity is also visible in Iraq, including in Baghdad and Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan Region. In August 2025, the Erbil Chamber of Commerce and Industry said 395 Iranian companies were operating across the Kurdistan Region, including 200 in Erbil. No comparable, current official figure was available for Baghdad.
These companies operate in many Iraqi sectors, including construction, trade, import-export, food, and energy. Contracting remains especially important because of Iraq’s extensive construction and housing needs.
“Iraqi militias backed by Iran are jeopardizing Iraq’s economy for the benefit of Iran,” Hatem al-Sulaimani, an Iraqi economist, told The Media Line.
Al-Sulaimani said illicit currency transfers, alleged trade fraud, and preferential treatment for Iranian goods could expose Iraq to further financial restrictions and increase pressure on the dinar. “All of this poses a threat to the Iraqi economy and could subject Iraq to sanctions, in addition to the risk of a dollar shortage,” he said.
He called on Baghdad to strengthen oversight of armed groups’ economic activities and protect Iraq’s recovering economy. He said the two countries’ stated goal of expanding annual trade to $20 billion, together with increased activity at border crossings, could complicate enforcement as US sanctions on Iran tighten.

====================================================================================================

Is 'Purity of Arms' holding the IDF back? Inside Israel’s battle over military ethics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:27:57 UTC
22:27:57 KST

You are a soldier, tasked with searching a house for a suspected terrorist and hidden weapons. The house is full of women, children, and an elderly, sick, bedridden man.
How do you proceed? Do you force the man out of bed immediately to complete a thorough search, or do you slow the search to treat him with kid gloves, possibly endangering your soldiers?
Judgment calls like these are everyday occurrences for 19-year-old soldiers – young men whose moral dilemmas only a year earlier involved not getting involved with their best friend’s girlfriend or resisting the urge to glance at the test paper of the nerd sitting in front of them.
But we send soldiers – not a cadre of lawyers – to the battlefield. How are these soldiers taught to make complex calls that could put them on the wrong end of an IED, or just as easily land them in military prison for taking an operation too far, according to the moral sensibilities of the most moral army in the world?
On August 9, according to Ynet, “The IDF raised the level of authorization required for certain strikes as high as the chief of staff, effectively requiring political approval in some cases. Commanders were also recently given explicit instructions to halt immediate-response fire, except in cases involving the removal of a direct threat.”
Per Hillel Biton Rosen, military and security correspondent for Channel 14, just days later Hamas operatives were identified crossing the Yellow Line ceasefire demarcation in Gaza, where they stole engineering equipment. Soldiers requested authorization to engage, but senior command denied the request.
The incursion was just one of more than 65 crossings, three times the number recorded the week before the rules of engagement changed.
A senior security official said: “Hamas is testing us, exactly as it did before Oct. 7. What happened last night could have ended with a soldier being abducted.”
Permission-to-open-fire orders clearly act as a deterrent and are necessary to maintain law and order.
Yet, the rules of engagement are fluid and always have been. They change with government policies and with diplomatic pressure from allies and enemies alike. Even while operating under the rules, there are days when the army is instructed by political echelons to hold its fire, even though the day before, it would have opened fire.
IDF soldiers are faced with numerous situations that require sensitivity and mindful awareness of civilian populations, but when an army is dealing with terror operatives, tunnels, and a malicious entity that disguises itself as civilian and totally controls its civilian population, it is hard for any soldier to know who in the scheme of things is who.
Israel's life-saving measures go beyond what international law requires
JOHN SPENCER – chairman of urban warfare studies at the Modern War Institute at West Point, and one of the most prominent Western experts on urban warfare – has been a leading voice on Israel’s conduct of operations in Gaza. His views are based on comparative historical analysis of urban battles.
In a March 2024 Newsweek op-ed, Spencer claimed: “Israel has done more and implemented more measures to prevent civilian harm than any military in the history of urban warfare.”
He said these measures go beyond what international law requires and beyond what the US and its partners did in comparable fights in Iraq, Afghanistan, and Mosul against ISIS.
Specific practices Spencer lauded:
• Mass evacuation warnings (days or weeks in advance in some cases)
• Phone calls, text messages, and recorded voice messages to specific buildings or neighborhoods
• “Roof-knocking” (firing a small, non-lethal munition onto a roof as a final warning)
• Distribution of maps showing safe routes and daily updates on humanitarian corridors
• Frequent tactical pauses and localized pauses during operations
• Extensive use of precision-guided munitions and formal targeting processes
He noted that no other military has systematically combined these actions at this scale while fighting an enemy deeply embedded in dense urban terrain with a vast tunnel network.
Which raises the question: Does that make the IDF highly moral or overly cautious?
A history of the ethos
Military ethics long predates the State of Israel.
Carl von Clausewitz, who joined the Prussian army at age 12 and served in the Imperial Russian Army during the 1812 campaign against France, is widely regarded as the father of modern strategic studies and a philosopher of war. His book On War remains one of the key texts used to teach soldiers and shape modern military and political strategy.
He stated that “war is the continuation of politics by other means,” balancing the people, the army, and the government. Thus, politics determines when a soldier is given permission to shoot.
Here in Israel, we have seen firsthand how diplomacy can get in the way of winning a war. In Israel, where “Never Again” is our battle cry, upon enlisting, each soldier is given a document called “Ruah Zahal,” “The Spirit of the IDF,” which includes a section on “Purity of Arms.”
The purity of arms (tohar haneshek) was an unwritten military tradition developed in the pre-state Jewish defense organizations, especially the Hagana and its strike force, the Palmah, and passed on to the present-day IDF.
“Tohar haneshek” means keeping one’s weapon “clean” from innocent blood. It means weapons and force should be used only for self-defense and the mission, and only to the extent necessary.
Fighters are expected to avoid harming noncombatants, including civilians, prisoners, and the defenseless, as much as possible, and to maintain their humanity even in the midst of combat, refusing to sink into unnecessary cruelty, looting, revenge, or abuse.
By the early 1990s, the IDF had spent several years dealing with the First Intifada, which began in 1987. New missions involved frequent operations in densely populated civilian areas against non-state actors, stone-throwers, and terrorists who did not wear uniforms or separate themselves from the civilian population.
Traditional army-versus-army doctrines were no longer sufficient on their own. Commanders needed clearer guidance for soldiers operating in complex, morally ambiguous environments.
In 1994, then-IDF chief of staff Ehud Barak called in Asa Kasher, who was already deeply familiar with the IDF through years of teaching its officers, a respected professional ethicist capable of turning military tradition into a coherent modern code, and someone who could lend the project both intellectual seriousness and legitimacy.
He is a professor emeritus of professional ethics and philosophy of practice at Tel Aviv University, a senior researcher (emeritus) at the Institute for National Security Studies, and the recipient of the 2000 Israel Prize for philosophy.
Together, they created “Ruah Zahal,” the IDF Code of Ethics, preserving the morals of the “purity of arms” in precise written language. The formal version retained the core ideas of tohar haneshek – the use of force only for the mission, only to the necessary extent, and the obligation to avoid harming noncombatants – while placing them within a broader ethical framework that also included human dignity, the sanctity of life, and the values of a democratic state.
The ethical code treats the drive to accomplish the mission and achieve victory as essential, but not absolute. Force must still be used only to the extent necessary, humanity must be maintained, and unnecessary harm to noncombatants must be avoided. Victory is a professional and moral obligation of the soldier and the army, yet it does not license the use of unrestricted means.
Victory: Is the IDF 'allowed' to win a war?
Kasher’s views on victory appear to be the most controversial aspect of his body of writing on IDF military ethics, especially “Ruah Zahal.” He treated “victory” differently, depending on the type of conflict.
He espoused the view that in classical interstate wars between regular armies, traditional concepts of military victory (defeating or destroying the enemy’s capacity to continue fighting) remain relevant.
In the fight against terrorism and non-state actors who embed among civilians, however, Kasher argued in his fall 2014 essay “The Ethics of Protective Edge” in the Jewish Review of Books – the classical notion of total victory is often obsolete or strategically unattainable.
He has further written that in recent decades “victory has been replaced by the ideal of successfully accomplishing given missions.”
One of the core members of the committee appointed in 2000 to drastically revise the original IDF Code of Ethics was Prof. Avi Sagi, a philosopher and leading public voice on modern Jewish identity, existentialism, and military ethics. He served as a professor of philosophy at Bar-Ilan University and a senior research fellow at the Shalom Hartman Institute.
In interviews with former Maariv journalist Tuvi (Toby) Pollack as late as 2024, Sagi argued that “victory is not a moral value” and warned that elevating it could justify the unrestrained use of force.
In a 2026 paper, “The IDF Needs to Return to Its Core Values,” published by Col. (res.) Prof. Gabi Siboni and Brig.-Gen. (ret.) Erez Winner, of the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security, described Sagi’s contribution to the “Purity of Arms” as “one of the most contentious changes” ever made to “Ruah Zahal.”
They continued, “The new language created a sense of ‘moral hygiene’ where the objective seemed not to be defeating the enemy but emerging from battle with a legal ‘clean sheet.’”
In his published paper “Correcting the IDF’s Ethical Code,” Dr. Ronen Shoval, an Israeli political philosopher and head of the Argaman Institute for Advanced Studies, quoted Sagi as saying (on the podcast On the Way: Conversations with Tuvi Pollack, episode 418, titled “Avi Sagi on the Ethics of Combat and Warfare, Dealing with Feelings of Revenge, and the Difficulty of Maintaining Human Dignity”): “Victory does not justify the use of force. If ‘victory’ meets the standard of self-defense, fine; if not, we should reserve the concept of victory for basketball or chess....”
Siboni and Winner argued that “in the end, victory was included only through a kind of compromise typical of Israel’s political culture, in the phrasing ‘commitment to the mission and striving for victory.’ Even so, the formulation of the value itself remained almost apologetic.
“For many in the fighting ranks, pushing victory to the margins of the value system conveyed a sense that the army had lost its bearings. If a military does not educate its soldiers to see victory as a central value, it risks losing its fundamental moral purpose: protecting the lives of the state’s citizens.”
'Israel is Just the Beginning'
IN A RECENT INTERVIEW with the Magazine, Moshe Feiglin – former MK and deputy speaker of the Knesset, and founder of the Zehut party, which recently announced it will be running in a technical election bloc with Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party – he explained, “The Purity of Arms reiterates again and again that the word ‘victory’ is immoral because you’re only allowed to fight to protect yourself. You’re not allowed to fight for justice, for example, or for your country, or for your land, or to achieve any kind of victory over evil forces, because there is no good and bad in the world.”
Feiglin’s new book, Israel is Just the Beginning, posits that Israel’s refusal to embrace its own Jewish identity is keeping it from winning existential wars it must win to survive.
“As long as Israel and its army are led by community-minded leaders and not national ones, the war will not end, because in truth the national war has yet to begin,” wrote Feiglin, who lost a grandchild in Operation Swords of Iron.
“Despite the terrible sacrifice of the soldiers and officers who gave their lives to save our country, this war will not end until Israel’s leadership is likewise drawn from their ranks – from those who have not lost their national consciousness. The war will not end because a community, even one whose sons are heroes, does not win wars. A community can only lick its wounds and redeem its captives.”
In our interview, Feiglin was clear: “When you are in war, there should be only one goal, and it is to win.”
He extended this credo to acts of terrorism. “If an Arab comes out of his town and throws a rock at an Israeli car or at Israeli people who are walking and touring the land, the reaction [of the Israeli civilian or soldier] should be to shoot in order to kill, because he is fighting against you in a national war. It is not a private altercation between people. We are at war.
“When the Egyptian soldiers crossed the Suez Canal in 1973, they didn’t look to see who was shooting at that moment and who was not. They understood that we are at war. Every Arab throwing a rock on you is a soldier in the Arab national war. And when you are at war, there should be only one goal, and it is to win.
“In Gaza we tried not to use methods that would have ended the war fast,” Feiglin said. “We sent soldiers into booby traps and tunnels – including my own grandson.”
He paused for a painful moment. “We think by acting this way, we will gain points with the international moral conscience, but we are actually showing the world that we don’t accept our own code of justice. We want to show the world how westerly civilized we are – but they look at us and say ‘polite colonialists are still colonialists.’”
Do the “don’t shoot” directives, the roof-thumping and flyer dropping advanced warnings go above and beyond the call of duty to warn enemy civilians and combatants that the IDF is about to attack?
“The idea that we can train our soldiers to understand this moral precipice in the classroom fails to take into account the very dynamic nature of war and the ‘fog of war’ that has been described so well by Clausewitz,” Dr. David Leitner shared with the Magazine. He is a strategy and leadership expert, the founder of Rhydl Consulting, and a lecturer at Bar-Ilan University.
“Soldiers face unique situations every single time they go out into the field, and they must make decisions based on what they are experiencing in the moment,” he added.
“To judge those decisions from a legal standpoint that does not understand or accept that war takes place within civilian populations who have, at the very bare minimum, supported the enemy and often are actively participating in enemy activities – it is, in and of itself, a recipe for hesitation that can cost soldiers’ lives.
“International politics are heavily impacting the ability of frontline soldiers to act for their own safety, or to act in ways they perceive as vital for the safety of the home front and the achievement of victory.
“This lack of a clear, shared understanding of what victory looks like – both in the military and the political realms – has led to significant friction between the political and upper echelons of the military and the soldiers out in the field who are experiencing the war through their feet.”
The IDF weighs in
In a conversation with a senior military official, the Magazine asked: "Is the IDF fighting to win?"
The official explained that the overall picture shows the IDF striving to create conditions in which Hamas is weakened and exhausted, no longer capable of operating as it once did, and ultimately defeated. The goal is to eliminate any threat to the residents of the State of Israel. Achieving this objective requires a continuous effort to balance the application of force, strategy, and tactics.
Regarding whether soldiers might refrain from firing to avoid legal consequences, the official expressed certainty that this is not the case. Of the thousands of decisions made during the war, only a very small percentage ultimately reach investigation. Many of these reviews, the official added, are not formal investigations but, rather, inquiries designed to ensure that protocols were properly followed.
Returning to the earlier example of soldiers entering a house that might contain terrorists, the official was asked how the army teaches its forces to respect other cultures while maintaining determination and authority.
The official explained that the IDF does not dictate one precise, specific method for entering a house. Instead, soldiers are given the values and ethics that underlie the mission. They are reminded that a clear, specific mission is the sole reason they entered the house; following the mission’s logic is essential. Respect is emphasized not only as an ethical requirement but also as a practical one – a lack of respect creates chaos, hysteria, and unnecessary noise that harm the mission itself.
Preparation for these complex situations relies on repeated drills and simulations. The simulations are filmed so that soldiers can review the footage and learn from their mistakes.
When asked whether the code of “Purity of Arms” needs to be updated, the official acknowledged that work remains to be done but argued that the original statement does not require rephrasing or rewriting. The code is strong enough as written, the official said. The priority is ensuring the right tools are used to implement it.
Rewriting the rules: Is 'Purity of Arms' due for an upgrade?
While “Purity of Arms” assumes a meaningful distinction between combatants and noncombatants and the possibility of limiting force to what is necessary, Israel’s adversaries – Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, Hezbollah, etc. – systematically reject that distinction.
They embed fighters, command centers, weapons, and tunnels inside and under civilian infrastructure, use human shields, and celebrate their own civilian deaths as strategic assets.
When the enemy deliberately creates mixed environments, the practical ability to apply force “only to the necessary extent” while still accomplishing the mission shrinks dramatically.
The Torah gives distinct guidelines for different kinds of wars, milhemet mitzvah and milhemet reshut, the former being the kind of war that must be fought under any circumstances. Then there is the Amalek war, where after being attacked by the merciless Amalekites, the fledgling nation of Israel was commanded to execute every man, woman, and child, and even livestock. The Talmud weighs in, saying, “If someone comes to kill you, you are obligated to kill him first.”
With that in mind, many individuals and political action groups hope that this year brings changes to the army’s document. These efforts reflect a broader post-Oct. 7 debate on the Right over whether the IDF’s formal ethical language adequately serves a Jewish army confronting existential threats.
In May 2026, MK Zvi Sukkot organized a letter, signed by about 30 coalition MKs, to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu demanding a full reexamination and rewrite of “Ruah Zahal.”
The signatories said lessons from the recent war and the changing security reality required reformulating the foundational principles so they strengthen fighters’ trust and align with the mission of defeating the enemy.
Sukkot criticized the existing version as having been written by “extreme leftists,” claimed Kasher had tried to damage the IDF, and insisted the code must state unequivocally that the lives of Israeli soldiers take precedence over those of the enemy.
Alongside Sukkot’s parliamentary push, a more ideological campaign has emerged from religious-Zionist circles seeking a fundamental rewrite of the IDF’s ethical protocols.
The Torat HaMedina institute, based in Jerusalem’s Beit Orot neighborhood, launched the book Mashiv HaRuah le-Zahal (Restoring the Spirit to the IDF) in spring 2026 as an explicit Jewish alternative to the existing “Ruah Zahal.”
Authored by rabbis Yair Kartman and Yaakov Yakir, the work argues that the current code is overly universalist and restraining, treating war as a necessary evil that risks moral corruption, rather than as a mitzvah and divine mission.
Drawing on Torah sources, it reframes combat as a continuation of the path of King David and the Maccabees, fought in the name of God and the people of Israel, and proposes five core values: defense of the Jewish people, sovereignty in the Land of Israel, decisive victory, Jewish morality rooted in tradition and prophecy, and the prioritization of Israeli soldiers’ lives in a collective national campaign.
The project has attracted visible support from senior religious and political figures, including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu, National Missions Minister Orit Strock, and MK Simcha Rothman, who attended related events.
A more measured corrective proposal, advanced by former IDF deputy chief of staff Maj.-Gen. (ret.) Uzi Dayan and Rabbi Oury Cherki similarly elevate victory as the supreme value and clarify the primacy of Israeli lives, while remaining closer to the existing framework.
Rabbi Cherki explained that war is a catastrophe according to the Torah. But, he said, the Torah recognizes that we are going to get into wars, and we must defend ourselves against barbarians. The Ramban, he said, points out that when it is necessary, we are obligated to prevent attacks.
That is part of the morality of war, Cherki told the Magazine. We first seek peace, but if that can’t be achieved, we fight to win.
“We must fight against terrorists who fight among civilian populations,” he explained. “The initial document [“Ruah Zahal”] reflects an immoral value. A fighter needs to have a sense of justice and legitimacy. We should never have to choose between the lives of our soldiers and the lives of civilians on the other side.”
Another notable voice in the critique of “Ruah Zahal” is Shoval’s. In his paper “Correcting the IDF’s Ethical Code,” he explained that “ethical codes for armies thus seek to fulfill three central functions:
“1. Morality and limitations: They establish a framework that defines the boundaries of combat.
“2. Maintaining public legitimacy: A code of ethics ensures that the actions of the military receive the support of the civilian population.
“3. Identity and heritage: The code of ethics strengthens the sense of purpose in military service by framing it not only as a means of defense but also as a mission grounded in values.
“The main problem is that, as it stands, this ‘moral guide’ [‘Ruah Zahal’] is simply not moral,” he explained. “There is a hidden assumption that to fight a war is unjust. But sometimes not killing the enemy is worse than killing them. There is an assumption that using force implies you are doing something wrong. It goes against the Christian ethos of turning the other cheek.”
He continued, “If the role of the soldier is to protect the civilian, the life of the soldier is worth more than the life of the terrorist.”
He pointed out in an interview that the questions come into play if there is an Israeli civilian victim and a Nukhba terrorist, both wounded on the ground. Who should the medics treat first? The current ethics in Israel, he said, is to triage the one who is more wounded, but he said the wounded civilian should morally come first.
In February 2016, Gadi Eisenkot (who was then IDF chief of staff and is currently party leader of Yashar), speaking to high school seniors about to enter the army, at Heichal Hatarbut in Bat Yam, said:
“When there’s a 13-year-old girl holding scissors or a knife, and there is distance between her and the soldiers, I don’t want to see a soldier open fire and empty his magazine at a girl like that, even if she is committing a very serious act. Rather, he should use the force necessary to fulfill the objective.”
He added that soldiers receive weapons to take a human life when required, but the rules of engagement are derived from the mission, and the IDF does not operate according to “slogans” such as “whoever comes to kill you, kill him first.” A soldier may remove the safety and shoot if there is real danger to himself or his comrades but must apply only the necessary force.
'Purity of Arms' is unlikely to change anytime soon
THE REAL QUESTION is how an ordinary soldier is to determine the severity of the threat in real time and under maximum pressure.
Shoval said that unless there is a concerted effort, the “Purity of Arms” is unlikely to change anytime soon. “The conception has not changed in the army, and it’s not likely to change. It can only change when we have a new generation of soldiers with fresh ideas, coming from the post-Oct. 7 crop of soldiers.”
Cherki admitted the IDF appears to be hesitating because it is not ready to make deep changes, but he does believe enough people want to see changes happen soon.
“Changing the ‘Purity of Arms’ document should be an election goal of the Right,” he said.
Hopefully, the candidates will clearly state their points of view. Some have already weighed in.
Voters will be left to determine whether the rules of engagement ultimately protect our soldiers and the Israeli nation they defend, and whether this new year will be safer for everyone in Israel.■
What would you do? Responses to a hypothetical army exercise in civilian areas
The mission: You have already given clear warnings to civilians to evacuate an area used by terrorists, to give the inhabitants time to flee. These include leaflets, phone calls, and “roof-knocking.” Some civilians remain. How does this affect your decision to engage a legitimate military target in that area?
Military figures weigh in:
Combat commander: I will never accept a greater risk to my own force to further reduce possible civilian harm. Obviously, we always try to avoid civilian harm. But not at the expense of our own troops’ safety. A properly coordinated and executed mission reduces the risk to my soldiers to zero. No one is more precious to me than my soldiers.
Remaining civilians do not affect my decision to engage the military target. Unless someone gives an order to call off the mission because the civilians refuse to evacuate, the mission proceeds as planned.
High-ranking elite combat soldier: If clear warnings were given (and in my view, even those warnings go above and beyond), anyone who chooses to remain in an active war zone understands the risks. As a combat soldier, I cannot compromise operational decision-making or soldier safety to account for those who remained after being warned to evacuate.
In a combat zone, I will almost always prioritize the safety and lives of my soldiers above other considerations.
Former US naval officer: If fair warning has been given, I’d authorize the bombing to commence immediately, regardless of how many civilians remain in the targeted area. If the civilians aren’t smart enough to clear the area, then whatever happens is on them. Of course, they might be loitering around either to buy time for the terrorists to get away or to prevent us from carrying out our bombing.
– J.S.
Moshe Feiglin’s book on identity and the fight against radical Islam
Moshe Feiglin’s new book, Israel is Just the Beginning: How Israel’s Fight Against Radical Islam and Progressivism Protects the Identity and Liberty of the Civilized World, is illuminating and sometimes deeply disturbing. He analyzes the unholy alliance between Islam and progressivism, attributing the connection to a quest to abolish identity – not just Jewish identity, but any identities all over the world.
Chapter by chapter, Feiglin – who was a Likud MK and deputy Knesset speaker from February 2013-March 2015, and now heads the Zehut (Identity) party, which recently joined in a technical bloc with Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party – lays out the facts. Issues span from Israel’s existential war, which he calls “The Temple War,” to the fight to abolish sexual identity, the ideological battle over climate change, how feminists conveniently ignored Islam’s Oct. 7 rapes, Israel’s rules of engagement, COVID coverups, and more.
Feiglin calls out the hypocrisy of Israelis’ blind eye to the government’s state-controlled “dominion over our lives,” submission to Oslo, while also exploring its overall tendency to suppress Jewish identity within the State of Israel. And he exposes Islam’s sometimes concealed, more often unhidden, agenda to destroy the Jewish state.
Embracing Judaism’s God-fearing identity, Feiglin says, is the answer – not only for Israel, but the world. He acknowledges the Jews’ rejection of faith provided “energy powerful enough to propel the Jewish people back to renewed nationhood.” But he says that civic nationalism “could no longer imbue Israeli life with meaning, nor sustain a national sense of justice, validity, and legitimacy.”
Feiglin’s book is a compelling read, even if you don’t agree with all his ideas or conclusions. Regardless of political point of view or religious orientation, he provides enough facts, observations, and simple truths for pro-Israel readers trying to make sense of today’s extremely confusing world situation. – J.S.

Israeli army has seized Lebanon's key Ali al-Taher ridge from Hezbollah
Israel has seized the strategically placed Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon from Hezbollah fighters, Defence Minister Israel Katz said Friday. The Iran-aligned Shiite group did not confirm losing the highland, which sits around 10 kilometres from the border with Israel and was pummelled by Israeli strikes in recent weeks despite a ceasefire.
Israeli troops have driven Hezbollah fighters from tunnels under the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Friday. The Iran-aligned Shiite group did not immediately comment.
Israel had said Hezbollah fighters were embedded in tunnels under the ridge, which overlooks a wide area and had become one of the most hotly contested areas in the Israel-Hezbollah war, despite a ceasefire announced in June.
Read moreIsraeli strikes kill 11 in southern Lebanon, Hezbollah threatens to retaliate
"The mission was completed and the tunnels were cleared of terrorists," Katz said on social media, after a statement by the military late on Thursday saying it had operational control of the ridge.
Reuters reported on Thursday that Iran had warned the United States last month that it would respond forcefully to an Israeli assault on its Hezbollah allies' positions within the ridge. For its part, the Shiite Muslim group had said it would resist any Israeli assault.
The Israeli military said some Hezbollah fighters had been "eliminated", while others had fled.
Hezbollah did not immediately respond to a request for comment and Reuters was not able to independently verify the status of the ridge.
Watch moreUNIFIL peacekeepers patrol south Lebanon, caught between Israel and Hezbollah
The ridge, a flashpoint since Tehran-backed Hezbollah drew Lebanon into the Middle East war in March following the US-Israeli killing of Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, lies close to the major city of Nabatieh and the Litani river.
It is just a few kilometres from UNESCO-listed Beaufort castle, another strategic site that Israel captured in recent months.
The Israeli military on Thursday said that the tunnel network included "command centres (and) weapons storage rooms".
"The infrastructure is a strategic underground network that was built over two decades and funded and planned by the Iranian terror regime," it added.
Kahwaji, who heads the INEGMA military analysis institute, said the hilltops overlook Iqlim al-Tuffah, an area further from the border where Hezbollah holds sway, as well as part of the country's east.
Control of the area would therefore "give the Israelis an easy passage to move on both sides".
Speaking to journalists including AFP last month, Hezbollah spokesman Youssef al-Zein refused to say how many of the group's fighters were at the Ali al-Taher position. He denied any Iranian personnel were there, as had been reported in some media outlets.
He said that Israel had "exaggerated the importance of Ali al-Taher" as a military objective but also vowed that Hezbollah would "defend this position as much as it can".
The ridge is located right above the Litani. Hezbollah agreed to disarm in areas south of the river under a 2024 ceasefire that sought to end its previous war with Israel.
Israel has expanded its military occupation over swathes of southern Lebanon since launching a new campaign against Hezbollah in March.
In June, Israel's army published an updated map showing the parts of southern Lebanon it considers within what it calls its "security zone" where its troops are operating, expanding the area to include the Ali al-Taher ridge.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters and AFP)

Russian technologies inside the EU: Is Germany ignoring the risks of cooperation with Rosatom?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:25:00 EEST
22:25:00 KST

Russian technologies inside the EU: Is Germany ignoring the risks of cooperation with Rosatom?
Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the European Union has been steadily reducing its dependence on Russian energy resources.
Gas, oil, coal – in almost every sector, this course has already become irreversible. Nuclear energy remains one of the few exceptions. This is precisely why the decision to allow French company Framatome to expand the production of nuclear fuel for Soviet-designed VVER reactors in Germany has sparked such a heated debate. Supporters of the project describe it as a step towards diversifying fuel supplies for European nuclear power plants. Yet there is a fundamental question:
Can this truly be called diversification if the new production relies on technologies provided by Russia’s TVEL, the nuclear fuel division of Rosatom?
The license published by the Lower Saxony authorities helps provide an answer.
The Most Interesting Part Is Not the Decision Itself, but Its Conditions
The public debate often revolves around whether cooperation with Rosatom creates additional security risks. Paradoxically, the most compelling answer comes not from the project’s critics, but from the German licensing authority itself.
The document examines in detail scenarios involving potential manipulation of fuel components, risks associated with the use of Russian equipment, espionage, sabotage and cyber interference.
It establishes specific additional security requirements for each of these scenarios.
For example, for certain VVER fuel designs, finished welded gadolinium-containing fuel rods will be supplied by the Russian manufacturer MSZ (Mashinostroitelny Zavod), which is part of TVEL. The permit specifically considers the risk of deliberate manipulation of these rods before their delivery to Germany, including the possibility of placing foreign substances or materials inside them, including explosive materials.
This is why 100% scanner inspection of such rods is required. In addition, one rod from a batch may be opened and internally examined as a sample.
Another scenario concerns the equipment and software supplied by TVEL for the manufacturing process.
The permit takes into account the risk that such equipment or software could theoretically be deliberately modified before arriving at the Lingen plant in a way that could affect the characteristics of the manufactured fuel elements or result in the production of defective fuel assemblies. Hardware components of the control systems must therefore undergo independent inspection. The source code, including software for programmable logic controllers and visualisation systems, must also be independently reviewed for hidden, modified or functionally unnecessary elements. The IT/OT infrastructure supplied by TVEL must also be separated from the plant’s other systems.
A separate set of conditions addresses the risks of espionage and sabotage.
Representatives of TVEL, Rosatom and persons associated with them are prohibited from accessing the facility, while contacts with them (both by telephone and in writing) are restricted to what is strictly necessary and must follow the "four-eyes principle".
However, this prohibition is not absolute. Access may still be granted in exceptional circumstances, subject to a dedicated risk-mitigation plan, a reliability assessment by the Lower Saxony Environment Ministry and prior approval by the nuclear supervisory authority.
Such mechanisms reduce the risks but do not eliminate them entirely,
as the human factor and the need to ensure compliance with the established rules remain.
In other words, the permit does not deny the existence of risks.
On the contrary, it assumes that they are serious enough to require specific control mechanisms. This is a crucial distinction. The document does not claim that Russian technologies automatically make production unsafe. But it acknowledges that their use creates new risk scenarios that would simply not exist without this cooperation.
The measures imposed by the permit conditions may significantly reduce the likelihood of such scenarios realisation, but they are designed to manage the risks rather than eliminate their underlying source – a Russian state-owned company.
It Is Not Just a Security Issue
The economic dimension is equally important. The expansion of the Lingen plant is presented as a way to reduce dependence on Russia. Yet the new production relies on Russian manufacturing licences, know-how, specialised equipment and certain components. In other words, part of the technological dependence does not disappear; it is merely relocated to the territory of the European Union. German officials themselves have raised this concern, and the issue therefore remains a matter of debate within Germany itself.
There are, however, fundamental limitations inherent in the German licensing procedure. The decision explicitly states that energy dependence and the security of European energy supply are not among the criteria considered when granting the permit. This means that strategic, economic and geopolitical risks are not assessed as part of the licensing procedure for nuclear fuel production. Nor does the decision assess whether a model of long-term technological cooperation between Framatome and Rosatom is consistent with the strategic interests of Germany and the EU, because this question lies outside the scope of the procedure.
This raises the central strategic question: if, in a few years, the EU tightens restrictions on the Russian nuclear sector or decides to phase out such technologies entirely, how quickly could this production model adapt? And could investments made today have to be scaled back long before they have paid off?
There are currently no answers to these questions.
Is Europe Supporting Two Different Visions of the Future?
The REPowerEU roadmap for ending Russian energy imports, presented in May 2025, envisages reducing dependence on Russia, including in the nuclear sector.
At the same time, the European Union is already funding the development of fully European fuel for VVER reactors. In particular, the SAVE project, funded under Horizon Europe and coordinated by Framatome itself, aims to develop fuel based on a European design, European manufacturing and a supply chain free from Russian technologies.
The Lingen project therefore goes far beyond the question of whether a particular manufacturing operation formally complies with the requirements of a German permit. The real issue is whether creating a new technological dependence on TVEL is consistent with the direction in which the EU intends to develop its energy policy.
In practice, two different models for the future of European VVER nuclear fuel production are currently being realised. The first envisages a gradual phase-out of Russian technological dependence. The second integrates part of that dependence within the EU itself. Both approaches cannot remain equally relevant indefinitely.
Sooner or later, a choice will have to be made.
Lingen Is About Much More Than One Plant
The debate surrounding the project has long moved beyond the question of a single additional production line. It is about how Europe defines its strategic autonomy.
This is where the logic of the manufacturing permit collides with the EU’s broader strategic logic. The licensing authority is tasked only with determining whether specific security risks can be mitigated to an acceptable level – and, as discussed above, it cannot completely eliminate their underlying source.
European policy, by contrast, must answer a different question: should these risks be created in the first place by establishing a long-term dependence on Russian technologies within critical infrastructure when the EU’s strategic objective is to move in the opposite direction?
The debate over the expansion of production in Lingen therefore did not end with the issuance of the permit. The security conditions imposed leave space for a legal assessment of whether they are sufficient to meet the standards of Section 7(2) of the German Atomic Energy Act. A legal challenge to the decision could therefore be one of the next steps.
At the political level, an even broader question remains: does the very fact that such a decision was taken contradict Europe’s overall course towards ending its dependence on Russian energy resources? This question is particularly relevant against the backdrop of Russia’s intensifying sabotage and other hybrid operations across Europe.
By Mykhailo Babiichuk,
General Manager on Security and Resilience, Kyiv-based think tank DiXi Group

Necva Tastan Sevinc
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis will visit Egypt next week as Athens closely follows improving relations between Cairo and Ankara and the possible expansion of a new regional collective-defense pact, local media reported Friday.
Mitsotakis is expected to meet Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi in El Alamein on Tuesday, according to Greek newspaper Ta Nea.
The visit is intended to signal continued close coordination between Athens and Cairo amid shifting regional dynamics, the report said.
Greek Cypriot administration leader Nikos Christodoulides may also attend.
A key issue expected to feature in the talks is the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement signed by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan on Aug. 7.
The agreement includes a collective-defense clause under which an armed attack on one member would be considered an attack on all.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has publicly raised the possibility of Egypt joining the arrangement, while Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has described Cairo as a “natural partner.”
Egypt already participates alongside the three founding countries in the emerging four-member consultation framework known as the R4.
Egyptian accession would give the pact greater strategic reach, as the country controls the Suez Canal, links the Mediterranean and Red Sea and possesses one of the region’s largest militaries.
Greek officials, however, reportedly believe Cairo is unlikely to join in the near term because it traditionally seeks to preserve its freedom of action and maintains important partnerships with the US and Europe.
The talks are also expected to cover Türkiye, Libya, migration, energy, investment and maritime disputes in the Eastern Mediterranean.

‘Forex, trade policies must be reviewed in line with current conditions’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:24:54 UTC
22:24:54 KST

‘Forex, trade policies must be reviewed in line with current conditions’
TEHRAN- The Head of Iran's Export Confederation, stating that the country's foreign trade conditions are no longer comparable to the past following the recent imposed war and subsequent developments, said: "Under current circumstances, continuing past policies in the areas of exports, imports, and currency repatriation is no longer effective, and a review of forex and trade policies is an absolute necessity."
Mohammad Lahouti, speaking to IRNA, stated: "Iran's sanctions situation and its relations with the United States have entered a different phase after the 12-day war, with tensions escalating from disputes and economic pressures to military confrontation. During and after the imposed war, new sanctions were imposed on Iran, and simultaneously with the issue of the Strait of Hormuz and restrictions on trade routes, the movement of goods and economic exchanges became more difficult for all parties."
He added: "Eventually, with the cessation of hostilities, some of the war-induced pressures eased, but sanctions remain in place and have even intensified in certain areas. On the other hand, some countries that previously had economic cooperation with Iran are now operating more cautiously under the new circumstances, and this too has affected the country's foreign trade."
The Head of Iran's Export Confederation, referring to the problems created in the foreign trade route, said: "Restrictions on the movement and transport of goods have made the trade process more difficult for economic activists. Furthermore, the damage inflicted on some industrial units during the war has affected production and, consequently, the country's foreign currency earning capacity."
He emphasized: "The combination of these factors shows that the current state of the country's economy and foreign trade is in no way comparable to pre-war conditions. To manage the existing situation, we cannot continue using the same regulations and prescriptions that were formulated under normal circumstances in the past."
Lahouti, stressing the need for a change in the government's approach to foreign trade, stated: "In the past, imposing restrictions on imports or creating complex processes for importers might have been manageable, but today, given the current conditions, such policies are no longer effective."
He added: "In the export sector as well, if the same strictness regarding currency repatriation and forex obligations continues under current circumstances, it could lead to a decline in the country's export capacity."
The Head of the Non-Oil Export Development Committee of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines, and Agriculture, said: "Now, pressure is being applied to Iran's economy from various directions, and the goal of these pressures is to weaken the country's economy. Therefore, the government must change its perspective on foreign trade management and make decisions regarding exports, imports, and even export bans in line with the new conditions."
Lahouti, referring to the country's limited foreign currency resources, stated: "Under current circumstances, import management must be proportionate to the country's export volume. Naturally, when foreign currency revenues from exports decline, import capacity is also affected, and economic activists understand this reality."
He added: "The decline in foreign trade, whether in exports or imports, is a direct result of reduced currency earnings and existing restrictions. However, the main issue is that current forex and trade policies have not been designed in line with the country's new conditions."
The Head of Iran's Export Confederation emphasized: "To overcome the current situation, a review of forex and trade policies is mandatory, and this cannot be considered an option or a postponable decision."
Lahouti, referring to the role of executive bodies in reforming the current conditions, said: "If serious changes and structural reforms in forex and trade policies—and the way foreign trade is managed—do not take place in institutions such as the Central Bank, the Ministry of Industry, Mine and Trade, and the Ministry of Agriculture, it will become even more difficult to navigate the current difficult situation."
He continued: "The currency policymaker must fulfill its duties regarding the forex sector, and the trade policymaker must also formulate policies in line with the country's foreign trade needs. The overlap of these two areas and the creation of complex processes, under current circumstances, can hinder the activities of exporters and importers."
Lahouti, stressing the need to move toward trade facilitation, said: "Under current conditions, instead of unnecessary strictness, a facilitation approach in foreign trade should be strengthened. Revising processes, reducing barriers, and redesigning forex and trade policies can help economic activists continue their activities under the current difficult circumstances."
He concluded: "If the policymaker's perspective changes and forex and trade policies are adjusted in line with the country's new conditions, we can hope that managing the existing situation will be achieved with lower costs and greater efficiency, and that the country's economy will have more capacity to withstand current pressures."

Conflicts and extreme weather pushing global food prices higher, warns UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:24:53 UTC

Conflicts and extreme weather pushing global food prices higher, warns UN
UN food price index rises to four-year high, illustrating impact of war and weather.
Global food prices have hit a four-year high, the United Nations has warned.
The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) reported on Friday that its Food Price Index climbed for a third straight month to 133.3 points in August.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items
- list 1 of 2El Nino: A phenomenon supercharged by climate change
- list 2 of 2Gulf insecurity fuels US energy dominance
That pushed the measure to its highest level since late 2022, as wars and weather impact supplies, the agency said.
Every category on the index – cereals, vegetable oils, sugar, meat and dairy – rose over the month.
FAO chief economist, Maximo Torero, said the rise is being driven by several factors.
“Climate shocks, geopolitical tensions and disrupted trade logistics are converging to tighten supply expectations,” he said in a statement.
That risk was clearest in sugar, which rose fastest of all the categories tracked, up almost 12 percent from July to its highest point in a year.
Cereal prices climbed more than two percent to their highest level in over two years.
Wheat and maize both became more expensive as military strikes disrupted shipping through the Black Sea, a major route for Russian and Ukrainian grain exports.
Fertiliser supplies faced separate strain from the conflict between the United States, Israel and Iran. The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway off Iran’s coast that is being blockaded by both the US and Iran, carries much of the world’s fertiliser trade.
Those increases matter well beyond supermarket shelves, since higher wholesale food costs tend to filter through to consumer prices in the months that follow.
The risk is heightened by global warming, as well as the return of El Nino, the naturally occurring Pacific Ocean warming pattern that disrupts weather worldwide.
The heatwaves that gripped Europe this summer led to a drop in crop yields, while El Nino threatens production in Asia.
The World Food Programme, the UN agency that coordinates emergency food aid, has warned that the weather phenomenon could push another 50 million people into acute hunger by the end of next year.

Malaysia declares emergency in Sarawak state amid worsening haze
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:24:34 UTC
22:24:34 KST

Saadet Gokce
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
Malaysia declared an emergency in Sarawak state's Serian district on Friday after thick haze linked to forest and peatland fires in neighboring Indonesia pushed air pollution to hazardous levels.
 
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said in a statement on US social media company X that Malaysia's King Sultan Ibrahim had approved the emergency declaration.
 
"The government will continue to monitor developments and ensure that all necessary actions are implemented promptly, including mitigation measures as well as the dissemination of information and health advice to the public," he added.
The Air Pollutant Index (API) in Serian surged above 500 on Friday, crossing the threshold for an emergency declaration. Malaysian authorities classify readings above 300 as hazardous.
 
Sarawak, on the Malaysian side of Borneo, has been heavily affected by smoke from forest and peatland fires in neighboring Indonesia's Kalimantan region.
 
Malaysia on Thursday launched a three-day cloud-seeding operation in Sarawak to replenish dam water levels and ease the haze.
Cloud seeding involves dispersing particles into suitable clouds to encourage rainfall.
 
Indonesia has also been carrying out cloud-seeding operations as it battles widespread forest and peatland fires.
Indonesia's National Disaster Management Agency spokesperson Berton Panjaitan told Anadolu on Friday that operations were conducted from Aug. 26 to Sept. 2 to make use of available rain, increase moisture in soil and peatlands, suppress existing fires and prevent new ones.
 
"Indonesia has deployed a total of 34 aircraft to support the cloud-seeding operations, or Operasi Modifikasi Cuaca (OMC), in different priority areas," he said.

Estonia puts Omniva up for sale – auction starting price set at 52 million euros
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:23:02 UTC
22:23:02 KST

Estonia on Friday launched a public sealed-bid auction for the sale of shares in the state-owned postal company Eesti Post, operating under the Omniva brand, with a starting price of 52 million euros, Omniva announced.
The auction offers 100% of the shares in Eesti Post. The deadline for submitting bids is 27 November 2026.
Eesti Post serves customers in all three Baltic states and operates an international logistics network spanning more than ten countries. The company’s revenue reached 155 million euros in 2025.
The sale follows the Estonian government’s decision of 6 April 2026 to sell Eesti Post shares through a public auction.
Estonian Minister of Regional Affairs and Agriculture Hendrik Johannes Terras said the sale would reduce the state’s exposure to business and investment-related risks while creating better conditions for the company to attract investment, improve service quality and strengthen its competitiveness.
“The state’s role in postal services should primarily be regulatory rather than providing services as the owner of the company. Even after the change of ownership, home delivery of letters, newspapers and other periodicals will continue, as universal postal service requirements and other obligations related to the provision of postal services are stipulated in the Postal Act,” Terras said.
In recent years, Eesti Post’s operations have changed significantly, shifting from traditional nationwide postal services towards international logistics services. The universal postal service accounted for 5% of the company’s revenue in 2025. With annual revenue of 155 million euros, Eesti Post has become one of the leading logistics groups in the Baltics.
The sale will not affect the provision of the universal postal service or the home delivery of newspapers and other periodicals in Estonia. Eesti Post will continue to provide these services in accordance with the requirements of the Postal Act, while the state will retain its regulatory and supervisory role.
The auction is being organised by advisers to the Ministry of Regional Affairs and Agriculture, Superia and Redgate Capital.
As previously reported, the Omniva Group delivered a total of 36 million parcels across the Baltic states last year.
In Latvia, SIA Omniva recorded revenue of 24.321 million euros last year, an increase of 4.3% compared with the previous year, while the company’s profit decreased by 11.3% to 1.711 million euros. Meanwhile, the Omniva Group generated revenue of 154.7 million euros last year, up 9.4% year-on-year, while its profit amounted to 5.9 million euros.
Omniva is an international technology and logistics group providing postal, parcel and e-commerce logistics services across the Baltic states and worldwide. The group consists of its parent company AS Eesti Post and its subsidiaries Finbite and Picapac in Estonia, Omniva in Latvia, and Omniva LT and Omniva LT Sorting in Lithuania. Eesti Post is wholly owned by the Estonian state.

British warship opens fire near Falklands to deter Argentina
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:22:23 BST
22:22:23 KST

HMS Medway carried out live machine gun firings at the edge of the Falkland Islands Conservation Zone during a four-day patrol at the end of July, British Forces South Atlantic Islands stated.
The patrol, designated Operation Southern Vigilance, ran from 26 to 29 July. The ship’s company fired mounted machine guns and worked through a man overboard exercise alongside an RAF A400M Atlas transport aircraft, work the command describes as maintaining operational readiness.
According to BFSAI, the deployment demonstrated the UK’s enduring commitment to the Falkland Islands by maintaining a visible presence and a capable force, helping to deter potential adversaries.
The Falkland Islands Conservation Zone extends 150 nautical miles from the centre of the archipelago and was established in 1990 to manage fish stocks, principally squid, which underpin a large share of the islands’ economy. Licensing and enforcement within it fall to the Falkland Islands Government, with the Royal Navy providing the deterrent presence and the fisheries patrol vessel Lilibet carrying out routine inspection work.
HMS Medway is a River-class offshore patrol vessel commissioned in 2019 and took over the South Atlantic Patrol Task from HMS Forth, which held the role for several years after replacing HMS Clyde. The class displaces around 2,000 tonnes and carries a 30mm gun, machine guns and a flight deck able to take a Merlin, with an endurance suited to long independent patrols in remote waters.
The ship is the only Royal Navy vessel permanently assigned to the region. British Forces South Atlantic Islands also operates Typhoon fighters and A400M and Voyager aircraft from RAF Mount Pleasant on East Falkland, alongside an infantry company, Rapier’s successor Sky Sabre air defence and a radar station on Mount Byron.
Argentina continues to claim the islands, which it calls the Malvinas, and raises the question annually at the United Nations Special Committee on Decolonisation. The British position rests on the 2013 referendum in which islanders voted by 1,513 votes to three to remain a British Overseas Territory.
Photography from the patrol was taken by Corporal Braithwaite.
Editor’s note: we have had an email asking us to explain this headline. I approved it and I’ll explain why.
BFSAI puts the live firing under training serials and applies the deterrence line to Operation Southern Vigilance as a whole. It is my view that the gunnery was highlighted precisely as part of the overall presence and deterrence point. Nobody publicises machine gun drills for the sake of it. A patrol vessel deters by being present and visibly able to do something about it, and a crew that has not fired its weapons in months is neither. Leaving that out would report the operation less accurately than the command described it. On Argentina, BFSAI says “potential adversaries” and stops. There is one country with a standing claim to the islands. Writing around that would be coy.

‘Arvand Martyrs Bridge is just beginning of a larger development path’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:22:22 UTC
22:22:22 KST

‘Arvand Martyrs Bridge is just beginning of a larger development path’
TEHRAN- The Secretary of the Supreme Council of Free Trade and Special Economic Zones, emphasizing the need to continue the development process in the Arvand Free Zone, stated that the inauguration of the Arvand Martyrs Bridge is not the end of a construction project, but rather the beginning of a larger path for implementing infrastructural, economic, and developmental projects in Abadan, Khorramshahr, and the Arvand Free Zone.
Hossein Forouzan, speaking at the official inauguration ceremony of the Arvand Martyrs Bridge mega-project, said: "The people of Abadan, Khorramshahr, and the Arvand region paid a heavy price during the eight years of the Sacred Defense [Iran-Iraq War] in defending the country. Today, it is the duty of officials to use all their capacity to compensate for part of this sacrifice and to strive for the development and prosperity of this region."
Forouzan, referring to his history of presence in Khuzestan and Khorramshahr, added: "My first presence in this region dates back to 1982, and being in a land where the sacred bodies of great martyrs such as Mehdi and Hamid Bakeri rest has always been an honor for me and a reminder of the heavy responsibility I bear toward the people and the martyrs."
Referring to the importance of inaugurating the Arvand Martyrs Bridge, he emphasized: "This project can resolve some of the problems faced by the people of the region, but it should not be seen as the end point of development efforts. Rather, this bridge should serve as a precursor to the implementation of a series of major infrastructural, economic, and developmental projects in Abadan, Khorramshahr, and the Arvand Free Zone."
The Secretary of the Supreme Council of Free Trade and Special Economic Zones continued: "The right of the people of this land upon officials goes far beyond the implementation of a single construction project. We must strive to make maximum use of the region's existing capacities to create welfare, employment, economic prosperity, and sustainable development."
Forouzan, referring to the meetings and reviews conducted in recent days in the Arvand Free Zone, said: "During my recent multi-day visit, a series of important priority projects for Abadan and Khorramshahr were identified, and plans have been made for their implementation. It is expected that a significant portion of these projects will reach the operational stage in the coming year."
Expressing appreciation for the performance of Mostafa Khanzadi, the CEO of the Arvand Free Zone Organization, he stated: "In recent days, numerous meetings have been held with the CEO and the management team of the organization. The prevailing approach of this team is a serious move toward development and gaining the satisfaction of the people."
The Secretary of the Supreme Council added: "Serving the people and striving to solve their problems must be the top priority of the region's management. We believe that the people's satisfaction paves the way for God's satisfaction."
Forouzan also pointed to the industrial capacities of the Arvand Free Zone and said: "Significant actions are also underway in the industrial sector. Some industrial projects currently being implemented could have considerable impacts on the region's economy and even the national economy in the future."
He emphasized: "Activating the region's industrial, economic, and investment capacities requires continued support and coordination among various agencies. All available capacities must be used to accelerate the development process."
The Secretary of the Supreme Council of Free and Special Economic Zones noted: "The success of the Arvand Free Zone Organization in implementing development programs requires the cooperation and support of the Governor of Khuzestan, representatives in the Islamic Consultative Assembly, and other executive bodies."
Forouzan added: "Coordination among various entities can speed up the implementation of infrastructural and economic projects and pave the way for achieving the region's development goals."
He also referred to the message from the Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance and the President for the people of the region, saying: "I conveyed the greetings and message of the President and the Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance to the noble people of Abadan, Khorramshahr, and the Arvand Free Zone, and emphasized their special attention to this region and their support for its development process."
The Secretary of the Supreme Council of Free and Special Economic Zones, emphasizing the historical standing of Abadan and Khorramshahr in contemporary Iranian history, said: "The people of this region deserve to enjoy the best infrastructure, facilities, and development opportunities."
Forouzan concluded: "The Secretariat of the Supreme Council of Free Zones will stand alongside the Arvand Free Zone Organization with all its capacity to ensure that the path of development and prosperity for Abadan, Khorramshahr, and this region is pursued with greater speed and seriousness."
The Secretary of the Supreme Council of Free Trade and Special Economic Zones, during his visit to the Arvand Free Zone, toured the Shalamcheh commercial terminal and its infrastructure.
Hossein Forouzan, leading a delegation from the Secretariat, visited various sections of the Shalamcheh commercial terminal, including its cargo yard and commercial and logistical infrastructure. He closely examined the capacities, issues, and operational processes of this terminal.
During the visit, the existing capacities of the Shalamcheh commercial terminal, cargo loading and unloading processes, support infrastructure for export activities, and the provision of services to economic activists and traders were reviewed.
The Shalamcheh commercial terminal, as one of the key commercial infrastructures of the Arvand Free Zone, plays an effective role in Iran-Iraq economic exchanges. Developing its infrastructure could increase export capacity, facilitate the movement of transport fleets, and improve logistical services at this international border crossing.
The 100-hectare cargo loading and unloading yard in Shalamcheh is also among the infrastructures established in this area, providing suitable capacity to support commercial and logistical activities at the Shalamcheh border.
Additionally, given Shalamcheh's commercial capacities and its position in developing trade with Iraq, removing implementation obstacles, strengthening logistical infrastructure, and increasing the terminal's productivity are among the key priorities in the path of developing economic activities in the Arvand Free Zone. Previously, the allocation of import codes to Shalamcheh port had also made it possible to import and clear goods through this route.
During the visit, Forouzan conducted a field review of the capacities and existing issues and was briefed on the latest status of the Shalamcheh commercial terminal's infrastructure and the progress of economic activities at this border crossing.
The CEO and a number of managers from the Arvand Free Zone Organization, along with officials related to the Shalamcheh commercial terminal, were also present during this visit.
The Arvand Free Trade-Industrial Zone is one of Iran's most strategically significant economic hubs, located in the southwestern Khuzestan province at the confluence of the Karun and Arvand rivers. Spanning over 37,000 hectares, it encompasses the cities of Abadan, Khorramshahr, and Minoo Island, sharing borders with Iraq and Kuwait.
The zone serves as a vital gateway for international trade, offering multi-modal transport advantages through the Abadan International Airport, Khorramshahr's second-largest container port, and the Shalamcheh border terminal – a key crossing for commercial activities with Iraq. Its logistics capacities are being further developed with a 700-hectare "Logistics Park" project.

Premiers of Bulgaria, Slovakia call for diplomatic solution to war in Ukraine

News
Premiers of Bulgaria, Slovakia call for diplomatic solution to war in Ukraine
Friday 4 September 2026 15:24
Friday, 4 September 2026, 15:24
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, right, and his Slovak counterpart Robert Fico issue a joint statement in Sofia, September 4, 2026.
PHOTO BGNES
Font size
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and his Slovak counterpart Robert Fico issued a joint call in Sofia for a diplomatic solution to Russia’s war against Ukraine, Radio Bulgaria’s Marta Mladenova reported.
“The war in Ukraine has no military solution. I always speak independently on behalf of the government when I say that the war in Ukraine is a violation of international law by the Russian Federation, but we do not see the world in black and white. In 2014, we saw the causes of this war, and I am not happy with the way the EU is supporting the war,” Fico said.
Prime Minister Radev, for his part, said: “We once again share our common view that attempts to find a military solution increase the risks and lead to dangerous escalation. That is why we once again call for reason. We call for dialogue. We call for a ceasefire and for the sides to sit down at the negotiating table, because diplomacy is the only sustainable and reliable solution to this conflict.”
During their meeting, the two prime ministers also discussed closer cooperation in nuclear energy and industry, particularly in the automotive and defence sectors.
Robert Fico is in Sofia on an official visit at Prime Minister Rumen Radev's invitation to discuss bilateral cooperation and current European and international issues.
