====================================================================================================

What a Record Hunting and Fishing Expansion Means for America’s Wildlife Refuges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:20:00 UTC
22:20:00 KST

The Department of the Interior implemented a massive expansion of fishing and hunting access in the United States, opening 1,488 opportunities across 32 states. With the rule in effect as of Monday, more than 92 million acres, or 95% of National Wildlife Refuge System land, are now available for the practices.
Expanded hunting and fishing are now allowed in areas where the practices were never before legal, including Rocky Flats National Wildlife Refuge in Colorado and Stewart Lake National Wildlife Refuge in North Dakota.
The rule also permits hunting and fishing for additional species and expands some seasons at locations where those activities were already allowed.
“America’s hunters and anglers now have something significant to look forward to in the fall,” said Interior Secretary Doug Burgum in the press release announcing the rule Aug. 13. “We are also promoting good government by reducing the regulatory burden and working with states to facilitate these outdoor activities.”
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) oversees more than 570 national wildlife refuges that were “established to serve a statutory purpose that targets the conservation of native species dependent on its lands and water,” according to the agency’s website.
Christopher Williams, a professor of wildlife ecology at the University of Delaware, says the refuges were initially created to protect wildlife and then later helped to combat “extreme market hunting,” or unregulated hunting of animals. They became safe habitats and breeding sanctuaries for endangered species under the 1966 Endangered Species Preservation Act.
Now, hunting and other forms of recreation are permitted across a majority of those refuges when “compatible with each station’s purpose and mission under federal law,” per FWS.
The very definition of a refuge seems to have “slowly morphed into an entity that was meant to provide an opportunity for hunting access,” Williams says.
The new rule raises a question of compatibility: How can the refuges fulfill their conservation mandate amid the nation’s largest-ever expansion of hunting and fishing?
Does hunting undermine the purpose of a wildlife refuge?
The FWS said this week’s expansion is about “maximizing access where compatible with conservation goals.”
It also said that the new rule will help revitalize rural economies, as hunters and anglers contribute more than $144 billion annually to the U.S. economy.
“These activities support jobs, fund conservation efforts, and sustain outdoor traditions that connect communities to the land and to each other,” the August announcement read.
Sporting groups touted the “historic expansion” and its potential ability to help retain hunters and fishers at these refuges, which may rely on them for curbing overabundant and invasive species.
Williams says it makes sense that conservation groups support the expansion, since hunters and anglers play an “enormously important role in American wildlife conservation.”
“And with long-term concerns about declining hunting participation, providing meaningful access remains an important part of recruitment, retention, and reactivation efforts,” he says.
“BHA applauds all efforts to responsibly expand and improve public access for hunters and anglers and appreciates the Administration’s recognition of the important role sportsmen and women play in the conservation and stewardship of public lands and waters,” Backcountry Hunters & Anglers said in a statement when the expansion was proposed in May.
This was not the first time the Trump Administration proposed such an expansion. A version of the rule from 2020 opened some 859 opportunities across 2.3 million acres. The increase in scope from his first term is about 73%.
The new rule also makes more than 1,000 modifications to existing federal regulations that previously guided access to the refuges, including simplifications and deletions. The Trump Administration has said the sweeping revisions aim to make it easier to understand and enforce guidelines from state to state. But some conservationists have concerns about how the abrupt elimination of that many regulatory mandates, all at once, will affect the refuges.
Robert Fischman, professor of environmental law at Indiana University Maurer School of Law, says that such a dramatic overhaul is worth noting. “I mean, 1,000 rules sounds pretty important,” he tells TIME.
The new rule reverses restrictions on lead ammunition
One significant change that comes with the new rule is a reversal on lead ammunition and tackle.
Following a lawsuit in 2021, the government said it would phase out the potentially harmful materials and require hunters and anglers to switch to non-toxic alternatives.
The Center for Biological Diversity sued FWS after it proposed an expansion on hunting opportunities during Trump’s first term. The lawsuit argued that the expansion could jeopardize protected species, which are susceptible to ingesting the lead ammunition and tackle. It also claimed that there would be residual harm to the greater ecosystem, as lead ammunition and tackle can contaminate fields and waterways.
The lawsuit was settled under the Biden Administration in 2022, with FWS saying it would phase out the use of lead ammunition and tackle at several refuges across the country.
Aaron Bloom, a senior attorney with nonprofit Earthjustice's Biodiversity Defense Program, said the phase-out was supposed to go into effect across eight refuges in September 2026. But with the new rule, the phase-outs will no longer take effect.
In response to the reversal, Bloom says Earthjustice will be looking at litigation—as will other environmentalist groups.
These phase-outs would have “protected both wildlife and human health, hunters and their families, from the adverse impacts of lead poisoning,” Bloom tells TIME. “There's absolutely no reason we should be allowing them in our wildlife refuges.”
Recent staffing cuts raise concerns about oversight
FWS staffing decreased by approximately 18% between April 2024 and May 2025, according to agency records obtained by the Center for Biological Diversity. The decline can be attributed in part to the “workforce optimization initiative” implemented by the Department of Government Efficiency at the beginning of 2025.
Fischman and Williams both express concern about the staffing cuts and how they will impact oversight amid expanded hunting and fishing access.
“What I'm hearing from people who are on the ground is you have whole national wildlife refuges that no longer have any staff there full-time,” Fischman says. “You have a refuge manager running around from one refuge to another, riding circuit to try to keep things together.”
Fischman questions whether there are enough staff left to “really understand” and document the impacts of the new rule. He says that streamlining refuge-specific regulations makes enforcement easier and may partially compensate for staffing reductions; however, he is skeptical that states have enough staff to patrol the affected refuges and ensure that hunters and anglers are complying with the regulations that do still apply.
“It’s dependent on there being people there to maintain trails, to monitor impacts on species, to enforce the law,” he says. “It could be that the rulemaking seems pretty logical [to the Administration], but on the ground can't be practically implemented in a way that is consistent with public safety and compatible with both the system mission and the refuge purposes.”
According to Williams, it's all a balancing act. He points out the need to preserve conservation efforts while boosting the economies of rural communities and reversing a long-term decline in hunting participation in the U.S.
“On one hand, are you reaching a point where you might be doing some harm of not having adequate sanctuary for wildlife? Or maybe you are making a net improvement to increase retention and recruitment of hunters, which provides a financial benefit?” he wonders. “The answer is probably yes on both sides of the house.”

Ingrid Neel and partner cruise past seeded pair in US Open round one
Estonian tennis player Ingrid Neel and her partner Giuliana Olmos (Mexico) made a winning start to the US Open women's doubles tournament, beating the 11th‑seeded pair Shuko Aoyama and Liang En‑shuo in straight sets.
The duo dropped just one game in the opening set, sealing a 6:1 victory in 25 minutes. Their opponents offered stronger resistance in the second set, but Neel and Olmos held firm to close out the match 6:4, taking just over an hour to advance.
Neel and Olmos converted four of five break points, while their opponents managed just one of two. The Estonian‑Mexican pair also won 75 of the total points played, with 17 winners to their opponents' 11.
In the next round, the round of 32 taking place on Saturday, they will face Ena Shibahara (Japan) and Lanlana Tararudee (Thailand), who beat Peyton Stearns (US) and Kimberly Birrell (Australia) in their round of 64 clash.
The U.S. Open runs to September 13.

Russia's 2026 grain harvest tops 110 mln tonnes — minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:18:47 UTC
22:18:47 KST

MOSCOW, September 4. /TASS/. Russia's grain harvest has surpassed 110 million tonnes so far in 2026, including 83.5 million tonnes of wheat, Russian Agriculture Minister Oksana Lut announced during an operational headquarters meeting on seasonal field works.
"About 70% of the grain and pulse harvested area has been threshed, and we have already gathered over 110 million tonnes of grain to date. This is 10.5 million tonnes more than on the same date last year. Wheat output has already reached 83.5 million tonnes," Lut said.
She noted that harvesting campaign is currently underway across all regions of the country. "We faced rather challenging conditions at the start. And, in fact, the harvesting itself is proceeding under difficult circumstances," the minister added.
Lut pointed out that, overall, the harvesting pace and crop yields for major commodities across the country are currently tracking ahead of last year's figures. "Thus, our domestic market is already fully secured with the required volumes of wheat and grains," the minister emphasized.

Northern Sea Route development emerges as priority amid global logistics crisis — aide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:18:03 UTC
22:18:03 KST

VLADIVOSTOK, September 4. /TASS/. The Northern Sea Route (NSR) stands out as a safe and highly cost-effective corridor amid the ongoing crisis in global logistics, Anton Kobyakov, Advisor to the Russian President and Executive Secretary of the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) Organizing Committee, told a press briefing.
"Today, against the backdrop of the global logistics crisis, the Northern Sea Route is one of the key, safe, and financially viable trade routes. It is a matter of pure economics: delivery times via the Northern Sea Route are 2 to 2.5 times shorter, if not more, compared to alternative routes," Kobyakov said.
He explained that bottleneck issues are currently being observed, particularly at the Panama Canal and the Strait of Hormuz. The crisis is disrupting cargo transit between Europe and Asia, slowing down trade between the two continents. In this situation, the trans-Arctic transport corridor - and the NSR in particular - looks increasingly critical. "The President has set a goal to transform the entire trans-Arctic transport corridor into a year-round, safe, and competitive route stretching from St. Petersburg and Murmansk, via the Northern Sea Route, to Vladivostok and the Asia-Pacific region. Leading Asian economies have grasped this; China has realized it, and the Republic of Korea has understood it as well," Kobyakov noted.
The Eastern Economic Forum took place on September 1-4 in Vladivostok at the Far Eastern Federal University campus. The main theme of the 2026 forum was "The Far East: Development for the Benefit of People." It was organized by the Roscongress Foundation with the support of the Government of the Russian Federation. TASS served as the general information partner.

Somali forces ‘decisively defeat’ Al-Shabaab-linked militias – authorities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:17:30 UTC
22:17:30 KST

Somali forces ‘decisively defeat’ Al-Shabaab-linked militias – authorities
Somali forces have “decisively defeated” militias allegedly operating alongside Al-Shabaab after they launched an attack on Baidoa, the capital of South West State, the authorities have said.
The assault began at around 4:15 a.m on Thursday with explosions intended to cause panic among civilians, the East African nation’s Defense Ministry said in a statement. Fighting continued for several hours before subsiding in the afternoon.
The ministry said government troops inflicted heavy losses on fighters loyal to former South West State President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen. It did not provide a casualty figure, but said an assessment was underway.
In a separate statement on Thursday, the South West State government said the attack began with two vehicle-borne explosive devices. It said its forces killed more than 40 Al-Shabaab fighters, wounded several others, and seized weapons and military equipment. Bay Regional Hospital received 71 wounded people, including 15 women, and one dead civilian, emergency department head Abdikafi Omar Mohamud told AP. Residents reportedly fled their homes as gunfire and explosions spread into residential areas.
Laftagareen’s camp acknowledged launching the assault. Former regional spokesperson Ugaas Hassan Abdi Mohamed told BBC Somali that it was a “planned” operation intended to incapacitate forces he accused of invading the country. He said two fighters from his side were killed and five others wounded.
The latest violence follows a prolonged standoff between Mogadishu and Laftagareen. The federal government rejected his disputed reelection in March and took control of Baidoa on March 30, prompting Laftagareen, who had governed South West since 2018, to announce his resignation. 
Regional lawmakers elected former Somali parliament speaker Sheikh Aden Mohamed Nur Madobe as president of South West State in June.
In August, at least four civilians were killed and 98 wounded when militias attacked government positions around the city. The federal authorities said nearly 30 attackers were killed, while regional officials put the toll at about 50. Both blamed Laftagareen loyalists and Al-Shabaab, allegations the former leader has repeatedly denied.
Baidoa, which is about 245km northwest of Mogadishu, hosts more than half a million people displaced by conflict and drought. Al-Shabaab has waged an insurgency against Somalia’s government for nearly two decades and continues to control territory in parts of the country.

Man jumps out of first-floor window to escape kidnappers in Lincoln
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:16:33 UTC
22:16:33 KST

Dramatic footage shows a kidnapped man jumping from a first-floor window into a tree before running into the street and, by chance, coming across a police car.
Lincolnshire police said the ordeal of the unnamed man had been “horrifying” and the presence of a marked police vehicle “may have saved his life”.
DC Liam Henderson said the CCTV footage captured a desperate moment in which the victim “quite literally risked everything to get away from those holding him captive”.
Lincoln crown court heard that the victim had been targeted and subjected to a terrifying ordeal linked to a past relationship breakdown. On 4 July 2025, he was lured to an address in Market Rasen where it soon became clear he would be unable to leave.
Inside the address were Brad’Lee Ranyard, Nathan Gladwell, Jackson Nicholson, Craig Ranyard and Danielle Thompson. For hours the victim endured violence and intimidation, police said. He was “repeatedly assaulted, threatened, humiliated and tormented” by his captors, who filmed the abuse on their mobile phones and laughed.
The next day the man was forced into the back of a Isuzu pickup truck and driven along back roads to a property in Lincoln. He arrived at 7.30am and was again held against his will.
At 11.23am the man seized his opportunity. He can be seen diving from the window into the tree, before getting to the ground and running into the street. Footage from a police car, which had turned into the street, shows the man running towards it saying: “Let me in, let me in”.
Police said the officer immediately recognised the man’s distress, realised he was fleeing a dangerous situation and took him to safety.
Henderson, who led the investigation, said: “This was a sustained and deeply distressing ordeal in which a man was subjected to violence, threats and humiliation at the hands of people who appeared to find amusement in his suffering.
“The victim showed remarkable courage in seizing the opportunity to escape.”
Henderson said it was sheer chance that a police car had entered the street. “That moment changed the course of events and allowed officers to get him to safety when he needed help most,” he said.
“We often hear concerns that victims may feel alone or that help will not arrive when it is needed. This case is a powerful reminder that when someone reaches out for help, we will do everything we can to protect them and bring those responsible to justice.”
Police said the victim had given permission for the footage, which also shows the arrests, to be shared.
A judge at Lincoln crown court gave nine-year jail terms to Brad’Lee Ranyard, 20, and Nicholson, 25, for kidnap and false imprisonment. Craig Ranyard, 42, was jailed for five years and three months after being convicted of false imprisonment.
Thompson, 38, was jailed for four years and nine months after being convicted of false imprisonment. Gladwell, 36, was jailed for three years and seven months after being convicted of false imprisonment.

TEHRAN- The President of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines, and Agriculture (ICCIMA) during a webinar meeting with the new Secretary-General of the International Road Transport Union (IRU), examined routes for facilitating money transfers between the Iran Chamber and the IRU.
According to IRNA, quoting the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Samad Hassanzadeh on Wednesday held a webinar meeting to discuss ways to facilitate fund transfers between the Iran Chamber and the IRU.
At the outset of the online meeting, the President of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines, and Agriculture congratulated the new IRU Secretary-General on assuming his role, stating: "We are very pleased that a scientific and economically cultured figure has accepted this responsibility."
Hassanzadeh, expressing hope for the beginning of a new era of effective cooperation between the Iran Chamber and the International Road Transport Union, emphasized: "The continued issuance of TIR carnets can strengthen Iran's position in the regional transit network."
Referring to the problems of money transfers due to sanctions, the Iran Chamber President outlined the efforts made to identify routes for facilitating fund transfers to the IRU.
Hassanzadeh also expressed readiness to establish a limited barter mechanism under IRU supervision, saying: "It is proposed that the IRU design a limited barter mechanism through which Iran could settle part of the value of services through non-sanctioned goods, or that these amounts be paid through a bank designated by the IRU."
Appreciating the IRU's continued support for the Iran Chamber, he requested: "The credit that this union allocates to Iran should be increased."
Hassanzadeh said: "We request that Iran's TIR carnet quota and credit line be increased by the IRU so that Iranian operators are not forced to resort to non-TIR methods."
The Iran Chamber President, commending the IRU's valuable cooperation with Iran over many years, called for facilitating operational pathways and said: "We hope this cooperation will continue in the new era with a fresh perspective and effective support, leading to the strengthening of Iran's position in the TIR system."
Keyvan Kashfi, a member of the Iran Chamber's Board of Directors, also congratulated the Tunisian nation on Habib Turki's election as Secretary-General of the International Road Transport Union, expressing hope that solutions would be offered to sustain and strengthen cooperation.
Habib Turki, in this online meeting, stated that his priority is the continuation of cooperation and problem-solving, emphasizing: "We stand firmly and resolutely by your side."
He referred to efforts to find channels for facilitating money transfers in light of international sanctions, and addressing the Iran Chamber President, said: "I thank you for acting proactively and responsibly to find methods for money transfers."
Habib Turki outlined three routes for facilitating money transfers between the Iran Chamber and the IRU and said: "With the channels we have evaluated so far, we are very hopeful that the problem of fund transfers between the Iran Chamber and the IRU will be resolved."
Increasing Iran's credit with the IRU, accelerating the process of sending carnets to Iran, and selecting new agents were among the key topics discussed in this online meeting.

‘Things happen’: How Vance’s comment on Iran wedding strike fits US pattern
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:15:36 UTC
22:15:36 KST

‘Things happen’: How Vance’s comment on Iran wedding strike fits US pattern
From My Lai to civilian killings in Afghanistan, Iraq, the US has often denied role before later quietly acknowledging.
United States Vice President JD Vance has expressed scepticism about reports of a deadly US attack on a wedding party in the Iranian town of Kuhestak on Tuesday this week, saying he does not trust Iran’s narrative.
However, he added: “Sometimes, things happen,” as he spoke about the claims.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iran, US exchange new attacks: Who was hit in latest strikes?
- list 2 of 3What do we know about the fatal US bombing of a wedding in Iran?
- list 3 of 3Abroad and at odds: How the war has divided Iranians in the diaspora
Speaking on Thursday at a White House news briefing, two days after the attack, Vance said he had no new information about the incident, but maintained that the US “never targets civilians in combat” and would investigate the incident.
Analysts say his comments reflect a long history of the US government minimising or disputing reports of civilian harm in military operations.
Here’s what we know about the strike on a wedding in Iran and how Vance’s response fits into a pattern of claims in US military history.
What happened in Iran?
A missile attack hit a wedding celebration in Iran’s southern town of Kuhestak, Hormozgan, on Tuesday night, killing four people – two women and two children – and injuring 67, according to the Iranian Red Crescent Society.
On Wednesday, the Hormozgan governor’s office identified the four killed as four-year-old Amir Ali Karimi, 16-year-old Mohammad Malahi, 43-year-old Kolsoum Malahi and 43-year-old Zarkhatoun Taheri.
The Iranian Red Crescent said the incident was thoroughly documented and released several images from the scene as well as of the children who were injured. It wrote to the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, seeking legal action against the perpetrators of the “grave” attack.
Footage showed that several projectiles had struck a telecommunications tower near the city’s shoreline and destroyed it, with locals saying they thought drones had been used. Based on fragments of shrapnel found in Kuhestak, defence experts said it might be a variant of the AGM-84K SLAM-ER, which manufacturer Boeing describes as an advanced precision-guided, air-launched cruise missile with “surgical strike capability”.
The Reuters news agency cited weapons experts who reviewed images and video and said the damage likely resulted from a direct hit by a US munition.
Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the strikes in Kuhestak completed a “catalogue of atrocities against the nation of Iran” by the US.
The US says it has launched an investigation.
What have Vance and other US government officials said?
On Tuesday, Tim Hawkins, spokesperson for US Central Command (CENTCOM), said the US was aware of reports of civilian casualties that “originated from Iranian state media” and was “looking into them”.
“The US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC,” he added, referring to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Vance later said he was “extremely sceptical” of the reports about the wedding strike.
He said the “Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe” about the ongoing conflict, despite the attack being documented by the Iranian Red Crescent Society.
“What I can say with 100 percent confidence is that, unlike the IRGC, the United States never targets civilians in combat,” Vance said. “We never will do that. We never have done that.”
He added: “Unfortunately, obviously, sometimes things happen.”
How does this compare to past military claims about attacks on civilians?
This is not the first time the US government has cast doubt on reports of alleged civilian harm during war, including in the current conflict with Iran.
Minab school strike, Iran
Following a deadly strike which hit a girls’ school in Iran’s Minab on February 28, US President Donald Trump at first stated that he believed Iran was responsible. But as a US probe into the attack progressed, and more satellite data, footage and expert analysis pointed to US responsibility – including the presence of fragments from a US Tomahawk missile – Trump later said: “Nobody did that on purpose” and “mistakes are made” during war.
Civilian casualties in Yemen
The US government has similarly shifted its messaging following several high-profile attacks that killed civilians in Afghanistan, Yemen and Iraq.
Last month, the US acknowledged for the first time that an air campaign against the Houthis in Yemen in April 2025 likely caused numerous civilian casualties, assessing that 153 civilians were killed and 243 wounded. The numbers mark a sharp increase from 2024, when the Pentagon assessed that US military operations had killed two civilians and injured two.
More civilian deaths in Afghanistan
The US government has similarly shifted its messaging following several high-profile attacks that killed civilians during wars in Afghanistan, Yemen and Iraq.
When a 2008 US air attack against Taliban fighters in the Afghan village of Azizabad prompted outrage over reported civilian casualties, the US military at first claimed there had been no civilian deaths. It later acknowledged seven civilian deaths, before revising that figure up to 33. The Afghan government said 90 civilians were killed, mostly women and children.
In the final days of the US withdrawal from the country in August 2021, the US carried out a drone strike on a car in Kabul. It first claimed fighters with the Islamic State in Khorasan Province, ISKP (ISIS-K), an affiliate of ISIL had been killed. Several weeks later, however, the US military admitted that an investigation had revealed the attack actually killed 10 civilians, including seven children. USS Air Force Lieutenant General Sami Said called it an “honest mistake”.
Abu Ghraib prison, Iraq
In Iraq, US officials initially downplayed the extent of crimes at the Abu Ghraib prison site after 2003 photos emerged of prisoners being abused by US guards. Subsequent inquiries uncovered a more extensive pattern of abuse, including sexual abuse, rape, and physical and psychological torture, resulting in the death of at least one inmate.
In the years that followed, 11 US soldiers were charged with dereliction of duty, maltreatment, aggravated assault and battery. They were convicted in military courts, and nine were sentenced to time in prison. In November 2024, a US jury ruled that Virginia-based defence contractor CACI must pay $42m to three Iraqi men who had been tortured at the prison in 2004.
Vietnam war
During the Vietnam War from 1955 to 1975, the US military at first hid reports of a massacre in My Lai, in which US soldiers killed and maimed up to 500 Vietnamese, many of them women and children. After evidence of the killings became public, a US inquiry found that US military officials had participated in a cover-up of the massacre.
What does Vance’s remark about the Iran wedding strike tell us?
Emily Tripp, executive director of Airwars, a watchdog that tracks cases of civilian harm during conflict, said Vance’s scepticism at the latest deadly US attack in Iran reflects a tendency to treat cases of civilian harm “like a PR crisis” rather than with due process.
“The odds are always stacked against civilians – from the moment they get harmed in a poorly planned operation, to when they try to show the world what happened, to when they ask for a response and acknowledgement,” Tripp told Al Jazeera.
“Vance pushing back at these claims, before an investigation is conducted by the military, reflects an instinctive disbelief in the most vulnerable people. And time and again that position has been shown to be false.”

How vulnerable is Germany's infrastructure?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:14:00 UTC
22:14:00 KST

How vulnerable is Germany's infrastructure?
September 4, 2026
On Tuesday morning, unknown perpetrators attempted to attack the power supply near the coal-fired power plant at Jänschwalde in the eastern state of Brandenburg, partly succeeding in their objective. Then, later the same evening, a substation near Cologne suffered a disruption in what is believed to have been an act of sabotage.
On Wednesday, an explosion occurred near the railway station in the Bavarian city of Augsburg, caused by a hand grenade, according to investigators.
In the early hours of Thursday, several incendiary devices were thrown onto a construction site in Munich, close to a number of defense companies. Then, on Thursday evening, a suspicious object was discovered at a power substation in Dormagen, between Cologne and Düsseldorf. Investigators say a claim of responsibility has since been received.
While it remains entirely unclear who was behind the attacks in Jänschwalde, Cologne and Augsburg, investigators in Munich have arrested at least two suspects, reportedly Bulgarian nationals.
Already 160 attacks on critical infrastructure this year
What all these incidents have in common is that they appear to have targeted so-called critical infrastructure: energy facilities, the rail network, companies of strategic importance to national security and defense contractors.
Taken together, these sites can hardly be protected in their entirety. According to media reports citing an internal document, the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) has recorded 160 potential acts of sabotage and more than 700 suspicious drone sightings so far this year.
People in Berlin express concern over Russia
Even if the exact circumstances of each incident remain unclear, their rapid succession has created a growing sense of constant threat among the public. To find out how people are reacting, DW spoke to residents on the streets of Berlin.
One woman described her immediate reaction: "Fear. I was just talking about it with a colleague. It makes me feel very uneasy. I think about it a lot, and yet no one really talks about it. Maybe it's because people are afraid and would rather push it out of their minds?"
One man added: "We first need to recognize that something is happening, that we are under attack. I have very close ties to Russia and very close Russian friends, and it is very, very painful to see what is happening."
A freeze in German-Russian relations
The fact that Russia is the first thing that comes to many people's minds when they hear about the recent wave of attacks is hardly surprising. On Tuesday, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), both members of the governing alliance with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), appeared before the press. They announced that the German government is convinced Russian actors were behind the attempted drone attack on Halle/Leipzig Airport on August 4.
The government responded by closing Russia's consulate general in Bonn and ending the lease on the Russian House in Berlin. Moscow, in turn, retaliated by shutting down the Goethe-Institut in Moscow. Relations between Germany and Russia are now at their lowest point in years.
"We are no longer at peace, but neither are we at war," Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) remarked last year.
The reality is that since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in the spring of 2022, Germany has been among Ukraine's strongest supporters, both financially and militarily. That holds true even though successive German governments, including the current one, have consistently maintained that the country is not itself a party to the war.
Germany's support for Ukraine as a motive?
Since then, the Bundeswehr, after years of continuous downsizing, has undergone rapid rearmament, driven in part by concerns that Russia could pose a threat even to central Europe.
Neither at war nor at peace: Sönke Marahrens, a colonel in the German armed forces and a security expert at Kiel University, believes Germans would be well advised to prepare for this new form of confrontation, whoever may be responsible for it.
He told DW: "Hybrid warfare and hybrid activities are, in my view, essentially the same thing because they rely on the same methods. Foreign states or organizations pursue their strategic interests without resorting to diplomacy. This can take the form of sabotage, disinformation or attacks on critical infrastructure."
At the same time, the researcher stresses that it would be difficult to describe the situation as a state of war.
Private firms urged to strengthen infrastructure security
But it would be too simplistic to attribute every such incident immediately and unequivocally to Russia. Earlier this year, for example, an attack on a cable bridge in southwest Berlin caused a power outage that lasted several days. Hundreds of thousands of people were affected in freezing temperatures. In that case, which remains unsolved, suspicion has fallen on far-left extremists.
A debate has long been underway in Germany over how best to prepare for such attacks in the future. This spring, the government passed legislation known as "KRITIS," aimed at strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure, although the law has yet to enter into force.
Herbert Reul (CDU), the interior minister of the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, noted in an interview with public broadcaster ZDF that critical facilities, including those operated by private companies, can already be monitored through video surveillance. Responsibility for securing the surrounding areas, however, lies with authorities such as the police.
As Reul put it: "In Germany, we are sensitive when it comes to video surveillance and, more generally, to measures that affect civil liberties or data protection."
Reul argued that companies themselves need to invest more in protecting their facilities. The German Police Union (DPolG) takes a similar view. Its chairman, Heiko Teggatz, said that safeguarding critical infrastructure is not primarily the responsibility of the police, but first and foremost of the operators themselves.
"Those responsible for the security of their facilities must also invest in their protection," Teggatz said.
What is lacking, he argued, is not technical capability but a consistent willingness to invest.
This article was translated from German.

Le Pen rivals seize on National Rally’s Ukraine divide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:12:38 UTC
22:12:38 KST

Marine Le Pen speaks during a National Assembly session at the French Parliament in Paris on March 3, 2025. | Magali Cohen/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — Marine Le Pen is facing a fight over military aid to Ukraine after two leading center-right rivals accused her party of playing into Russia’s hands.
The dispute underlines the lack of clarity around the far-right National Rally's views on Ukraine and Russia, something that its opponents hope to exploit to undermine the party's credibility ahead of next year's crucial presidential election.
On Friday, center-right candidates and former Prime Ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal slammed comments made by Louis Aliot, a National Rally vice president, who hinted on Thursday that France would limit military assistance to Kyiv if his boss Le Pen wins next year.
Advertisement
"We turn off the tap," Aliot said of aid to Ukraine in a television interview, pointing to France's fiscal overstretch and problems in financing areas like health and education. He stressed his party's strong support for Ukraine and condemned Russia for its invasion, but underlined: "Who pays for the war?"
Philippe and Attal — fighting to become the main center-right presidential candidate — both fired back.
"Cutting off aid to Ukraine means playing into Russia’s hands," Philippe posted on X. "The National Rally has changed its position on just about everything, except for its support of Putin’s regime — a stance that runs counter to French and European interests."
"You’ve just heard the 'foreign-backed' party speak ... The National Rally is once again demonstrating its subservience to Russia," echoed Attal.
Le Pen, who's currently leading in opinion polls, responded: "Since Russia's aggression against Ukraine, I have been demanding that France urgently convene a major conference for peace in order to contribute, not to the prolongation of a bloodbath, but to a diplomatic resolution of this abominable war."
However, she didn't repeat Aliot's comments on France's inability to continuing to provide military aid to Ukraine.
Advertisement
POLITICO has previously reported that the far-right party is internally divided over Russia, Ukraine and NATO.
Jordan Bardella, the National Rally president and a member of the European Parliament, leads the more pro-European wing of the party. Le Pen's own views have been more pro-Russia; she has met Russian President Vladimir Putin in the past and her party took a €9.4 million loan from a Czech-Russian bank with links to the Kremlin, since repaid.
Bardella and Le Pen also differ on NATO, although both would break with French President Emmanuel Macron's strong support for the alliance. Bardella wants to wait for the Ukraine war to end to pull France out of NATO's integrated command, while Le Pen pledged to do so in the next five years regardless of what's happening in the conflict.
The National Rally will release its campaign platform before the end of the year, potentially clarifying its positions on Ukraine and Russia.
The spat among Philippe, Attal and Le Pen also shows that center-right parties are trying to paint the National Rally as Putin allies in a bid to damage her electoral prospects.
"Did you think the [National Rally] had changed its stance on Ukraine? You were naive. The masks are coming off, and Marine Le Pen’s support for Vladimir Putin remains what it has always been: unwavering," said MEP Nathalie Loiseau, a Philippe ally.

Breaking: Russian drone hits Kyiv's center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04

Breaking: Russian drone strikes SBU headquarters in central Kyiv, injuring at least 9
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
A Russian drone struck the headquarters of Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) opposite St. Sophia's Cathedral in central Kyiv on Sept. 4, injuring at least nine people, local authorities said.
An air raid alert was activated in Kyiv at around 3 p.m. local time, followed by explosions in the city center about half an hour later. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the attack damaged a non-residential building in the Shevchenkivskyi district, without providing further details.
The drone was targeting the office of SBU acting head Oleksandr Poklad, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Speaking to the Kyiv Independent, a former intelligence officer also confirmed that the Russian drone had appeared to strike the location of Poklad's office.
"I gave Poklad the task of responding to this Russian attack in an appropriate, significant, and — if possible — symmetrical manner once everything is ready," Zelensky said.
Nine people were injured in the attack, seven of whom had been hospitalized as of 5 p.m. local time, Klitschko said. The fire at the site was extinguished, but the attack damaged the building's exterior wall, the mayor added.
The drone strike in the heart of the city center has shaken those who live and work nearby.
"All the time we've been walking around this area, we felt safe," Alina Zamanova, an artist whose studio is close to the site of the impact, told the Kyiv Independent.
"I slept in the studio today, and whenever I sleep here, I feel like I'm super safe — I don't even think about going to a shelter at all," she said. "I guess not anymore, though."
Asked whether the strike would make her consider relocating, Zamanova said her first reaction was, "I'm going to leave," but acknowledged that making such a drastic move would be difficult.
"I have my studio, my dog is here, and my home is here," she said.
Dmytro, 43, was driving to a meeting when the drone hit. He heard a "very loud explosion" but carried on to his meeting anyway "to do my job."
Dmytro, who asked to be identified by his first name only because he works in the defense tech sector, said he was "definitely not surprised" that such a building was targeted. He added that Russia's newer jet-powered drones are far harder to intercept than previous piston-engined versions.
"So I just hope that we'll have enough finance for (defense) companies to protect Ukraine and the sky, as well as upgraded air defense drones," he added.
Dmytro urged those abroad to "keep supporting Ukraine" in its fight against "these barbarian eastern tribes which we have on our border now."
"You should help the one who is fighting them, otherwise you'll be fighting next," he added.
This is the first known Russian attack on the SBU headquarters in central Kyiv. On March 18, a Russian drone targeted Lviv, more than 460 kilometers (285 miles) from the capital, with debris from the downed drone falling on the grounds of the SBU's regional office.
"The Russian attack on Ukraine's Security Service Headquarters is a major escalation that demands resolute responses," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X.
"Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace — laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy."
Sybiha urged international partners to condemn the attack unequivocally and intensify pressure on the Kremlin regime. The minister also called on UNESCO to "act decisively" to protect Ukraine's endangered cultural heritage, after the attack struck near the UNESCO World Heritage Site of St. Sophia's Cathedral.
The Russian attack also damaged the Zavertailo restaurant, located near the SBU building, the restaurant's co-owner, Stanislav Zavertailo, said on Telegram.
Zavertailo said one restaurant guest was injured in the strike and hospitalized. People were sheltering in the building's basement during the attack, he added.
"Everyone is safe and unharmed, but they are still in shock, so everyone will need to be examined again," Zavertailo wrote.
The Russian attack marked the second time a Zavertailo restaurant has been damaged. Another Zavertailo branch in Kyiv's Podil district was damaged overnight on May 24. The blast wave shattered the restaurant's windows and damaged the building's facade, but the restaurant resumed operations later that day.
Zavertailo is also a co-owner of the Honey restaurant chain. One of its branches was damaged in a Russian attack on Aug. 28, 2025. The restaurant near St. Sophia's Cathedral is therefore the third Zavertailo-owned establishment to be damaged in Russian attacks.
The attack came on the ninth consecutive day of Russian strikes on Kyiv, with the capital facing near-constant attacks by jet-powered Shahed-type drones, as well as a ballistic missile attack earlier in the week.
Constant air raid alerts, air defense fire and explosions have taken a toll on Kyiv residents, depriving them of sleep and increasing anxiety throughout the day.
"We're tired. We're very, very tired," Diana To Hang, a student, told the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 2 after a Russian drone strike on a university in the capital.
"A lot of people right now are patriotic and they're doing everything they can to help people who aren't safe right now get out of those situations. But looking at the situation, I can see that it’s simply not getting any better, and we still have winter ahead of us," she added.
The onslaught has prompted Zelensky to announce a change in Ukraine's aerial alert system.
Under the new plan, alerts will be divided into red and yellow levels, with yellow corresponding to drone threats and red signaling incoming missiles and massive combined attacks.

Canada’s labor market is losing momentum — how much did employment decline, and did the “dispute” with the US have an impact?

Canada’s labor market is losing momentum — how much did employment decline, and did the “dispute” with the US have an impact?
Kyiv • UNN
In August, Canada lost 41,700 jobs, while unemployment remained at 6.4%. New US tariffs threaten further slowdown.
In August, Canada's economy lost 41,700 jobs, signaling a sharp slowdown in hiring after an exceptionally active summer period; meanwhile, the unemployment rate remained unchanged at 6.4%, reports UNN, citing Reuters.
Details
The August report provides one of the last "clean" pictures of the state of Canada's labor market before the effects of new 50% tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump begin to affect the economy.
These tariffs affect a relatively small share of Canadian exports, but they target vulnerable industries — including wood product manufacturing — increasing the risk that the recent growth in labor-market activity could practically evaporate.
Analysts surveyed by Reuters had forecast an increase of approximately 15,000 jobs (following a significant increase of 75,100 in July). The forecast for the unemployment rate matched the actual figure.
The Canadian dollar fell 0.51% to 1.3860 Canadian dollars per U.S. dollar (or 72.15 U.S. cents). The yield on two-year government bonds rose after the labor-market data were published, increasing by 1.3 basis points to 2.469%.
According to Statistics Canada, the main reduction in employment occurred in the full-time sector (down 35,900 positions), while the number of part-time jobs decreased by 5,800.
Recent hiring figures were inflated by temporary factors, such as hiring staff to conduct the census and work related to the FIFA World Cup; together, these factors generated an increase of 181,000 jobs from April to July.
The growth in recent months was also explained by the fact that the economy as a whole demonstrated considerable resilience to U.S. trade restrictions that have been in effect for more than 18 months, and mass layoffs have so far been avoided.
However, the entry into force of the new U.S. tariffs and Canada's retaliatory measures (starting early next week) is expected to slow this growth somewhat. Four out of five members of the labor force are employed in the services sector, including health care, education, transportation, and finance; this sector bore the brunt of the employment decline in August.
According to Statistics Canada (StatsCan), 51,500 jobs were eliminated in this sector in August; the greatest losses occurred in industries such as business and support services (including building services), as well as wholesale and retail trade.
The unemployment rate remained at its lowest level in two years, despite the economy facing a wave of tariffs imposed by the Trump administration.
Slower labor-force growth, caused by stricter immigration rules and an aging workforce, also contributed to improved unemployment figures in recent months.
The labor force, which stood at 22.632 million people, declined for the first time since February.
The youth unemployment rate rose by 0.3 percentage points in August, reaching 12.9%, interrupting the downward trend observed from April through July.
Average hourly wages for permanent employees — an important indicator of inflationary pressures — fell to 2% in August (from 3% a month earlier), reaching their lowest level in more than seven years (excluding the pandemic period).

Philippines' Vice President Sara Duterte Faces Arrest Over Alleged Grave Threat to President Marcos

13:09:39 UTC
22:09:39 KST

A Philippine court on Friday ordered the arrest of Vice President Sara Duterte over alleged grave threats to her former ally, President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr., his wife, and a former House Speaker.
The warrant against Duterte, 48, set the bail at 120,000 pesos ($1,900) for each of the three counts against her.
“Regardless of the question on jurisdiction, she has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies,” Duterte’s lawyer said in a statement.
Duterte has been charged with threatening the lives of Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and his cousin, former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.
The case stems from a November 2024 virtual press conference where the Vice President revealed an apparent assassination plot against Marcos, his wife, and Romualdez.
“I already talked to someone—I told him, If I’m killed, kill [Marcos], Liza Araneta, and Martin Romualdez,” she said in Filipino, “No joke, no joke. I already gave orders. If I die, I told them, ‘Don’t stop until they’re dead.’ And then he said, ‘Yes.’”
The threat is also one of the allegations included in the impeachment complaint against Duterte, on top of alleged misuse of public funds as Vice President and during her stint as Education Secretary. Duterte has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing.
The Vice President is currently standing trial at the Philippine Senate, serving as an impeachment court, following her second impeachment in May. If convicted in the impeachment court, she could be removed from office and barred from running in the 2028 national elections, where she said she plans to contest the presidency.
Philippine law typically allows candidates to run for public office even if they face pending criminal charges.
Duterte controversies and public standing
Duterte is the daughter of former President Rodrigo Duterte, who is awaiting trial before the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands, for the thousands of deaths attributed to his violent anti-drug campaign.
The Duterte family still enjoys broad public support in the Philippines, despite the controversies. Recent surveys show Sara Duterte herself is the top preferred candidate by Filipinos to succeed Marcos, whom she had a falling out with. Marcos, who took office in 2022, is limited to a lone six-year term.
The presidential office said in a statement that it “respects the decision of the court” to issue an arrest warrant.
Jean Encinas-Franco, a political science professor at the University of the Philippines, tells TIME that “the law has finally caught up with the Vice President,” but questioned the timing of the arrest warrant’s release. Franco said Duterte’s arrest warrant could successfully repel criticisms that Marcos is a “weak” leader as the impeachment proceedings have dragged on.
However, Franco says it remains unclear which political camp—if any—will benefit from the latest political development. “We don't know what will happen because it's still 1-½ years [until the elections] and that's a lifetime in Philippine politics.”

Russia training record-high number of African students – EEF experts

Unknown Publisher

Russia training record-high number of African students – EEF experts
Russia is now training more African students than the Soviet Union did, Andrey Maslov, director of the HSE Center for African Studies, said on Friday at the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) in Vladivostok.
The number of students from African countries enrolled at Russian universities has reached a historic high of over 37,000 this year, Olga Petrova, Russian deputy minister of science and higher education, reported at the same session. The figure is up from around 17,500 in 2020, according to Fernando Jose Sambu, the head of Direction for Work with Government Bodies and Diplomatic Missions of African Countries.
Russia has also expanded state-funded education opportunities for African students, a policy promoted by President Vladimir Putin at the 2023 Russia-Africa Summit.
In August, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said the government-funded quota for Ghanaian students would nearly double from 120 places beginning with the current academic year. Ghanaian Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa later said the allocation had been increased to 240 places.
Beyond university education, Russia has also expanded programs aimed at training African government officials. Maslov said the HSE Center for African Studies is working with government agencies in more than 20 African countries, including on digitalization, financial monitoring, and cybersecurity.
The expert noted there is strong demand among African governments for Russian expertise in financial monitoring and cybersecurity.
“This is an area that African states are only just beginning to approach systematically in terms of understanding their role in protecting their national digital environments from external influence,” Maslov stated.
The HSE Center for African Studies has been running its E-Governance Knowledge Sharing Program since 2022, providing training for African government officials in the digitalization of public administration. Its first major training school in Moscow in 2023 brought together over 40 mid- and senior-level officials from 23 African countries. The program has since expanded to activities on the continent, including a training school on e-governance held in Tanzania in May 2026.
The 11th Eastern Economic Forum is being held in Vladivostok from September 1 to 4 under the theme ‘The Far East – Development for the Benefit of People’. More than 7,000 participants from 78 countries and territories have attended this year’s forum, according to organizers.

From naval blockade to land corridors: Iran's strategic pivot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:07:45 UTC
22:07:45 KST

From naval blockade to land corridors: Iran's strategic pivot
TEHRAN- Iran's maritime trade has faced serious disruption due to geopolitical tensions and sanctions, but this challenge has unexpectedly accelerated the development of land-based transit routes. What initially appeared as a strategic vulnerability—over-reliance on the Strait of Hormuz—is now forcing a fundamental shift in the country's trade infrastructure. The result could transform Iran from a sea-dependent economy into a regional transit hub connecting East, West, North, and South.
The recent naval pressures, intensified after failed military confrontations, have exposed a long-standing weakness: Iran's trade was disproportionately channeled through a single maritime choke point. Rather than simply imposing costs, however, this constraint has made the diversification of trade routes an urgent necessity. In response, Iran is actively developing four major land corridors that could redefine its economic geography.
First, the East-West Railway Corridor links China to Iran via Central Asia, passing through Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan. This 10,400-kilometer route can cut shipping times from 30 days by sea to just 15 days by rail, significantly reducing costs and risks. Second, the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), through Pakistan's Gwadar port and Iran's Rimdan border, offers an eastern bypass of the Strait of Hormuz. Third, the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) connects Iran to Russia and India, providing access to northern and southern markets. Fourth, the Shalamcheh-Basra railway—only 32 kilometers short of completion—can open Iran to Iraq, Turkey, and the Mediterranean.
According to Ahmad Bakhshayesh, a member of Iran's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, the government has actively expanded trade cooperation with neighbors like Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkey, Pakistan, and Oman. He emphasized that these corridors have prevented shortages of essential goods during the crisis, ensuring price hikes rather than outright scarcity.
The activation of the Iran-Pakistan transit corridor is particularly significant. With instability on Pakistan-Afghanistan border routes, Islamabad now looks to Iran for access to Central Asian markets. Iran's Mirjaveh and Rimdan terminals are central to this exchange, with a bilateral trade target of $10 billion. Rimdan has been developed since 2020, with passenger facilities and infrastructure upgrades underway.
These corridors must not remain temporary fixes. If completed and sustained, they can offer lasting competitive advantages, attract investment from China, India, and Russia, and reduce Iran's vulnerability to maritime disruptions. What began as a forced response to containment can become a permanent pillar of Iran's economic strategy. The lesson is clear: a country with Iran's geography cannot be blockaded when it turns its land borders into bridges rather than barriers.

‘Life-saving assistance’

"Human remains and thousands of dead livestock still lie in the debris, raising the risk of communicable disease outbreaks."
Communities near the epicentre remain cut off.
"Families whose homes are gone need durable shelter in weeks, not months," the appeal said.
A UN preliminary assessment estimated building damage from Nepal's floods at $158 million alone, warning that total losses - including damage to roads and bridges, agricultural land and humanitarian costs - would be far higher.
Nepal has suggested the reconstruction bill could run into "billions" of dollars.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News ) – Feitsui Reservoir Administration said Friday that it has sped up inspections with drones and big data.
The management said that flying has not only increased efficiency but also allowed inspectors to examine issues from a safe distance.
Acting Director Chou Po‑kai (周伯愷) said that manual inspections could not cover the 122.5-meter-tall dam as its curved structure made it difficult to see up close with binoculars, leaving many areas unchecked. He noted that drones and AI image recognition fixed these issues and provided data for a comprehensive database, allowing for 24-hour monitoring.
Safety Inspection Chief He Chin‑yu (何謹余) said the program began last year with drones flying up close to photograph dam surfaces, with AI-supported cameras identifying defects. He added that engineers mapped flight paths and fixed camera angles for consistency.
Inspection officer Tseng Jui‑wen (曾瑞文) said the AI is trained to recognize leakage, cracks, cavities, and growth with 90% accuracy. He noted that management plans to check the interior structure and installations, such as the dam's 300-meter-long, 500-meter-high spillway tunnel. Drones can easily survey the dark and slippery tube that is difficult and dangerous to cover on foot.
The dam is owned by Taipei City Government and operated by the dam administration. It is Taiwan's second-largest dam after Tsengwen Reservoir and supplies water and electricity to all of Taipei and some of New Taipei.

Russia’s proposed telecom licensing reform would leave 27 regions without local internet providers
A Digital Development Ministry initiative to tighten requirements for telecom operators would leave 27 regions without local internet providers, the Russian business news outlet RBC reported. Aleksei Leontyev, director of the Association of Telecommunications Operators (ASTO), cited the figure at a roundtable discussing proposed amendments to the legislation.
In April, the Digital Development Ministry planned to introduce three telecom licenses — basic, universal, and general — replacing the current 17. Depending on the license type, the cost would range from one million to 50 million rubles. The ministry also plans new requirements for companies’ minimum authorized capital and for how extensively their communications infrastructure must cover the regions.
About 4,700 operators currently work in Russia, not counting major federal companies and their subsidiaries. Only those with revenue exceeding 400 million rubles would be able to meet the new requirements, the outlet Frank Media reported.
Leontyev said these companies would be hit hardest: by his estimate, 21% of operators have revenue below 100 million rubles, and 36% have revenue below 200 million rubles. Regional operators, he said, together account for 45% of Russia’s broadband internet market.
Oleg Grishchenko, head of the Rosteleset association, said the reform would also hit the “new regions” — Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine, where mostly local providers operate — as well as small towns, where telecom service is usually built by local entrepreneurs with modest revenues.
Experts say the reform itself would require substantial spending to reconnect subscribers — spending that would have to come from the state budget, since Russia’s largest operators are all heavily in debt. Leontyev believes the cost could run into “hundreds of billions of rubles.”
The Digital Development Ministry believes the new measures will improve the quality and availability of communications services, leaving only “reliable” operators in the telecom market. The ministry stresses, however, that no final decisions have been made and that the initiative is still only being discussed with businesses.

Germany has begun mass production of more than 5,000 medium- and long-range strike drones for Ukraine, defense company Auterion and its Ukrainian joint-venture partner Airlogix said.
The first units have already been manufactured in the greater Munich area under a German government order that industry sources estimate at about €300 million ($348 million).
The companies said the contract is due to be completed by mid-2027.
The drones are part of Germany’s military assistance to Ukraine, amid the conflict with Russia that began in February 2022.
The joint venture, founded in February, said it expects follow-on orders and a long-term commissioning.
“Germany now has a production line for affordable precision weapons in large quantities,” Auterion Chief Executive Lorenz Meier told local media.
“We will deliver already proven and tested systems this year -- at costs and at a manufacturing pace that actually make large stockpiles for deterrence possible,” Meier added.
Production is underway at an undisclosed site near Munich and is also planned at a second plant in eastern Germany, German news agency dpa reported.
Two models are being manufactured, according to company sources.
One has a medium range, while the other can fly up to 1,500 kilometers (about 930 miles), the sources said.
Auterion supplies the software and operating system, while Airlogix provides the hardware.
The one-way strike drones carry explosives and are designed to hit and destroy their targets rather than return.
Artificial intelligence is intended to keep the drones on course even when electronic warfare systems attempt to jam them.

How knowledge and media can challenge misconceptions about Islam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:00:40 UTC
22:00:40 KST

Organised by the Islamic Civilization Center in Uzbekistan, the forum gathered nearly 300 participants from around 50 countries. Discussions ranged from responsibility for misrepresentations of Islam and journalistic independence to Europe’s closer engagement with Central Asia.
The International Media Forum “Islamic Civilization: A New Perspective - New Discoveries”, organised by the Islamic Civilization Center in Uzbekistan, brought to Tashkent a series of debates that extend well beyond the event itself.
Nearly 300 media professionals, researchers, publishers, filmmakers and technology specialists from around 50 countries discussed how the history and heritage of Islamic societies are represented, how stereotypes are challenged and how old sources can be made relevant to new audiences.
Organisers linked the forum’s wider purpose to President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s 2017 address to the UN General Assembly, when he rejected attempts to associate Islam with violence and bloodshed and proposed a resolution on “Enlightenment and Religious Tolerance”, which was adopted the following year.
The forum translated that broad idea into debates about media, evidence, technology and historical interpretation.
Islamophobia, knowledge and responsibility
Firdavs Abdukhalikov, the centre’s director, argued that misconceptions about Islam should be addressed through knowledge and explanation rather than confrontation.
“In the media space, we should speak not to argue, but to explain,” he said. “The most effective response to Islamophobia is enlightenment. The strongest response to misconceptions is truth. The most effective weapon against ignorance is knowledge.”
Abdukhalikov also focused on the scientific and cultural history of Islamic societies, arguing that it should be presented more widely and on the basis of research and evidence.
Hasanbey Kondu, who heads Turkish publishing house Mega Basım, added another layer to the debate. He argued that distorted perceptions could not simply be blamed on Europe or the modern West.
“Islam is misunderstood and misrepresented, intentionally or unintentionally — and I include Muslims in that,” Kondu said. “It is not enough to blame Europeans or the modern world. As a Muslim, how are you presenting Islam? How have you understood it yourself? Perhaps we need to look first at our own shortcomings.”
Reporting a region Europe long overlooked
The question of representation also extended to Uzbekistan and Central Asia themselves.
Sherzod Asadov, press secretary to Uzbekistan’s president, told foreign journalists that they were not being asked simply to speak positively about the country.
“We invite you to see it with your own eyes, talk to people, ask questions and draw your own conclusions,” he said.
In the same speech, Asadov addressed the impact of artificial intelligence on journalism. AI could expand a journalist’s capabilities but could not replace the journalist, he argued, adding that however technology changes, truth, impartiality, conscience and the interests of people should remain central.
Euronews CEO Claus Strunz placed that debate in a wider European context. He recalled how Central Asia had once been largely absent from European public discussion, except in reports about disasters or romanticised stories about the Silk Road.
“That was arrogant and blind then,” he said.
Institutional ties have deepened in recent years. In April 2025, the first EU-Central Asia summit was held in Samarkand, where the two regions upgraded their relationship to a strategic partnership.
For Strunz, that shift reflects Central Asia’s growing economic, political and cultural importance to Europe. “It is time to look East again,” he said.
But greater attention, he argued, should remain grounded in independent reporting. Journalists should be present on the ground, report what they find and give audiences enough information to form their own views.
“We are not here to teach them. We are here to inform them.”
Europe and Central Asia: links that go back centuries
The forum also placed today’s rapprochement against a much longer history of exchange between Europe, Central Asia and the wider Silk Road world.
Italian researcher Dr Mario Taddei, a specialist in Leonardo da Vinci’s manuscripts and inventions, described what he calls a “Knowledge Silk Road”, his term for the movement of scientific ideas from China through the Middle East and into Renaissance Europe.
Speaking about Western perceptions of scientific history, Taddei said: “We believe that we invented everything, but it’s not true.”
Dr Taddei cited medieval engineers Al-Muradi and Al-Jazari as part of a wider history of mechanical and scientific exchange.
A different connection emerged through publisher Charlotte Kramer. Spanish envoy Ruy González de Clavijo was sent by King Henry III of Castile to Timur and reached Samarkand in 1404, leaving a detailed account of the journey. Kramer presented a publishing project based on that historical record.
“We already see a very strong connection from Europe to Central Asia,” she said, pointing to both the Silk Road and diplomatic dialogue.
The forum also explored how such material can reach audiences today. Presentations included books, documentaries, digital avatars, immersive platforms and other new formats for presenting historical figures and sources.
Hungarian media executive Alpar Kato summed up that approach as bringing together “something modern and an old, traditional story.”
The setting itself reflected much of that discussion. The forum was held at the centre in Tashkent, where historical research, publishing and new media projects were presented side by side.
Firdavs Abdukhalikov, the centre’s director, summed up that ambition in his address: “History should speak. Cultural heritage should communicate with people. The past should inspire today’s generation to new discoveries.”

Psychiatrists detail mother’s sudden descent into severe psychosis and delirious mania following childbirth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:00:38 UTC
22:00:38 KST

A recent case report published in Frontiers in Psychiatry details the experience of a 27-year-old woman who developed a rare and severe condition known as delirious mania shortly after giving birth. The case highlights how women with bipolar disorder may face an increased risk of complex manic episodes following multiple pregnancies and deliveries. The findings suggest that electroconvulsive therapy can be an effective and rapid treatment for this life-threatening psychiatric emergency.
Bipolar disorder is a mental health condition characterized by extreme mood swings, including emotional highs known as mania and lows known as depression. Following childbirth, women with bipolar disorder experience a heightened risk of recurrent psychiatric episodes. These postpartum episodes typically present as depression or standard mania. Postpartum psychosis is another related condition where mothers experience an abrupt onset of psychotic symptoms shortly following childbirth.
Delirious mania is an unusually severe neuropsychiatric condition that is rarely documented. It combines the hyperactive and erratic behaviors of mania with delirium, which is a state of profound confusion and disorientation. Patients may also experience psychosis, meaning they lose touch with reality through hallucinations or delusions.
Diagnosing delirious mania is challenging because doctors must first rule out a variety of physical illnesses that can cause similar symptoms. Infections, drug toxicity, and severe metabolic imbalances can all produce a state of delirium. Medical teams typically conduct extensive blood tests, brain imaging, and neurological exams to ensure the symptoms are not caused by an underlying physical disease.
Because delirious mania is poorly understood and infrequently documented, it often goes unrecognized in clinical settings. Lead author Bowen Song, a researcher at Sichuan University’s Mental Health Center in China, and a team of scientists documented this specific case to build a medical literature base that helps other doctors recognize the condition. By detailing the patient’s symptoms and treatment, the authors aim to provide evidence on how to identify and manage postpartum delirious mania before it escalates into a life-threatening situation.
The patient in this report was a 27-year-old Chinese woman with a documented history of bipolar disorder type I. She had previously experienced manic episodes characterized by excessive talking, a decreased need for sleep, and impulsive behavior. During her first pregnancy in 2020, she experienced a manic episode with psychotic symptoms following a routine amniocentesis. An amniocentesis is a medical procedure used to test amniotic fluid, and the physical stress of the event appeared to trigger her symptoms.
She was treated with medication and later delivered her first child via a cesarean section without further postpartum psychiatric issues. In 2024, she became pregnant again and delivered her second child, also via a cesarean section. Her mood had remained stable throughout the pregnancy on a low dose of an antipsychotic medication called quetiapine.
On the first day after her second surgery, her behavior changed drastically. She became highly excitable, talked excessively, and showed uncharacteristic aggression toward her family members. Over the next three days, she did not sleep and began experiencing auditory hallucinations, hearing voices mocking her. She also developed paranoid delusions, believing her husband had been unfaithful.
Her condition quickly deteriorated into a state of severe confusion and physical restlessness. She exhibited inappropriate behaviors, such as bedwetting, and became completely disoriented. She claimed to have lived for hundreds of years and could no longer recognize familiar people, places, or the current time.
Her family brought her to the emergency department, where doctors initially attempted to calm her using various medications. These initial treatments included sodium valproate, a mood stabilizer, and propofol, a strong sedative. These medications did not improve her symptoms. Her extreme agitation posed a risk to herself and the medical staff, requiring continuous sedation and physical restraints.
Given the severe and life-threatening nature of her symptoms, the medical team recommended electroconvulsive therapy, commonly known as ECT, on her seventh day of hospitalization. ECT is a medical procedure that involves passing small electric currents through the brain to intentionally trigger a brief seizure. This process appears to alter brain chemistry in a way that can quickly reverse symptoms of certain severe mental health conditions.
The patient received daily ECT sessions for the first three days, followed by treatments every other day. After the third session, her mood began to stabilize, and her consciousness returned to normal. She was once again able to recognize her surroundings and interact amicably with her family members.
Following the eighth ECT session, her emotional state stabilized entirely. Her hallucinations, delusions, and severe agitation resolved. She was discharged on the 19th day of her hospital stay and prescribed maintenance doses of oral psychiatric medications.
During a follow-up visit four weeks later, the patient remained alert and emotionally stable. She reported complete amnesia regarding the acute phase of her illness. She remembered nothing from the delivery until her third ECT treatment.
This single account cannot establish that multiple pregnancies or cesarean sections directly cause delirious mania in women with bipolar disorder. Biological changes during childbirth are complex, and individual medical events do not indicate a direct cause-and-effect relationship. The onset of psychiatric symptoms after delivery likely involves a combination of hormonal fluctuations, physical stress from surgery, and underlying genetic vulnerabilities.
These findings also do not imply that standard psychiatric medications are ineffective for postpartum psychiatric emergencies. For this specific patient, standard drugs did not stabilize her condition quickly enough, necessitating electroconvulsive therapy. Different individuals respond uniquely to treatments, and medications remain the standard initial approach for managing acute mania.
During the diagnostic process, the patient’s family declined a lumbar puncture, a routine procedure used to test the fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord. This meant doctors could not definitively test for autoimmune encephalitis, a condition where the immune system attacks the brain and produces similar psychiatric symptoms. The patient’s rapid recovery following ECT indicates an underlying psychiatric condition rather than an autoimmune disease, but the absence of this test leaves a small degree of diagnostic uncertainty.
Case reports describe the unique experiences of individual patients. They cannot be used to determine how common a condition is within the broader population or to create universal treatment guidelines. They are highly useful in medicine because they document rare clinical presentations, helping other doctors recognize unusual symptoms and consider alternative treatment options when standard therapies fail.
The report, “Postpartum delirious mania in a patient with diagnosis of bipolar disorder after cesarean delivery: a case report,” was authored by Bowen Song, Yiwen Yuan, Zhixiong Li, Zhongrui Ma, Xiufang Yang, and Zhe Li.
