This Greek island solved its rubbish problem - by getting rid of its landfill entirely
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:00:09 UTC
22:00:09 KST

Most small islands have little choice but to bury their rubbish in a landfill. Tilos in Greece has found another way. Euronews visited the world's first zero-waste island to see how its system works, and whether other places can do the same.
Tilos, a small Greek island, used to bury its rubbish on a hillside. The landfill kept growing. Wind scattered plastic across the beaches below.
It's a familiar problem for small islands. Residents and tourists produce waste, but shipping it elsewhere for recycling rarely makes economic sense. So most islands sacrifice a patch of scarce land and bury the problem. Out of sight, out of mind.
A few years ago, Tilos tried something different. Working with Greek circular economy company Polygreen and backed by the Region of South Aegean, the island removed its street bins entirely and replaced them with door-to-door collection. Every household and business received separate bags for recyclables and organic waste, each tagged with a QR code.
As a result, Tilos is now the world's first island to hold the Zero Waste Cities Certification, with a recycling and composting rate of close to 90% - well above both the Greek national figure and the EU average.
How it works
All waste collected from the residents and businesses goes to the Centre of Circular Innovation, built on the old landfill site.
"This is an island that produces waste but buries nothing," project manager Spyros Kastanakis told Euronews. “330 tonnes a year - 60% recyclable, 30% organic, and the remaining 10% goes as fuel to cement factories.”
Organic waste is composted into fertiliser and given free to local farmers. Non-recyclables are turned into alternative fuel. Everything else is sorted into 15 categories, compressed, and shipped to the mainland as economically valuable raw material. “This is no longer waste - it's raw material,” says Tilos Secretary General Stathis Kontos. “Everything has a second life.”
The system only works if residents sort properly at home. Getting them there took effort. “First we went to the schools and convinced the children,” Mayor Maria Kamma told Euronews. “The children passed it on to their parents, and from there it spread.”
The Just Go Zero Tilos project is ready to grow. Regional authorities are planning to extend the model so that more small islands across Greece can stop burying their waste - and start dealing with it properly.

Why are fuel and petrochemical prices outpacing crude – and how long will it last?
Global refined-product exports were down 25 per cent year on year in August, with losses concentrated in Russia and the Persian Gulf, analysts say
This summer, David Chen, a Chinese national living in Japan, got an unexpected lesson in global industrial supply chains – delivered through a bag of potato chips.
When popular Japanese snack brand Calbee replaced its signature colourful packaging with monochrome designs, Chen initially assumed it was a marketing gimmick. “Then news reports explained the switch stemmed from a naphtha supply crunch. I even looked up the word,” Chen said.
Naphtha, a flammable liquid processed from crude oil, might not be a household name, yet it serves as a foundational input in polyester fibres, packaging and industrial solvents. The squeeze has prompted Japanese media to coin a new term: “naphtha bankruptcies”, reflecting mounting anxiety among some companies over securing vital oil-derived inputs.
A June survey by corporate research firm Tokyo Shoko Research underscored the widespread impact, finding that about 80 per cent of more than 7,000 responding firms had difficulty procuring oil-derived products.
However, behind Japan’s localised squeeze lies a wider strain on global supply. According to late-August estimates by Goldman Sachs analysts led by Yulia Zhestkova Grigsby, global refinery outages – which take refining capacity offline or force facilities to reduce output – stood 60 per cent above seasonal norms.
Market and industry analysts attributed the tight conditions to two main pressures: mounting geopolitical conflict and fuel export controls from China, which has the world’s largest oil-refining capacity.

Estonia fuel prices swing daily as retailer price war becomes 'new norm'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Estonia fuel prices swing daily as retailer price war becomes 'new norm'
Fuel prices in Estonia are now fluctuating daily or even several times a day, driven more by an ongoing price war between filling station chains than by the Iran crisis.
While the price of diesel had exceeded the €2 per liter mark at some filling stations in Estonia on Wednesday, prices had dropped again by Thursday, the result of a price war between competitors.
"We've had a fuel price war going on for a year. More than a year, actually. It started on September 1 last year, but since then there has been greater volatility. Even this week — prices were hiked on Monday, but by Wednesday morning they had already fallen by 18.5 cents. Yesterday (Wednesday, September 2 — ed.) prices were raised — diesel even went above €2 per liter — while today prices are already as much as 16.5 cents lower in some places," Terminal management board member Alan Vaht told "Aktuaalne kaamera."
"Primarily, I think, it is the continuing price competition between filling stations on the Estonian market, which has already been going on for a year. Intra-week price fluctuations of 10 to 15 cents, and sometimes even more, have now become a weekly occurrence. That is the main reason when we look at the daily price changes here. Local competition is currently clearly having a stronger impact than movements on the global market," said Alexela head of business development Tarmo Kärsna.
The price war began a year ago when another chain, Neste, abandoned its loyalty programs and lowered the quoted prices at its filling stations below those of its competitors. In a game theory in action scenario, its competitors have followed suit.
"In fact, the other market participants have responded to this and have likewise scaled back their loyalty programs or abandoned them altogether, as Neste did. Consumers are price-sensitive, and if the posted price somewhere is higher, they will notice it in the long run," Vaht added.
Neste Estonia CEO Polina Tkatšuk noted that: "Estonia's fuel market is highly competitive. That is positive news for Estonian customers, because intense competition means there is also a very broad range of offers, and customers have a great deal of choice and high expectations of fuel retailers. As a result, fuel retailers keep a very close eye on what is happening in the market and react quickly."
Consequently, whereas a year ago the thinking was the price war could not be sustained for very long, it has since become the new norm.
"Today, we can say that this is the new reality, which on the one hand is good for consumers — at times prices are very good — but on the other, creates a lot of confusion about when to buy," Kärsna concluded.
Up-to-date fuel prices in Estonia can be viewed by scrolling down the front page of ERR News.

New island emerges in Norway’s Svalbard as glacier retreats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:59:45 UTC
21:59:45 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
A new island has emerged in Norway’s Svalbard archipelago after the Austfonna glacier retreated, Norwegian public broadcaster NRK reported Friday.
The island, covering roughly 0.45 square kilometers (0.17 square miles), was first identified in satellite images taken this summer, according to Geir Moholdt, a glaciologist at the Norwegian Polar Institute.
Radar images indicate that the landmass became separated from the glacier in late autumn last year. It now lies about 400 meters (1,312 feet) from the glacier front.
Austfonna, Norway’s largest glacier, has been melting at a record rate. Its glacier front stretches for more than 180 kilometers (112 miles), making it the longest in the Northern Hemisphere, according to the institute.
“In recent years, glaciers in Svalbard have lost more than one meter of ice on the surface on average per year,” Moholdt said, adding that the rate was far higher than previously observed.
He said Svalbard’s glaciers are retreating further onto land, causing fjords to lengthen while the ice becomes thinner because of warmer summers and extensive melting.
The rapidly changing terrain also makes updated maps increasingly important for researchers, local authorities, police, aircraft operators, and people traveling outdoors, said Anne Urset, a geodesist at the institute.
Moholdt warned that other landmasses could emerge as warming and glacial retreat continue.
“There are several candidates for new islands that could emerge with rapid warming and melting,” he said, adding that some glaciers could eventually disappear entirely.

====================================================================================================

Alleged Confession Video Raises More Questions About Ukrainian Security Agencies Shoot-Out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:58:30 UTC
21:58:30 KST

A shoot-out between Ukraine’s two leading security agencies on the streets of Kyiv has caused concern among residents already coming under intense Russian drone and missile attacks.
Days later, there are still more questions than answers about what happened and why. A video showing a man confessing to being a Russian spy -- which he has since said was recorded under duress -- has added to the confusion.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has taken swift action, firing the deputy heads of each organization on September 3 -- declaring "both agencies must be held accountable.” He'd previously said the gunfight was "disgraceful."
Who Was Involved?
The gun battle pitted Ukraine’s main domestic intelligence agency, known as the SBU, against the country’s military intelligence outlet, the HUR. Both have been carrying out armed operations against Russian forces.
Their firefight erupted on September 2, as the Ukrainian capital was targeted by Russian air strikes for the sixth day in a row.
“Both acted in a way that is absolutely unacceptable,” Zelenskyy said, adding that “two individuals implicated in the shooting” had been formally named as suspects amid an ongoing investigation.
Still, the details of the incident known to the public remain murky.
The jarring shoot-out appears to be connected to the earlier arrest of Stepan Kaplunov, deputy commander of the notorious Ukrainian-backed paramilitary group the Russian Volunteer Corps.
The corps first came to prominence with cross-border raids inside Russia in 2023.
Effectively overseen by the HUR's Tymur's Special Unit, it is mostly made up of Russian nationals.
'Kidnap' And 'Confession'
Kaplunov was "abducted" on August 23, without a detention record or legal counsel present, his lawyer, Taras Borovskiy, told RFE/RL.
Borovskiy said Kaplunov’s whereabouts were unknown until the early hours of September 2, when SBU officials brought him to his apartment to conduct a search.
HUR representatives were already waiting at the scene.
As the developments unfolded, “comrades and supporters of the HUR’s Tymur’s Special Unit began arriving” in the area as well, the lawyer added, saying that it was then that “the first groups that came here were attacked.”
Local residents told RFE/RL they were afraid to leave their apartments, having no idea what was going on in their street: Armed men wearing no identifying insignia were moving between the buildings, with the only way to tell them apart being the green and blue tapes they wore.
According to Borovskiy, three HUR servicemen were injured in the incident, with one suffering a bullet wound that severed an artery in his leg.
The SBU said the search of Kaplunov's apartment was part of a pretrial investigation into a "terrorist attack" allegedly organized by Russian special services and that an armed group of people was trying to disrupt measures being taken to collect and document evidence.
According to the agency, Russia was planning an assassination attempt against one of the leaders of the Russian opposition movement. During what it called “counter-sabotage efforts,” the SBU said it uncovered contacts between Kaplunov and Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB).
On September 3, the SBU published a video of Kaplunov confessing that he had been “approached by an agent acting in the interests of the [FSB] with the aim of recruiting him to carry out active measures to eliminate Ukrainian Defense Forces personnel.”
Kaplunov, who had earlier been released, said in an interview with Ukraine's Radio NV that he had agreed with the SBU version of events only "under psychological pressure.”
Inter-Agency Rivalry
Kaplunov's commander, Denis Nikitin, earlier told RFE/RL the SBU did not find anything compromising in their search of his apartment. The HUR claimed that there was a “targeted disinformation campaign” aimed at discrediting its combat units.
While the investigation into the incident is yet to unfold, it's been widely suggested that the clash lifted the lid on an ongoing rivalry between the two agencies. Indeed, this is not the first time they have clashed.
On March 5, 2022, just 12 days after Russia began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Denys Kiryeyev, a member of a Ukrainian delegation to negotiate with Russia in Belarus, was found dead on a Kyiv sidewalk.
The SBU did not publicly disclose its own version of the circumstances surrounding Kiryeyev’s death. But later that month, the agency reported that it had eliminated a Russian agent without naming him.
A 2023 report by The Wall Street Journal, citing then-head of the HUR Kyrylo Budanov, said Kiryeyev had been working with Ukrainian intelligence and had provided it with Russia’s invasion plans.
Following the incident, there were changes to the leaderships of both agencies. Budanov was recently appointed head of Zelenskyy's office.

====================================================================================================

South Korea’s military turns to AI as low birth rate shrinks pool of recruits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:57:44 UTC
21:57:44 KST

As South Korea's population rapidly ages and the pool of military recruits shrinks, Seoul is increasingly looking to artificial intelligence, robots and autonomous systems to help defend one of the world's most heavily militarized borders with fewer soldiers.
Earlier this month, President Lee Jae Myung called for selective conscription and a shift toward a smaller, technology-driven force, describing his goal as a “smart, elite and strong military centered on advanced equipment and technologies.”
The push is already moving beyond plans and policy.
In July, South Korea conducted its first test of a humanoid robot performing a ship's helmsman duties, with the robot successfully executing steering commands under simulated conditions including narrow waterways, bad weather and nighttime operations.
The Navy also carried out its first minesweeping trial using AI technology and unmanned vessels earlier this month.
The Army, meanwhile, has commissioned a study into automating key maintenance operations, including through AI-powered predictive maintenance, automated information management, maintenance robots and wearable strength-assist suits.
The push is part of South Korea's broader embrace of AI. In June, Lee unveiled investment plans worth more than $1 trillion for projects including semiconductors, physical AI and data centers.
But for the military, the technology is intended to address a particularly pressing problem – South Korea is running out of people to fill its ranks.
South Korean men are required to complete at least 18 months of military service, with some exempted or assigned alternative service.
But decades of falling birth rates are rapidly shrinking the population from which the military can draw its conscripts.
South Korea's total fertility rate stood at 0.8 in 2025, far below the 2.1 children per woman generally considered necessary to maintain a stable population without migration.
Around 1 million babies were born annually in South Korea in the early 1970s. By 2022, that number had fallen to just 249,000 and the fertility rate had dropped to 0.78, a level the government described as “unprecedented in world history.”
South Korea's population is projected to fall from around 52 million in 2024 to 36 million by 2072. Within the same time frame, the proportion of people aged 65 and older is projected to surge from 19.2% to 47.7% – meaning nearly half the population could be elderly.
“The demographic rationale is explicit and quantifiable,” Dongyoun Cho, a senior fellow for advanced technologies, national security and defense at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS-Europe), told Anadolu. “The active force has fallen to around 450,000, at just over 90% of required manning.”
But AI cannot simply replace every soldier who disappears from the ranks, she cautioned.
“AI substitutes selectively, not one-for-one – it is most credible in persistent surveillance, logistics and other manpower-intensive tasks,” Cho said. “The force will shrink regardless of AI. The question is what a smaller force can still do.”
South Korea is pursuing several programs aimed at building autonomous and AI capabilities across its armed forces, with the Future National Defense Strategy Committee putting AI and unmanned forces on the agenda, she said.
The Army aims to introduce more than 50,000 training drones by 2029, enough to provide one drone per squad, the Korea Herald reported in April, enabling service members to acquire basic drone operating skills and practical experience.
The Army's TIGER Plus program also envisions integrating AI, drones and other advanced technologies across the force by 2040.
In the air, South Korea is developing the LOWUS unmanned combat aircraft, envisioned as a “loyal wingman” that could operate alongside crewed fighters such as the country's KF-21.
At sea, the Navy's Sea Ghost concept is aimed at creating a force in which crewed warships operate alongside unmanned systems using AI.
But Cho argued that Seoul's technological ambitions are moving faster than its ability to put them into practice.
“Political will is running ahead of the ecosystem that has to deliver it,” she said, pointing to the reorganization of the Drone Operations Command after its initial creation was acknowledged as hasty.
And the biggest obstacles may not be the AI models themselves.
“The practical obstacles are less about algorithms than about integration – interoperability across platforms and services, test and certification bottlenecks, communications resilience under jamming, safety assurance and operator training,” Cho said.
Those challenges are compounded, she added, by military acquisition systems designed to purchase hardware rather than software that is continuously updated.
The gap between South Korea's ambitions and its ability to implement them will be “the defining feature of the next several years,” she said.
South Korea is hardly alone in racing to integrate AI and autonomous systems into its armed forces.
But Cho said Seoul differs from Washington and Beijing “less in scale than in motivation and structure.”
The US and China are investing in military AI on a much larger scale and across a wider range of applications.
South Korea, however, has an “unusually explicit demographic rationale,” Cho said, alongside an export-oriented defense industry and the need to ensure its systems remain interoperable with those of its US ally.
Japan has historically taken a more incremental approach, though that may now be changing, she added.
Tokyo is moving to revise its three major national security documents, with AI-enabled decision-making and unmanned systems reportedly among the issues under consideration.
According to media reports, Japan is also considering utilizing cutting-edge AI systems under its preemptive cyber defense policy such as US company Anthropic's Claude Mythos.
Rather than seeing the developments as a single race for AI military supremacy, Cho said each country is responding to its own strategic pressures.
“Rather than a race with a single scoreboard, these are programs shaped by quite different drivers and constraints – and (South) Korea's may prove one of the more instructive cases of adoption under demographic pressure,” she said.
Putting increasingly autonomous technology into military operations brings a different set of problems.
For Cho, three are particularly concerning: AI systems could misidentify targets or make errors in chaotic environments; human operators could place too much trust in machine-generated recommendations; and faster automated decision-making could increase the risk of military escalation.
All three carry particular weight on the Korean Peninsula.
Real-world conditions, Cho said, are “far harder than those in which systems are trained and tested.”
Under intense pressure, operators could also defer to recommendations generated by AI, weakening meaningful human control even when formal “human-in-the-loop” requirements remain in place.
Speed is another issue.
AI can process information and recommend action far more quickly than conventional military decision-making systems. While that can provide an advantage, it could also leave humans with less time to question what a system is telling them, Cho said.
That, Cho said, is “particularly consequential on a peninsula where warning times are already measured in minutes.”
Cho expects AI to move from an experimental capability to a structural part of South Korea's defense posture, shaping how the country designs its military rather than simply being added to existing forces.
The Army's TIGER Plus blueprint, which targets force-wide application by 2040, already points in that direction.
AI could help accelerate the process from detecting a potential target to deciding how to respond, including by integrating information from reconnaissance satellites. It could also support military command decisions and use predictive logistics to identify equipment problems before they occur, she said.
“The trajectory points toward a smaller but more automated force, and toward autonomy becoming a component of Korea's defense-export offer as well,” Cho added.
But whether that transformation succeeds, she argued, will depend on more than technological capability.
“The decisive variable will be whether governance keeps pace with adoption – assurance and safety cases, doctrine and interoperability with the United States and other partners.”
Countries that deploy military AI “responsibly and demonstrably will also be the ones trusted as suppliers and allies,” she predicted.

Brazilian exports of meat and other animal products to the European Union have been suspended following the introduction of updated EU animal health and food safety requirements, but shipments can resume once Brazilian authorities demonstrate compliance with the new rules, the European Commission said Friday.
"Once they can show compliance, exports to the European Union of these products from Brazil will be able to resume," European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill told reporters in Brussels.
The EU suspended imports of Brazilian animals and animal-origin products intended for human consumption on Thursday, pending assurances that the country's exports comply with EU rules.
The measures affect products including beef, poultry, eggs, honey and animal casings.
EU rules require imports of animal-origin products for human consumption to meet the bloc's animal and public health standards, including requirements concerning residues from veterinary medicines.
Gill said the EU's rules on antimicrobial resistance apply equally and without discrimination to European producers and those from third countries seeking access to the bloc's single market.
He said the EU had engaged with its trading partners and provided support to help them meet the new requirements.

Netanyahu partners renew calls for removal of Gazans as Israeli election nears
JERUSALEM, Sept 4 - Two Israeli ministers floated proposals this week for the mass removal of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, resurfacing an idea voiced repeatedly by right-wing politicians over the past three years as they seek to rally supporters ahead of an election.
The calls by two of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political allies have revived Palestinian fears that Israel ultimately aims to forcibly expel them from Gaza despite U.S.-led diplomatic efforts to end the conflict there.
Far-right security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir laid out a seven-year plan for removing Gaza's population through "voluntary emigration" during a press conference on Thursday night. He said he would seek the creation of a "ministry in charge of emigration" in the next government.
"Instead of illusions of peace now, we need actions of emigration now," he said. "Instead of (them) digging tunnels, it’s time to pack suitcases," referring to tunnels dug under Gaza by Hamas before the war.
Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party said in a statement on Thursday that Turkey, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of Congo were being considered as potential destinations.
Ismail Al-Thawabta, director of the Hamas government media office, said: "The Palestinian people are deeply rooted in their land and will not be intimidated by such threats."
Israel is due to hold a general election on October 27. It will be the first since Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, triggered an Israeli military campaign that laid waste to Gaza, which has a population of more than two million.
An October 2025, U.S.-backed, ceasefire halted large-scale fighting, but it has not ended Israeli strikes or produced progress on a plan for permanent peace.
FEARS OF A NEW 'NAKBA'
Ben-Gvir's comments followed those of Defence Minister Israel Katz, from Netanyahu's Likud party, who said on Wednesday there was "no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration".
“We are fully prepared to move them out if it becomes possible — by sea, by air, by every way possible. Egypt is not willing, so it won’t be through them," he said during an online conference hosted by Israel’s Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper.
Netanyahu's office did not immediately provide comment.
Polls suggest Netanyahu, who has led the most right-wing coalition in Israeli history, could lose power next month, his security credentials still shaken by the 2023 attack — though analysts say he can't be written off.
Israel's defence ministry in 2025 established an office tasked with overseeing “voluntary emigration” from Gaza, after comments by U.S. President Donald Trump suggesting Gazans could be permanently displaced.
Trump later backed away from the idea, which faced strong resistance from Arab states and was widely rejected internationally. Israel reportedly sounded out several African countries as potential resettlement sites.
Netanyahu has said he supports what his government has described as "voluntary emigration" from Gaza, but that far-right ministers' goals of re-establishing Jewish settlements in the territory are unrealistic. Israeli officials have denied intending to transfer Gaza's population out by force.
Calls for resettlement of Gazans have prompted fears among Palestinians of a new "Nakba" (catastrophe), the name given to the displacement of hundreds of thousands of Palestinians who fled or were driven from their homes in the wake of the 1948 war that accompanied the founding of the state of Israel.
The Gaza Strip is central to Palestinian hopes of statehood in territory captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.
GENOCIDE ACCUSATIONS
The 2023 Hamas-led attacks killed 1,200 people in Israel while another 251 were taken hostage, according to Israeli tallies.
More than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel's military campaign, according to Gaza health authorities.
A U.N. inquiry determined that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, arguing that its killings, siege and destruction were carried out with the intent to destroy Palestinian life in the enclave.
Israel, which is fighting a genocide case at the International Court of Justice, rejects genocide allegations as politically motivated and says that its military campaign targets Hamas, not Gaza’s civilian population.
This week, Ben-Gvir posted an AI-generated video depicting dozens of Palestinian prisoners on a conveyor belt, entering a prison facility. They emerge from the other side emaciated, distressed and in tears.
Ben-Gvir later deleted the video, after it had amassed millions of views on X. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In a crowded Gaza City displacement camp, some Palestinians said that they believed the latest Israeli calls were an election ploy.
They also said Gaza was their land and they would never leave it.
"We will die on the land of Gaza," said one resident, 52-year-old Mohammed Abu Al-Qumbuz. "We were born on it, our children grew up on it, so it is very difficult to think of leaving." REUTERS

Kyiv schools are gradually returning to in-person learning — 11 institutions will remain online
Kyiv • UNN
In Kyiv, most schools are gradually transitioning to in-person learning with safety considerations in mind. Eleven institutions will remain online due to the lack of shelters.
After the first week of the school year, schools in Kyiv are gradually returning students to in-person learning, taking the security situation into account. The Kyiv City State Administration reported this, UNN writes.
In total, more than 248,000 students study at 412 schools in the capital. This week, more than 45% of schoolchildren studied in person in shelters—mostly primary school students; nearly 30% studied in a blended format, more than 17% remotely, and another 7% according to an individual learning format. Now, students in grades 5–11 are also returning to in-person learning in most schools
At the same time, 11 Kyiv schools will continue studying remotely for now. These are primarily institutions that do not have their own shelters and, for various reasons, are unable to set them up on their premises.
Previously, during air raid alerts, students at such schools could move to the nearest shelters at metro stations. However, due to the changing nature of military threats, this model is no longer a safe option for organizing the educational process.
Valentyn Mondryivskyi, Deputy Head of the Kyiv City State Administration, emphasized that the format of schooling may continue to change. At the same time, the safety of children and employees of educational institutions remains the main criterion.

Finland holds Europe’s largest civil defence drill since WWII
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
15:54:36 EEST
21:54:36 KST

More than 2,000 people took part in a civil defence exercise in Kuopio this week, testing how authorities and residents would respond to cyberattacks, infrastructure failures and the threat of missile strikes. Organisers described Shelter 2026 as Europe’s largest civil defence exercise since the Second World War.
The exercise centred on Luola, an underground sports and events complex in the Savilahti district.
The facility, completed two years ago, serves as a sports centre during normal conditions but converts into a civil defence shelter during an emergency.
Students from Savonia University of Applied Sciences, Savo Vocational College and Luovi Vocational College were among those taking part.
Participants received instructions at around 11.30am on Wednesday to move to the shelter. They had around 30 minutes to reach Luola, where the shelter doors were then closed for about two hours.
The exercise simulated cyberattacks that had disrupted electricity and water supplies in Kuopio while authorities faced an increased threat of missile strikes.
Inside Luola, organisers divided the main sports hall into sections holding around 200 people each. Participants had to share a limited number of dry toilets, and there were not enough beds for everyone to sleep at the same time.
More than 100 people remained underground overnight as the exercise continued into Thursday morning.
Luola holds around 2,500 people during normal operations and has space for up to 7,000 during emergency conditions. The facility has drawn attention outside Finland because of its dual civilian and emergency role.
Finnish conscripts wearing protective suits practised measuring radiation levels inside the shelter. Doors at the site are designed to provide protection during nuclear or biological emergencies.
Retired Army Colonel Asko Muhonen, who helped organise the exercise, told the Associated Press that Finland’s preparedness depends not only on the armed forces but also on civilians accepting responsibility during a crisis.
He said Finland has also studied lessons from Ukraine, where residents facing missile attacks often have only minutes to reach underground stations, car parks or other shelters.
The exercise took place as Finland continues to expand civil and military preparedness following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Finland shares a border of about 1,340 kilometres with Russia and joined NATO in April 2023.
Organisers also used the drill to test how ordinary residents would cope when public services were disrupted. Finland’s emergency preparedness guidance advises households to be ready to manage for at least 72 hours without outside assistance during disruptions to electricity, water or other services.

EU sends more aid to Nepal to care for flood survivors

12:53:57 UTC
21:53:57 KST

As families across Nepal face the human toll of one of the country's deadliest floods in decades, the EU is adding to the relief effort led by Nepalese authorities and humanitarian partners. A first EU humanitarian air bridge flight is delivering 82 tonnes of essential supplies, while the European Commission is providing a further €500,000 for response and coordinating further help offered by European countries.
Organised with UNICEF, the Air Bridge flight has landed this morning carrying supplies for nutrition, health, water and sanitation, shelter, education and protection from EU stocks. The additional €500,000 will be channelled through the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies' disaster response emergency fund, allowing local teams to cover urgent needs. Separately, through the EU civil protection mechanism, Luxembourg, Germany, Latvia and Norway are sending equipment including life jackets, hygiene and kitchen kits, blankets, medical supplies, protective equipment and emergency energy equipment.
This further assistance builds on the EU response already underway. On 28 August, the Commission allocated €2 million in emergency humanitarian aid, on top of almost €3 million already allocated to Nepal in 2026 for disaster preparedness. EU-funded partners have been providing assistance on the ground, while Copernicus emergency satellite mapping has been activated and the EU Rapid Response and Logistic Coordinators for Asia are deployed.
Commissioner for Crisis Management Hadja Lahbib said:
‘In a single night, rivers of mud and water swept away what generations had built: homes, schools, entire communities. Nepal has suffered a devastating loss of life, and thousands of families are facing the unimaginable. The grief is only beginning to sink in. Europe stands with the Nepalese people. We are supporting emergency responders and getting emergency aid to those who need it: clean water, medicine for hospitals, shelter for families sleeping in the open, and psychological support for the grieving. European solidarity crosses oceans. We will help Nepal not just survive this tragedy, but rebuild. Stronger and never alone.’
Background
The European Commission's emergency response coordination centre operates 24/7; it ensures rapid deployment of emergency support and acts as a coordination hub between all EU Member States, the 10 additional participating states, the affected country, and civil protection and humanitarian aid experts.

BIRMINGHAM, England — Nigel Farage dined with business executives Thursday night — and seemed determined not to allow Reform UK’s party conference to be commandeered by a swirling new scandal. But by Friday morning, two of his closest advisers were gone.
Jukes is known as Farage’s most loyal attack dog — a communications chief who began unflinchingly batting for his boss as a teenager and has lasted for more than a decade in the Farage orbit. They are so close that their relationship is often spoken of as being more like father and son. Orr was Reform’s big policy brain. A Cambridge academic who was leading work to build a robust platform for governance, Orr is a theologian with deep links into the MAGA movement, including a friendship with U.S. Vice President JD Vance.
Advertisement
Aides had billed this get-together of the party faithful as the moment Farage got “serious” after a summer dominated by his Clacton by-election battle against comedy candidate Count Binface. That was a fight Farage started himself to try to extinguish separate allegations he had failed to declare millions of pounds in donations from crypto businessman Christopher Harborne.
Now fresh headlines in which Farage insists the party has “broken no laws” and denies his team has taken any “dodgy money” are overshadowing the right-wing outfit’s Birmingham gathering.
‘Clandestine projects’
Smoked trout and fillet of beef was on the menu Thursday evening as anxious attendees of the Reform UK business dinner at the National Exhibition Centre watched the Channel 4 footage of the sting on their phones.
There was Orr caught on camera arranging potentially rule-breaking funding from a foreign benefactor — via a middle-man in the U.K — to produce favorable polling. There was Jukes discussing “little clandestine projects” that he deems “so valuable” to the party.
There was Farage, too, speaking to a fake U.S. donor in his Clacton constituency, appearing to celebrate the great “bang for buck” that the poll — carried in national newspapers with no declaration of its links to Reform UK — had provided.
Jukes was uncharacteristically not seen at Farage’s side during Thursday night’s dinner. He had been there at his boss’s drinks with political editors shortly before the investigation aired. But his presence on the mind of Reform’s top brass was evident.
“The impression over dinner was Nigel was going to back them to the hilt,” said one senior figure in the party who was present at the business event. They were granted anonymity like others in this article to speak frankly about an internal party matter. The argument was that there had been “no law breaking” and that Farage could stand by the embattled duo.
“Different combinations of [deputy leader Richard] Tice, Orr etc. were regularly stepping away from tables, having hushed chats in the corners, then coming back,” said a second attendee. “They didn’t acknowledge or mention it to anyone, they certainly weren’t laughing it off.”
Meanwhile, there was what one invitee described as a “watch party” of the Channel 4 footage in a hotel room, where senior officials discussed how to handle the situation.
At the fifth-floor Sky Bar where many of the conference revelers gathered, senior figures in the party were asking each other “how bad is bad?” over 11.30 p.m. gin and tonics.
Most were insistent the row would blow over. If the support for Orr felt more rudimentary, the expectation that Jukes would be fine seemed certain.
Advertisement
“At the bars it was obviously the central topic of conversation, but I don’t think anyone predicted that this morning Orr and Jukes would resign,” the second business dinner attendee said. “The assumption was they would try and brush off and basically fight back, say it’s a hoax etc.”
By breakfast there was clarity. Ed Sumner, now indisputably Farage’s most senior communications adviser, spent his birthday morning confirming Jukes and Orr had “stepped down” pending an internal investigation.
“The party believes it is important that the investigation is allowed to proceed independently and without prejudice. No further comment will be made while the investigation is ongoing,” read a statement.
What prompted the about-turn was unclear, but one senior adviser said Jukes is a “rational thinker,” adding: “When the time was up, he knew the time was up.”
The fightback
After the defiance over late-night drinks at the Sky Bar, talk of a fightback came at Friday morning’s breakfast buffet. Reform remains neck-and-neck with the governing Labour Party in the polls, and had intended to use Friday to show their readiness for government.
“No way is our conference going to get derailed by some stupid posh boy and a Channel 4 investigation,” fumed one of Reform’s gruffer, high-profile champions.
Advertisement
Lee Anderson, who serves as Reform UK’s chief whip, told broadcasters “there’s no chance” of Orr or Jukes coming back — but privately some at the top of the party are holding out for exactly that.
The senior figure quoted above predicted the loss of the two aides represented a “tactical retreat” to “take the heat off today” — a “temporary thing,” where an investigation paves the way for a potential return.
They also discussed how the party might go on the attack, trying to paint the investigation carried out by journalists at Verbatim, an organization founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, as the work of an “activist.” One Reform MP was overheard reassuring a supporter of Jukes, “It’s alright — we’ll look after him.”
Tice, who serves as Farage’s deputy, publicly made the case that Channel 4 itself may have “broken the rules” with an “entrapment” operation.
But there was no doubt the conference mood had been sullied. “What a sh*tshow,” raged one prospective candidate for Westminster as he joined the long queue into the venue.
The senior party figure who spoke of a tactical retreat described Orr as a “very good interlocutor between different people in the party,” a particularly crucial role considering some of the fractures involving Farage’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf.
Advertisement
“He gets on with Nigel, he gets on with Zia. So he would sort of broker stuff,” the figure said of Orr. “It will be a major loss.”
Farage’s set-piece conference moment with Jordan Bardella, the president of France’s far-right National Rally party, now comes against the backdrop of scandal. And the scrutiny is unlikely to die down beyond Birmingham. Farage separately expects to be interviewed by parliament’s standards commissioner over the Harborne funding row in the next few weeks.
“We clearly need not to create negative headlines that make it harder for people of all stripes [to support us], whether they’re from the respectable tendency or anti-establishment people, who don’t like stories of dodgy money and all that,” the senior party figure said. “It’s bad from all points of view.”

US envoys headed to Russia and Ukraine to relaunch mediation
The return of Washington’s negotiators raises hope of progress towards a settlement to end Moscow’s war on Ukraine.
United States envoys are expected to arrive in Kyiv and Moscow over the weekend, in an apparent bid to revive negotiations aimed at ending Russia’s war on Ukraine.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said late on Thursday that US negotiators were set for meetings in both capitals “in the coming days” and that Ukraine is ready for substantive, high-level negotiations.

Russia’s state news agency TASS reported on Friday that Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner would be in Moscow on September 5 and 6.
President Donald Trump’s envoys, who have not previously visited Kyiv, were most recently in the Russian capital in January. However, Washington’s mediation efforts have all but halted since the US and Israel launched war on Iran in March.

Strikes persist
However, in the eight months since Witkoff and Kushner were last in Moscow, Russia and Ukraine have ramped up air attacks deep inside the other’s territory and at sea, as well as the fighting along the front line in eastern Ukraine.
Russian attacks overnight killed at least three people in Ukraine, local officials said on Friday. Moscow’s forces have relentlessly struck civilian areas over the four and a half years since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
A “massive” overnight Russian attack on the southern Odesa region killed one person and injured at least five others, including a child, regional head Oleh Kiper said in a post on Telegram. The attacks damaged multiple residential buildings, including two multistorey blocks.
Strikes in Dnipro in the east killed two police officers, officials said, while a drone attack in Kyiv injured three people after hitting a residential building.
Ukraine, meanwhile, continues to concentrate strikes on Russia’s energy infrastructure and other economic targets, as it seeks to drain Moscow’s funding for its war and encourage public anger over the conflict and its impact on the Russian population.
A large-scale Ukrainian drone strike hit the Black Sea resort city of Sochi and the nearby district of Sirius, regional officials said, with fires reported at both locations.

Brazil’s EU ambassador, Pedro Miguel da Costa e Silva, told Euronews "all options are on the table" after Brasília threatened retaliation over the EU’s ban on Brazilian meat imports due to antibiotic use.
Brazil’s EU ambassador, Pedro Miguel da Costa e Silva, told Euronews on Friday that an inspection of Brazilian meat was unnecessary, and signalled that “all options are on the table” for Brazil to respond if the EU ban remains in place.
The European Commission’s decision came into force this week, after Brazil was removed from a list of countries complying with EU food safety rules over its use of antibiotics to stimulate animal growth.
The EU ban prompted anger from the Brazilian government on Thursday, which threatened to adopt countermeasures.
"There wasn't a need for an audit, not for poultry, not for honey, not bovine meat, because no audits were conducted for the other countries," da Costa e Silva said. "We have provided sufficient guarantees."
An EU audit of Brazilian poultry and honey is ongoing, but the Commission said that Brasília had not provided guarantees that would allow for an audit of its beef.
The ambassador added that while Brazil will continue discussing the issue with the Commission, and that "all options were on the table” if the imports did not resume.
The Commission pushed back on Friday against Brasília's accusation of unfair treatment, with the Commission's deputy Chief spokesperson Olof Gill saying: “Our approach is non-discriminatory, and we've given our partners sufficient time and all the information they need to adjust."
The dispute comes as a free trade deal between Mercosur countries — Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay — and the EU provisionally came into force in May, despite strong opposition from EU farmers, who fear that Latin American products that do not comply with the bloc’s phytosanitary and food safety standards will be dumped in Europe.
"Food safety rules are a matter of the highest priority for EU citizens," Gill added. "These rules have been well known for a long time, with third countries having been informed going back many years."
The EU introduced new rules to combat antimicrobial resistance in 2018, which have been applied to EU producers since 2022 and to foreign importers since Thursday.

Migrants accused of beating baby dolphin to death in Spain (VIDEO)
A group of migrants in the Spanish North African enclave of Ceuta have been accused of pulling a baby dolphin from the sea and beating it to death, after disturbing footage sparked outrage online.
The bottlenose dolphin calf was spotted swimming close to the shore at El Trampolin beach on Wednesday before several men dragged it from the water, according to local newspaper El Faro de Ceuta. One of them allegedly struck the animal in the head with a stick, leaving it mortally wounded.
A beach worker reportedly confronted the group and told them not to touch the dolphin and to call wildlife services. They then tried to return it to the sea, but the animal appeared already dead.
Ceuta-based blogger Juan Ruiz filmed members of the group raising the dolphin like a trophy as he approached them. “You can’t take that, it’s a dolphin, you don’t eat that!” he shouted, before demanding to know who had killed it.
When people in the group apparently claimed the animal had already been dead in the water, Ruiz responded sarcastically: “Yeah, it died in the water on its own, right.”
Local environmental group DAUBMA has filed a complaint with Spanish law enforcement, demanding the authorities investigate the incident and identify those involved.
The footage triggered widespread anger on Spanish social media, with users calling for those involved to be prosecuted and expelled from the country. The reaction has fed into broader anti-immigrant sentiment in Ceuta, where residents have already marched demanding deportations and chanting “Out with the invaders.”
Ceuta has been gripped by chaos since an unprecedented migrant influx from neighboring Morocco in late July, when around 72,000 people crossed into the tiny Spanish territory.

Israeli-backed militia kills Islamic Jihad member in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:46:08 UTC
21:46:08 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli-backed militia kills PIJ member in Gaza amid string of attacks by Tel Aviv's proxy forces
An Israeli-backed Palestinian militia killed a member of the Al-Quds Brigades, the armed wing of the Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ), on Friday during an attempt to abduct him in al-Qarara, north of Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip, according to the group.
In a press statement, the Al-Quds Brigades said a militia force advanced towards al-Qarara at dawn, with support from Israeli drones, in an attempt to abduct one of its members.
The Al-Quds Brigades said its fighters detected the force and engaged it with grenades and medium weapons at close range.
Several militia members were killed or wounded before Israeli drones intervened to cover their withdrawal, according to the group.
The drones then allegedly killed Fadi al-Abadla, a member of the Al-Qarara Battalion of the Khan Younis Brigade, leaving his body at the scene, according to the statement. The militia withdrew with its dead and wounded.
There was no immediate comment from the Israeli military or the alleged militia.
Separately, speaking with The New Arab, local residents in Khan Younis said they heard gunfire and clashes in al-Qarara during the early morning, coinciding with the presence of Israeli drones.
One eyewitness said the area had recently seen a growing presence of armed groups, while residents were unable to identify the force or determine its objective.
The incident came two days after Moen al-Arabeed, head of Hamas's internal security apparatus in Gaza, was abducted from Gaza City.
Palestinian sources initially suggested Israeli-backed militias were responsible, but Hamas sources later said an Israeli special forces unit had carried out the operation directly.
The two incidents have brought renewed attention to the activities of Palestinian armed groups reportedly operating with Israeli support.
Israel's Palestinian proxies
An investigation published by Haaretz in late August, based on testimonies from Israeli soldiers and officers, satellite imagery and conversations with Gaza residents, identified five-armed militias operating at six locations across the Strip and receiving Israeli financial and military support.
According to the investigation, the Israeli army and Shin Bet maintain close coordination with the groups, which are primarily hostile to Hamas.
An Israeli Air Force officer quoted by Haaretz said the government, army and Shin Bet send armed and trained militias into Gaza to carry out security missions, while the Air Force is instructed to protect them during their operations.
The groups are tasked with pursuing Hamas and other Palestinian faction members, conducting raids and kidnappings, gathering intelligence and operating in areas where Israeli forces face difficulties moving directly, according to Haaretz.
They have also been accused of attacking Palestinian civilians, looting property and burning homes, as well as participating in efforts to drive residents from certain areas.
The Yasser Abu Shabab group has emerged as one of the most prominent of these formations. It operated mainly in southern Gaza, particularly Rafah, and openly acknowledged cooperation with Israel.
In July 2025, Abu Shabab told an Israeli television channel that his group received support from the Israeli military.
Despite Abu Shabab's subsequent death under unclear circumstances, Haaretz reported that Israel's militia strategy continued to develop, particularly following the October 2025 ceasefire.
The groups do not appear capable of replacing the Israeli military or independently controlling Gaza. Instead, their role appears focused on specific security and intelligence operations, allowing Israel to use local Palestinian actors against its opponents.
'Tools of Israel'
Gaza-based political analyst Ahed Ferwana told TNA that Israel's reliance on the militias forms part of a strategy to create local Palestinian forces capable of carrying out operations inside Gaza.
"The militias cannot be regarded as independent Palestinian forces given their Israeli funding, weapons and operational coordination," he said.
He warned that their expansion could deepen Palestinian divisions by shifting confrontation towards armed clashes between Palestinian groups.
Akram Attallah, a political analyst in Gaza, told TNA that the militias are "tools of Israel […] Tel Aviv uses them when it wants to conduct operations indirectly but deploys its own forces when an operation exceeds their capabilities".
Attallah said the abduction of Moen al-Arabeed demonstrated the overlap between direct Israeli military operations and those carried out through locally backed armed groups.
He added that Israel can shift between using Palestinian proxies and deploying its own forces depending on an operation's nature and scale, making the distinction between the militias and the Israeli military increasingly difficult to separate.
For Attallah, the development of these groups reflects a broader Israeli effort to create Palestinian actors capable of performing security functions inside Gaza, potentially reshaping the Strip's security landscape and deepening divisions between Palestinian factions.

Civil society opposition to Sudan's Burhan-led dialogue mounts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:43:35 UTC
21:43:35 KST

Breadcrumb
Sudan's civil society 'stronger than credited' as opposition mounts to Burhan's dialogue, AU Commission endorsement
Sudan's civil society is "stronger than people give it credit for", analysts told The New Arab, after a Sudanese political coalition condemned the endorsement of a new intra-Sudanese dialogue led by Abdel Fattah al-Burhan by the African Union's (AU) Commission.
The Sudanese Declaration of Principles coalition issued a formal complaint to the AU's Peace and Security Council on Wednesday over the commission's endorsement of Burhan's 'Sudanese-Sudanese dialogue.'
The coalition, made up of several political groups including the Somoud alliance and the Sudan Liberation Movement, accused the endorsement of contradicting previous AU statements on a humanitarian truce, effectively endorsing the partition of the country.
They also accused the commission of violating the 2021 suspension of Sudan from the AU that followed Burhan's coup against the civilian post-revolutionary government, and said the move gave political cover to Burhan's regime and neglected their own efforts to promote an alternative dialogue led by civil society.
Kholood Khair, founder and director of Confluence Advisory, a think-and-do-tank founded in Khartoum, told The New Arab: "The opposition believes it's important to register their lack of support for Burhan's process, but also register their discontent with the African Union because there have been concerns that the African Union would be pushing for recognition of Burhan's process as part of their efforts to bring about a national political process in Sudan."
The dialogue was announced by Burhan earlier in May with a stated intention of completing a transition to civilian rule.
The AU Commission said on Monday that it "welcomes" Burhan's initiative and that it "reinforces the African Union's roadmap and the track of the Quintet Mechanism within a coherent strategy led by Sudanese stakeholders."
The Quintet, which includes the AU, UN, Intergovernmental Authority on Development, EU and Arab League, was formed to bring about an end to the war that erupted in 2023 after fighting broke out between the Sudanese army and the rival Rapid Support Forces.
Khair explained that Burhan's initiative initially excluded most of Sudan's anti-military opposition, but later gave amnesty to groups and figures to participate in the dialogue.
"The problem with that is that, if some agreed and came and accepted temporary immunity, it would be like them accepting they had actually done wrong, that they had deserved the indictments in the first place, that they had been guilty of crimes, and that they were now coming to the talk in part so they would not be liable for prosecution."
Khair added that former dictator Omar al-Bashir, who was ousted in a revolution that preceded the 2021 coup and civil war, did a similar thing between 2014 and 2017: "we've seen this all before."
Leena Badri, a nonresident fellow for TIMEP, told The New Arab that the condemnation from the group was "no surprise", given the opposition's aversion to the Sudanese Armed Forces and the former National Congress Party that had for decades ruled the country.
"They envision that such efforts [by Burhan] carry a high risk of normalising the return of individuals formally affiliated with the party, in addition to normalising military rule and control over a political process."
African Union Commission endorsement 'win' for Burhan, but civilians needed for government
Badri added that the commission's endorsement was a "win for the SAF [Sudanese armed forces] because it offers legitimacy to their political efforts, and solidifies their position as being a party capable of developing and seeking out processes for dialogue and incorporating civilians into that process".
Sudan's armed forces have, in recent months, won a string of battlefield victories against the RSF, reconnecting a vital road between the semi-besieged city of El-Obeid in North Kordofan and Omdurman, the sister city of the capital Khartoum.
The army has also taken in a wave of defections from the RSF, despite the group's moves to form and solidify its own parallel government.
Despite the battlefield success, however, Khair said that the opposition's statement against the initiative and the AU Commission's endorsement show that "civil society has been stronger than people give it credit for, and that's what has changed since the revolution".
"The war, despite wanting to diminish the power of civilian actors, has not managed to do that," she said, adding, "even if Burhan makes territorial gains, he will not be able to rule without some kind of buy-in from civilian actors and politicians."
Further complicating the situation is the fact that the endorsement of the AU Commission of Burhan's dialogue reveals "a bit of schizophrenia within the AU", where one side of the body has moved against Burhan politically while the other endorses it.
Khair explained that the AU Commissioner, Mahmoud Ali Yousif, is pro-Burhan, but that his position runs against major concerns within the AU about legitimising coups and the formation of parallel governments in Africa, which has been rocked by several coups across the continent, in particular the Sahel, in recent years.
"The biggest danger is actually that the AU can undermine itself and it can undermine the quintet," in their efforts to push for a peace process.
The backlash to Burhan's initiative has also prompted rumours that those involved in the process may pull out on grounds that being involved with the military is becoming a huge liability.
Ultimately, Khair said that the opposition's condemnation of both processes has revealed that "It's very difficult for armed actors now in Sudan to rule by themselves as a result of the popular political movement that has been a key part of civilian Sudanese politics since the revolution".

U.S. Air Force’s EC-130H flies final mission alongside EA-37B
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:43:04 UTC
21:43:04 KST

- A U.S. Air Force EC-130H flew its final flight on September 3, in formation for the first time with its EA-37B replacement over Southern Arizona.
- The EC-130H has flown the Compass Call electronic attack mission since 1982, while the EA-37B has flown its own combat missions against Iran since March.
A U.S. Air Force EC-130H Compass Call aircraft flew in formation with an EA-37B Compass Call for the first time on September 3, in what the Air Force identified as the EC-130H’s final flight, marking the end of the propeller-driven aircraft’s role in the service’s electronic attack mission.
Both aircraft belong to the 55th Electronic Combat Group, flying together over Southern Arizona near the group’s base at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base. The formation flight represented the handoff between the two aircraft types: the EC-130H, a modified C-130 that has flown the Compass Call jamming mission since 1982, and the EA-37B, its Gulfstream G550-based successor.
The Compass Call mission disrupts, denies and degrades enemy command-and-control networks, using electronic attack to jam communications and radar systems that adversaries rely on to coordinate their forces. The 55th Electronic Combat Group, a geographically separated unit under the 55th Wing at Offutt Air Force Base, Nebraska, has been the Air Force’s only unit flying that mission.
The Air Force began retiring individual EC-130H aircraft years ago as EA-37Bs entered service. The 43rd Electronic Combat Squadron flew its last EC-130H mission in February 2024, becoming the first squadron under the 55th Electronic Combat Group to complete the switch. By this past spring, only a handful of EC-130H aircraft remained in the fleet, according to earlier reporting on the transition. The Air Force plans to field 10 EA-37Bs in total.
The EA-37B has already flown in combat. Two of the aircraft deployed from Davis-Monthan through RAF Mildenhall in the United Kingdom to Souda Bay, Crete, in late March, then entered the fight against Iran as part of Operation Epic Fury, which began February 28. Their mission there mirrored the EC-130H’s traditional role: jamming enemy communications and blinding air defense radar.
Over nearly four decades, EC-130H aircraft supported combat operations including Desert Storm, Iraqi Freedom, Enduring Freedom and Inherent Resolve. One of the type’s original aircraft, tail number 1587, flew close to 29,000 hours before its own retirement in 2020, including almost 11,000 hours in direct support of combat missions.

Spain will send Ukraine more Patriot interceptor missiles, Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares confirmed, according to Le Monde.
Patriot interceptors are among the few weapons Ukraine has that can stop Russian ballistic missiles. The specialized rounds are scarce worldwide, and manufacturer Raytheon cannot build them fast enough to meet demand. Each costs $3 million to $4 million.
Spain confirms the flow will grow
Albares spoke at an informal meeting of European Union foreign ministers in Ireland on 2 September. He reaffirmed Madrid's support as Kyiv pressed for more interceptors. "We have been doing this for a long time, and we will continue to do so," he said. He confirmed that Madrid is preparing a new batch. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc is also working with non-member states to lift Ukraine's air defenses.
Madrid and Kyiv meet in Wicklow
The confirmation followed talks with Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. They met on the sidelines of the same EU gathering, in Wicklow. Sybiha said he pressed Ukraine's urgent need to strengthen its air and ballistic missile defenses. He also thanked Spain for its solidarity. Albares reaffirmed Spain's role as a founding member of the Integrated Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, which ten countries launched in Paris on 13 July. The group aims to build a shared anti-ballistic capability, and its declaration calls the coalition purely defensive. Spanish military instructors are training Ukrainian technicians to maintain the systems.
What Spain has promised so far
Spain is not just giving—it is also buying. In December 2025, Madrid signed a $1.7 billion contract with US arms maker Raytheon for four new Patriot systems. It was Spain's largest Patriot order yet. The deal covers radars, launchers, command-and-control stations, and training. Spanish firm Sener builds the control system for the GEM-T interceptor those launchers fire. Spain is one of only a handful of European countries that operate Patriots.
What Spain has already sent
Spain has supplied Ukraine with Patriot missiles before. In March, Madrid pledged five older PAC-2 interceptors from an air-defense artillery regiment at Marines, near Valencia. Madrid has pledged €1 billion ($1.16 billion) in military aid for 2026. Ukraine has spent months urging partners to release interceptors from their stockpiles.

EU court rules against Lithuania’s sanctions on Russia -linked energy company
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:42:00 UTC
21:42:00 KST

The European Union’s top court ruled Thursday that the EU or an individual member state cannot sanction an EU-based company solely because it is indirectly owned by the Russian state.
The ruling came in a dispute between Lithuania’s Financial Crime Investigation Service (FNTT), and Inter RAO Lietuva, an electricity supplier controlled by Russian energy giant Inter RAO.
The European Court of Justice said the control of a company by a person subject to EU restrictive measures must be established through objective and sufficiently strong evidence.
“The autocratic nature of the Russian political regime is not, in itself, sufficiently strong evidence capable of establishing that the Russian president controls a company,” the court said in a statement.
The case was referred to the EU court by Lithuania’s Supreme Administrative Court, which suspended proceedings last year while seeking clarification on how EU sanctions rules should be applied.
Lithuanian authorities had argued that Russian President Vladimir Putin could influence decisions at Inter RAO Lietuva even without direct ownership or capital links to the company.
The European court rejected the argument that the autocratic and oligarchic nature of Russia’s political system was sufficient on its own to establish such control.
Lithuania’s Supreme Administrative Court will now have to issue a final ruling in the dispute, taking the EU court’s interpretation into account.
Inter RAO Lietuva is 51% owned by Finland-based RAO Nordic, which is controlled by Inter RAO. The Russian energy company’s board is headed by Igor Sechin, a Russian oligarch who is under Western sanctions over his ties to the Kremlin.
FNTT restricted Inter RAO Lietuva’s ability to conduct banking transactions in March 2022, citing its links to Sechin. In May of that year, the agency said it had frozen the company’s funds, shares and real estate.
The measures were subsequently linked to Putin rather than Sechin.
The ruling could affect how Lithuanian authorities assess sanctions involving companies with indirect ownership or alleged links to sanctioned Russian individuals and entities.

New Stryker brigade at Fort Carson receives first vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:40:09 UTC
21:40:09 KST

- The newly redesignated 3rd Stryker Brigade, 4th Infantry Division, began receiving Stryker vehicles at Fort Carson, Colorado, on September 2.
- The brigade, formerly an armored unit built around M1A2 Abrams tanks, completed its conversion after testing at Fort Irwin's Project Convergence Capstone 6 exercise.
Soldiers assigned to the newly redesignated 3rd Stryker Brigade, 4th Infantry Division, began receiving Stryker vehicles at Fort Carson, Colorado, on September 2, marking the next step in the unit’s conversion from a tank formation to a wheeled Stryker force.
The brigade, known as the Iron Brigade, previously operated as the 3rd Armored Brigade Combat Team, built around M1A2 Abrams tanks and Bradley Fighting Vehicles. Its last Abrams tank left Fort Carson in mid-July, heading to Fort Irwin, California, for Project Convergence Capstone 6, an exercise where the brigade tested emerging technology including a new digital command-and-control system before completing its final conversion steps and taking on the Stryker Brigade designation.
The tanks the brigade gave up are headed to Army depots for overhaul, after which they will be redistributed to other armored units across the service, according to earlier Army reporting on the transition.
With Strykers now arriving at Fort Carson, soldiers will move into new equipment training, platform familiarization and leader development, covering vehicle capabilities, maintenance and digital systems. The Army has said the brigade will also see a personnel realignment as infantry soldiers arrive to fill out the battalions needed for a Stryker-based force structure, which relies more heavily on dismounted infantry than an armored formation built around tanks.
The Stryker is an eight-wheeled, armored combat vehicle that trades the heavier armor and firepower of a tank for greater speed and lower logistical demands, letting units move under their own power over longer distances instead of requiring the heavy-equipment transporters and rail movements that come with fielding tanks.
The conversion is tied to a larger organizational shift. The 4th Infantry Division has been reassigned to America’s First Corps, which supports U.S. Army Pacific, a headquarters focused on projecting land power across the Pacific and sustaining a regional military presence. Army officials have said the Iron Brigade’s move to Strykers is meant to give the division a more rapidly deployable, digitally connected force to support that mission.
“We absolutely honor the legacy of the 3rd Armored Brigade and their storied history,” said early Col. Nick Sinclair, the brigade’s commander, in July as the unit prepared for its final conversion steps. The brigade has spent decades as one of the Army’s principal armored formations, deploying to the Middle East and Europe and rotating repeatedly through the Army’s National Training Center.

Seeds of hope: how a local farming project is offering a lifeline to Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
12:37:57 UTC
21:37:57 KST

Salama Ayesh Muhanna still remembers the first seeds he planted on his family’s land in al-Qarara, Gaza. At just 17, Muhanna had proudly sprouted cucumbers.
“I was very happy because I saw the results,” Muhanna says. “We were farmers at heart.”
Now 71, he is an agronomist, a community leader and the founder of the Al-Qarara Seed Bank.
The original project, founded in 2017, was situated near the eastern border of Gaza in al-Qarara, an area now completely flattened and inaccessible. Back then, Muhanna had a large home, olive trees, land of his own, and a successful seed bank operation with dedicated storage and equipment. Everything was destroyed early in Israel’s brutal military campaign, but after being displaced to Deir al-Balah in 2024, Muhanna and his daughter Hanadi, 38, are now hard at work, regrowing seed collections at Gaza’s only seed bank.
Outside the tent where they currently live in a displacement camp, summer temperatures climb to almost 35C. Another tent houses their small but growing collection of open-pollinated, non-GMO seeds, including local wheat and vegetables such as okra and spinach.
Each day, Muhanna rises early to check on the project, a 200-metre-wide plot of land where the family lives, collects seeds, and experiments with new crops. He inspects the seeds to assess their quality, waters crops and checks on seedlings. As the manager of the seed bank, Hanadi deals with local farmers and oversees the growing seed collection – all while studying agriculture and food sovereignty online via a programme partly tied to Coventry University and the Gaza Urban Agriculture Forum. Muhanna jokes that his hard-working daughter will be “managing her father” by next year.
The project has two main aims. One is to collect and preserve the seeds of local plants that may thrive better in this landscape. “The war forced farmers to resort to local seeds,” says Hanadi, because of the ongoing blockades on seed imports, rocketing food prices and growing hunger across Gaza. Yet it appears that this focus on local seed varieties – “baladi” seeds – may prove more effective. That, Muhanna says, is because “local seeds are resistant to drought, fungi, and pests”.
“During the war, they’ve been our lifeline,” he adds.
The project’s other aim is to create a node for seed distribution for farmers who need to save every possible penny. The seeds, once collected, are distributed among Palestinian farmers and families in Deir al-Balah who then return the same amount after harvest. Approximately 200 farmers have so far benefited thanks to Muhanna and Hanadi’s seeds, with support from the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). Beyond multiplying seed collections, it is helping Palestinian farmers reclaim agricultural agency and self-reliance – providing for families despite devastating restrictions on resources including vital humanitarian aid.
The seeds are deeply connected to memories of the Palestinian land Muhanna has always called home – and could, he hopes, be key to future food sovereignty in Gaza. “The pumpkin plant reminds me of my father and mother,” he says. “It grew on the vineyard where we lived when I was little.”
The needs have never been more urgent. At least 1.2 million people in Gaza now face acute food insecurity amid an escalating humanitarian crisis, according to a new report by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC). Despite growing alarm among humanitarian organisations, Israel continues to block access to agricultural land and the import of seeds and organic fertiliser. Meanwhile, dwindling water supplies, degraded soil and deadly remnants of explosives make farming a treacherous practice.
“Walking in the streets is unsafe, and walking on the land is unsafe,” Muhanna says, adding that the psychological impact affects their work. “The war destroyed my hope.”
Despite immense challenges, the family know their seeds are helping the community while preserving indigenous species against agricultural monopolies, and safeguarding Palestine’s agricultural heritage.
As Muhanna puts it, seeds are “my identity, my patriotism, my nationality”.
Pat Griffiths, ICRC’ spokesperson in Jerusalem, said: “This is about agency. It’s about dignity. It’s about being less dependent on what is or is not allowed to enter Gaza. As the occupying power, Israel has an obligation to make sure that Palestinians in Gaza have access to the food, goods and items that they need to live.”
There is still a long way to go in returning the seed bank to its former size. Muhanna says that before the war, they had about 42 types of local seeds. “Now we have about 28.”
There is also another looming challenge that could affect the seed bank’s future.
“Climate change is what controls us,” Muhanna says, as he sips his tea and shelters inside from the sun. “When the weather is hot, the seeds spoil.” Sometimes he has to plant almost a month later than normal, delaying harvests in a race against time to gather resilient seeds for the future. Still they keep going, experimenting in their fields to see which local seeds produce the best yields. And with almost 2.5 tonnes of seeds collected so far – better than last year – there are signs that the efforts are working.
With each seed, there is hope in Gaza that sovereignty over food security can soon take root.
“Any country in the world that doesn’t have sovereignty over food security isn’t a country,” Muhanna says. “If we establish sovereignty over food security, then we’ll be a real country.”
