Ali said the family's pursuit of justice in the US has so far produced no results.
“I think this is an extremely hypocritical stance. But it is not surprising. We have seen this for the past 20 years, ever since Rachel Corrie,” he said.
Corrie was an American peace activist killed by an Israeli bulldozer in Gaza in 2003 while trying to prevent the demolition of a Palestinian family's home.
“She was an American, born and raised in the US, and her parents were American too. Yet justice was not delivered for her either,” Ali said.
“This is disappointing and it makes me angry. But when it comes to Israel, this double standard is not surprising,” he added.
“Looking at America's approach towards Israel and its record of not holding it accountable, its talk about justice seems extremely hypocritical.”
Ali said they would continue seeking justice at both the state level in Washington and the federal level.
“We will continue doing this because we know the issue is not only Aysenur. It is everyone who has been unjustly killed around the world, including by Israel,” he said.
Killing of Aysenur Ezgi Eygi
Israeli soldiers opened fire during a peaceful demonstration in the occupied West Bank, seriously wounding Eygi, who had joined the protest in support of Palestinians and also held US citizenship.
Eygi was taken to a Palestinian hospital after being shot in the head and died on Sept. 6, 2024.
She was laid to rest in Didim, Aydin, on September 14.
Eygi was a human rights activist and volunteer with the International Solidarity Movement, which supports Palestinians through peaceful and civilian means against Israel's occupation of Palestinian territories.
Israel has killed more than 73,000 people and injured over 174,000 others in Gaza since October 8 2023.
Israeli army and illegal settler attacks in the occupied West Bank since the start of the Gaza genocide have killed more than 1,000 Palestinians and injured over 12,000 others, while around 24,000 have been arrested.

Association of Stevedoring Companies: Latvian grain is given priority at ports and is not displaced by transit cargo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:48:51 UTC
20:48:51 KST

Latvian grain shipments are not being displaced by transit cargo at ports, and the necessary capacity for handling domestic grain is being ensured, the Latvian Stevedoring Companies Association stresses, noting that Latvian-origin cargo is given priority during the grain season.
The Association explains that the primary function of Latvia’s ports and transport infrastructure is to serve the needs of the Latvian economy, including the import and export activities of domestic companies. Latvian grain represents one of the most significant seasonal cargo volumes, and ports, terminals and the railway therefore take these shipments into account in advance when planning their operations.
Members of the Latvian Stevedoring Companies Association confirm that domestic grain shipments are handled in accordance with the volumes that have been requested and agreed upon, and are not being displaced by transit cargo. Latvian grain is accepted and handled, while individual situations in which additional capacity is required at a particular terminal at a given time are resolved in cooperation with customers.
The Association stresses that the overall capacity of Latvian ports makes it possible to handle Latvian grain while simultaneously using available spare capacity for other types of cargo.
At the same time, terminal infrastructure, warehouses and workforce must be maintained throughout the year, even though the most intensive period for handling Latvian grain is seasonal. Therefore, spare port capacity is also used to handle legal transit cargo and grain originating from other countries.
According to the Association, a regular flow of cargo is essential for maintaining port infrastructure and the workforce throughout the year, which in turn enables ports to provide high-quality services for cargo handled on behalf of Latvian companies.
Regarding the control of transit cargo, the Latvian Stevedoring Companies Association notes that shipments are inspected in accordance with the responsibilities of the relevant authorities. Terminals cooperate with the Customs Board of the State Revenue Service, the Food and Veterinary Service and other competent authorities in verifying cargo documentation, origin and compliance with other requirements established by law.
The industry is interested in ensuring that controls are as effective as possible and that sanctioned cargo, cargo of non-compliant origin or otherwise illegal shipments do not enter Latvia’s transport system. If the competent authorities and experts conclude that additional control mechanisms are necessary, stevedoring companies are prepared to cooperate in their implementation.
The Association stresses that the industry’s task is to maintain a safe, economically viable transport system that remains accessible to Latvian businesses, while preserving priority for Latvian cargo and making efficient use of available infrastructure capacity.

====================================================================================================

This UAE-backed Fatah dissident is allying with Hamas and pushing a proposal to change Palestinian politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:48:06 UTC
20:48:06 KST

The Palestinian legislative elections scheduled for next November are already shaking up Palestinian politics in ways not seen in years, with different actors across the Palestinian political spectrum making power moves in an attempt to secure their position within a shifting political landscape in the fallout from the Gaza genocide. The latest of these moves is the announcement of a plan by UAE-based dissident Fatah leader Muhammad Dahlan to “end Palestinian division.”
Dahlan’s plan is more than an election program, going so far as to propose a complete remaking of the Palestinian political system and a change to the decades-old way power balances have been managed in Palestinian institutions.
Dahlan’s move doesn’t come in a vacuum. It follows the earlier announcement of an electoral alliance between Hamas, the Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ), and the two main dissident currents in Fatah — one led by former Palestinian diplomat and nephew of the late Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat, Nasser Al-Qudwah, and the other led by Dahlan.
The alliance brings together most of the main Palestinian political forces, with the exception of the leftist factions and the dominant Fatah leadership of Mahmoud Abbas, who runs the Palestinian Authority (PA) and serves as its President.
Dahlan’s plan hasn’t been endorsed yet by his electoral allies, but they haven’t disavowed it either. The presentation of the plan right after forming the alliance establishes Dahlan as the alliance’s leading figure and puts him at the center of the Palestinian political game, closer than ever to a comeback to Palestinian leadership and decision-making.
Long exiled to the UAE and declared persona non grata in both Gaza and the West Bank, Dahlan now seeks to claw his way back into political relevance with the financial backing of his Gulf sponsors. The reason he has a chance of succeeding is that his plan offers all sides — Hamas, Abbas, and the UAE-U.S. axis pushing Gaza’s postwar order — a way to claim national unity without settling who actually governs. That ambiguity is precisely what has kept such plans alive.
Who is Muhammad Dahlan?
Muhammad Yousef Shaker Dahlan was born in 1961 in the Khan Younis refugee camp in the southern Gaza Strip to a Palestinian refugee family from the village of Hamama near Asqalan, destroyed by Israeli forces in 1948. He joined Fatah as a teenager and spent five years in Israeli jails for his activism.
In 1987, he was released and later deported by Israel shortly before the start of the first Palestinian Intifada. He joined Fatah’s exile apparatus, moving among multiple Arab capitals for several years, during which he grew closer to Yasser Arafat and eventually returned to Palestine with him after the Oslo Accords.
Upon the establishment of the Palestinian Authority, Arafat named Dahlan head of the Palestinian Preventive Security Forces in Gaza, making him the main security officer in the Strip. As the man in charge in his own hometown, Dahlan increased his support base among Gaza’s Fatah supporters, all while strengthening his contacts with Israeli intelligence through his role in security coordination between the PA security and Israel.
This role also allowed Dahlan to cultivate contacts within regional governments, mainly the Egyptian government, and with U.S. officials. Dahlan became an outspoken critic of Hamas and was accused by the group of arresting many of its members.
Hamas and Dahlan: a complicated relationship
During the Fatah-Hamas conflict in 2007, Dahlan was seen as Hamas’s number-one nemesis in Gaza, publicly challenging the group and trading accusations of treason. Dahlan was one of the first Fatah leaders to leave the Strip after Hamas’s takeover of the PA’s institutions in Gaza in June 2007.
In 2011, tensions grew between Dahlan and the dominant current in Fatah, led by PA President Abbas, culminating in Abbas’s official expulsion of Dahlan from Fatah. Dahlan left for the UAE, where he began to reorganize his alliances.
In 2017, while Gaza was marking 10 years of strict Israeli blockade and isolation from Palestinian political life, Hamas was scrambling to find a way out of the crisis. The group released a new “political charter” that year, in which it accepted the PLO’s legitimacy to represent the Palestinian people, as well as the principle of a Palestinian state within a two-state solution framework. The same year, Hamas announced its complete organizational disconnection from the global Muslim Brotherhood and its independence as a Palestinian movement.
These moves to achieve progress in Palestinian reconciliation reached a dead-end as the PA imposed its own set of restrictions on Gaza’s bureaucracy, halting the payment of salaries to thousands of employees hired by the Hamas administration. Hamas needed a political lifeline, and it found an unlikely one in its old foe: Muhammad Dahlan.
Dahlan and Hamas announced an understanding which included a “social reconciliation,” paying reparations to families of victims of the inter-Palestinian fighting of 2007 through a special fund supported by the UAE. It also included a plan to facilitate humanitarian and social aid, and the entry of fuel through Qatar. The implementation of the plan would involve Gulf states and Egypt, in addition to U.S. approval.
While some parts of the understanding were implemented, namely the social reconciliation part, the political part of reaching a full agreement didn’t go through, as both the PA and Hamas saw that the political part of the reconciliation needs to be reached between them, and not between Hamas and Dahlan. The continuous stagnation of the political scene, the continuation of the Israeli blockade, and the deteriorating conditions of Gaza’s population led to the 2018 Great March of Return protests, which were violently repressed by Israel and ignored by the international community. Dahlan went back to the shadows, but only for a while.
What is Dahlan’s plan?
Dahlan’s plan is based on a simple idea: separating political competition between Palestinian factions from the running of Palestinian institutions, by making the Palestinian Authority a “neutral” body, where decisions on who gets to hold key positions are irrelevant to power balances between parties. Dahlan’s plan calls this a “national partnership instead of a struggle for power.”
This would mean a dramatic change from the way things have been handled in Palestinian politics for decades, where the larger and more dominant factions controlled most positions in the PLO and the PA, to the point that public institutions became practically an extension of party organizations. Political affiliation, or loyalty, has also been a criterion for holding office and even getting a job in government, which was one of the reasons why the reconciliation between Fatah and Hamas became so difficult, since thousands of Hamas-hired public servants in Gaza were payrolled on the Ramallah-based, Fatah-run PA budget. Dahlan’s proposal is to keep the competition between factions limited to elections for political office, and leave the rest of the PA body of institutions separated from politics.
To do this, Dahlan’s plan proposes a “new national social contract,” through a new Palestinian constitution that recognizes the people as the only source of legitimacy, and elections as the only way through which a Palestinian may hold office. The current Palestinian Basic Law already stipulates popular legitimacy through elections, as well as the separation of powers and the impartiality of public institutions, but political practice has been following unwritten rules inherited from the “revolutionary” era of the PLO in the 1960s and 1970s, where parties secured their share in the PLO institutions based on the size of their support base.
Even in that era, the idea of “national partnership” through collective decision-making among factions was a celebrated principle, practiced or ignored depending on the particular conditions of any given day. Dahlan’s plan doesn’t offer a practical approach to solving these inherited gaps between principles and practice. It only reaffirms the principles.
Gaza: the gateway to Palestinian politics and regional deals
For both Hamas and Dahlan, the main goal remains finding a way back into Palestinian politics and participation in the Palestinian decision-making process, which has been monopolized by the PA leadership represented by Fatah’s dominant faction under Abbas. Both Hamas and Dahlan have their main support bases in Gaza, at precisely the same moment that Gaza has now become the center of gravity of the Palestinian cause.
After the Israeli genocide in Gaza, international and regional focus shifted to how Gaza will be run in the future phase, after Hamas’s handing over of its control over the Strip. The plan of U.S. President Trump, including handing the administration of Gaza to a Palestinian technocratic committee under the so-called “Board of Peace,” remains in limbo, waiting in Egypt and unable to enter Gaza due to Israel’s insistence that the reconstruction will not move forward without Hamas’s total disarmament. Israel has also continued to reverse its partial withdrawal to the so-called “Yellow Line” during the October 2025 ceasefire by moving the Line further west, eating up more territory under Israeli control while hemming Gaza’s population into tighter spaces.
Politically, moving Trump’s plan to its second phase depends largely on the potential understandings over who would be in charge of Gaza on the Palestinian side. Hamas has agreed to give up its control of the strip, and even to disarm. But its main focus is to keep a place in Palestinian politics as a partner in national decision-making. But this internal Palestinian issue has been affected by the international dimension of the future of Gaza, which has become a regional political question in which several forces are vying for influence.
To the U.S., resolving the question of the future of Gaza is important to move on with the normalization efforts between Israel and Arab countries, which are themselves important for larger economic mega-projects in the region. The UAE is a key player in this regional normalization and in regional economic plans, and Dahlan — being the Palestinian leader enjoying the lion’s share of support from the UAE — has positioned himself as the figure to secure the missing piece of the puzzle: a Palestinian administration of Gaza with roots in internal Palestinian politics, enjoying a support base in Palestine, and capable of garnering the trust of regional players and the U.S.
What does this mean for Palestinian politics?
Dahlan’s election allies, namely Hamas, haven’t officially endorsed his plan, but they haven’t rejected it either. This places Dahlan as the leading figure in the alliance and makes his plan the de facto election platform of the alliance. The overall logic of the plan gives space for all players, including Hamas and Abbas, to maintain their status and their influence, while providing a patriotic, reconciliatory, and democratic discourse to present the Palestinian need to accept Trump’s plan in order to alleviate the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza.
The core idea of the plan is already the product of a Palestinian consensus: Palestinians need national unity to have any leverage over their own destiny. But the idea of this unity being reached through a figure who has been at odds with every party to the Palestinian division — sponsored by an Arab country leading normalization efforts with Israel, and aligned with Trump’s agenda — was not expected to have a serious chance of success under different conditions.
Today, it does have a chance, and in the background are the Palestinians’ hope to bring some relief to Gaza’s devastated population and have some chance to face Israel’s offensive in the West Bank united. Dahlan’s serious attempt to make a comeback in Palestinian politics through an alliance with Hamas speaks to how much Palestinians are ready to reconsider and politically accept under the shock of three years of genocide, destruction, and devastation.

Fury across India after Delhi Police assault two Muslim women journalists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:46:35 UTC
20:46:35 KST

A political and media storm has erupted in India after two women journalists said they were detained and brutally assaulted by Delhi Police while covering an event in south Delhi, with the assault becoming worse after officers learned that they were Muslim.
The journalists, Shaheen Khan and Nafisa Khan, work with digital news platform 4PM News Network. Videos showing their bruises and injuries have gone viral on social media, prompting condemnation from opposition parties, journalists' organisations and the Press Council of India.
Delhi Police, meanwhile, have strongly denied the allegations, saying the two women were taken to the Saket police station after allegedly obstructing a designated VVIP route during an event attended by Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta.
Rejecting the journalists' account, the police described the allegations as "factually incorrect", "misleading" and "baseless."
What happened in Saket?
The incident took place on Thursday, when Shah and Gupta were attending the inauguration of a new wing at Max Smart Super Speciality Hospital in Saket.
According to Khan and her colleague, they had gone to cover the event and were attempting to ask questions from the chief minister. They allege that police personnel stopped them, detained them and took them to Saket police station.
In videos circulated by 4PM News Network, Shaheen Khan is seen inside the police station describing the assault and showing injuries. Another video shows Nafisa Khan unable to walk and being carried away. The journalists have alleged that they were beaten with sticks and slapped.
Shaheen has said that police personnel asked her name and, after hearing "Khan", asked which community she belonged to. She alleges that the assault subsequently intensified after officers learned that she was Muslim.
According to Shaheen, an officer saw an incoming call from someone identified as “Mohammed” on her phone and said: “Muslim hai… do dande zyada maaro (She’s Muslim… hit her twice more with sticks).”
Videos fuel public outrage
The controversy escalated after 4PM News Network released videos in which the two journalists displayed visible bruising and described their treatment inside the police station.
The footage has been widely reposted, including by political leaders and news organisations.
The Press Club of India, Indian Women's Press Corps, Delhi Union of Journalists, Press Association and Kerala Union of Working Journalists jointly condemned what they described as a brutal assault on the two freelance journalists.
They called for punitive action against the police personnel involved, including the station house officer, and urged Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar to order a free and fair investigation.
The organisations also called on the Press Council of India to take suo motu cognisance of the matter and conduct an independent investigation.
Opposition parties condemn the beating
Opposition party Congress’ spokesperson Pawan Khera described the visuals as “horrifying” and questioned whether Delhi was becoming a "police state".
The Congress itself circulated the video and accused the BJP government and Delhi Police of detaining and assaulting Khan after she attempted to question the chief minister. The party demanded strict action against the police personnel involved.
The Aam Aadmi Party has also attacked the Delhi government, with leader Saurabh Bharadwaj alleging that the journalists had been brutally beaten for asking the chief minister questions, while party leader Somnath Bharti called for intervention by Delhi's Lieutenant Governor.
Indian politician leader Tejashwi Yadav from Rashtriya Janata Dal party also joined the chorus of opposition condemnation. In a post on X, Yadav called the incident a serious assault on press freedom and democratic accountability.
“In Modi ji's so-called Amrit Kaal New India, being a Muslim, being a woman, and being an impartial journalist is now the greatest sin,” he wrote, adding that the BJP has crossed every limit of twenty-four tyrannical authoritarianism across the country.
“Amrit Kaal” is the Indian government’s term for its vision of India’s development towards 2047 and “New India” is its broader slogan for a modern, transformed India.
The journalists’ own organisation, 4PM News Network, has also taken the matter to the highest constitutional office, petitioning Indian President Droupadi Murmu for intervention and seeking an impartial investigation into the alleged assault.
The organisation has also called for relevant CCTV and video evidence to be preserved and for action against any police personnel found responsible.

VLADIVOSTOK, September 4. /TASS/. Russia and China are currently discussing the Power of Baikal gas pipeline project, formerly known as Power of Siberia 2, for Russian gas supplies to China, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said at a meeting of the Russian-Chinese Intergovernmental Commission on Energy Cooperation.
On the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF), he said that most independent gas stations in Russia are already receiving fuel supplies, with more stations to be supplied going forward.
At the Russia-China Energy Business Forum, Novak stressed that amid the conflict in the Middle East, Russian companies have once again proven themselves to be reliable long-term partners supplying oil at fair market prices.
TASS has compiled the deputy prime minister's key statements.
Fuel situation in Russia
Russian authorities intend to prevent an oversupply of diesel fuel and will allow exports if necessary: "Our key task is to prevent this. If sufficient diesel inventories are built up to prevent an oversupply, we will naturally decide to reopen exports. For now, the Energy Ministry considers it appropriate, based on the overall balance and the situation it is monitoring, not to export."
Most independent gas stations in Russia are already receiving fuel supplies, with more stations to be supplied going forward: "Most gas stations are receiving supplies, yes. Unfortunately, not all of them are receiving full supplies yet. As for gasoline - the situation with diesel fuel, as I have said, is stable - as the gasoline market becomes saturated, we will naturally ensure supplies to all gas stations."
The Russian government does not plan to make changes to the fuel market's damping mechanism: "All the necessary changes were adopted during the spring session. No changes are currently planned."
Novak will hold a meeting on the fuel market situation on September 7, where agreements between regions and independent gas stations will be discussed: "I will hold a meeting on Monday, where we will hear from everyone - the Energy Ministry, the Federal Antimonopoly Service and the regions - on the signing of these agreements."
Power of Baikal
Russia and China are currently discussing the Power of Baikal gas pipeline project, formerly known as Power of Siberia 2, for Russian gas supplies to China: "Pipeline gas exports via the Power of Siberia pipeline are growing steadily. We are preparing to launch the Far Eastern route and continuing dialogue on other promising routes for Russian gas supplies to China, including the Power of Baikal project."
Russia and China have agreed to continue preparations for a contract on Russian gas supplies via the Power of Baikal pipeline: "We discussed these issues within the framework of the existing intergovernmental commission. It has now been deemed appropriate to continue work on preparing the contract itself so that our companies can reach concrete agreements more quickly."
Cooperation with China
Russia and China are currently developing a joint LNG project in the Arctic and building a gas processing complex on the Baltic Sea: "A joint gas production and liquefaction project in the Arctic is also being developed, along with the construction of an ethane-rich gas processing complex on the Baltic Sea."
Russia is ready to discuss new nuclear energy projects and research with China: "We are ready to discuss new joint projects, specialist training and research into advanced nuclear technologies."
Russia has become one of the top three LNG suppliers to the Chinese market: "Liquefied natural gas is showing record growth - volumes have increased more than 50-fold over the past decade, and Russia has become one of the top three LNG suppliers to the Chinese market."
Russia increased oil supplies to China by 25% in the first seven months of 2026 and remains China's leading oil supplier: "The best confirmation of this is the record growth in oil exports. Russia remains the leading supplier to China, with exports rising 25% in the first seven months of this year."
Russia and China need to build and upgrade gas and oil pipelines, ports and energy facilities to make energy cooperation more resilient: "The next stage of cooperation is to make our energy ties even more resilient to external factors. To achieve this, we need to develop infrastructure for cross-border projects -- build and upgrade gas and oil pipelines, port capacity, energy facilities and transport and logistics corridors, as well as address insurance issues."
Russia is China's largest supplier of pipeline gas, while further expansion of projects will significantly increase total supplies: "Gas is now reshaping the map of energy connectivity across Eurasia. A total of 38.8 bln cubic meters was transported via the Power of Siberia pipeline in 2025, a quarter more than a year earlier and above contractual commitments. Daily records are being set regularly. Russia is China's largest supplier of pipeline gas."
Russia is one of the leading coal exporters to China, with coking coal supplies to China rising 16% in the first six months of 2026: "Demand is recovering this year, with coking coal exports rising 16% in the first half. We continue to develop the Zashulanskoye deposit in the Trans-Baikal Region. Russian fuel is in demand among Chinese power plants and steelmakers."
Russia and China cooperate on digital solutions for the oil and gas sector and protection against cyberthreats: "We will continue cooperation on renewable energy, hydrogen, energy storage systems and carbon credit markets, as well as on energy system modeling, operational dispatch management and renewable energy generation forecasting, digital solutions for the oil and gas sector and protection against cyberthreats."
Oil exports
Russia currently sends 94% of its oil exports to friendly countries: "Overall, 94% of Russian oil exports currently go to friendly countries."
"The main thing Russia offers the market along with its resources is reliability. Even amid external pressure, the Russian fuel and energy sector fully meets its commitments, playing a stabilizing role in the global energy market."
Amid the conflict in the Middle East, Russian companies have once again proven themselves to be reliable long-term partners supplying oil at fair market prices: "Disruptions to Middle Eastern supplies amid the worsening military and political situation have also had an impact. Under these conditions, Russian companies have once again proven themselves to be guarantors of uninterrupted long-term supplies at fair market prices.".

Russian-made spy drone washes up on Finnish shore near Porvoo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:44:43 UTC
20:44:43 KST

- Finnish authorities said a drone found near Porvoo appears to be a Russian-made Geoscan 701 surveying aircraft, though President Stubb said Finland faces no direct threat.
- The find is part of a pattern of drone incidents in Finland through 2026, most previously tied to stray Ukrainian drones rather than Russian devices.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb said Wednesday that Finland faces no direct threat after a drone was found on a shoreline in the Pellinki archipelago near Porvoo, even as Finnish authorities said the device now appears to be Russian-made.
A resident discovered the drone on September 1 on the shore of an island in the archipelago, roughly a two-hour drive east of Helsinki. The Finnish Border Guard identified it as a Geoscan 701, a fixed-wing aircraft built by the Russian company Geoscan for aerial surveying and mapping. The Border Guard confirmed the device carried no explosives.
“We are not worried, we need to be calm,” Stubb said, adding that authorities were still investigating the drone and would release more information once confirmed.
Finland’s Ministry of Defence said it is investigating the incident as a possible violation of Finnish territory, with the Border Guard and police working to determine the drone’s origin and how it reached the shoreline. Two officials told Finnish broadcaster Yle they now believe the drone is Russian, a shift from authorities’ initial description of it only as a surveying aircraft that posed no danger.
The Geoscan 701 is a civilian fixed-wing drone designed for aerial photography and mapping. It launches from a catapult, lands by parachute, and can fly for up to 10 hours and cover as much as 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) on a single flight, according to the manufacturer. The aircraft has a maximum takeoff weight of 22 kilograms (49 pounds) and a wingspan of about 3.3 meters (11 feet). Geoscan markets the drone for civilian survey work, including projects in Siberia, the Russian Arctic and Antarctica.
Stubb said the discovery fits into what he called a “new normal” Finland must prepare for, and warned that hybrid attacks, including sabotage, cyberattacks and information warfare, are likely to increase. He said Russia’s aim is to make Europeans afraid.
Finland has reported a string of drone incidents through 2026, most involving stray Ukrainian drones that drifted off course during Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure along the Gulf of Finland. In late March, Finnish officials confirmed drones that landed near Kouvola came from Ukraine, and an F/A-18 Hornet was scrambled to identify one aircraft as a Ukrainian AN-196 drone. A separate drone crossed into Finnish airspace near Virolahti in May. Not every incident has been tied to Ukraine, however; the Pellinki find is the latest case where Finnish authorities have pointed to a Russian origin instead.
Finland has moved to build up its counter-drone defenses over the past year. In December, the Finnish Armed Forces confirmed they had purchased hundreds of SkyWiper Omni Max jamming devices from Lithuanian manufacturer NT Service, intended to block drone control and navigation signals around critical infrastructure such as military bases.
Finnish authorities have not said when the investigation into the Pellinki drone will conclude or whether they can determine how it reached Finnish territory.

daniel arsham turns barley grains into moving sculpture for the balvenie at frieze seoul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:43:15 UTC
20:43:15 KST

daniel arsham TIME-WORNs BRONZE sculpture for the balvenie
A circular bed of grain welcomes designboom to the floor of Space S50 in Seongdong-gu, Seoul. Four performers move within the material, gathering, spreading, and reshaping the loose barley using sweeping, continuous gestures. Choreographed by Sukyung Yoo to a soundscape recorded inside The Balvenie distillery, the eight-part performance translates the manual labor of turning grain on a traditional malting floor into kinetic art. Conceptualised by artist Daniel Arsham, the live performance marks the debut of The 1931 Collection, created by the Speyside whiskey maker and unveiled during Frieze Seoul 2026.
daniel arsham’s circular bed of barley grains becomes a canvas for movement during frieze seoul 2026
the installation at space s50 references traditional techniques inside the balvenie’s historic home malting floor
The performative installation centers on a specific historical milestone for The Balvenie. In 1931, the whiskey maker opened its Home Malting Floor — a space that remains functional today. That same year, workers filled a European oak sherry butt from Jerez, Spain, labeled cask #239. The spirit matured for eighty-eight years until Malt Master Kelsey McKechnie bottled seventeen decanters in 2019. Rather than presenting the liquid within standard glasswork, Arsham developed an architectural vessel that treats the decades-long maturation process as a physical, geological transformation.
The Balvenie opened its Home Malting Floor — a space that remains functional today – in 1931
Daniel aArsham inspects malt during a research visit to the distillery in Speyside, Scotland
images courtesy of The Balvenie
eight layers of hand-patinated bronze and eighty-eight of oak
The sculpture housing the 88-year-old single malt is built as a split vessel made of contrasting industrial and natural materials. Its front fascia comprises eight flowing layers — each representing a decade of aging — cast in hand-patinated bronze. The surface treatment reproduces the verdigris textures and oxidation that naturally occur over time on copper stills.
The back half of the sculptural form consists of 88 layered sections of oak. Positioned at the core of the piece is a round copper disc salvaged directly from a decommissioned distillery still. Inside this enclosure sits a hand-blown crystal decanter detailed with 18-karat gold gilding and topped with a stopper shaped after the distillery’s copper pot stills.
‘At The Balvenie, I encountered a spirit that has been carefully shaped by generations of people who have protected and refined their craft, while remaining deeply connected to their origins,‘ artist Daniel Arsham explains. ‘Much of my work explores time, material transformation and the histories that objects carry. This collaboration has brought these themes together naturally; I wanted to create something that feels both ancient and contemporary, to make the passage of time tangible.‘
Arsham and malt master Kelsey McKechnie introduce the project alongside the immersive installation in Seoul
liquid expressions of the balvenie: the 1931 collection
The visual language of the central sculpture extends to two additional limited-edition releases within The 1931 Collection: a Twelve-Year-Old and a Fifteen-Year-Old single malt. Both expression packages feature heavily debossed exterior surfaces with green verdigris undertones fading into warm copper hues. Inside, a textured copper-colored substrate lines the box, referencing the raw metals of the production floor.
The Fifteen-Year-Old expression relies on 100 percent home-grown and home-malted barley, matured in American oak before finishing in ex-sherry European oak butts from Jerez. The Twelve-Year-Old mirrors the technical maturation process of cask #239, combining home-malted barley with the same sherry finish.
The installation at Space S50 transitions visitors, like designboom, from the live grain performance into an adjoining gallery space displaying Arsham’s bronze relic, accompanied by guided tastings led by McKechnie. Following its initial showing during Frieze Seoul, the performance and collection will travel to New York, Shanghai, and Taipei.
the eight-layered bronze fascia patinas over time, mirroring oxidation on the distillery’s copper stills | image courtesy of The Balvenie
at the sculpture’s core lies a central copper disc cut from a decommissioned distillery still

Bulgaria's prime minister suggests Western support for Ukraine provoked Russia's Leipzig Airport attack
Bulgaria's Prime Minister Rumen Radev suggested on Sept. 4 that the alleged Russian attack on Germany's Leipzig Airport last month was provoked by the West's military support for Ukraine.
"What can we expect when we attack... another country with our long-range weapons? Will (the country) stand by or will it respond?" Radev asked in the Bulgarian parliamentary chamber, according to the Bulgarian news agency Novinite.
No Western country has directly attacked Russia with weapons, long-range or otherwise. Several countries have supplied long-range weapons to Kyiv to help it defend itself against Russia's full-scale invasion.
Radev repeatedly characterized Europe's sending of long-range weapons to Ukraine as "a reckless act" and accused Western countries of warmongering.
"The collective West is trying to achieve a conventional victory over Russia, without taking into account the fact that it is the largest nuclear power and we cannot resist its hypersonic weapons," he said.
"Europe must finally start calculating the risk and sit down at the negotiating table as soon as possible, because this war is expanding its spatial scope and the risk is growing with each passing day."
The EU and several European countries held multiple discussions earlier in the year about peace talks with Russia, but all have drawn the same conclusion that Moscow is not yet interested in ending its war against Ukraine.
read also
Germany's interior and foreign ministers on Sept. 1 officially accused Russia of an attempted sabotage of Leipzig Airport in early August using explosive-laden drones.
It was the first time Berlin formally acknowledged Russia was responsible for a hybrid attack against the country.
"We will not allow Russia's attacks to divide us or intimidate us," German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said, while announcing several countermeasures against Moscow.
The Kremlin has denied responsibility and accused Germany of escalating tensions.
While claiming to "stand firmly by Germany, by our biggest, closest ally," Radev has a track record of sympathizing with Russia.
After resigning as president, Radev led his new party to victory in Bulgaria's parliamentary election in April. The day after, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov praised Radev for his pro-Russian messaging and "willingness to resolve issues through pragmatic dialogue with the Russian Federation."
Radev in June blocked an EU attempt to impose sanctions on the head of Russia's Orthodox Church, Archbishop Kirill, with a vague allusion to the two countries' shared past in fighting the Ottoman Empire. And in July, Radev withdrew Bulgaria from the Coalition of the Willing, a group of over 30 countries preparing security guarantees for Ukraine.

Ukraine Unveils Highest-Denomination Banknote Featuring Vasyl Stus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:40:15 UTC
20:40:15 KST

Ukraine’s central bank on Friday introduced a new Hr. 2,000 banknote, the country’s highest-denomination bill, featuring Ukrainian poet and Soviet-era dissident Vasyl Stus.
The banknote is worth approximately $45. From Sept. 4, banks can obtain the notes from the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) and issue them to customers through their cash desks, the central bank said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The front of the banknote features a portrait of Stus, one of Ukraine’s most prominent 20th-century poets and a vocal opponent of Soviet repression. The reverse depicts the philology faculty building of Donetsk National University, where he studied.
The NBU said the date chosen for the banknote’s introduction carries symbolic significance.
On Sept. 4, 1965, Stus joined Ukrainian dissidents Viacheslav Chornovil and Ivan Dziuba in staging what the central bank described as the first open public protest against political repression in the Soviet Union. The protest took place during the premiere of Sergei Parajanov’s film “Shadows of Forgotten Ancestors.”
Exactly 20 years later, on Sept. 4, 1985, Stus died at the Perm-36 maximum-security prison camp in Russia.
The NBU said the decision to introduce the higher denomination reflected changes in Ukraine’s economy, including rising incomes and prices, the volume of cash in circulation and changes in how people use banknotes.
India’s Double Game with Russia: Peace Rhetoric vs Record Oil Trade
Since Ukraine introduced the Hr. 1,000 banknote seven years ago, the country’s average monthly salary has tripled, while prices have doubled according to the inflation index, the central bank said.
The new denomination is also expected to reduce the cost of transporting, processing and maintaining cash.
The NBU said issuing the Hr. 2,000 note did not amount to “printing money” and would not by itself increase inflation or cause fluctuations in the foreign exchange market.
The banknotes will enter circulation only in exchange for noncash funds or as replacements for worn notes of other denominations, according to the central bank.
The initial issue will consist of several million banknotes.
Until Friday, Ukraine’s highest-denomination banknote was the Hr. 1,000 bill, introduced in 2019.

Hannah Life in Bulgaria: Beyond the tourist clichés

What does Bulgaria look like through the eyes of someone who has chosen to make it their permanent home? That is the story Hannah Dwight tells through Hannah Life in Bulgaria, a Facebook page chronicling the everyday life of a foreign family in a Bulgarian village.
Hannah lives here with her husband Steve and their daughter Nyx. The family discovered Bulgaria while travelling and bought a home here in 2019. In 2023, they made the move permanent, settling in a village near Veliko Tarnovo. Before that, they lived in Wrexham, Wales, where Hannah is from, while Steve comes from New Zealand. He now works at the school in the nearby village of Rusalia and plays with the rock band Hinterlands.
A graphic designer by profession, Hannah now also creates content about her life in Bulgaria – from gardening and home-cooked food to local traditions and family life, sharing her experience of the country with an international audience.
The Bulgarian language has a special place in her stories. She documents everything from her first steps with the Cyrillic alphabet to the words and expressions that occasionally land her in unexpected – and amusing – situations.
In the process, Hannah Life in Bulgaria has become more than a diary of one foreign family’s life. It offers a view of Bulgaria from the outside, where things Bulgarians barely notice in their everyday lives can look surprisingly different through Hannah’s eyes.

Belgian PM’s chocolate gift to Modi doesn’t survive journey to India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:39:26 UTC
20:39:26 KST

Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever shakes hands with his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi at the Hyderabad House in New Delhi on September 3, 2026. | Sajjad Hussain/AFP via Getty Images
Diplomatic protocol is like a box of chocolates. You never know what you’re going to get — or whether it’ll survive the flight.
A chocolate replica of New Delhi’s India Gate intended as Belgium’s gift to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi was damaged on its way to India, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever said Thursday.
De Wever joked about the mishap at a press conference alongside Modi. He had planned to present him with a sculpture “made out of the best Belgian chocolate.”
Advertisement
“But unlike the real India Gate, which has stood almost for a century, the chocolate version didn’t even survive the journey to India,” De Wever said. “Chocolate is excellent for diplomacy, but not excellent for diplomatic travel.”
The gift carried a more serious message. India Gate is a war memorial in New Delhi, and De Wever said the replica was meant to honor the more than 9,000 Indian soldiers who fought and died in Belgium’s Flanders Fields during World War I.
A backup version is still waiting in Belgium, De Wever said. He promised the replacement would fare better: “One way or another, I will get it to Prime Minister Modi in one piece.”
Diplomatic gifts have produced stranger outcomes.
A camel given to former French President François Hollande by Mali was left with a family in Timbuktu, which later slaughtered and ate it. In 2014, then-U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry presented Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov with two Idaho potatoes.
Beyond the protocol hiccup, De Wever and Modi agreed to deepen cooperation on defense, organized crime and renewable energy, while aiming to boost trade. De Wever also invited Modi to visit Belgium.

The seizures are reportedly intended to facilitate a road connecting the planned Emek Dotan and Noa settlements, which are among 34 new settlements approved by the Israeli government earlier this year, it added.
Area A has formally been under the Palestinian Authority’s civil and security administration since the Oslo Accords.
Citing Israeli settlement watchdog Peace Now, Amnesty said this was the first time since the accords that military seizure orders had openly targeted Area A for civilian projects benefiting settlers rather than purported security purposes.
The confiscated land is largely privately owned by Palestinians from several villages in Jenin, according to the statement.
The Jenin governor’s office told Amnesty that implementation had begun and could cut off hundreds of families from agricultural land and olive groves ahead of the harvest season.
It said the planned road and other settlement projects could sever Jenin from the neighboring governorates of Tulkarem, Tubas, and Nablus, further fragmenting Palestinian communities and disrupting economic and social ties.
Amnesty urged countries with close relations with Israel to press its government to withdraw the orders and called on Israeli authorities to halt settlement expansion.
Under international law, Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, are illegal. Israel disputes this characterization.

The commission’s proposal calls for “targeted restrictive visa measures to address security risks stemming from hostile actions of third countries,” according to a Sept. 3 statement by European Commission spokesperson Markus Lammert, who did not specify what the restrictions would be. The new measures are expected to be presented as part of an upcoming review of the EU visa code, though no timeline has yet been announced.
Before the start of Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine, Russian citizens received about 4 million Schengen visas a year. By 2025, that number had fallen to 618,000, Lammert said. He added that it was “very important that the figures stay down and that the figures go further down.” Decisions on individual visa applications will still be made by the authorities of each EU member state, Lammert added:
“The issuance of visas is a member state competence, so each individual visa application has to be assessed on a case by case basis by the national authorities. It's the national authorities who decide on every individual application and issue visas, but what we can do at the EU level is that we can take action, and we have taken action to further restrict the issuance of visas.
One of the elements that we started in 2022 was that we fully suspended the visa facilitation agreement with Russia. Also in 2022, we have adopted clear guidelines for member states to deprioritize visas for Russians and to focus on security and border controls. So now we are monitoring these guidelines and the implementation of these guidelines, and we're working with member states to promote [their] consistent implementation.”
Germany is also preparing to tighten its own entry rules for Russian citizens. After the incident in Leipzig, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said controls on Russian citizens entering Germany would be strengthened, though he did not announce specific measures.
According to a report by the outlets Süddeutsche Zeitung, NDR and WDR, the suspected perpetrators of the failed August drone attack are a Russian-born man who holds a Latvian passport and a Belarus-born man who holds a Russian passport. German media reported that the latter entered Germany on a Schengen tourist visa issued by Italy in Minsk.
In addition to tightening entry controls, Berlin has decided to close Russia’s consulate general in Bonn and the Russian House cultural center in the German capital. Travelling to Europe? EES border checks are changing from 6 September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:34:38 UTC
20:34:38 KST

Industry experts are concerned the removal of the Entry/Exit System’s temporary flexibilities will see border chaos return.
On Sunday 6 September, the EU’s Entry/Exit System (EES) emergency flexibility measures will come to an end.
Over the summer, member states were granted authority to temporarily suspend the collection of travellers' biometric data through fingerprints and facial scans to ease congestion in exceptional circumstances.
Industry bodies are now pushing for these flexibilities to be extended beyond September amid concerns of renewed border delays.
Less flexibility at airports and borders
The biometric system became fully operational across participating European borders on 10 April 2026, following a progressive rollout that began in October 2025.
However, European authorities have had a vital safety valve available during the transition.
Under EU rules, countries have been permitted to temporarily suspend the collection of biometric information at individual border crossings when passenger volumes become so high that waiting times become excessive.
From 6 September, that temporary period is expected to expire, meaning airports and border authorities will have less flexibility to ease biometric requirements simply because passport control areas have become overwhelmed.
At a press briefing on 1 September, a European Commission (EC) spokesperson said the EES had "broadly worked well" over the summer while underlining that "the advantages of the new system for the EU are evident".
Referring to the end of flexibility measures on 6 September, the EC spokesperson said: "When it comes to the time after the summer, we are in close and constructive contact with those few member states where some adjustments are needed at certain border crossing points.
"Overall, we can see that there is a strong joint will to make the system work everywhere."
After 6 September, Jurgen Himmelmann, co-founder and CEO of Global Work & Travel, says travellers should build significantly more time into journeys involving European border controls.
"Getting to the airport early is sensible, but there is a limit to how much control that gives you,” he says. “Bag-drop desks may not be open four hours before departure, and once you're in a passport-control queue, you can't simply skip ahead because your flight is boarding.
“I'd avoid planning a journey around the minimum connection time over the next few weeks. A connection that looks perfectly reasonable on paper can become uncomfortable very quickly if you lose an hour or more at the border."
Fears of renewed border delays in September
Industry experts are concerned the removal of EES temporary flexibilities will see border chaos return.
“We continue to push the European Commission to allow these measures to be used beyond September, recognising that there is still some way to go until EES is fully and consistently operational across all participating countries,” said Luke Petherbridge, Director of Public Affairs at ABTA, a UK trade association for tour operators and travel agents.
According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), standard passport checks that previously took around 20 to 25 seconds now require about 90 seconds under the EES.
Data shows wait times have doubled at major hubs as the scheme struggles to cope with the sheer number of non-EU passengers passing through.
The study by UK-based newspaper the Financial Times and travel analytics group Qsensor shows that in Frankfurt, the average wait time reached 120 minutes in July, up from 60 minutes the same month last year.
At Munich airport, waits are up to 60 minutes from 31 last year and, in Amsterdam, maximum waiting times have rocketed from 80 to 120 minutes in the same period.
IATA has also urged the European Union to grant an extension of the “safety valve”.
“Extending the possibility of partial suspension beyond 6 September is absolutely necessary until the end of the winter season,” Thomas Reynaert, Senior Vice President, External Affairs at IATA, said at a media briefing this week.
Reynaert stressed that the association is “fully supportive of EES” but that certain conditions should be met before flexibilities are removed.
Writing in a LinkedIn post, he added: “Reliable systems, fully deployed self-service kiosks and automated border controls, together with adequate staffing, remain essential if EES is to operate effectively during peak periods without creating unnecessary disruption for passengers, border authorities and transport operators.”

The Russian House is the informal name for Russia’s state cultural center abroad, run by the cultural outreach organization Rossotrudnichestvo.
Officially, the Goethe-Institut is still operating in Russia. Lavrov, however, has already said its branches “will, of course, be closed.” Joost said Moscow’s decision would mean the “end of an era” in Russian-German cultural relations:

It was the beginning of a new chapter, which enabled us to bring the societies of both countries closer together through the work of the Goethe-Institut and, consequently, through culture and language. In 2019, another institute in Novosibirsk opened its doors.
For people in Russia who are learning our language and visiting our libraries, today’s announcement is unfortunate news.
In recent years, our work has been increasingly restricted – in 2023, we were forced to reduce our staff numbers. Our work in Russia was and remains important: promoting German language learning and fostering a mutual understanding between people. Our staff have carried out important work under the most difficult conditions. We are in close contact with all of them regarding how things will proceed in the coming hours.
We are also working together with the Federal Foreign Office to continuously monitor the situation and determine the next steps together.”
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul expressed regret that “Russia has taken such a step,” saying the Goethe-Institut had served as an important cultural bridge. German authorities, he said, “were prepared to continue this work.” Lavrov earlier said Berlin had “deliberately” moved to close the Russian House — a step that, he said, “they could not fail to understand clearly means the end of their cultural presence” in Russia.
Despite the statements from Russian and German officials, as of the evening of Sept. 3 in Moscow, it was still possible to register for a Goethe-Institut German-language exam. The schedule for those tests, which certify levels of language proficiency, runs through the end of November 2026. In St. Petersburg, the exam schedule also runs through the end of November. Places for the A1, A2, and B1 exams — beginner to intermediate levels under the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages — were fully booked through the end of September.

A longer exhale may push your brain toward bolder decisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:33:12 UTC
20:33:12 KST

A longer exhale may push your brain toward bolder decisions
- Date:
- September 4, 2026
- Source:
- German Center for Diabetes Research (DZD)
- Summary:
- Slow breathing with a prolonged exhale made people more willing to take risks by changing heart activity and increasing the brain’s sensitivity to rewards. The findings suggest that something as simple as controlling your breath can directly influence how you evaluate choices.
- Share:
A new study suggests that deliberately changing the rhythm of your breathing can influence how you make decisions by altering activity in both the heart and brain. Researchers from the German Institute of Human Nutrition Potsdam-Rehbruecke (DIfE) and Charité -- Universitätsmedizin Berlin found that longer exhalations increased heart rate variability and made the brain more responsive to rewards, which was associated with bolder choices. The findings were published in Neuron.
Fast breathing and an elevated heart rate are often linked with rapid decision-making. Under pressure, people may become more cautious in an effort to avoid losses, whether they are making an investment, handling a tense workplace situation, or choosing a meal quickly. Slower breathing and a calmer cardiovascular state, by contrast, may encourage a more positive assessment of potential outcomes and make people more willing to take risks.
How Breathing Connects the Body and Brain
Decision-making has traditionally been viewed as a process centered mainly in the brain. The new research examined a broader possibility: that signals from other parts of the body can change brain activity and influence the choices people make.
The study was led by Prof. Soyoung Q Park in collaboration with researchers from institutions including the Neuroscience Research Center at Charité -- Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Freie Universität Berlin, and the German Naval Institute of Maritime Medicine.
"Our decisions are rarely determined solely by external information. Rather, our judgment emerges from the interplay between cognitive processes and our current bodily state. It was previously unknown how the conscious regulation of our body, for example through targeted breathing, could actively control our decision-making process. We wanted to create a physiological shift using a slow breathing pattern to change the quality of our decisions," explains Soyoung Q Park, head of the Department of Decision Neuroscience and Nutrition at DIfE, summarizing the research question.
Testing Whether Longer Exhales Change Decisions
The researchers studied 41 healthy participants while they made risky choices under carefully controlled breathing conditions. Participants followed visual breathing instructions and either breathed at their normal individual pace or slowed their breathing while extending the exhalation phase (2:8 inhale-exhale ratio).
As the participants completed a series of risk-related decisions, the research team measured several aspects of their physical and neurological responses. Functional magnetic resonance imaging was used to track brain activity, while breathing patterns, heart activity, skin conductance, and pupil responses were monitored at the same time.
This combination of measurements allowed the researchers to test whether extending the exhale did more than simply lower heart rate. They also wanted to determine whether the breathing pattern directly changed how the brain processed potential rewards.
Longer Exhalation Shifted Choices Toward Reward
The results showed that extended exhalation slowed heart rate and was associated with riskier choices. Importantly, the change appeared to come from greater attention to possible rewards rather than reduced concern about potential losses. Participants still responded to losses in a similar way.
The researchers also detected stronger activity in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the precuneus. These brain regions are involved in reward processing and in regulating the timing between heartbeats, a measure known as heart rate variability.
"Our study thus underscores the transformative role of breath-based interventions. The interplay between breathing and cardiac dynamics makes the brain more receptive to rewards," explains lead author Wenhao Huang, interpreting the results.
What the Findings Could Mean for Breathing Techniques
The work adds to a growing field focused on body-brain communication and supports neurovisceral models, which propose that a person's physical state can strongly shape cognitive processes.
Park explains: "Breathing techniques have accompanied humanity for millennia across various religions and cultures. With this study, we provide scientific proof that it is a reliable and targeted method capable of controlling our decisions."
Because controlled breathing is simple, inexpensive, and relatively easy to learn, the researchers say it could have value as a tool for everyday self-regulation. It may also have potential as a supportive, non-pharmacological approach in clinical settings, particularly for conditions such as anxiety disorders or depression, which can involve disrupted autonomic regulation and altered responses to reward.
Could Breathing Influence Eating Behavior?
Future studies will need to determine whether the same effects appear in broader clinical populations, including people with overweight. The researchers are particularly interested in whether breathing techniques could influence food-related decisions, since eating behavior is strongly affected by both reward processing and a person's physical state.
"Since dietary decisions are strongly influenced by reward assessment and physical state, targeted breath regulation could also play a role in consciously perceiving and more effectively managing eating behavior," Park summarizes for future research activities.
This study was supported by the Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space [Grant 01GP2210C (DecEnt-Project), Grant 01EE2301E for the conceptual development of the German Center for Mental Health; Grant 82DZD03D03 (German Center for Diabetes Research)], the Ministry for Science, Research and Culture of the State of Brandenburg (MWFK). Ignacio Rebollo was supported by the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Action (MSCA) BRAINSTOM (grant agreement no. 101028203).
Story Source:
Materials provided by German Center for Diabetes Research (DZD). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Wenhao Huang, Mine Schmidt, Ignacio Rebollo, Felix Molter, Min Pu, Beatrix Keweloh, Lok Yan Lam, Peter N.C. Mohr, Gabriele Bellucci, Stefan Röttger, Soyoung Q. Park. Slow breathing impacts inter-organ dynamics modulating brain function and risk behavior. Neuron, 2026; DOI: 10.1016/j.neuron.2026.04.044

Mass burial reveals hidden toll of Algeria’s deadly ‘Black Wednesday’ wildfires
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:33:04 UTC
20:33:04 KST

Mass burial reveals hidden toll of Algeria’s deadly ‘Black Wednesday’ wildfires
Wildfires ripped across northeastern Algeria in late August. Photos and videos showing the mass burial of several dozen people have raised questions about the real death toll of the fires as Algerian authorities haven’t shared new numbers since August 26. A number of Moroccan social media accounts have also been sharing disinformation about the fires.
It’s after sundown, and a person is digging a rectangular hole in the ground as around 20 men watch. The image was captured in a TikTok live shared on August 27, narrated by a man speaking in Algerian Arabic.
 "Each time, they bring 30 or 40 [bodies]. Many people have died. There are people who are looking for their parents, for their children and they haven’t found them yet. El Ancer, Texenna, El Milia, [almost all of the region of] Jijel has been affected."
Jijel is the name of both a town and a wilaya – a province – located on the northeastern coast of Algeria. It was one of the main regions affected by a wave of forest fires that began on August 26, nicknamed “Black Wednesday” by locals and some officials. The flames reached the outskirts of the towns listed above between August 26 and 27, as shown on the FIRMS site, run by the US space agency NASA, which enables the public to watch the progression of wildfires in real time.
The person who filmed the video is a young resident of Jijel. Before the fires, he mostly posted about sports and fitness. But since they began, he’s been documenting the situation.
He says the mass grave was being dug in "Djemaa Beni Habibi, which was badly hit”. This detail enabled us to verify that the video was filmed in the cemetery of a small town, 30 kilometres east of Jijel.
No official numbers despite PM attending funeral
The next day, other videos posted by residents give a sense of the scale of the tragedy.
To display this content from TikTok, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
In some of the images, you can see up to 13 caskets at once.
Another video, recorded at the cemetery after part of the mass grave had been filled, shows more than twenty individual graves, each a simple mound of earth, marked only by a water bottle or a stick. The excavator, still operating when the footage was taken, is covering at least three more coffins with dirt. A large section of the trench remains empty, seemingly capable of holding several more bodies.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Algerian Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb, as well as several other government officials, attended the burial. Official local authority social media accounts also reported on the burial, but did not say how many people were buried.
However, other sources are helping us establish the human toll. On the evening of August 27, the night before the burial, the village of Djemaa Beni Habibi posted two statements on Facebook (here and here) listing the names of wildfire victims recorded by two hospitals. The lists were meant for families, so that they could come to see the bodies.
FRANCE 24 Observers team documented a total of 72 names after examining both lists, accounting for duplications.
Death toll rising sharply from preliminary figures
The Algerian authorities have stopped publishing official numbers of dead and wounded from the fires in late August. The initial toll, given on August 26 by the Ministry of the Interior, cited 12 deaths and 54 people injured. But the numbers are clearly higher than that, as more people were buried in the mass grave in Djemaa Beni Habibi alone.
Moreover, information from the ground also contradicts the official numbers. An Algerian congressman who visited the affected zone on August 31 said on Facebook that 19 members of the same family died in the village of El Ancer during the Black Wednesday fires.
Our team counted at least 98 victims from the Jiljel region after examining statements made by officials, local governments and families. If you include people mentioned in articles published in local media outlets – difficult to verify because they don’t always name the victims – our toll rose to nearly 130 potential victims. Journalist Nozha Khelalef, quoted by Algerian media outlets and French newspaper Le Monde, documented more than 200 names using a similar method.
The number of victims is likely even higher than that. Pan-African media outlet Jeune Afrique cited, on August 28, quotes from anonymous sources close to the Algerian Ministry of Defence. They said that 385 people died in the fires, and more are missing.
Our team contacted the Algerian Civil Defence to ask them if the official death toll has risen since August 26. They did not respond to our question. We will update this article when and if they do.
A tragedy instrumentalised by pro-Morocco social media accounts
On X, the uncertainty around the death toll has been exploited by accounts that support Morocco, Algeria’s geopolitical rival.
One of them posted a video showing what he claimed were “more than 20 victims” who were “buried at 3am”.
"Another video that contradicts the version of events given by the Algerian military regime,” he said. The FRANCE 24 Observers team was unable to independently verify this video or his claims.
Others have been using photos and videos of the mass burial in Djemaa Beni Habibi. An account called "Opinion Marocaine" shared the real images from the TikTok live showing the mass grave being dug. However, it claimed it showed “burial operations under the cover of darkness in mass graves for the fire victims in Algeria, and a total absence of Algerian official media”.
However, this footage doesn’t show the funeral, but preparations for it, which likely took place the night of August 27 to August 28. The burial didn’t take place in secret, at night, as this account claims. It took place during the day, and a large number of people attended, including local and national dignitaries, as shown above. Several Algerian media outlets critical of the government also covered it.

How US military presence spurred Pattaya’s rise into Thailand’s city of pleasure
Military links have brought waves of Americans to Thailand since the 1940s, with the crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln the latest to visit
The Amazon deliveries stopped reaching the USS Abraham Lincoln in February as it entered the conflict zone with Iran. A few weeks later – much to the chagrin of the sailors on board – even that most American of meals, the hamburger, was compromised by supply shortages when burger buns ran out.
“I lost a lot of weight on board,” said one young sailor, who was not authorised to speak to the media. “But I’m putting it back on here. We’re just eating and drinking as much as we can.”
The Lincoln, whose fighter jet squadrons have launched strikes on Iran, has spent a record time at sea, with complaints over food shortages and even the crew’s mental health reaching American media.
The length of its deployment without shore leave has stirred fierce debate over the White House’s treatment of its service personnel during the war on Iran.
It is a conflict, fought alongside Israel, that was meant to take a few days or weeks but is now in its seventh month as Tehran fights to a stalemate.
