Germany’s state election becomes a test of who belongs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:04:04 UTC
20:04:04 KST

On August 26, migrant business owners in Magdeburg, the capital of the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, closed their shops for five hours and gathered outside the state parliament.
The Migra-Streik (migrant strike) came days before the state election on September 6. It targeted the prevailing political climate.
Most participants are German citizens who work, employ people, and pay taxes in the state, yet find their place in the country once again under discussion.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is polling around 41 percent in Saxony-Anhalt, compared with roughly 23 percent for the Christian Democrats (CDU).
If that holds, AfD's lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, could become the first far-right politician to lead a German state government since 1945, heading a party branch that the domestic intelligence agency, the Verfassungsschutz, has classified as “confirmed right-wing extremist”.
On Sunday, voters in Saxony-Anhalt will elect a new state government. They will also answer a second question: is the citizenship of people born here fair game in an election campaign?
The answer becomes uncomfortable when considering who Germany's migration debate actually describes.
The debate started in 1961, not 2015
Germans usually date the migration debate to 2015, when close to a million asylum seekers arrived and “Wir schaffen das” (we can handle this) entered the political vocabulary. But the debate is older.
Under the 1961 labour recruitment agreement between West Germany and Türkiye, hundreds of thousands of “guest workers” arrived assuming they would one day leave. Many did not.
They settled, brought their families, built businesses and raised children and grandchildren who speak German as a first language and staff the country’s schools, hospitals and town halls.
According to federal statistics, around three million people of Turkish origin live in Germany, and roughly half hold German citizenship.
Not every complaint about “too much migration” is about new arrivals. Some of it lands on Germans.
In Munich, far from Saxony-Anhalt, three German citizens with Turkish family backgrounds spoke on condition of anonymity.
The first, a public-sector employee in her late twenties, was born and raised in Germany. “I was born here. I work here. I pay taxes here,” she tells TRT World.
“I should not have to explain, again and again, that I belong here.”
She does not object to Germany discussing migration policy. Her concern is that migration has become a catch-all explanation for problems with housing, schools, public safety and local administration.
The second, a logistics worker in his early forties who was also born in Germany, has little patience for parties that treat public frustration as prejudice.
“People see crowded schools, long waits at public offices and rents going up,” he says. “If politicians call everyone racist for talking about that, they leave the argument to AfD.”
He supports stricter migration rules but made clear that this should not put his own place in Germany into question. “This is my country too.”
The third, a corporate lawyer in her early thirties, was born in Munich to a family that arrived from Türkiye in the late 1960s. “My generation did everything the integration textbook asked of us,” she says.
“We went to university, we speak German better than we speak Turkish, we pay into the system.”
Watching mainstream politicians discuss whether citizenship can be withdrawn has changed how she views that record.
“If three generations are not enough to make you permanent, then nothing is. The requirements move whenever you meet them.”
Their views differ, but together they point to a double failure: a political debate that turns citizens with migrant roots into permanent suspects while dismissing concerns about strain as prejudice.
What happens when a state election is fought over belonging is not hypothetical. Germany has been here before.
In 1999, the CDU's Roland Koch won the election in the western state of Hesse after campaigning against the Schröder government's plan to allow dual citizenship. The result cost the governing coalition its majority in the Bundesrat, Germany's upper house, and the citizenship law that took effect in 2000 was narrower than originally proposed.
Children born in Germany could acquire German citizenship, but many had to choose between German and another nationality by age 23. That compromise shaped the debate for two decades.
Koch's CDU was not the AfD. The mechanism, however, was similar: a state election fought over belonging had national consequences for people who were hardly the subject of the vote.
What Sunday's vote could mean
The same mechanism — a state election that turns belonging into a campaign issue — is at work again.
The difference is that in 1999, the mainstream led it; today, it follows. The CDU and the Social Democrats (SPD) have responded to the AfD by moving between avoidance and imitation, and that imitation is no longer just rhetorical.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government has rolled back the three-year fast track to naturalisation introduced by the Scholz coalition in 2024, while proposals to strip dual nationals of German citizenship have moved from the AfD's platform into mainstream political debate.
Each step has been presented as a way to win voters back. But polls in Saxony-Anhalt suggest this has done little to slow the AfD.
Instead, mainstream parties have adopted parts of its framing while leaving the AfD as its most prominent advocate. Its influence on Germany's migration debate has extended well beyond its own vote share.
That is the choice the Migra-Streik pointed to in Magdeburg: whether to discuss migration as a policy issue or allow it to become a question of who counts as German. Germany faced a similar question in 1999, and its answer shaped the debate for two decades.
It faces that question again. How mainstream parties respond could determine whether German citizens with migrant backgrounds, in Munich as much as Magdeburg, once again feel that their place in the country is up for debate.

Polish military centers have begun sending mobilization cards to citizens
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Polish military centers have begun sending mobilization cards to citizens
Kyiv • UNN
Poland sends mobilization cards to reservists and civilian specialists every year. The authorities emphasize that this does not mean that mobilization has been declared.
In Poland, military recruitment centers have begun sending mobilization cards to citizens. The documents are primarily being issued to reserve soldiers, although they may also be handed to civilians. RMF24 reports, writes UNN.
Details
It is noted that a mobilization card is issued during peacetime. It specifies the unit and location where a person must report in the event mobilization is declared or war breaks out.
The Central Military Recruitment Center of Poland emphasizes that the distribution of such documents is a standard annual procedure. In other words, the current issuance of the cards does not in itself mean that mobilization has been declared in the country.
Mobilization cards may be received not only by reserve service members. They are also sent to specialists who may be needed by the army during wartime, including doctors, IT specialists, and logisticians.
Some documents may be issued to civilians who, in the event of war, are planned to be involved in tasks related to energy, transport, communications, or administrative work. Similar measures apply to employees of law enforcement and security agencies.
The Polish military explains that this arrangement makes it possible to determine people's duties and place of service in advance, so that if a crisis situation arises, time is not wasted organizing this process from scratch.

Serbia: How the funeral of Ratko Mladic is dividing a nation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:03:00 UTC
20:03:00 KST

Serbia: How the funeral of Ratko Mladic is dividing a nation
September 4, 2026
The body of the former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic, who died last week in The Hague, where he was serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina, has arrived back in Serbia.
Wrapped in the Serbian flag, Mladic's coffin was carried by members of the Serbian Armed Forces from the plane to a vehicle that transported his remains to the Military Medical Academy for autopsy.
Several groups of citizens gathered along the route from the airport to the hospital. Standing on overpasses, they greeted the motorcade carrying Mladic's body, holding banners that read "Thank you, General" and "Heroes never die."
Pro-government tabloids provided minute-by-minute coverage, referring to Mladic as a "Serbian general" and claiming that he had been "killed in The Hague."
A funeral with full state honors?
Ratko Mladic was sentenced in 2017 to life imprisonment by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in The Hague for the genocide in Srebrenica, in which more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed, the years-long siege of Sarajevo during the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and other war crimes, including the establishment of detention camps for non-Serb civilians and prisoners of war.
Belgrade media report that Mladic will be buried in Belgrade on Monday. Justice Minister Nenad Vujic had previously announced that the funeral would be held with the highest state honors.
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, however, says the decision will be left to the family.
Security agencies estimate that tens of thousands of people could attend the funeral.
"We will be there to provide all kinds of logistical and transport support and to maintain public order and security," said the president, adding, "It is very difficult to ensure and guarantee the safety of everyone."
Glorification that has continued for decades
For Jasmina Lazovic, executive director of the Belgrade-based Humanitarian Law Center, which has spent decades working on transitional justice and dealing with the past, none of this comes as a surprise.
She points to the long-standing glorification of Ratko Mladic in Serbia and his legacy.
"There is no small town in Serbia without at least one mural glorifying Ratko Mladic. The narrative that he was unjustly convicted has existed for years," she tells DW. "Now a narrative has emerged that he was killed, despite the fact that he died at the age of 85 after suffering several strokes."
Lazovic says that these narratives suit the state leadership's portrayal of Serbia as a country that fought exclusively defensive wars and do not leave enough room for a discussion of the consequences of those wars and the victims they left behind — neither in the media nor in the education system and institutions.
"And there are hundreds of thousands of victims across Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo. Above all, these were crimes committed against civilians, crimes that left the countries of the region — particularly Bosnia and Herzegovina — with a completely transformed ethnic structure," she said.
Lazovic says that the list of victims also includes those who survived rape and torture, as well as those who were forcibly displaced. "The list is long, and our knowledge is limited," she adds.
A general without a rank
The announcement that Mladic could be buried with the highest state honors drew swift responses from the international community.
"Glorification of war criminals is contrary to European values. There is no place for it either in EU member states or in candidate countries. I hope the government in Belgrade is aware of that," said European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos.
Aleksandar Vucic responded by accusing the West and the Hague Tribunal of blaming only Serbs for war crimes and failing to deliver justice for Serbian victims. But for now, he has officially left the decision on whether the deceased general will receive state honors to Mladic's family.
Jasmina Lazovic believes Vucic will once again take a pragmatic approach and that the final decision will depend on an assessment of what brings the authorities greater political benefit and what could cause greater damage.
She also points out that the issue is not only political, but legal.
"What is being overlooked here is the fact that Ratko Mladic was indeed a general, but he was sentenced to life in prison. Under the Law on the Serbian Armed Forces, anyone sentenced to more than one year in prison for a criminal offense loses their rank and, therefore, all the privileges that come with that rank," she says.
"If Ratko Mladic were buried with the highest state honors in accordance with the rank he held during the armed conflicts, that would be a direct violation of the law of this country."
What do Serbs want?
On the question as to how they view Ratko Mladic, Serbian citizens interviewed by DW in several cities across the multi-ethnic autonomous province of Vojvodina expressed sharply differing views, ranging from those who are convinced that Mladic was unjustly convicted to those who accept the genocide designation without reservation.
"What was he supposed to do, let them kill all the Serbs? Thank you [Mladic], for everything," one man from Ruma told DW.
"For me, the matter was settled when the genocide verdict was handed down," said a student from Novi Sad.
But most people simply wave the question away. "I have enough of my own problems," said Svetlana from Zrenjanin.
Goran, from Novi Sad, believes that it is simply another political issue. "They've been making fools of us for years. Nothing is different now," he told DW.
Lazovic believes that most Serbs are apathetic about the matter.
For her, this is a greater problem than just the pro-government media portraying Serbia as wanting to say goodbye to Mladic as a general. She argues that confronting Mladic's legacy and the past is essential if Serbian society is to move forward.

Haze is a recurring seasonal problem in Southeast Asia, where smoke from forest and peat fires in Indonesia can travel across national borders and affect neighbouring Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore.
Malaysia declared an emergency in a town in Sarawak state on Borneo Island on Friday after air pollution breached the country's emergency-level threshold linked to fires in neighbouring Indonesia.
The Air Pollutant Index in Serian, a small agricultural town of just under 90,000 near the border of Indonesia's Kalimantan province, surged to 521 on Friday, according to Malaysia's environment department.
Sarawak's much-larger capital, Kuching, also showed a hazardous reading of 311.
Malaysia's King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar has consented to the declaration of an emergency in Serian, which would allow more effective measures to be taken, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s office said in a statement.
It didn't provide details but officials have said a reading above 500 could provide for nonessential work and outdoor activities to be halted. Schools are already shut if the index is above 200.
Haze is a recurring seasonal problem in Southeast Asia, where smoke from forest and peat fires in Indonesia can travel across national borders and affect neighbouring Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore.
Sarawak has been the worst-hit Malaysian state by the haze, with several areas having hazardous air levels in the past few days.
The haze this year has been particularly severe, with elevated fire activity in several provinces in Indonesia, including Kalimantan, and prolonged dry conditions contributing to worsening pollution across parts of Borneo.
Satellite data from Indonesia's Forestry Ministry on Friday detected 717 hot spots nationwide likely caused by forest fires since 1 August. The data showed 103 active hot spots in the past 24 hours alone.
Indonesian authorities have deployed firefighting resources and attempted to induce rain.
Indonesian police announced Friday that they have arrested 112 people suspected of starting the recent forest and peatland fires in 10 provinces on Sumatra and Borneo islands. The suspects were local farmers accused of deliberately burning land to clear areas at lower cost.
Indonesia has also suspended the business licenses of five companies over alleged forest and land fires within their concessions in the Kalimantan province.
Pipit Subiyanto, a senior police official at Indonesia’s National Police criminal investigation agency, said authorities are investigating 167 cases involving the deliberate burning of some 4,700 hectares of land across nine provinces.

The strangest sky in the galaxy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:01:48 UTC
20:01:48 KST

There are a lot of weird stars in the universe, but if I had to pick the very weirdest, it would be S301.
The name is prosaic, but it hides profundity. Ironically the star itself isn’t really peculiar at all. It’s much like the sun, though somewhat more massive, hotter and more luminous. There are billions more just like it in the galaxy at large.
If this star was almost anywhere else in the universe, it would be downright mundane. But as any cosmic real estate agent will tell you, it’s all about location, location, location. It’s not the star; it’s the neighborhood.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
S301, you see, orbits Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), the supermassive black hole that inhabits the exact geometric center of our Milky Way galaxy. And from there, its view of the cosmos is odd—more than odd, really, because the star experiences severely warped time and space.
At 4.3 million times the sun’s mass, Sgr A* dominates the region. Its gravity is extremely strong, of course, holding sway over a menagerie of objects around it. This includes a swarm of stars called the S-star cluster. Dozens of very luminous stellar cluster members are known, but this area likely has far more stars that are fainter hidden behind a vast smog of opaque dust between the center of the galaxy and the sun.
Using huge infrared telescopes that can see through that veil of dust, astronomers have been able to watch some of these stars swirling around the black hole. Most are on elliptical trajectories, dipping closer in and then sweeping farther out over their orbits. Until recently the black-hole-diving record holder was a star called S2, which got as close as 18 billion kilometers to Sgr A*.
But then, in August 2026, that record was shattered when astronomers announced the discovery of a star they dubbed S301. On its greatly elongated orbit, S301 gets as close to the black hole as about 1.7 billion km—not much farther out than the average distance between the sun and Saturn.
And that makes the sky from S301 unlike any other known place in the galaxy.
In 2022 a global consortium of astronomers announced that they had captured images of Sgr A* that showed a doughnut-shaped ring of material swirling around it. The hole in the center of the ring is SgrA*’s “shadow,” the volume of space around it where light can actually orbit the black hole before falling in; because no light gets out, this region appears dark. S301 gets so close to the black hole that this shadow is more than a degree across in the star’s sky—that is, more than twice the size of our full moon, as seen from Earth. The ring of material surrounding Sgr A* would be about four degrees across—about half the apparent size of your outstretched fist.
Mind you, the combined might of radio telescopes spread across our planet could just barely make out the shape of that material, showing only a fuzzy ring. From S301, you’d have a far better view by simply looking up.
That would come with a cost, though. Astronomers have found that, just 200 years or so ago, material falling into Sgr A* got so hot that it emitted bright flares in x-rays—blasting them out at a rate hundreds of thousands of times the sun’s entire luminosity. Even from 1.7 billion km away, that’s a lethal dose of radiation.
Happily—if that’s the right word to use—there are probably no planets orbiting S301. At that distance from Sgr A*, the black hole’s gravity is so powerful that it would destabilize any world orbiting more than just a few million kilometers from the star. While it’s possible planets could persist with a closer orbit to S301, the star itself is so hot that they’d be cooked.
That is too bad. Discounting those deadly, ultrapowerful x-ray outbursts, what a view it would be!
Seeing a supermassive black hole up close is a spectacular, if unsettling, thought, but that’s not the only oddity to be seen from S301. What matters in this case is not so much the star’s location but its velocity. When the star is at perigalacticon (a delightful term meaning “closest point in its orbit to the galactic center,” which is Sgr A* for S301), the gravity of the black hole is so strong that S301 whips around Sgr A* at a speed of 90 million kilometers per hour.
That’s 8 percent the speed of light.
If we looked out from the star, this demonically rapid motion would change what we’d see—literally.
At such high velocities, light becomes noticeably redshifted and blueshifted because of the relativistic Doppler effect. This is similar to how the sound of, say, a passing motorcycle drops in pitch as the vehicle zooms away from you. At S301’s speed around the black hole, that shift is substantial, changing the perceived color of cosmic objects. For example, the iconic red color of hydrogen clouds in the Milky Way would look to us to be orange as S301 swung toward them and a deeper red as it moved away.
Even weirder is the aberration of light. Despite the strange terminology, you’re already familiar with this effect: when you drive a car through rain, the drops always appear to come at you at an angle from vertical no matter what direction you move. This is a result of the combination of the velocity of the raindrops as they fall downward and your velocity as you move toward them.
This also happens with light. The effect is extremely small unless you’re moving very rapidly, but at S301’s speed around Sgr A*, that angle can change by more than four degrees. This means the stars on one side of the sky will appear to shift their positions by about nine degrees, relative to stars on the other side of the sky! This would make mapping the sky difficult, to say the least. Entire constellations would appear to shift positions over the star’s 8.7-Earth-year-long orbit.
Even time itself changes for S301. Einstein’s special theory of relativity shows that, compared with a stationary observer, time flows more slowly for moving objects. Again, this effect is small until speeds get large; at 8 percent the speed of light, this time dilation effect is really obvious. At the star’s maximum speed, clocks on S301 would lose about 11 seconds per hour relative to clocks on Earth. Worse, that difference itself would change as the star moved to the other side of its orbit and lost some velocity. Anyone traveling along with the star would say their clocks moved at a constant speed, whereas clocks very far away would be off—that’s relativity in a nutshell. But in the end, trying to time celestial events from S301 would be irksome.
All this is, frankly, bizarre. A sky that twists and changes color and flagrantly disobeys the idea of linear time is difficult to comprehend. And yet it could be worse: S301 is decently bright yet still difficult to spot, meaning as-yet undiscovered, fainter stars could very well be orbiting closer to Sgr A*, where all these effects would be magnified even more.
Theoretically speaking, being an astronomer there would be amazing. In practical terms, though, I think I prefer the sky from Earth.

A computational model explains the sudden rise in societal division
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:00:34 UTC
20:00:34 KST

As modern communication technology has doubled the number of close social ties people maintain, societies have fractured into deeply divided political camps. A computational model simulating human social behavior shows that simply having more connections past a certain threshold forces communities to splinter into polarized echo chambers. The research was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Political polarization has risen sharply in the United States and other Western nations over the past two decades. During this same period, the average number of close friendships reported by individuals has nearly doubled, a trend coinciding with the public debut of smartphones and mass social media networks around 2008.
Stefan Thurner, Markus Hofer, and Jan Korbel, researchers at the Medical University of Vienna and the Complexity Science Hub Vienna, noticed the parallel timing of these two trends. They wanted to test whether the sheer volume of social connections might be driving the ideological divide.
To investigate this, the researchers focused on two well-documented features of human behavior: homophily and social balance. Homophily is the human tendency to seek out and befriend like-minded individuals. When people interact with those who share their views, they often reinforce each other’s beliefs, causing their opinions to align even more closely.
Social balance describes how groups of three people naturally seek comfortable, stable relationship dynamics. A balanced triad occurs when all three people are friends, or when two friends mutually dislike a third person.
Unbalanced triads cause psychological tension or social stress. This happens if one person tries to remain friends with two people who despise each other, or if three people all dislike one another. People naturally try to resolve this tension by either changing their opinions to match their friends or by distancing themselves from people who disagree with them.
To see how these basic social rules play out on a large scale, the research team built an agent-based computational model. In this virtual society, each simulated individual was assigned a mathematical profile representing a set of binary political stances on different topics.
Individuals in the simulation were connected in a network where relationships could be either positive or negative. A positive connection formed if two individuals shared a majority of their stances, acting as a virtual friendship. A negative connection formed if their stances opposed one another, acting as a rivalry or enmity.
The researchers used a mathematical algorithm to randomly select individuals and flip one of their political stances. After flipping an opinion, the model calculated the individual’s new level of cognitive dissonance, measured by how much they now agreed with their friends and disagreed with their enemies.
If the new opinion lowered their overall social stress, the individual kept the new stance. If the opinion increased their social stress, the individual rejected the change, though the model allowed a small probability of keeping it to represent occasional irrational behavior. As individuals updated their views, their positive and negative relationships shifted to maintain social balance.
The researchers ran this simulation multiple times, varying the average number of close connections each individual possessed. They tracked how the distribution of opinions across the entire population changed as the network became more interconnected.
The simulation revealed a sudden tipping point, which physicists call a phase transition. When the average number of close connections remained low, the virtual society maintained a diverse, cohesive blend of opinions. Small friend groups shared similar views, but these groups remained scattered and tolerant of the broader population.
Once the average number of connections surpassed a critical threshold of about five close friends, the societal structure abruptly collapsed into a highly polarized state. The numerous small, diverse clusters merged into two massive, opposing groups of roughly equal size.
Within each massive group, individuals held nearly identical opinions. Between the two groups, individuals held entirely opposite views and maintained strictly negative relationships with anyone on the other side.
Next, the researchers introduced radical influencers to the model. They assigned extreme, unchanging opinions to just two percent of the simulated population. These influencers never adjusted their stances to reduce social stress, but they still formed friendships and rivalries based on ideological alignment.
The presence of these rigid influencers changed the nature of the polarization tipping point. The transition from a cohesive society to a divided one became gradual rather than sudden. However, the splintering into opposing echo chambers began at an even lower threshold, occurring when individuals averaged just four and a half close connections.
To test if their model reflected reality, the research team compared their simulated results to real-world survey data. They analyzed data from large, multi-year surveys, including the Pew Research Center, which track both political ideology and the average number of close friendships among thousands of respondents.
The empirical data showed that ideological polarization in the United States remained relatively low and stable before 2010. Shortly after that time, the average number of close social ties increased, and polarization spiked rapidly.
The researchers found that their computational model accurately predicted both the timing and the magnitude of this real-world polarization spike. The model required no outside factors like economic changes or political campaigns to explain the divide. The mathematical rules of homophily and social balance, combined with an increasing number of social ties, were enough to produce the exact polarization trend seen in the survey data.
The study does present certain caveats. The computational model assumes every individual has the exact same sensitivity to cognitive dissonance and social stress. In reality, human beings display varied levels of tolerance for disagreement and differing levels of political engagement.
The simulation also uses a relatively fixed network structure. While relationships can switch between positive and negative, the underlying web of who knows whom does not fluidly dissolve and rewire over time. The authors note that real social media platforms use recommendation algorithms that constantly suggest new connections, which might amplify the clustering effect beyond what the current model captures.
One concerning finding from the model is a hysteresis effect, meaning the process is difficult to reverse. Once a society crosses the connectivity threshold and becomes highly polarized, simply reducing the number of connections back to the original level will not depolarize the population. A fractured society must drop its connectivity far below the initial tipping point to restore ideological cohesion.
Since reducing human connectivity is likely impossible in the digital age, the authors suggest alternative ways to raise the critical threshold. They suggest that educational efforts could train individuals to have a higher tolerance for opposing opinions, which mathematically prevents the phase transition. Disrupting the reach of radical influencers through content moderation could also delay the onset of extreme societal division.
The study, “Why more social interactions lead to more polarization in societies,” was authored by Stefan Thurner, Markus Hofer, and Jan Korbel.

How a Secret Orangutan Breeding Program Is Creating a Baby Boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

“It’s a girl!” Melissa Peterson exclaims.
Just outside the operating room, the hallway erupts in cheers. Joseph Dewane, an ob-gyn, has just delivered a healthy baby via C-section; Autumn Joi Goodwin-Samson, a neonatalist, tends to the newborn still slick with a waxy film.
It’s a successful delivery just like any other except for one, minor, difference: The patient is an orangutan.
Ruhana—or just “Ru” for short—is one of eight orangutan babies born in a collection of US zoos since the beginning of 2025. For these critically endangered primates, that’s a staggering figure. It’s also not random: The baby boom is the result of a meticulous breeding plan and decades of research to weave a conservation safety net, one birth at a time.
“It might seem like it was all a coincidence that everyone was born at the same time, but it was very carefully planned,” says Angie Selzer, a senior animal care specialist with the Fort Wayne Zoo in Indiana and the Orangutan Species Survival Plan (SSP) program coordinator.
The SSP has been coordinating breeding recommendations since 1985; every two years, the program creates a breeding and transfer plan for animals at zoos accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA). Geneticists from the SSP consult a “studbook,” which contains the pedigree of all the animals in their system.
“We want to maintain a healthy and sustainable population that mimics the natural history of wild orangutans while ensuring successful mother-rearing of offspring,” Seltzer tells WIRED. Their recommendation accounts for a number of breeding factors, including underrepresented genetic lines, each animal’s unique personality, and group dynamics—always aiming for the lowest relation between breeding pairs.
“We’ve had a very good, happy outcome,” she says. It all started in February 2025 when the Indianapolis Zoo welcomed Edi, a healthy baby boy. After that, Weila was delivered at the Hogle Zoo in Utah in June; Bintang arrived at the Los Angeles Zoo, and in December, the Memphis Zoo welcomed Ruhana. Peterson, the associate primates curator at the Memphis Zoo says being present for that moment was a “remarkable experience.” The run of babies has continued this year, with baby girls born at the Cameron Park Zoo in Waco, Texas, Sedgwick County Zoo in Wichita, Kansas, and Fort Wayne Zoo in Indiana. Just a few months ago, the Denver Zoo welcomed a baby boy named Rambutan.
Humans share over 90 percent of their DNA with orangutans, a figure well-evidenced in how they breed and give birth. Orangutans in the program are routinely given human birth control and human prenatal vitamins; they’re taught to pee on human pregnancy tests; they gestate for nearly nine months; and after humans, their offspring have the longest childhood of any mammal. While C-sections like Jahe’s are rare, some zoos keep ob-gyns on call for their orangutans and other primates.
“Looking at their eyes and their hands, it’s like a mirror,” says Matthew Lenyo, assistant curator of predators at Denver Zoo. “It’s humbling.”
As with humans, maternal behaviors are learned; training is a critical part of ensuring the health of orangutan babies. For first-time mom Hesty, the Sumatran orangutan at the Denver Zoo, training involved teaching her to pass the baby to and from keepers for essential health checks and nursing since Hesty’s mother had struggled with it.
For many zoos, prebirth training involves other orangutans in their care too. To be successful, this training requires a deep and hard-earned trust between keepers and these animals, and can prove invaluable if an orangutan cannot be cared for by their biological mother.
That happened at the Hogle Zoo, when Weila’s biological mom failed to bond with her. She was hand-reared by keepers while they prepared Acara—a proven foster who raised her younger brother—to take over as mom using a stuffed animal as a proxy. They slowly introduced the two to each other, rewarding Acara for properly handling Weila. “She also has a gentle behavior” and uses a very gentle touch, says Hannah Comstock, the animal care supervisor of primates at Hogle Zoo. The pair live together full-time now. Acara is a model parent, and Weila is thriving; she has even started adopting some of Acara’s mannerisms.
Still, zookeepers aim to be as hands-off as possible. “We do all this work, but then at the same time, the best outcome is when you’re not needed,” says Lenyo.
It’s estimated that there are around 100,000 Bornean orangutans and 11,000 Sumatran orangutans left in the wild. The population of Tapanuli orangutans is even more dire, with estimates indicating a few more than 700 are left in the wild. The rainforest habitat they rely on in their native Borneo and Sumatra is being razed to create palm oil plantations, and the great apes are also targeted by traffickers who kill orangutan mothers, kidnap their babies, and sell them on the black market as pets. Some estimates indicate that orangutans could go extinct in the wild within 50 years; some experts caution it could be even sooner, in the next 10 to 20 years.
While these new orangutan babies will not be released into the wild, they are a critical part of species conservation. Zookeepers call them ambassadors; when visitors can see the apes, abstract ideas like climate change and deforestation become more real.
But the captive population also has a direct impact on the well-being of wild and rehabilitated populations: Research conducted at AZA zoos on everything from disease management to quality of life is then relayed back to teams in Southeast Asia. Felicity Oram is a conservation practitioner and co-director of OrangJUGA, a Borneo-based conservation organization. Her research on orangutan’s teeth has been critical in the care of young orangutans rescued from the pet trade who live in rehabilitation and rescue centers. She quips that “captive orangutans can help their cousins in the wild and in rehabilitation centers just by opening their mouths.”
Before Oram’s research, estimating age was an imperfect science at best. “It’s very difficult with size,” Oram says. “It’s just like with human children—you go, ‘Isn’t that a cute 4-year-old!’ And then they tell you it’s 2.” She partnered with zoos, using data collected from captive orangutans to link tooth stages to behavioral and developmental stages. In turn, this research allowed rescuers to more accurately make critical decisions about nutrition, medical care, and socialization, giving these orangutans the best shot at having a successful life—and maybe one day having offspring of their own.

EXPLAINER: How a state election in Germany tests the far-right’s path to power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:59:50 UTC
19:59:50 KST

A state election in little-known Saxony-Anhalt is being watched across Europe for the shockwaves it could send through German national politics.
Voters on Sunday will elect a new state parliament in the mid-sized eastern region, home to less than 3% of Germany’s electorate.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) leads the polls and may form a state government, which would be the first far-right administration in a German state since 1949, after the Nazi regime fell and the Federal Republic was founded.
The political stakes far outweigh the state’s size. The AfD, which campaigns against immigration and is already the main opposition in the national parliament, is testing the “firewall” other parties have built to keep it from office.
A strong showing would hit Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s already-fragile coalition in Berlin, which has been weakened by a sluggish economy and infighting.
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel has framed the contest as more than a state race. “We will form the government in Saxony-Anhalt,” she said. “We will also govern at the federal level.”
The far-right AfD has more than doubled its support in Saxony-Anhalt in five years. It took 20.8% in 2021. It now polls above 40%. 
 
Many observers credit lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund for driving the surge.
The 35-year-old lawmaker sells himself as a candidate of change and has already issued a “government program” plus a 100-day plan.
Immigration is the core of his pitch. He pledges to expel people without legal status “from the first minute,” expand deportation detention from dozens of places to hundreds and make asylum seekers work or lose benefits.
Weekly magazine Der Spiegel put him on its cover as “Germany’s most dangerous man.” Siegmund leaned into the label, signing copies for cameras and social media.
Critics say his moderate public image hides his ties to a tougher, more hardline network around him. The country’s domestic intelligence service has classified the AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch as a “confirmed right-wing extremist” organization, citing anti-democratic goals and members’ ties to far-right groups.
Far-right candidate Siegmund’s closest rival is Premier Sven Schulze of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU). 
 
The 47-year-old conservative took office only in January, after longtime leader Reiner Haseloff stepped down following nearly 15 years in power.
Schulze is less established than his predecessor and has struggled to turn name recognition into votes. The CDU presents itself as the responsible center-right choice and argues that an AfD government would scare off investors and isolate a state that lives from the European single market.
Schulze has repeatedly warned on the campaign trail that an AfD government would be an “economic catastrophe” for Saxony-Anhalt, since the far-right party is seeking to take Germany out of the euro and the visa-free Schengen area, causing alarm among investors.
“The AfD has no contacts whatsoever to make things better in Europe. It only wants out of the EU. That would be an economic catastrophe,” he said in a recent interview.
“I am the only one who, with the CDU, can keep the AfD from power and avert harm from Saxony-Anhalt.”
Polls from several institutes put the AfD at about 40% to 43%, well ahead of every other party. However, coming first is not the same as winning the state.
Seats are shared only among parties that clear the 5% threshold and enter the Landtag, so how many make it across that line can decide whether the poll leader also gets a majority.
The CDU, the center-right party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Premier Sven Schulze, is at about 22% to 23%, down from 37.1% in the 2021 state election. Of Schulze’s coalition partners, the Social Democrats are at about 7% to 9%. The pro-business Free Democrats are at about 3%, below the threshold.
The socialist Left Party is at about 11% to 13%. The Greens sit at about 5% to 6%, on the edge of the cutoff. The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance, a newer left-populist party that opposes military support for Ukraine, is at about 3% to 4%.
Sunday night will therefore turn as much on the small parties as on the AfD. If enough of them miss 5%, AfD leader Ulrich Siegmund could take a majority. If they squeeze in, he could finish first and still fall short.
Merz’s CDU has ruled out any coalition or cooperation with the AfD, citing the party’s record and intelligence findings that the Saxony-Anhalt branch is a confirmed far-right extremist organization. Other mainstream parties have taken the same stance.
Far-right candidate Siegmund is not seeking a partner and is running to govern alone. Estimates suggest he needs at least 45% to 48% to win a majority of seats in the state parliament.
The Landtag’s standard size is 83 seats. A party needs 42 to govern alone. If the AfD falls short of a majority of seats, Magdeburg could spend weeks arguing over who becomes premier.
The option raised most often is a CDU-led minority government with the Social Democrats and perhaps the Greens, surviving vote by vote.
Schulze has said he will not make himself dependent on the Left Party. Sahra Wagenknecht, founder of the BSW, insisted that they want a “non-party” premier and will not serve as the majority-maker keeping the CDU in power.
German officials and analysts say Sunday’s result will echo in federal politics even if no one expects a snap election.
Calling early Bundestag elections would itself be read as an admission of failure by the co-ruling Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and Social Democrats.
Pressure would fall first on Merz’s conservatives. A large AfD win and a weak night for the CDU would reopen debate over his future.
According to the latest opinion polls by public broadcaster ARD, 83% of eligible voters say they are dissatisfied with Chancellor Friedrich Merz - a historically poor rating. Only 13% say they are satisfied with his work, the lowest figure the poll has recorded for a sitting chancellor.
A leadership fight within the Christian Democrats would not automatically bring down the federal government. If party pressure forces Merz to resign, parliament could elect a new chancellor without dissolving the Bundestag.

Germany: Is Saxony-Anhalt's economy really struggling?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:59:00 UTC
19:59:00 KST

Germany: Is Saxony-Anhalt's economy really struggling?
September 4, 2026
Germany is watching the upcoming state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt with keen interest. Much of the attention is focused on the performance of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), whose state branch in Saxony-Anhalt has been classified by the domestic intelligence agency as "confirmed right-wing extremist."
According to opinion polls, the AfD could emerge as the clear election winner.
In the last state election in 2021, the AfD won around 20% of the vote and has since been the largest opposition party. The state is governed by a coalition of the center-right Christian Democrats (CDU), the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP), with the CDU's Sven Schulze serving as state premier.
Where does Saxony-Anhalt stand?
The AfD is campaigning on the claim that Saxony-Anhalt has been left behind — both socially and economically.
The unemployment rate in Saxony-Anhalt is higher than the national average, while median earnings for full-time employees are lower than across Germany as a whole.
Of Saxony-Anhalt's roughly 2.1 million residents, just under 800,000 are in jobs subject to social security contributions. The chemical industry has traditionally been one of the state's major employers and among the most productive sectors of the economy, particularly in the so-called chemical triangle around the cities of Leuna, Merseburg and Bitterfeld-Wolfen.
Machinery and plant engineering companies, including suppliers to the struggling automotive industry, also play an important role in the manufacturing sector.
The retail, transport and hospitality sector accounts for around one-fifth of jobs, including many positions in tourism. The Harz Mountains, the Luther cities of Wittenberg and Eisleben, and Quedlinburg, with its UNESCO World Heritage status, are key destinations.
Saxony-Anhalt's economy growing more slowly than the national average
The perception that the eastern German states have still not caught up with the former West German states appears to resonate with voters. The AfD has built broad support around this message, particularly among younger voters.
It is often claimed that pensions are lower in eastern Germany than in the west, but this is no longer the case. It is true, however, that the proportion of pensioners in Saxony-Anhalt is slightly higher than the national average. Many pensioners in the east also rely solely on their state pension, whereas many in the west receive company pensions or income from private retirement savings in addition to their state pension.
Partly because of its higher proportion of pensioners, Saxony-Anhalt has one of the lowest levels of economic output per capita in Germany, at just three-quarters of the national average. The state's economy has also generally grown more slowly than the national economy in recent years.
'Foreigners are to blame'
The AfD has also made immigration a central campaign issue in Saxony-Anhalt, warning of "too much immigration" and "foreign influence" — and appears to be gaining support with this message. This is even though, compared with other German states, relatively few non-Germans live there.
Although Saxony-Anhalt is one of Germany's economically weaker states, it has gained population in recent years, according to migration figures.
Since 2016, more non-Germans have moved to Saxony-Anhalt than have left. The net migration balance for German citizens has also been positive for the past six years.
At the end of 2025, foreign nationals accounted for around 9% of Saxony-Anhalt's population — roughly half the share in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state.
The claim that "foreigners are living off taxpayers" is also misleading. Compared with other German states, Saxony-Anhalt has a relatively low proportion of foreign nationals among potential recipients of welfare benefits such as basic income support.
However far the political and economic reality may diverge from the bleak picture painted by extremist parties, particularly the AfD, one trend appears evident: support for radical parties is becoming increasingly entrenched.
The two formerly dominant parties, the CDU and SPD, are bearing the brunt of this shift and steadily losing ground. The CDU is increasingly struggling to maintain its status as a broad-based mainstream party, while the SPD is edging closer to the 5% threshold, raising the prospect that it could eventually struggle to win seats in some state parliaments.
This article was originally written in German.

99% of Ireland's population growth 'driven by foreigners': True or false?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:55:31 UTC
19:55:31 KST

The short answer is 'false', but the truth is not much far from that.
As fertility rates plunge across the EU, the impact of migration on demographics is becoming increasingly evident.
Since 2012, more people have been dying in the EU than have been born, and last year, new births reached their lowest point on record, at 3.46 million.
Although migration is indeed helping to keep demographic collapse at bay, figures circulating online are not always accurate.
Take this video shared by Tommy Robinson, a British far-right activist, which was watched nearly 700,000 times, claiming that nearly all population growth last year was driven by foreigners.
The video doesn't cite sources, but data from Ireland's Central Statistics Office can clear up a few things.
First of all, the majority of all births last year — about 70% — were to Irish citizens.
However, that rate is falling steeply and rapidly; it stood at 76% in 2022.
Then migration comes into play.
The latest estimates — April 2025 to April 2026 — say that there was a net flow of around 53,000 non-Irish migrants coming to the country, so around 72% of the total population growth.
At the same time, more Irish citizens left the country than those who arrived, with a net loss of around 5,000.
For context, Ireland's population grew by nearly 67,000 people between April 2025 and April 2026, and about 28% of that growth came from "natural increase", meaning there were almost 19,000 more births than deaths.
So migrant arrivals are significantly contributing to Ireland's population growth.
That's also been certified by Eurostat, which classified Ireland as a country where population growth is mainly due to net migration.
This aspect is even more pronounced in countries such as Spain, Portugal, the UK and France, where, Eurostat says, population growth last year was "only due to positive net migration" last year.
In no country surveyed by Eurostat is population growth happening only due to natural change.

A new opinion poll showed Israel’s opposition ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc in the Knesset, with 57 seats against 51 if general elections were held on Friday.
The poll, conducted by the private Lazar Research Institute on a random sample of 600 Israelis with a 4.4% margin of error, came a day after a separate survey showed both camps tied at 53 seats each.
According to the latest poll, neither camp would be able to reach the 61-seat threshold needed to form a government, Israeli daily Maariv reported.
The results come ahead of general elections scheduled for Oct. 27, amid intense competition over the shape of political blocs and the premiership.
Jewish opposition parties would win 57 seats if elections were held today, compared with 51 for the bloc supporting Netanyahu, Maariv said.
Arab lawmakers would win 12 seats in the 120-seat Knesset.
A Channel 13 poll published Thursday showed Netanyahu’s camp and the opposition tied at 53 seats each, with Arab parties receiving 14 seats.
The latest results shift the bloc map from a tie to a six-seat lead for the opposition within one day, but neither camp secures a governing majority.
Most leaders of Jewish opposition parties say they refuse to rely on Arab lawmakers to form a government.
Bloc shifts
Maariv said Netanyahu’s coalition bloc strengthened to 51 seats for the first time since May.
It said the opposition bloc dropped by two seats to 57, while Arab parties lost one seat.

The far-right Your People Israel party, led by Ofer Winter, also received four seats.

Seat map

In the opposition, Yashar, led by Gadi Eisenkot, came first with 23 seats.

Thursday’s Channel 13 poll also showed Eisenkot ahead of Netanyahu, 47% to 37%.
 
Fear of war

By contrast, 39% said they do not fear such a war, while 6% were undecided.
 
Genocide on Gaza

By political affiliation, 61% of coalition voters believed there had been “internal betrayal,” while 64% of opposition voters said no such thing had happened.
Israel, backed by the US, launched its genocide in Gaza on Oct. 8, 2023, killing 73,470 Palestinians and injuring 174,540 as of Thursday, while victims remain under the rubble and on roads that rescue teams cannot reach.
Israel’s general elections are scheduled for Oct. 27 and are seen as decisive for Netanyahu’s political future, as he faces accusations of corruption, authoritarianism, and failure.
The current government, described as the most right-wing in Israel’s history, has been led since late December 2022 by Netanyahu, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes in the Gaza Strip.

Emil Rusev blends his Bulgarian and Colombian worlds in music
Friday 4 September 2026 13:00
Friday, 4 September 2026, 13:00
PHOTO remezcla.com
Font size
At 22, Emil Rusev already has a rather unusual musical résumé – Colombian rhythms, Bulgarian roots, a TikTok hit and a spot at an Ed Sheeran concert. Born in Medellín, the singer describes himself as a “Euro-paisa”, a nod to his life between Colombia and Bulgaria. BTA tells his story in a recent article.
Emil’s connection with music actually began before he was born. His mother is Colombian and sang in a choir, while his Bulgarian father plays the double bass. The two met in a lift while on tour in Cali and, according to Rusev, fell in love on the spot – even though she spoke no Bulgarian and he understood no Spanish.
“The power of music ultimately brought them together. Literally, my entire existence in this world is because of music,” Rusev told Remezcla.
As a child, he took singing lessons from his mother, while his father introduced him to music theory. Justin Bieber and Post Malone are among his biggest influences, and Rusev jokingly describes himself as “the Latin American Justin Bieber”.
His breakthrough came in 2026, when “Va Uno a Ver y Ve” took off on TikTok. Around the same time, Ed Sheeran chose him as an opening act for his concert in Bogotá. It was then that Rusev began weaving his Bulgarian roots more noticeably into his music. His latest single, “Ando (Bye, Ya Me Voy…)”, even includes words in Bulgarian.
“I’m trying to start incorporating my Bulgarian culture into my music,” he says.
Rusev sees belonging to two very different cultures as an advantage. 
“I’ve always been proud to be Colombian and Bulgarian. I’ve always tried to show both sides how much respect I have for them,” he says.
His next big goal is a debut album, which is already in the works. His list of dream collaborators also bridges his two worlds: among the names he mentions are DARA and Maluma, Remezcla writes.

Russian occupation court sentences captured Ukrainian journalist Levchenko to 15 years in prison
The ruling was published by occupation-linked channels, Ukrinform reports.
According to Russian sources, after the occupation of Melitopol, the journalist remained in the city and did not renounce her Ukrainian citizenship.
"After contacting a resident of Ukrainian-controlled territory via the Telegram messenger, the woman agreed to assist the Ukrainian special services by providing information about the locations of administrative buildings and employees of Russian authorities, as well as the routes used by Russian military personnel, military equipment, weapons and other troops and military formations in the Zaporizhzhia region," the Institute of Mass Information quoted the occupation-linked channels as saying.
According to information from the occupation court cited by the media, in February 2023, the woman allegedly provided information about Russian state ministries and agencies, including security and defense bodies, along with their addresses and lists of employees.
"The transfer of this information to the Ukrainian side could have resulted in strikes against the locations of these strategic facilities," the occupation court claimed.
The occupiers also alleged that Levchenko failed to delete the information from her phone.
The Russian authorities charged her with espionage under Article 276 of the Russian Criminal Code, which concerns the transfer, collection or storage, for the purpose of passing to the enemy, of information that can be used against the Russian Armed Forces.
The so-called "Zaporizhzhia Regional Court" found the former journalist guilty and sentenced her to 15 years in prison.
Russian forces abducted Iryna Levchenko and her husband, Oleksandr, in early May 2023 in temporarily occupied Melitopol and held them for some time in basements in the city. The couple were detained on the street and initially held together before being separated.
According to Levchenko's sister, Olena Rudenko, the journalist was held in a detention center in Donetsk in a cell measuring approximately 3 by 4 meters together with three other women.
In June 2026, it emerged that Iryna Levchenko had been transferred from a detention center in Simferopol to a detention center in Krasnodar, Russia.
According to RIA South, Oleksandr Levchenko was released in August 2024. He had been held in occupied Melitopol throughout his detention. Upon his release, he was given a document stating that he had allegedly served 21 days of administrative arrest for "violating the curfew."
His passport, bank cards and money seized during the search were not returned. During his entire period in detention, he saw his wife only once, while they were both out for a walk at the detention center, but they were not allowed to speak to each other.
According to the Institute of Mass Information, Iryna Levchenko has worked in journalism since 1981. She worked for factory newspapers, the Melitopol district newspaper Novyi Den, and served as a correspondent for regional and national print media outlets.

Crimea under attack: what the 2026 holiday season was like for Russians
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:50:07 EEST
19:50:07 KST

Crimea under attack: what the 2026 holiday season was like for Russians
Kyiv • UNN
Systematic strikes complicated logistics, weakened air defenses, and caused disruptions to energy and fuel supplies in Crimea. The 2026 holiday season has effectively been ruined.
Systematic strikes by the Defense Forces of Ukraine against the energy, fuel, transport, and military infrastructure of occupied Crimea throughout the spring and summer have significantly complicated Russia’s use of the peninsula as a military hub. Operation "Crimean Switch off" did not lead to the immediate collapse of the Russian grouping or the energy system of occupied Crimea, but it has had a cumulative effect: problems with logistics and fuel supplies, power outages, and reduced air defense capabilities. A collateral but tangible consequence was the effective disruption of the holiday season, on which a significant share of local small businesses depends. UNN discussed the consequences of the systematic Ukrainian strikes on facilities in the occupied peninsula with experts.
"Crimean Switch off": what kind of operation is it?
"Crimean Switch off" is the name of a campaign by the Unmanned Systems Forces aimed primarily at energy infrastructure in the occupied territories. It is being conducted in parallel with Operation "MoLoChKa," whose targets include tankers and other vessels providing Russian logistics in the Black and Azov Seas.
"Crimean Switch off" began on July 1, while "MoLoChKa" began on July 6. Both special operations fit into Kyiv’s strategy of coercing Russia into peace.
One of the first targets of Ukraine’s middle strikes was the "TES-Terminal-1" terminal in Kerch. It is a large facility for storing light petroleum products. Substations with voltages of 110–220 kV in Yalta, Kerch, Sudak, Feodosia, Alushta, and other populated areas were systematically targeted.
According to the Unmanned Systems Forces, by August 28, 315 energy facilities had been hit since the start of the operation. The targets included the Balaklava Thermal Power Plant in Sevastopol and gas-turbine stations in Karierne and Naumivka.
In parallel, Ukraine carried out strikes against maritime logistics. As of August 22, according to the commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Robert "Madyar" Brovdi, 242 vessels in the Black and Azov Seas had been hit. It was separately reported that four of the five key ferries of the Kerch crossing had been disabled.
The Unmanned Systems Forces carried out the main strikes on tankers using attack UAVs manufactured by FirePoint
In addition, at the beginning of the summer, Ukrainian troops destroyed the main bridges connecting the peninsula with mainland Ukraine, which significantly complicated logistics for Russian occupation forces.
How strikes on Crimea affect the front
For Russia, Crimea remains primarily a major military and logistical hub through which, among other things, the occupying forces in southern Ukraine are supplied. That is why strikes by the Ukrainian military are not limited to the energy sector.
According to military expert Ivan Stupak, this summer Ukraine has been systematically targeting air defense, electronic warfare systems, warehouses, bases, fuel infrastructure, and Russian logistics.
This is important because Crimea is not simply territory for Russia, but a major military hub. And Ukraine is precisely trying to gradually undermine its capabilities. This concerns strikes on warehouses, bases, logistics, fuel infrastructure, and other military infrastructure. The goal here is absolutely clear—to reduce Russia’s ability to supply its grouping in southern Ukraine. In particular, this concerns Zaporizhzhia Oblast—the areas of Huliaipole, Orikhiv, and Stepnohirsk. We are trying to create conditions for Russia under which it will be more difficult for it to support its offensive operations
According to him, the fight against Russian road logistics has become a separate area.
And I would say that we have already significantly undermined their capabilities in Crimea. Over the past three months, according to the data I have seen and that can be verified, Ukraine has destroyed about 600 trucks every month. These are very large figures. In fact, this represents a serious reduction in the volumes that Russia can transport and supply
However, this does not yet mean the destruction of the entire Russian supply system on the southern front. Military expert Mykhailo Zhyrokhov draws attention to the key role of the Crimean Bridge and railway connections.
As long as such an important strategic structure as the Crimean Bridge exists, Russia has the ability to maintain more or less normal supplies for the troops stationed on the occupied peninsula. We understand that a single train can deliver more fuel than dozens of fuel trucks, which can then be destroyed on the road from Novorossiysk. Rail supply is the foundation
At the same time, experts identify the gradual weakening of Russian air defenses on the occupied peninsula as one of the most noticeable results of the Ukrainian campaign.
“Madyar” showed strikes by Ukrainian UAVs of the Fire Point company against Russian air defense systems
If we are talking specifically about military capabilities, I would say that Russia’s air defense capabilities have been severely undermined. Almost every day, reports emerged that either a radar station, an anti-aircraft missile system, or even some aircraft at an airfield had been destroyed. This is gradually reducing the Russians’ ability to shoot down our drones
But in his view, this is not yet a strategic turning point in this area.
Stupak also does not expect an immediate effect from the Crimean operations. In his assessment, this is rather a cumulative effect and a gradual reduction in the capabilities of Russia’s military machine in Crimea.
If this trend continues in the autumn and winter, I would not speak of some immediate collapse of Crimea. I am more inclined toward a different scenario - Russia may gradually reduce its presence on the peninsula
In his view, the Russians could potentially move some administrative and military structures to the mainland, change their basing locations, and reduce their use of airfields in Crimea.
Such a reduction in presence is quite likely. I think that Ukraine could potentially further reduce Crimea’s importance by 20–30%. And this, accordingly, could reduce the Russians’ ability to use the peninsula to launch attacks on Ukraine’s southern regions
Strikes on energy infrastructure: disruptions are already occurring, but the system is holding for now
Energy infrastructure became a separate area of the operation. Systematic attacks on substations, generation facilities, fuel terminals, and oil depots have caused disruptions both to civilian infrastructure and to the occupying forces. According to Zhirokhov, prolonged power outages in Crimea were reported in Russia.
Then a campaign of strikes on Crimea’s energy infrastructure began. What did this lead to? To certain shifts. Reports appeared on Russian public channels that individual districts had been left without electricity for one, two, or three days at a time
According to Zhirokhov, the key factor enabling Russia to compensate for some of its losses remains the energy bridge between Crimea and Krasnodar Krai.
Along with the construction of the Crimean Bridge, the Russians built what is known as an energy bridge, through which they transmit electricity from Krasnodar Krai. Therefore, without destroying this energy bridge, all these strikes are, you know, for now merely figures in the General Staff’s reports: so many electrical substations hit, some other facilities hit. This certainly creates problems, but it does not break the system
At the same time, fuel problems arising from strikes on tankers and oil depots could directly affect Russian units at the front. According to Stupak, internal Russian reports recorded a reduction in fuel supplies.
One separate and important issue is fuel and energy infrastructure. Strikes on oil depots, fuel terminals, and other facilities create problems for the Russians. I saw their internal reports and their response to Ukrainian strikes. At certain points, they acknowledged a reduction in fuel supplies to the front by approximately 20–25%
In modern warfare, fuel is needed not only for armored vehicles and automobiles, but also to operate generators, on which, among other things, the ability to charge FPV drone batteries, maintain communications, and so on depends.
And at certain moments, the Russians complained that they were short of fuel for their generators by approximately 20%. This means they have to conserve their batteries and launch fewer reconnaissance and strike drones. But I cannot say that this is already a widespread problem along the entire front line. Nevertheless, the local problems are noticeable
The situation in Crimea may become even more complicated in winter. Economist and former spokesperson for NJSC "Naftogaz of Ukraine" in the Lviv region Viktor Halchynskyi predicts problems with supplying the peninsula with gas as well.
If the gas issue is further addressed, it will be cold in Crimea. As far as I know, the storage facilities located there have also been damaged. If the Defense Forces take certain further actions, combined with the shortage of liquid fuel and electricity, this could lead to an extremely uncomfortable winter on the peninsula, even taking into account the fact that the climate there is warmer
Resort season under attack: Crimea has lost tourists and money
The disruption of the resort season was the most tangible consequence for the civilian population of occupied Crimea. Problems with fuel and electricity, constant strikes, disruptions to transport logistics, and the overall danger made vacationing in occupied Crimea almost impossible. At the end of June, Russians who had come to vacation on the occupied peninsula fled en masse. Even 15-kilometre queues to leave Crimea were recorded.
According to Halchynskyi's estimate, the 2026 resort season became the worst for the occupied peninsula since 2014.
It is difficult to assess the damage in absolute figures because we can see the situation in the temporarily occupied territory exclusively through media estimates and reports that leak onto the internet from individual users. But we can say with confidence that the damage from the 2026 resort season, which in fact did not take place, is probably the greatest since the occupation, that is, since 2014
In his opinion, the actual disruption of the resort season became the culmination of a process that began immediately after the occupation of Crimea, when Ukrainian and European tourists stopped visiting the peninsula.
Due to the lack of fuel and electricity, constant air attacks, and the blocking of transport connections, the season had effectively ended prematurely in June. Accordingly, the tourism sector failed to receive substantial funds
According to experts, the consequences are being felt primarily by local small businesses, whose earnings had been tied to the summer for decades. Mykhailo Zhyrokhov notes that the model was simple: the money earned in summer enabled many Crimeans to live through the rest of the year.
But psychologically and socially, this is undoubtedly a major blow for the residents of Crimea. Most small businesses in Crimea—both under Ukraine and under Russia—were built specifically around the resort season. People earned money in summer and then effectively lived on it in autumn and winter. Now this model has been disrupted. Certain economic problems have arisen, and people have failed to earn the expected amount of money
Halchynskyi also speaks of the gradual winding down of businesses and the possible outflow of the economically active population from the peninsula.
If we are talking about business in Crimea, it is obvious that a very large number of people earned their living specifically from tourism. Now businesses are closing. There are problems with energy and problems with security. And, judging indirectly from what we see, this process has gradually begun
According to him, there is no mass evacuation at present, but people may move their economic activity outside Crimea or leave the peninsula altogether.
At the same time, experts remind us that Crimea has always received subsidies from the state budget. For the occupation administration, a decline in tourist flows also means reduced revenues and greater dependence on Russia's federal budget.
Most likely, the Crimean authorities will once again have to appeal to Russia's federal budget and request more direct transfers for 2027. Crimea is already the most heavily subsidized region, and the reduction in tourist flows only increases this dependence
This, in his view, is one of the additional effects of the Ukrainian campaign of strikes on Crimea. After all, any additional Russian budget expenditures on Crimea reduce the possibilities for military spending.
It is beneficial for us if money from the Russian budget is spent not on military purposes. If Russia is forced to direct more funds toward supporting Crimea, compensating for losses in the tourism sector, restoring infrastructure, and making direct transfers, this already works to our advantage. Because Russia never has an excess of money. And the more the Russian budget is forced to spend on problems arising from Ukrainian strikes, the fewer resources potentially remain for the war
At the same time, Zhirokhov believes that losses suffered by small businesses due to the disrupted resort season will not be a problem for the Russian authorities, since the Kremlin will not consider the interests of Crimeans a priority.
Thus, the main effect of Ukrainian operations in Crimea lies in the gradual increase in the cost of occupying Crimea for Russia. Moscow is forced to simultaneously compensate for losses to military logistics, restore energy facilities, strengthen air defenses, support the subsidized economy of the peninsula, and respond to Crimea's growing unattractiveness to tourists.
And if the systematic nature of such strikes is maintained, occupied Crimea will become increasingly difficult to use simultaneously as a military bridgehead, a logistics center, and a symbolic "showcase" for Russians.

No Evidence of FPV Drones Launched From Jet-Powered Shaheds in Kyiv, Expert Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:49:32 UTC
19:49:32 KST

Three days of searches have failed to uncover evidence that Russia used jet-powered Shahed drones to carry and launch FPV drones during attacks on Kyiv, Ukrainian military technology expert Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said.
“For three days, we have not been able to find a single piece of evidence of FPVs being used from jet-powered Shaheds in Kyiv,” Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president on defense technology, said in a Facebook post.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The statement challenges recent reports that Russia may be using Shaheds as “mother drones” to deliver smaller FPV attack drones deeper into Ukrainian territory.
Reports of Shaheds carrying FPVs
Reports of the tactic emerged earlier this week. The Ukrainian monitoring channel eRadar said on Thursday, Sept. 3, that an FPV drone had been found attached to a Shahed in the Kyiv region.
Ukraine’s Wild Hornets volunteer group also published footage on Aug. 27 of a Shahed shot down by a drone operated by the 36th Separate Assault Brigade. The group said the Shahed was carrying two FPV drones.
Such a configuration could allow Russia to use a long-range Shahed as a carrier, releasing smaller drones closer to their targets and potentially complicating Ukraine’s air defenses.
However, Beskrestnov’s latest statement indicates that no evidence of the specific tactic has been confirmed in Kyiv over the past three days.
52% Back Ukraine Arms, 42% Say Germany Has Gone Too Far, Deutschland Poll Finds
How the technology works
The use of FPV drones attached to larger strike drones is not a new Russian tactic. Beskrestnov previously said Russian forces had been using the configuration for more than a year.
According to the expert, two FPV drones can be attached to a standard Shahed or Gerbera drone and controlled using LTE modems.
The system has limited effectiveness, however, and is therefore used relatively infrequently, Beskrestnov said. The smaller FPV drones can lose their communications or control link during flight and crash before reaching their targets.
There is also an important distinction between standard and jet-powered Shaheds.
FPV drones are attached to conventional Shaheds, Beskrestnov said, because the much higher speed of jet-powered drones makes carrying and deploying FPVs extremely difficult.
As a result, evidence that FPVs were found in the Kyiv region does not establish that they were launched from jet-powered Shaheds.
Beskrestnov urged against treating a connection between the two types of drones as confirmed without supporting evidence.
Jet-powered Shaheds extend their reach
The reports come as Russia continues deploying modified, jet-powered versions of the Shahed drone, which can travel significantly farther than earlier variants.
During Russia’s Aug. 28 attack, a jet-powered Shahed reportedly flew about 960 kilometers (597 miles) and reached Volyn region in western Ukraine, according to OSINT analysts.
On Aug. 18, another jet-powered Shahed reportedly reached the Rivne region for the first time, covering an estimated 900 kilometers (597 miles).
The increasing range of the modified drones is adding another challenge for Ukraine as Russia continues adapting its long-range drone campaign against the country.
