17:18:02 KST

A contract within the supply chain for Britain’s new Dreadnought-class nuclear ballistic missile submarines was terminated following security reviews by the Defence Nuclear Enterprise, the Ministry of Defence has confirmed.
The disclosure came in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked the Defence Secretary about a “fruitless payment” associated with the Dreadnought supply chain recorded in the MOD’s Annual Report and Accounts for 2025-26.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard replied: “A contract within the Dreadnought supply chain was terminated following security reviews by the Defence Nuclear Enterprise. The detail is unsuitable for disclosure due to the classification and sensitivity of the programme.”
The answer does not identify the contractor, of course, or the part of the Dreadnought programme affected or the circumstances which led the Defence Nuclear Enterprise to terminate the agreement.
The reference to a fruitless payment comes from the MOD’s annual accounts. Such payments are recorded in government accounts where expenditure has been incurred without the intended benefit being received, although Pollard’s answer does not provide the value or nature of the payment associated with this particular case.
The Dreadnought programme is delivering the four submarines intended to replace the Royal Navy’s existing Vanguard-class boats and carry the UK’s submarine-launched nuclear deterrent. Construction is centred at BAE Systems’ submarine shipyard in Barrow-in-Furness, supported by a large industrial and nuclear supply chain across the country.
The programme sits within the wider Defence Nuclear Enterprise, which covers the organisations, infrastructure, personnel and industrial capacity needed to support Britain’s nuclear deterrent. Security controls around the enterprise are correspondingly stringent, with detailed information on individual suppliers and sensitive components often withheld.
The first Dreadnought-class submarine, HMS Dreadnought, is being built alongside the other boats in the class as the Royal Navy prepares to transition from Vanguard while maintaining continuous at-sea deterrence.

UN slams foreign networks for helping fuel Sudan’s brutal war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:15:00 UTC
17:15:00 KST

The United Nations said Thursday that foreign networks are helping fuel Sudan’s brutal war, which has raged between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since 2023, killing at least 59,000 people, displacing about 13 million and pushing large parts of the country into famine.
A U.N. investigation found that a network of companies based in the United Arab Emirates, Colombia, Chad and other countries supplied the RSF with military contractors, weapons, logistics and training.
“The mission finds reasonable grounds to believe that a transnational network supplied the Rapid Support Forces with weapons, logistics, training and foreign personnel, including Colombian contractors involved in advanced weapons and drone systems,” according to a summary of the investigation by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan.
The mission is an independent body established by the U.N. Human Rights Council to investigate violations of international human rights and humanitarian law in Sudan.
It found that “individuals and entities operating from, registered in or linked to the United Arab Emirates played a significant role in networks involved in the recruitment, financing, transportation and deployment of foreign military contractors and the provision of military-related support benefiting the Rapid Support Forces.”
The UAE regularly denies that it backs the RSF militarily.
The report also said foreign-supplied drones “expanded” the Sudanese army’s drone capabilities, though it added that its findings on external support for the army “remain preliminary.”
The investigators called on the U.N. Security Council to extend its arms embargo on Sudan.
“The weapons, financing, personnel and technology that sustain this war must be constrained,” it said.
Investigators said they had documented drone attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure by both sides that may amount to war crimes.
They also linked foreign-trained fighters to two massacres in 2025 at Zamzam camp and in El Fasher.
Survivors among the more than 100,000 people who fled El Fasher reported that RSF fighters gunned down civilians in homes and on the streets, leaving the city littered with bodies. Satellite images have since appeared to show the RSF disposing of bodies in mass graves or by burning them.
Chad, Colombia and the United Arab Emirates cooperated with the investigators, but “no substantive response” came from Ethiopia, Libya, South Sudan and Somalia. Panama, whose financial industry has faced accusations of industrial-scale money laundering, requested more time to respond. So far, the U.N. said neither the Sudanese military nor the RSF has cooperated with the investigation.
An AP investigation in July showed that Colombian mercenaries had trained children to fight for the RSF. Rights groups say the Colombians were recruited by a state-linked firm in the UAE, which denies providing arms or military support to any warring party in Sudan.
The United States has urged the U.N. to impose new sanctions to bring the warring parties to the negotiating table.
A draft of the U.S. resolution, seen by The Associated Press in August, deplores “the continuous influx of external military assistance, weapons and ammunition to the warring parties, which is prolonging the conflict and undermining mediation efforts,” including the launching of drones and unmanned aerial systems from third countries.
The proposed resolution demands that all countries “cease any direct or indirect support to the warring parties, be it logistical, financial or military, which enables conflict to continue.”

Meloni's government becomes Italian Republic's longest
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
10:13:38 CEST
17:13:38 KST

ROME, 04 SET -Premier Giorgia Meloni's government on Friday became Italy's longest since the country became a republic after World War II, having lasted 1,413 days - one more than Silvio Berlusconi's second administration between June 2001 and April 2005. 
    "Today, our government becomes the longest-serving in the history of the Italian Republic," Meloni, the leader of the right-wing Brothers of Italy (FdI) party who became Italy's first woman prime minister when the coalition she heads won the 2022 general election, said via social media. 
    "It is a fact that I welcome with gratitude and a strong sense of responsibility. Because stability is not a record to flaunt, it is a condition that enables a nation to plan, make decisions, keep its commitments, and command respect". 
    The stability is unusual for Italy, where governments usually collapse with ease. 
    Meloni, who is celebrating the milestone with a rally in the southern city of Bari, says this has enabled Italy to bolster its standing on the international arena and secure key victories, such as those regarding changes to the EU's rules on migration. 
    She can boast having increased the number of people in employment by over one million under her watch and having reduced income taxes for lower earners and the middle class by around 21 billion euros. 
    Her government has also won plaudits for its prudent management of the nation's public finances, which has helping bring down bond yields. 
    "In recent years we have worked to increase employment, reduce unemployment, support families and businesses, strengthen security, manage public finances responsibly, and restore Italy's influence and credibility on the international stage," Meloni said. 
    "We have achieved results, but we are well aware of how much still remains to be done". 
    Italy's opposition parties, however, say the last four years have been wasted. 
    They point to low levels of economic growth, the fact that, while income taxes have been reduced, the overall tax burden has increased, a drop in health spending in relation to GDP and the failure to deliver major reforms. 
    Meloni's biggest defeat since taking office was the rejection of her government's Constitutional reform to overhaul the judiciary in a referendum earlier this year.

Iran has bypassed US naval blockade: oil minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:09:47 UTC
17:09:47 KST

“During the 40-day war, despite the wartime conditions, the country’s crude oil exports did not stop even for one hour from February 28 until the temporary ceasefire was established,” Paknejad said, according local Iranian media.
Paknejad was referring to the joint US-Israeli act of aggression against Iran, which began on February 28. According to the minister, the war failed to halt Iran’s crude exports, even as Iranian energy infrastructure came under repeated attack.
The attacks included strikes on oil storage and distribution facilities as well as major gas-processing infrastructure. The South Pars gas complex, one of the country’s most strategically important energy assets, was among the facilities targeted during the fighting.
The challenge to Iran’s oil exports extended beyond the physical damage caused by the attacks. Tehran subsequently faced a maritime blockade that threatened to complicate both the sale and delivery of crude to international customers.
Paknejad said the first blockade involved a line stretching from Ras al-Hadd to Pakistan’s Gwadar port. In response, Iranian authorities adopted measures intended to keep oil sales and deliveries moving despite the restrictions.
“The process of selling oil and delivering it to customers was carried out thousands of kilometers away from the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman,” the minister said.
According to Paknejad, the first blockade lasted from around April 13 until June 18. A temporary pause in the blockade gave Iran an opportunity to move a significant volume of crude outside the waters of the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman and position it in locations from which it could subsequently be delivered to customers.
That pause, he said, was used to reduce Iran’s exposure to the maritime restrictions and preserve its ability to fulfill oil deliveries.
The pressure resumed on July 15, when a second blockade was imposed and, according to Paknejad, remains in place.
“The oil industry has not sat idle and has not stopped,” he said. “We are pursuing various solutions and different measures so that we can reach a day when we are able to completely bypass this blockade.”
Oil production and gas recovery
At the same time, the Petroleum Ministry says it has continued efforts to expand domestic production despite the wartime conditions.
Paknejad said a program targeting an additional 250,000 barrels per day of crude production has moved into the implementation phase, with around 70,000 to 80,000 barrels per day already realized.
The ministry has also reported progress in collecting associated gas that would otherwise be burned off through flaring.
Since the beginning of the current administration, around 11.5 million cubic meters per day of flare gas has been collected through various projects, Paknejad said.
Combined with the roughly 5.5 million cubic meters per day already being captured before the administration took office, total flare-gas collection has now reached about 17 million cubic meters per day.
The increase is significant both from an energy-efficiency perspective and because captured associated gas can be returned to productive use rather than being wasted through routine flaring.
The resilience of Iran’s energy system was also tested by direct attacks on its gas-processing infrastructure.
Paknejad recalled that on March 18, the enemy struck four gas refineries in Asaluyeh, covering the third through sixth refineries. The attacks forced Iran to reduce a significant portion of its gas production capacity.
According to the minister, however, specialists from Iran’s oil and gas industries were able to restore a substantial part of the lost capacity, while reconstruction work began shortly after the strikes.
“Perhaps within the next few months, we will be able to see the results and witness an increase in the country’s gas production,” Paknejad said.

Fake customer service drives 56% jump in phone scam losses to HK$900 million
“Every one hour, a resident falls for a scam after answering a fraudulent call,” police superintendent says, as force reveals latest figures
Impersonating customer service staff is the “most rampant tactic” used by phone scammers, Hong Kong police have said, revealing the number of such fraud cases rose by 45 per cent to 4,830 in the first half of 2026 compared with a year ago.
Despite the increase, deception cases overall fell slightly between January and June, dropping by 0.7 per cent compared with the same period last year, Superintendent Kwok Ching-yee of the commercial crime bureau said on Friday.
Losses also fell by 0.8 per cent to HK$3.51 billion (US$447.6 million), she noted.
“Among phone scams, impersonating customer service was the most rampant tactic, accounting for nearly half of the cases. In other words, in the first half of this year, one resident fell victim to a phishing scam every four hours,” Kwok said.
“Every one hour, a resident falls for a scam after answering a fraudulent call. On average, victims of each phone scam lost at least around HK$270,000.”
Although the numbers of most online scam cases registered a year-on-year decline, phishing scams rose by 61 per cent to 1,113 cases, and phone scams rose by 45 per cent to 4,830.

Backing all of that is a criminal offence in the legislation that set up the Electoral Commission. That’s the Political Parties Elections and Referendums Act 2000.

Fon-Ce blends Latin heritage and Taiwan produce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:06:24 UTC
17:06:24 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Latin American restaurant Fon-Ce, recommended in the Michelin Guide Taipei, is celebrating its first anniversary with a new tasting menu titled “Sunrise and Sunset.”
Chef and founder Leonardo Fonseca Celis, previously worked at world-renowned restaurants including Noma in Denmark, Central in Peru and Disfrutar in Spain.
Inspired by the 13-hour time difference between his native Colombia and Taiwan, Celis combines Latin American culinary heritage with seasonal Taiwanese ingredients in an eight-course menu. Though soft-spoken, Celis delivers bold, spice-forward flavors without clashing.
The menu opens with a dish inspired by Latin American breakfast culture: cassava cake stuffed with surf clam and yellowtail, served with house-made plantain vinegar sauce and a broth made from Taiwanese high-mountain loquat.
Another highlight, a chickpea bunuelo, reinterprets the traditional Colombian holiday treat. Made with a chickpea puree shell, it features slow-caramelized coconut milk, chicken liver mousse, and Taiwanese guava pickled in dark beer.
The signature tuna bone marrow draws inspiration from Mexican aguachile and the experience of eating oysters. Seared bone marrow brushed with house sauce is topped with lacto-fermented tree tomato water and kiwi.
Diners sip the marrow jelly before eating the surrounding fish, which is finished with guava pectin and a fresh herb salad.
For the fish course, three-day dry-aged, charcoal-grilled yellowtail is served with an encocado sauce of clam stock, mole and coconut milk, accompanied by roasted hazelnut salad and charred water bamboo. Guests can also order a limited add-on of grilled amberjack collar, ideal for sharing among two to three people.
The meat course features 24-hour slow-cooked pork cheeks paired with a private-recipe mole, toasted yeast, fermented green papaya and cabbage heart.
Dessert incorporates the ancient Latin American technique of nixtamalization applied to pumpkin, resulting in a crisp outer layer and tender interior, served with green mango sorbet and pine buttermilk foam.
In celebration of Colombia's annual Flower Festival in August, Fon-Ce is also offering a limited weekend lunch menu paired with cold-brew floral Colombian coffees. The eight-course menu is priced at NT$2,980 (US$94) per person plus a 10% service charge, with reservations now open.

Ukrainian drones attack Russia’s Black Sea coast, sparking a fire at an oil depot

The oil depot’s owner has not been officially identified, though the independent Telegram channel Astra claimed the facility belongs to Rosneft-Kubanneftprodukt in the Adler district.
Preliminary reports indicated no one was injured, though windows were damaged in several residential buildings and other structures. Black smoke could be seen over Sochi.
The Ukrainian monitoring Telegram channels Exilenova+ and Supernova+ claimed that Ukrainian drones also struck air defense installations: S-300 or S-400 surface-to-air missile systems.
Astra, citing eyewitness photos and videos, reported that one of the strikes hit near the town of Sirius, close to the Psou River, where an air defense battalion equipped with S-300 or S-400 systems is stationed, sparking a fire at the site. This spring, Ukraine’s armed forces repeatedly targeted another city in Krasnodar Krai, Tuapse, striking the local oil refinery and a marine terminal that together form a single complex with the refinery. Nearly 12% of NMT-2026 participants failed to reach the threshold score in at least one subject

A total of 329,709 people took part in NMT-2026, with more than 48,500 failing at least one subject. The threshold was most often not reached in mathematics.
In 2026, more than 48,500 students failed to reach the threshold score in at least one subject of the NMT. This is stated in a report by the Ukrainian Center for Education Quality Assessment, reports UNN.
Details
This year, nearly 360,000 people registered for the National Multi-Subject Test, and 329,709 participants took the test.
A total of 39,888 participants failed to reach the threshold score in mathematics. This amounts to 12.1% of all those who took the test.
At the same time, 6,217 people failed the Ukrainian language test, while 1,283 failed the Ukrainian history test.

CSIC develops magnetic "nanoflowers" to capture and convert water nanoplastics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:03:58 UTC
17:03:58 KST

ICMM-CSIC researchers have created magnetic iron-oxide nanoflowers that trap PET nanoplastics and turn them into tools to remove other water pollutants, supporting circular, advanced water treatment.
From plastic that pollutes water to a tool that helps clean it up. Researchers at Madrid’s Institute of Materials Science (ICMM), part of the CSIC, have developed flower-shaped iron oxide nanoparticles capable of capturing nanoplastics, fragments a thousand times smaller than a microplastic, derived from PET, one of the most common materials used in bottles, packaging and polyester clothing. The study has been published in the Chemical Engineering Journal.
The secret lies in the shape. "Iron oxide is a magnetic material that allows many pollutants to be trapped at once. In addition, its nanoflower structure means that the particles have several cores that cooperate to enhance their magnetic properties," explains Álvaro Gallo-Córdova, a researcher at ICMM-CSIC and one of the lead authors of the study, together with Rafael Herrera-Aquino and María del Puerto Morales.
From the microplastics in make-up to PET nanoplastics
It is not the first time these particles have proved their usefulness: in 2024 they already managed to extract and degrade microplastics measuring between 0.001 and 5 millimetres, originating from cosmetics. The step forward now is one of scale. Nanoplastics measure a billionth of a metre, a thousand times smaller than those microplastics.
"When they reach the end of their useful life, a large proportion of PET plastics ends up in the environment, where sunlight and physical wear act like sandpaper, grinding them down and turning them into nanoplastics, a kind of ultra-fine dust that contaminates our soils and water sources," adds Gallo-Córdova.
Just one gram of these magnetic nanoflowers can capture up to 10,000 milligrams of nanoplastics, a figure the team itself describes as unprecedented until now.
The pollutant that helps clean up other pollutants
The work does not end with capture. Once the nanoplastic has been trapped, the team turns it into a magnetic material capable of extracting heavy metals or organic dyes from water, and can even take part in catalytic degradation processes.
"After capturing the nanoplastics thanks to our magnetic nanoparticles, we upcycle them into functional materials, turning a polluting waste into a new raw material within a circular economy approach," the researcher sums up. In other words, they use the waste itself to remove other pollution, giving a second life to something that would normally end up in the bin.
The process uses barely any energy, because magnetic heating works locally, right on the surface of the nanoparticles, without the need to heat all the water.
And it stands up to repeated use: after five cycles, the nanoflowers retained 88% of their decontamination capacity and released into the water less than 0.82% of the iron they contained at the start, confirming that they are stable, reusable and safe. The ICMM-CSIC team is now looking towards advanced water treatment as the next field in which to apply this technology.

Naftali Bennett’s reset: Why the former PM broke his promises - and his plan to 'repair' Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:03:37 UTC
17:03:37 KST

"My name is Jimmy Carter, and I’m running for president of the United States.”
That was how Carter, a little-known peanut farmer and former Georgia governor, introduced himself to voters while campaigning in 1976 for the highest office in the land.
Naftali Bennett seems to be taking a page out of Carter’s campaign playbook.
Granted, Bennett – who already served a short stint as Israel’s prime minister – is well known in the country. But, like Carter, he is traversing the width and breadth of the land, talking to “regular people” in informal street-corner “parliaments.”
While Carter introduced himself to the American people, Bennett is trying to reintroduce himself to the Israeli public – especially right-wing voters who feel that, after he formed a government with Ra’am’s Mansour Abbas and Yesh Atid’s Yair Lapid in 2021, they no longer really know him.
In a video clip posted on Bennett’s Facebook page, a man named Yankele describes, at one such “parliament” in Beersheba, how betrayed he felt by Bennett, for whom he had previously voted.
“Do you know why the hurt was so great?” he said, as a black-T-shirted Bennett sat and listened. “Because we know that you come from us – from our camp, from our ideology – and because, excuse me, you turned your back on ideology for a job.”
Bennett’s “parliaments” are punctuated – as in the Knesset – by hecklers yelling “liar” and “traitor.” He told Yankele that he was not going to try to convince him that he had been right but rather explain his motivations. Bennett finds himself doing that over and over, hoping – as Carter did – that one conversation at a time can change the way voters see him.
“I JUST come in, sit, have coffee, and they start cursing,” Bennett said this week during an hour-long interview with The Jerusalem Post, describing these encounters.
“It’s tough, but you know what? I learn a lot. First of all, I listen. I agree with some of the criticism, which is just, and then I try and unpack– and it’s working.”
Asked which criticism he accepts, Bennett replied, “That I broke a promise. Yeah, and they feel that I zigzagged.”
That broken promise – to refrain from joining a government with Abbas – has dogged Bennett ever since among the right-wing camp from which he emerged and of which he still considers himself a part. He once served as director-general of the Yesha Council, remains adamantly opposed to a Palestinian state, and supports settlement in Judea and Samaria.
“I did break a promise. That’s just a fact. Unfortunately, I had promised not to form a government with Abbas, and I did. I can’t change history, but I stand behind that decision, and I explain why I made that decision.”
His 30-second explanation can be boiled down to this: After four elections, Bennett gave Netanyahu his party’s seven seats following the 2021 vote, but Netanyahu still had only 59 mandates. Netanyahu then sought Abbas’s support and, according to Bennett, persuaded nearly everyone in the right-wing bloc – including the haredi parties and Itamar Ben-Gvir – to accept the idea. Religious Zionist Party head Bezalel Smotrich refused, however, and the effort collapsed.
Bennett said he ultimately faced a choice: “I had an option to go to fifth, sixth, seventh elections and tear Israel apart, but I will have met my promise, or do the right thing for Israel, which I thought was to form a government – which would be a good government – and try and pull Israel out of the hole, and that’s what I did.
“I think even my detractors agreed that it was a competent, effective government,” he said. “It didn’t last long because of the coalition, but we got stuff done.”
'October 7 changes a lot of things'
What about this time? Could Bennett again form a government with Abbas’s Ra’am if the alternative were yet another election?
“No,” he replied. “October 7 changes a lot of things.”
One of those changes, he said, is that a post-October 7 government cannot include non-Zionist parties. Bennett stressed the term “non-Zionist” rather than “Arab,” noting that Yosef Haddad, an Arab candidate running with Ofer Winter’s party, is also a Zionist.
“This is not based on race,” he stressed. “But we are a Zionist country.”
Bennett did not say explicitly that he would refuse to sit with the haredi parties. He did, however, set criteria that would make their participation all but impossible.
He said the next government must be Zionist and institute national service for all. Anyone who dodges service, he added, should receive “not one shekel” from the state.
BENNETT’S PARTY offices occupy the seventh and eighth floors of a glass high-rise in Ra’anana, the city where he lives. A calendar counting down the days to the election greets visitors.
If the campaign is taking a toll on him, it doesn’t show. Bennett, in his ubiquitous black T-shirt, was full of energy.
His advisers made sure that a new book by Ari Shavit, titled Bennett, sat prominently on the table in front of him. Its cover shows Bennett, eyes closed, hugging a soldier.
Hugs appear in many of the clips he posts and seem almost a campaign theme, projecting an empathy that – when one meets him – feels genuine.
“My goal and the reason I’m coming back to politics is to repair Israel. Israel went through a horrible trauma on October 7, the worst trauma. We failed in our most fundamental goal, which is to protect Jews. We failed.”
Bennett repeatedly used the words “fix” and “repair” during the interview. The most urgent repair, he said, is to bring haredim into the army and integrate them more fully into the country’s economy.
“There’s a lot of things we’ve got to do. There’s one that will save Israel,” he said.
That one thing is bringing Israel’s 1.5 million haredim into the military and the workforce, turning them into taxpayers rather than having the state subsidize them, and ensuring that their schools teach math and English alongside Torah and Gemara.
“That’s the single most important thing for Israel’s long-term future because of demography. Right now, every year, we are carrying more tax burden, more weight, and more military service on our shoulders, and something’s got to give. Now’s the time.”
Several parties – from Ofer Winter’s new People of Israel party to Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar and Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu – have made this a central campaign issue.
Asked what distinguishes his policy from those of Eisenkot and Liberman, Bennett said Eisenkot favors military exemptions for 30% of haredim, while Liberman wants to arrest draft dodgers. Bennett rejects both approaches. His answer is to cut off state funding.
Or, as the man he hopes to succeed might once have put it: You serve, you get. You don’t serve, you don’t get anything. Not a shekel.
Bennett said his policy would operate in three areas: military service, employment and taxation, and education.
In the military sphere, Bennett proposes establishing haredi hesder yeshivot along Israel’s borders with Jordan and Egypt, where participants would divide their days among Torah study, guard duty and patrols, and sleep.
The all-male frameworks, he said, would significantly reduce the burden on reservists, since one soldier in the regular army is the equivalent of 12 reservists serving one month a year.
He also wants to provide haredim with vocational training that will enable them to work.
Most importantly, however, he wants to carry out sweeping reforms in the haredi educational system, something he said he has changed his mind on, since in the past he did not want to get involved in the haredi “value system.”
“No, I will get involved because when you teach your kids to be anti-Zionist, anti-IDF, anti-going-to-work from the age of three to the age of 18, then at the age of 18, they go out and demonstrate, saying they will rather die than serve.”
He wants to set up state haredi schools that will teach a 60% core curriculum, including English, math, Hebrew, Bible, and Zionism, and another 40% that will concentrate, at least for boys, on Talmud. Once these schools are set up, he added, “I’m going to stop funding a school that teaches anti-Zionism and doesn’t teach math and English.”
The “big insight,” Bennett said, is that the country “cannot kick the can down the road forever” on this issue.
The term “conceptzia” applies not only to entrenched thinking on security matters, but also to these types of issues, he said, adding that Israel has operated under the mistaken assumption that it could preserve the status quo with the haredim indefinitely. That may have been sustainable when they constituted 3% of the population, but not when their numbers are approaching 15%.
“Thirty percent of Jewish kids in first grade are haredi. So it’s now or never,” he said.
Bennett opposes granting draft exemptions to 30% of haredim, as Eisenkot has suggested, because that raises the question of who would decide who receives them. He also opposes arrests of draft dodgers, arguing that this merely turns those jailed into heroes.
Nor does he favor continuing the dialogue on this issue with the haredi parties that, he said, has led nowhere for years.
Instead, he wants to turn off the financial spigot. Economic incentives work, he stressed.
The differences between Bennett's approach to Gaza and Netanyahu's approach
IF HAREDI integration is one major issue hovering over the campaign, October 7 is another. Bennett highlighted – in the interview, as he does in his informal “parliaments” – the differences between his approach toward Gaza and Netanyahu’s.
Bennett described his policies toward Gaza as “diametrically opposite” to Netanyahu’s. Netanyahu, he said, pursued a policy of containment, tolerating rockets, incendiary balloons, and disturbances along the border fence, while Bennett adopted a “zero tolerance policy”: “Not one balloon, not one terror kite or rocket.”
He also criticized Netanyahu’s decision to permit the monthly transfer of $30 million in Qatari cash to Hamas. Bennett ended this policy when he became PM in June 2021 and replaced the cash transfers with prepaid cards for Gazan families that Israel could track. But he acknowledged that he neither solved the problem nor foresaw what was coming.
“I inherited a really bad situation and improved it. But I didn’t solve it,” he said. “I admit I didn’t imagine the October 7 scenario in Gaza. I did imagine the October 7 scenario from Lebanon.”
Unlike some of the other candidates in the race, Bennett does not drip with contempt for Netanyahu.
“I am not a hater of Bibi. I never was,” he said. “In fact, in the past, I very much admired him. I think he entered politics for the right reason. His heart was in the right place. I think 30 years is enough.”
Nor does Bennett want to see Netanyahu jailed. “I think he should go home. He should be pardoned.”
Bennett also agrees that it is an exaggeration to blame Netanyahu entirely for Israel’s deteriorating standing in American public opinion. He attributed half the problem to deep progressive, anti-Israel, and antisemitic currents that have taken hold all over the world.
The other half, he said, is of Israel’s own making, citing Ben-Gvir’s selfies with bound prisoners, Zvi Sukkot taking a sledgehammer to a monument in a Palestinian city, and ministers saying that Gaza should be nuked.
Fifty percent is self-inflicted, he said, adding this advice: “Stop doing stupid things. That would be a pretty interesting policy. Don’t be an idiot. A non-idiotic government would be a good step.”
Bennett says he is optimistic about Israeli youth
DESPITE ALL this, Bennett said he is optimistic about the country’s future because of the way its young people have risen to the occasion since October 7.
“I’m optimistic about Israel’s future because there’s a simple formula. I call it the Bennett formula. Israel’s the only Western country in the world that’s having kids – that’s positive. And the kids we have, I look at this younger generation, and I believe it’s Israel’s finest generation.”
His use of the term “finest generation” was deliberate, drawing a parallel to America’s Greatest Generation – the generation that fought and lived through World War II.
“After October 7, what they’ve gone through and what they’ve done on October 7 and thereafter, it’s sort of embedded them with idealism and a drive to fix Israel, similar to post-World War II veterans who came home from America. They built America, right? 1945 to the 90s, the finest generation. This is our finest generation.
“So here’s the formula. Lots of kids times great kids equals a great future. All we need to do is change the leadership.”
And that he hopes to do in over the next two months, one street-corner “parliament” at a time – Jimmy Carter-style.

Suspect deemed unfit to stand trial for alleged role in deadly hold-up 35 years ago
Jury rules Wen Wenye, 61, cannot be held criminally liable for murder and attempted robbery in 1991 due to cognitive impairment caused by lung cancer
A mainland Chinese man has been deemed unfit to stand trial for his alleged involvement in a deadly shooting during a botched robbery in Hong Kong 35 years ago, after he was diagnosed with a cognitive impairment caused by lung cancer.
A High Court jury of four men and three women ruled on Friday that Shenzhen resident Wen Wenye, 61, could not be held criminally liable for murder and attempted robbery because he was unable to understand the legal proceedings and give instructions to his lawyers.
A “special hearing” will still be held before the jury to decide whether Wen indeed took part in the crimes at Shun Fat Company, a second-hand goods shop on Pei Ho Street in Sham Shui Po, on June 9, 1991.
The defendant will not be convicted in any event, but the court can impose appropriate measures if the jury decides that he committed all the acts alleged in the original indictment.
Wen has been remanded in custody since his arrest at the Shenzhen Bay control point on November 11, 2023.
During his incarceration, he was diagnosed with stage IV lung cancer, with mutated cells spreading to his brain.
He underwent surgery to remove damaged brain tissue on July 24, 2024, but has used a wheelchair since.

Russia and India expanding industrial cooperation – Moscow
Russia is willing to share high-end technology and expand industrial cooperation with India to help develop its industries, the deputy minister of industry and trade, Roman Chekushov, has said.
”We are ready to share our technologies with them,” Chekushov said on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok on Thursday. He added that India has been seeking technologies from Russia as the two countries move beyond their robust trade relationship.
Chekushov said some Russian companies, mostly in the transportation and chemical sectors, already have production facilities in India. Calling this the initial stage, he said more Russian companies are exploring production in India and expanding in the Indian market. The initiative will also be in line with the Make-in-India policies promoted by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi as he seeks to boost economic growth and jobs in the world’s most populous nation.
The INNOPROM. India trade fair will open in New Delhi next week just ahead of the 18th BRICS Summit. The organizers say the event will showcase advanced technologies and explore cooperation across sectors ranging from aviation to AI.
'Russia–India Moving Beyond Trade Relations & Into Industrial Cooperation' - Roman Chekushov
‘Made in India’ partnerships will create added value, and Russia is ‘ready to share its technologies with 🇮🇳,’ the 🇷🇺 Deputy Minister of Industry & Trade said at EEF. pic.twitter.com/dOKUTrx3nZ
Russian aviation, technology, energy, and industrial heavyweights are attending, along with several big Indian companies.
India has long been a major buyer of Russian military hardware, a relationship that deepened after India and Pakistan clashed last year following a terrorist attack in Kashmir that killed 26 civilians. India is now the second largest buyer of Russian oil after it stepped up purchases following the Middle East conflict which disrupted energy supplies from the Persian Gulf states.
India is also keen on the Northern Sea Route, which Russia is developing as a shorter, more competitive trade route to northern Europe via the Arctic ocean and its Far East.
The two countries have set a bilateral trade target of $100 billion to be reached by 2030.

Fury grows as Israel plans to displace 1.86M Palestinians from Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:02:00 UTC
17:02:00 KST

Israel’s far-right national security minister has unveiled a plan to facilitate the departure of nearly 1.9 million Palestinians from the Gaza Strip over seven years, drawing immediate criticism from Palestinians, Arab countries and rights groups over a proposal they say could amount to forced displacement despite being presented as voluntary.
Itamar Ben-Gvir, leader of the far-right Jewish Power party, presented the plan, called “Disengagement 710,” on Thursday as a centerpiece of his party’s campaign ahead of Israel’s Oct. 27 parliamentary election.
The proposal calls for about 250,000 Palestinians to leave Gaza during the first year, roughly 1.11 million within three years and 1.86 million within seven years.
With Gaza’s population estimated at roughly 2.1 million, the plan would seek to relocate the vast majority of the territory’s Palestinians.
Ben-Gvir said the initiative would provide Palestinians with a voluntary pathway to leave Gaza, with Israel offering financial and logistical assistance and working with countries willing to receive them.
Critics argue that Gaza’s widespread destruction, displacement, restricted humanitarian access and continuing insecurity make it impossible to regard mass departures as genuinely voluntary.
The proposal is based on a 20-page document outlining a system for encouraging and organizing Palestinian departures.
It calls for a dedicated government ministry to implement the program, negotiate with potential destination countries and oversee the movement and integration of Palestinians who leave Gaza.
Under the proposal, each Palestinian leaving Gaza would need a receiving country willing to accept them and provide legal status.
The assistance package would include travel documents and visas, transportation, initial housing, vocational training, employment assistance and financial support for up to 24 months.
The plan also proposes payments to countries and organizations involved in receiving Palestinians. Individuals would undergo security screening, while Israeli authorities would receive regular reports on applications, approvals, departures, costs and integration outcomes.
The initial Israeli investment is estimated at about 10 billion shekels, or roughly $3.3 billion. The broader financing framework could reach 50 billion shekels, or about $16.6 billion, depending on international participation and agreements with destination countries.
Ben-Gvir has described the proposal as the product of months of work and presented it as a practical solution for Gaza’s future after the war.
“We must seize this historic opportunity to bring about a historic solution,” he said.
The proposal mentions Türkiye, Ethiopia, the Democratic Republic of Congo and unspecified Arab countries as potential destinations.
However, no country has publicly confirmed an agreement to accept Palestinians on the scale proposed.
That presents a major obstacle. Relocating 1.86 million people would require agreements with multiple governments, extensive transportation and housing arrangements, legal status for those arriving and billions of dollars in funding.
Ben-Gvir has claimed that countries are prepared to receive Palestinians and that many people in Gaza want to leave. Israeli media reports have noted the lack of publicly confirmed large-scale commitments.
Ben-Gvir and his supporters insist the plan involves no forced removals.
Human rights groups, Palestinian officials and legal experts argue that the circumstances under which people make the decision to leave must also be considered.
Much of Gaza has been devastated by the war that began after Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. Large parts of the territory’s housing and infrastructure have been destroyed or damaged, while repeated military operations have displaced much of the population.
Critics say offering people a choice between remaining amid destruction and insecurity or accepting assistance to leave can undermine the claim that departures are genuinely voluntary.
International humanitarian law prohibits the forcible transfer or deportation of protected civilians from occupied territory. Depending on the circumstances, such transfers can constitute serious violations of international law and war crimes.
UN officials and rights organizations have previously warned that proposals encouraging Palestinians to leave Gaza could amount to forcible transfer if conditions effectively deprive residents of a meaningful choice.
Ben-Gvir rejects that characterization and says Palestinians who choose to leave would receive assistance and legal status in their new countries.
Palestinian officials and residents have repeatedly rejected proposals for large-scale relocation outside Gaza, arguing that Palestinians should remain on their land and eventually rebuild.
The proposal has revived memories of the Nakba, or catastrophe, when hundreds of thousands of Palestinians were displaced during the 1948 war surrounding Israel’s creation.
The scale of Ben-Gvir’s plan has intensified those fears because it would leave only a fraction of Gaza’s current population in the territory if fully implemented.
Israel’s Defense Minister Israel Katz has also advocated Palestinian emigration from Gaza, adding to concerns that the idea is gaining support among senior government officials.
Katz said Wednesday that Israel was prepared to facilitate Palestinian departures by sea, air and other means once the United States approved the plan and destination countries were secured.
He said there could be no lasting solution for Gaza without Palestinian emigration.
Egypt has strongly opposed allowing Palestinians to leave Gaza through its territory, while Arab governments have repeatedly rejected proposals that could result in permanent demographic change.
The initiative also revives an idea that drew widespread condemnation after U.S. President Donald Trump proposed in February 2025 that Palestinians could be relocated from Gaza as the territory was rebuilt.
Trump envisioned transforming Gaza into what he called a prosperous “Riviera of the Middle East.”
The proposal was rejected by Palestinian leaders and Arab governments and faced opposition internationally over concerns that Palestinians could be permanently displaced.
Trump later backed away from mass resettlement as a formal objective, while earlier Israeli efforts to identify countries willing to receive Palestinians failed to produce publicly confirmed large-scale agreements.
Ben-Gvir’s proposal nevertheless reflects the continued influence of the idea among Israel’s far right.
The proposal is closely tied to Israeli domestic politics.
Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party plans to make adoption of the relocation program, including the creation of a dedicated ministry, a key demand in negotiations over participation in Israel’s next government.
The initiative is therefore both a policy proposal and an electoral message aimed at voters who favor a tougher approach toward Gaza and oppose the establishment of a Palestinian state.
Ben-Gvir has repeatedly challenged Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from the right and used the Gaza war to push for more aggressive policies.
But the proposal faces significant practical and diplomatic obstacles, particularly the absence of confirmed destination countries.
Its implementation would also depend on the election outcome, coalition negotiations, the position of the Trump administration and the willingness of foreign governments to participate.
Ben-Gvir’s plan is the latest in a series of calls by Israeli far-right politicians for Palestinians to leave Gaza.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has previously advocated policies encouraging Palestinian emigration, while other Israeli officials have discussed ways to facilitate departures.
Those proposals have consistently faced opposition from Palestinian representatives, Arab governments, international organizations and rights groups.
The central dispute remains whether Palestinians leaving Gaza under current wartime conditions could genuinely be considered to have made a free choice.
As of early September, “Disengagement 710” remains a proposal by Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party rather than adopted Israeli government policy.
Its prospects depend on the Oct. 27 election, coalition negotiations, U.S. policy and the willingness of third countries to accept Palestinians.

Serbians targeted with spyware in country’s ‘largest documented wave of surveillance’
Aisha Down
Global technology reporter
Meanwhile, it emerged that at least 14 people from across Serbian civil society were targeted with advanced spyware earlier this year in what the digital rights group Share Foundation said was the largest documented wave of such infection in Serbia to date.
The wave of spyware infections was discovered in August after Apple notified people in 110 countries that they had probably been victims of mercenary spyware.
The Citizen Lab, which carries out forensic analyses of spyware attacks, released an analysis on Wednesday showing that at least one of the Serbians had been targeted with the NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware, which would have given the attacker “total access to the device”.
Share said those targeted included members of a Serbian student movement that has been a thorn in the side of the government of Aleksandar Vučić since 2024. Coalescing out of countrywide protests that followed the collapse of a train station that winter, it is one of the largest student movements in Europe.
Vučić has been in power for more than a decade, during which time critics have said he has overseen a hollowing-out of institutions while steering the country closer to Moscow.
There is no evidence that Vučić’s government was the entity that targeted the student with the Pegasus spyware. However, other spyware used against the students, including a software called NoviSpy, has been previously connected to Serbian authorities.
EU enlargement commissioner calls off Serbia visit over Mladić's 'glorification'
EU’s enlargement commissioner Marta Kos has called off her planned visit to Serbia in protest at what she called “the glorification surrounding the death” of Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladić.
Mladić, who died last week while serving a life sentence for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity during the 1992-1995 Bosnian war, will be commemorated at a public event in Belgrade on Saturday afternoon before his burial on Monday.
Upon landing in Belgrade last night, Mladić’s coffin was wrapped in the national flag and Serbian army soldiers carried his body from the plane to a van for transport to the military hospital, AP reported.
In a strongly worded statement, Kos, a Slovenian diplomat and politician, said:
“Ratko Mladić was convicted of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. The return of his remains to Belgrade reminds Europe of the darkest pages in our recent history.
The glorification surrounding his death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built. That path requires confronting the past, genuine reconciliation and respecting the victims of war crimes.
The values that underpin our common future are not negotiable. In this context, I have decided not to proceed with my planned visit to Serbia at this time.”

Israel and Turkey's uneasy contest to shape Syria's future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
08:00:21 UTC
17:00:21 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel and Turkey's uneasy contest to shape Syria's future
Damascus - Syria’s Foreign Minister Asaad Al-Shaibani met with Israel’s Mossad chief Roman Gofman in Jordan on 23 August following days of escalating tensions that resulted in an Israeli strike on a Syrian airbase in northern Idlib.
According to reports, the two met in order to “lower the temperature” following this latest bout of tensions.
Whilst it was not the first round of direct diplomacy between Syrian and Israeli officials, it represented the first instance of direct meetings at such a senior level.
The renewed risk of escalation comes amid growing competition between Israel and Turkey, as each regional power pursues a different - largely incongruous - strategy over Syria’s future.
Yet US efforts to restrain Israeli aggression have achieved some limited success, say analysts.
Growing competition
Israel claimed the strike on Abu al-Duhur airbase on 18 August was due to Turkey being close to breaching “the status quo on security matters” by deploying troops into Syria. Turkey denied that any of its forces had been at the base before or during the attack,
The airstrike was “clearly a message not just to the Syrian administration but also to Turkey,” Caroline Rose, a senior director at The Soufan Centre, told The New Arab.
“They want Turkey to know that they have the ability to strike them anywhere in Syria in order to deter further perceived encroachment.”
According to Muaz Al-Abdullah, Middle East Research Manager at the conflict-tracking organisation, Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), this follows a pattern of behaviour in which Israel strikes any military installation that Turkey seeks to redevelop.
“They also struck T4, Hama and Palmyra airbases following Turkish attempts to redevelop them,” he explained to The New Arab. “It serves a dual purpose of limiting Turkish influence within Syria and preventing the Syrian military from redeveloping.”
This comes amid what Rose describes as “a growing competition” between Turkey and Israel regionally.
Turkish-Israeli relations have soured massively since 7 October. Whilst both countries have full diplomatic relations, Turkey recalled its ambassador in November 2023 in protest over Israeli actions in Gaza.
In February, meanwhile, former Israeli prime minister Naftali Bennett described Turkey as belonging to a “monstrous axis,” alongside Qatar, in part for its hosting of Hamas officials.
A recent article in Israel Hayom, a pro-Likud outlet, assessed the possibility of an Israeli strike on Turkish forces in Syria triggering NATO’s self-defence clause. It concluded that such an attack would not draw in Turkey’s NATO allies.
Turkey recently signed a mutual defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan - what some commentators have taken to calling an ‘Islamic NATO.’
“The mutual defence agreement is a major step,” Issam Al-Reis, a researcher with ETANA, a Syrian research group, told The New Arab.
“For Saudi Arabia, it is a counter to a possible Iranian attack, and for Turkey it is important to deter a possible future scenario in which it's attacked by Israel,” he added.
“There is a sense of increased recklessness from the Israelis and Turkey is likely wondering if after Iran, they are next on the hit list.”
Divided strategies
Part of the tensions are driven by Israel and Turkey’s conflicting strategies in Syria. “Turkey was one of the primary supporters of the Syrian revolution,” says Al-Reis.
“Now their strategy is driven by a desire for a stable Syria that will allow the millions of refugees within Turkey to return home and provide a calm southern border.”
As such, they have sought to develop Syria’s state capacity, and “expand its military footprint in order to stabilise the country and counter groups that they consider to be terrorist organisations like the Syrian Democratic Forces,” explains Al-Reis.
Yet Al-Abdullah cautions about wholly conflating Israel’s attempts to counter Turkey with its own strategy within Syria. “These two dynamics are linked but also separate,” he argues. Israel has its reasons to oppose the Syrian government.
It sees “a Syria capable of launching attacks as a threat and so wants to see Syria weak and fragmented,” believes Rose. “They seek to counter or at the very least delay Syrian rearmament.”
Similarly, Israel has supported non-state actors within Syria, such as Druze Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri’s National Guard in Suweida, in order to keep Damascus weak.
The US, seeking a stable centralised Syria, has been attempting to restrain Israel with mixed results. US Special Envoy for Syria, Tom Barrack, condemned Israel’s recent strike as “an unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability”.
However, Al-Abdullah notes that according to ACLED’s data, the number of Israeli strikes on Syria is consistently decreasing over time, but that “occasionally Israel still decides to act without the US greenlight”.
Stalled talks
Syrian and Israeli officials have taken part in several rounds of talks in Paris, the latest being on 6 January 2026, designed to establish a ‘deconfliction mechanism’ and set out the ground for the possible future security architecture between the two countries.
According to analysts, these talks have been largely inconclusive and have failed to halt Israeli violations both within the newly occupied territories in Quneitra and Daraa and beyond.
On 14 August, following the resumption of Syrian air force training flights, Israel had reportedly planned on striking a number of airbases in order to disable the last vestiges of Syria’s air force.
It is worth noting that 80% of Assad’s air force was destroyed by Israel in the days following the fall of the Assad regime, leaving Syria now with barely a handful of old Soviet fighter jets.
Whilst the planned strikes were reportedly blocked by the White House, the days after saw numerous attempts to resolve the dispute - including a reported phone call between Shaibani and Gofman - which failed to prevent escalation.
Part of the reasoning behind the recent meeting in Jordan is likely to correct this, with both sides discussing the possibility of establishing “a special operations room” in Jordan under US supervision to prevent any confrontation in Syria.
“This meeting is significant both because Syria’s senior leadership actually met with the Israelis but also because it was publicly acknowledged by the Syrians,” says Al-Abdullah.
This represents a step change in Syrian officials' willingness to candidly acknowledge their attempts to foster dialogue with Israel. Despite that, he remains pessimistic about the outcome of talks.
“The two actors are negotiating different things,” he explains. Syria is hoping to return to a status quo ante, which would see Israel leave the newly occupied areas in return for a deconfliction arrangement similar to the 1974 deconfliction arrangement.
Whereas Israel, reflecting a new post-7 October security mindset that is also visible in Lebanon and Gaza, wants to create “an unliveable buffer zone close to their borders through demolitions, eviction and the poisoning of agriculture”.
Ultimately, this would entail Israel leveraging its position to pressure Syria into accepting major concessions like diplomatic normalisation or the recognition of Israel’s 1981 annexation of the Golan Heights - both of which are political non-starters in Damascus.
It is for this reason that he expects this pattern of latent tensions that sporadically erupt to continue.
However, Al-Abdullah stresses that despite the fierce rhetoric on all sides, neither side is seeking a full-blown conflict and so for now “whilst Syria might be a theatre for confrontation, it is not yet the Middle East’s next battleground”.
Cian Ward is a journalist based in Damascus, covering conflict, migration, and humanitarian issues

Since its launch in 2020, the ArchDaily Next Practices Awards have spotlighted forward-thinking architecture practices that are redefining the boundaries of the discipline. Over five editions, the initiative has recognized 105 practices from 44 countries, amplifying voices from around the world and fostering a global conversation about architecture's evolving role in society. Across the winning practices, recurring values emerge: contextual sensitivity, sustainable material use, co-creation with communities, experimental and interdisciplinary approaches, memory and heritage, social responsibility, and human-scale interventions.
The program reflects what is next: the ideas, practices, and projects that should be brought forward. 'Next' embodies practices that find solutions to today's urgent challenges while anticipating the needs of tomorrow. By spotlighting these practices, we hope to illuminate the paths that can lead to a more meaningful and resilient future for architecture and beyond.
As we move into the 6th edition, we are proud to introduce the jury that will help shape this year's selection. Bringing together voices from Latin America, Southwest Asia, North America, Africa, and Europe, this year's panel includes architects, landscape practitioners, preservation specialists, and institutional leaders whose work is deeply engaged with the questions Next Practices seeks to address. We sincerely thank each of them for their time, expertise, and commitment to the future of architecture.
Jury of the ArchDaily Next Practices Awards 2026
Sumayya Vally
Sumayya Vally is the principal of Counterspace, an architecture and research practice exploring hybrid identities and spatial relationships, with a particular interest in the complex relationships between territories and places. A WEF Young Global Leader, TIME100 honoree, and Art Basel Medallist, she is the youngest architect ever commissioned to design the Serpentine Pavilion in London. Vally is also Resident Architect at Ibraaz, which she conceived as a living, evolving space shaped by the artists, collaborators, and communities that gather there. Her practice is in constant conversation with her teaching at leading institutions, including Columbia's Graduate School of Architecture, Planning and Preservation (GSAPP) and UCL's Bartlett School of Architecture.
Susana Rojas Saviñón
Susana Rojas Saviñón is co-founder of Estudio Ome, an award-winning landscape architecture practice based in Mexico City and London — and a Next Practices winner herself, recognized in a previous edition of this very initiative. She holds an MPhil in Architecture and Urban Design from the Architectural Association and a professional degree in Architecture from Universidad Iberoamericana, and completed the Wood Program in Architecture and Design at Aalto University. A registered architect in Mexico, she has lectured across Latin America, the United States, Canada, and Europe, and taught architecture at Universidad Iberoamericana from 2019 to 2024. In 2020, she was awarded the Young Creators Scholarship from Mexico's National Fund for Culture and the Arts.
Oanh Nguyen Henriksen
Oanh Nguyen Henriksen is Partner and Director of Business Development & Communications at Dorte Mandrup, bringing nearly two decades of experience cultivating new markets and developing strategies for some of the world's most recognized architecture firms, including BIG and 3XN. Her background in urban design informs a deep understanding of the synergy between architecture, business, and societal issues. Beyond her role at Dorte Mandrup, she serves as a board member and mentor for the Dreyers Foundation and the Danish Architectural Association's Grant Program for start-up architecture firms.
Nicolas Fayad and Charles Kettaneh
Nicolas Fayad and Charles Kettaneh are the founders of EAST Architecture Studio, a collective practice working across housing, cultural buildings, exhibitions, master planning, and research. The studio integrates history, traditional culture, and contemporary life through a collaborative, tactile approach that brings together artisanal techniques, innovative design, and expertise from artists, engineers, and environmental specialists. In 2022, EAST received the Aga Khan Award for Architecture, becoming one of the youngest practices to earn this globally recognized distinction; in 2024, the studio won the AlMusalla Prize for a space of prayer and contemplation unveiled at the Islamic Arts Biennale in Jeddah. Their built work and research have been exhibited at the 17th and 19th Venice Architecture Biennales and featured in leading publications including Wallpaper, The Architectural Review, Architectural Record, and Domus.
Javier Ors Ausín
Javier Ors Ausín is an architect and preservation specialist serving as Director of Thematic Programs at the World Monuments Fund, where he oversees a global portfolio spanning three strategic programs: Modernist architecture with a focus on the Global South, Jewish Heritage, and Crisis Response — dedicated to protecting cultural heritage threatened by conflict and natural disasters. His work integrates architecture, international project management, and community-based conservation across Africa, Asia, and Europe. He has lectured at Harvard, Columbia, the University of Toronto, and the University of Miami. He holds a Master in Architecture from the Universidad Politécnica de Valencia and a Master in Design Studies from Harvard University's Graduate School of Design.

Most Poles say formal education falls short for lifelong careers, poll shows
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
09:59:16 CEST
16:59:16 KST

Most Poles say formal education falls short for lifelong careers, poll shows
Three-quarters of Poles (75 percent) believe the knowledge and skills acquired during formal school or university education are no longer sufficient for an entire professional career, according to a new survey commissioned by PAP.
Despite this widespread awareness, the study conducted by the Market and Social Research Institute (IBRiS) found that one in three respondents (34 percent) failed to learn anything new on their own initiative over the past year, primarily due to a lack of time.
The belief that formal education falls short varies across demographics. By education level, this conviction is highest among university graduates (86 percent), compared to those with secondary (75 percent) or primary and vocational education (64 percent). By gender, more women (80 percent) than men (69 percent) view formal schooling as insufficient. Across age groups, disbelief in the adequacy of formal education peaks among those aged 40–59 (81 percent), followed by young adults aged 18–39 (75 percent) and seniors (70 percent). On the other hand, 24 percent of Poles still believe formal education suffices for a lifetime career.
While 66 percent of Poles engaged in self-initiated learning over the past year, participation rates vary significantly. By age, 80 percent of adults aged 40–59 and 73 percent of those aged 18–39 learned something new, while 55 percent of seniors over 60 reported no such activity. By education, 80 percent of university-educated respondents pursued new skills, compared with 63 percent with secondary education and 54 percent with primary or vocational backgrounds.
The primary drivers for continuing education among Poles are developing hobbies (25 percent), maintaining mental sharpness (19 percent), finding a better job (18 percent), and improving tech literacy (18 percent). However, motivations vary widely across generations. Finding a better job motivates 37 percent of young adults aged 18–39, compared to 18 percent of the 40–59 group and just 1 percent of seniors. For the middle-aged cohort (40–59), the main incentives are hobbies (32 percent) and technology (29 percent), while seniors over 60 primarily learn to maintain mental acuity (29 percent).
A lack of time is the leading barrier to learning (44 percent), peaking at 55 percent among adults aged 40–59. Financial costs deter 17 percent of all respondents, rising to 26 percent among young adults aged 18–39. Other hurdles include a lack of motivation (11 percent), transit or accessibility issues (9 percent), and health problems (7 percent), while only 16 percent face no obstacles at all.
The survey was conducted between August 26 and September 1 on a representative nationwide sample of 1,000 Poles. (PAP)

A court in the Philippines has issued a warrant of arrest against Vice-President Sara Duterte-Carpio over death threats she made against President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr.
The warrant involves three counts of grave threats, according to a court order that also set bail at 120,000 pesos (US$1,900) for each count. The charges were first filed last month, based on a National Bureau of Investigation criminal complaint in February 2025.
Duterte’s lawyer, Paul Lawrence Lim, on Friday confirmed the Quezon City regional trial court “has issued a warrant of arrest against the vice-president”.
His client “has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies”, he added.
In November 2024, the vice-president claimed after a late night news briefing that she had hired an assassin and instructed him, if she were ever murdered, to kill Marcos, his wife, First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and his cousin, then house speaker Martin Romualdez. Duterte-Carpio has since denied making those threats.
The alleged threats are also among the allegations included in the impeachment complaint against Duterte, who is being tried before the Senate sitting as an impeachment court. A conviction could remove her from office and derail her presidential bid in 2028.

US claims EU joined new Iran sanctions push, yet Brussels only endorsed it

16:55:15 KST

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has declared that the European Union formally joined Washington's campaign to sever Iran from the global financial system. Yet a Brussels statement issued at this week's G20 finance meeting in fact stops well short of that.
Washington says it has a new partner in its financial war on Tehran.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced on Friday that the EU had "officially joined" Operation Economic Outcast, the aptly named American sanctions effort to cut Iran out of the international banking system, praising the bloc for moving early.
The European Commission statement Bessent refers to, published on Monday, however, welcomes the US campaign without formally committing the EU to it.
"We appreciate their strong and early stance," the US Treasury Secretary wrote, framing the development as proof that international pressure on Iran is mounting.
Bessent added that the world was "sending a clear message to the Iranian regime" and that Washington "will not stop until every remaining financial lifeline has been severed," saying the US "stands firm with our allies in ensuring the murderous Iranian regime cannot exploit the global financial system."
What Brussels actually said
The document the US Treasury Secretary cited was published on 31 August, the opening day of the meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors in Asheville, North Carolina.
The US chairs the group this year, and Bessent hosted the gathering alongside Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, using it to press counterparts to cut financial ties with Tehran or risk secondary sanctions of their own.
The EU statement opens by listing the bloc's longstanding complaints, such as Iran's nuclear and ballistic missile programmes, its destabilising activities in the region and in Europe, its military support for Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and the repression of the Iranian population.
It notes that the EU "has adopted extensive sanctions to prevent Iran from exploiting the global economy and financial system" and "remains ready to take further measures, where necessary, to safeguard its security and interests, including freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz."
On the American sanctions campaign itself, the wording is carefully limited.
The EU "welcomes efforts at ensuring that Iran ceases its destabilising activities and engages in peace negotiations with good faith, also through additional economic pressure, including through the US-led Operation Economic Outcast," and says it will "continue to work closely with the United States and other G7 and international partners."
Nowhere does the statement say the EU is joining the operation, as Brussels announced no new sanctions, no alignment with US designations and no change to its own regime, which already covers Iran's nuclear and missile programmes and its support for Moscow.
It also restated a preference Washington does not share with equal emphasis, saying it "believes continued diplomatic efforts are necessary to reach a peace settlement."
Endorsement, not participation
The characterisation of the EU as having formally joined Operation Economic Outcast is Bessent's, and several news organisations have adopted his framing.
Questioned by Euronews on the issue during the European Commission's midday press briefing on Friday, a spokesperson referred to the same statement from Monday and did not clarify further.
What Brussels has offered so far is an endorsement of American pressure rather than direct involvement in it, and the distinction matters because of what Operation Economic Outcast involves.
Launched in late August, it aims to target Iran's access to digital assets, advanced technology, gold, commercial aviation and shipping, and relies on secondary sanctions, meaning penalties against foreign firms and banks that keep dealing with Iran.
The US Treasury designated close to 60 companies, individuals and vessels at the outset and has signalled fresh measures weekly, starting with banks.
European companies could be exposed to those penalties, and the EU's Blocking Statute bars them from complying with US sanctions on Iran without permission from the European Commission.
"Officially joining" the sanctions effort would likely mean the EU adopting equivalent measures of its own and threatening European companies with European penalties if they continued trading with Iran, which it has not committed to at the moment.
That is a decision requiring unanimity among member states, and one with direct consequences for firms in countries such as Germany, Italy and the Netherlands, which together account for around two-thirds of the bloc's remaining trade with Tehran after years of sanctions.
For now, the gap between what Washington claims and what Europe has announced — and actually done — remains unbridged, and for European banks and exporters, the difference between endorsing the campaign and joining it is the difference between watching it play out and being bound by it.
This story has been updated with a statement from the European Commission spokesperson.

World first in Leuven: Surgeons rebuild damaged torso with donor tissue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
07:51:46 UTC
16:51:46 KST

A team at the Leuven university-hospital have developed a technique to repair major damage to the midsection of the body using tissue from a deceased donor. The new procedure saves the patient from a lifetime use of anti-rejection medication.
Surgeons at UZ Leuven have carried out the first transplant in the world using donor tissue to repair damage to the torso. The new technique, developed at the university-hospital, frees the patient from a lifetime of having to take anti-rejection drugs.
“The tissue from the deceased donor is fully incorporated into the recipient’s own tissue,” says Laurens Ceulemans, a thoracic and transplant surgeon at UZ Leuven. “The vessels that supply blood to the transplanted tissue come from the recipient, not the donor. And you cannot reject your own blood vessels. So the donated tissue essentially becomes part of the patient’s own body.”
Six-pack
Today, large, gaping wounds in the abdomen, chest or diaphragm are usually repaired using a synthetic mesh. This can cause problems in the case of an infection as the material itself can get infected and may have to be removed.
An alternative has been biological material derived from animals, but this is expensive to produce and isn’t always strong enough for a human transplant. So the Leuven surgeons have been working on another solution, which has now been carried out: strong connective tissue from the abdominal wall of a deceased donor.
Our hypothesis is that the body will completely take over the tissue
Dr Laurens Ceulemans
This involves the so-called rectus sheath, a strong layer of connective tissue surrounding the rectus abdominis muscles, the muscles that form the so-called “six-pack.” This tissue is both strong and flexible.
An additional major advantage is that the patient does not require immunosuppressive drugs. In conventional organ transplants, such as with the kidney, liver or lungs, these drugs are necessary, often for life, to prevent the body from rejecting the transplanted organ.
The researchers even suspect that, over time, no donor cells will remain in the transplanted tissue. “Our hypothesis is that the body will completely take over the tissue,” says Ceulemans.
The technique also offers several practical advantages. Donor tissue can be stored for up to one month so can be available for a patient who immediately needs surgery. In addition, the blood type of the donor and the patient don’t need to match.
The results of the research have been published in both the Annals of Surgery and The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery. Ceulemans also recently presented the findings at the annual meeting of the European Surgical Association in Rome, where he was awarded the event’s first prize for his research.

Teacher says winning teens' attention is a daily battle in literature class
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
07:50:00 UTC
16:50:00 KST

Teacher says winning teens' attention is a daily battle in literature class
Writer and Tabasalu High School literature teacher Jürgen Rooste says that teaching is often a daily struggle for students' attention, but some encounters and moments also give a great deal of energy.
Rooste began working at Tabasalu High School five years ago, when the school opened in 2021. Standing in front of a class is often stressful for him.
"It's a daily fight. When you walk to the front of the class as a teacher, every day is a battle or a war. Some days you come home broken and worn out. That's 90 percent of the days. And then there are some days that are great and give you energy," he said.
According to Rooste, one of a teacher's biggest tasks is to spark interest in students and make them notice what is happening in class. He says literature is not inherently interesting for young people, and teachers must work hard to make it so.
"You face the fact that you have to fight for every moment just to get them to notice anything at all. Some sense of interest or excitement is broken. Literature as such simply isn't interesting. To make literature interesting, you have to fight enormously."
He noted that a teacher must be both demanding and able to find ways to spark curiosity. His own deep love of literature does not mean students automatically share it.
"I'm not the best teacher just because I love literature. I want everyone to be fans of literature, of these texts and things like I am, but of course it doesn't work that way," he admitted.
For teachers, fighting for students' attention has become an everyday issue. This includes phone use. One option, he says, is a rule that phones are not used at all in class unless needed for learning. But that also means the teacher takes responsibility onto themselves.
"If one teacher alone starts banning phones — saying that in my class you can't use them — then there's always the chance you take the hit yourself. I have that option, that choice, but I haven't taken it," he said.
Rooste teaches in upper secondary school, and he believes students at that level should be more capable of being present in their studies. Now he sees attitudes in high school that he previously associated more with basic school.
"I remember that high‑school classes were already a transition phase — they wanted to be more adult, they wanted to be a bit present and show it, not that every moment they could chat with a friend, they would."
Reading checks have not disappeared from his classes. Students can do them with the book and their own notes. The teacher cannot fully control the use of artificial intelligence in note‑taking. "At least it has been digested in some secondary or tertiary form," he said.
When choosing works, he gives students a list of options but also experiments with reading different texts side by side. His literature program also includes younger Estonian authors.
