Houthi attacks on Yemen’s Taiz escalate, triggering new displacement wave
Government-Houthi clashes in Taiz intensify, displacing thousands and threatening vital roadways to the Red Sea coast.
Taiz, Yemen – Abdullah Saeed, 47, fled his home in the Maqbanah district west of Taiz in 2022, leaving everything behind and settling in al-Rahabah camp in the Jabal Habashi area 90km (55 miles) south.
While he and around 300 other families in the camp have since struggled to meet their basic needs, they at least enjoyed a peaceful life far from the frontlines.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Houthi fighters clash with Yemeni government forces in country’s southwest
- list 2 of 3Saudi Arabia condemns deadly Iranian attack on tanker in Strait of Hormuz
- list 3 of 3China’s Xi urges new Middle East security framework during rare Egypt visit
That is, until the battles came to Jabal Habashi. An attack from Yemen’s Houthi rebels early on Thursday targeted the district and other areas in southwest Yemen, with heavy fighting continuing.
As the Houthis advanced towards al-Rahabah, Saeed and hundreds of other families fled once again.
“Fighting erupted suddenly at night. We were far from the battlefield, but in the morning, we were shocked to see the frontlines near our camp. There was no solution but to take our basic belongings and flee,” he told Al Jazeera. “We had a bad experience when we were stuck in the crossfire in 2022, so we didn’t want to experience a similar situation and fled before the battles reached our camp.”
Saeed said it wasn’t just displaced families at his camp who had fled, but also people from neighbouring camps and villages.
“We have fled for the second time, but there are also families who fled for the first time. We are all now in dire need of shelter and basic services,” said Saeed, who is now staying with relatives at another camp for displaced people.
After four years of quiet along Yemen’s frontlines, Saeed had held out the hope that he would soon be able to return to his home in Maqbanah. But now, with all-out war between the Houthis and the Yemeni government looking ever more likely, he would be happy just to be able to get back to al-Rahabah, where he at least had shelter, a source of water and a familiar place.
“I do not support any military side, but I hope the battles stop soon and we manage to return to our camp, as all we need now is stability,” he said.
Sudden Houthi attacks
The Houthis launched an offensive against government forces on the western fronts of Taiz governorate – including positions in Maqbanah district – early Thursday morning, using missiles and drones before initiating ground fighting described as the fiercest since 2022.
The pro-Iranian Houthis managed to advance across several fronts in Maqbanah, Mawzaa and Jabal Habashi districts, triggering a new wave of displacement. Saudi-backed government forces say they are confronting the attacks and have retaken some areas.
Military reinforcements, including fighters and military vehicles, have been arriving for both the government and the Houthis. The fighting has grown fiercer, with dozens fighters killed on both sides.
It’s the latest escalation in Yemen’s more than decade-long conflict, which has intensified in recent months. The conflict began in 2014, when the Houthis launched a coup against Yemen’s government, and then seized much of northwest Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.
Since early August, the Houthis have launched deadly missile, drone and ground attacks against government forces across several governorates, including Marib, Taiz, Hodeidah and al-Dhale.
The Houthis have also targeted al-Makha (Mocha) port in an apparent attempt to push government forces out of the southern Red Sea coast, allowing the Houthis to have more control over the key waterway where they have been attacking Saudi shipping.
Government forces have also attacked the Houthis across multiple governorates, reporting dozens of drone strikes against Houthi targets.
The escalating conflict may draw in Saudi Arabia, four years after it last officially conducted airstrikes in Yemen in support of the government.
Casualties
Yahiya Lutf, a pro-government fighter in Jabal Habashi district, confirmed that the Houthis had launched sudden attacks across different fronts in western Taiz governorate but claimed that government forces have retaken several areas.
“The Houthis launched these attacks attempting to cut the main road between Taiz city and the Red Sea coast, but they failed,” Lutf told Al Jazeera. “Our goal is not only to liberate what they took [on Thursday]; we will press forward beyond that, as our morale is high and we are fully prepared for battle.”
He added that there were casualties on both sides.
“The true outcome of these battles will be clear in the near future,” Lutf said. “I call on those reporting Houthi advances to wait, and I promise them good news.”
Lutf added that troops from various military units are participating in the battles.
The frontlines lie near the main road connecting Taiz city with the Red Sea Coast, which serves as the headquarters for the National Resistance Forces, a government-aligned military faction led by Tareq Saleh, nephew of the late former President Ali Abdullah Saleh.
A Houthi source in Sanaa told Al Jazeera that the recent battles are part of the group’s “efforts to break the siege on Yemenis”.
“We are engaged in battle to break the siege on Yemen, especially at sea. This is not just the goal of Ansar Allah [the Houthis], but the desire of all Yemenis,” he said.
The source declined to provide further details, while Houthi media outlets have also refrained from publishing details on the fighting.
Regional factor
Yemeni journalist Odai al-Dokhaini believes the frontlines hold strategic importance as severing the road linking Taiz to al-Makha – as Houthi fighters attempted on Thursday – would impact both cities. The route serves as a vital lifeline for transporting food and goods from al-Makha.
“The Houthis selected these current frontlines for their strategic location,” al-Dokhaini said. “If they succeed in isolating the Red Sea coast fronts, they can begin targeting them individually.”
Yemeni political analyst Abdulsattar al-Shamiri tied the developments to wider events in the region – most notably the US war on Iran.
“This battle cannot be viewed in isolation,” al-Shamiri said. “The Houthis have been pushing to seize more territory along the Red Sea.”
He believes that the attacks are part of a wider strategy by Iran and its allies to project strength, “giving Tehran another point of leverage alongside the Strait of Hormuz”.

Rents rise 4.4% nationally, Rotterdam hit hardest
Unknown

Rents rise 4.4% nationally, Rotterdam hit hardest
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Rents in the Netherlands rose by an average of 4.4% in July compared with a year earlier, national statistics office CBS has reported, a slower increase than in either of the past two years.
The rise was lower than the 4.9% recorded in 2025 and the 5.4% in 2024, then the steepest increase in more than 30 years. Most landlords in the Netherlands raise rents once a year, in July.
The average covers two different things. Tenants who stayed where they were saw a 3.8% rise but rents rose faster when a new tenant moved in.
Where rents rose most
 Among the four big cities, rents rose most in Rotterdam, at 4.7%, and least in Amsterdam, at 4.3%. The Hague saw 4.4% and the city of Utrecht 4.5%. By province, the steepest rises were in Overijssel and Noord-Brabant, both at 4.6%, and the smallest in Friesland, at 4%.
The government sets annual caps on rents for each part of the market, at 4.1% for social housing this year. Rents can still rise above the cap when a home is re-let, or when higher earners are charged an extra €50 or €100 a month.
For private-sector tenants, housing already takes a bigger share of income than for any other group, up to 35% for those entering the market, CBS reported earlier this year.

After Gen Z, India’s Gen Alpha rises, demanding education reforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:20:33 UTC
15:20:33 KST

After Gen Z, India’s Gen Alpha rises, demanding education reforms
School students across multiple states have held protests in recent weeks, seeking better conditions — seemingly inspired by the Gen Z protests that challenged the Narendra Modi government.
Bengaluru, India — It was past time for class, but none of the 122 students at the government-run primary school in Samuhi Bhatpurwa village in India’s Uttar Pradesh were ready for lessons.
For once, they had something to teach the school authorities.
Dressed in their red-and-white checked uniforms, the students — some as young as six — refused to enter their classrooms until they received an assurance that the school would build the new building authorities had promised. Some, such as eight-year-old Priya*, held India’s national flag.
The current structure is old and dilapidated. A portion of the school lies in rubble — unrepaired — after a wall fell on a girl, severely injuring her in 2023.
Since then, the children have been asking for a new building for their safety. But no one listened to them until they launched their unlikely protest on August 22 , children no older than 10 challenging school and government authorities. As news spread that the youngsters were on strike, a senior education department official visited the school.
Block education officer Deepak Awasthi told the children that a new building would be constructed soon. That was when the pupils agreed to go back home as it was already close to evening.
“I am happy. We will get a new building. We (the children) dread the school building would one day fall. Its condition is poor,” Priya told Al Jazeera. “The fear does not let us concentrate on our studies. That is why we all protested.”
Priya and her friends aren’t alone. Children in at least 10 Indian states, including Maharashtra, Bihar, Rajasthan, Jharkhand and Madhya Pradesh, among others, have launched similar protests in schools since late July. Protests have been reported in rural areas where government-run schools are crumbling under neglect.
The protests represent a challenge, not only for India’s education system, but also point to a new political test for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government when it is already struggling to retain the support of young people.
From Gen Z to Gen Alpha
Starting in early June, thousands of Gen Z protesters flooded Jantar Mantar, the protest hub in the heart of India’s capital city, New Delhi. Their most pressing demand was accountability after a series of high-profile examination paper leaks, which in turn were seen as responsible for dozens of young Indians dying by suicide.
But as the Modi government tried to cast the protesters as extremists backed by foreign forces rather than engaging with their grievances, their questions of those in power grew: India’s vast unemployment and underemployment crisis became another flashpoint for the protests.
The popular youth movement was led by the Cockroach Janata Party, or CJP, a satirical society formed in May to express angst over large-scale unemployment and systematic flaws in the education system.
When security forces that report directly to Modi’s de facto deputy, Amit Shah, brutally cracked down on protesters peacefully marching towards the Indian parliament, the Gen Z youth movement drew widespread popular support from across the nation.
As the numbers of protesters swelled and their anger at being beaten up simply for demanding education reforms grew, the Modi government relented. Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, from Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party, resigned.
The CJP has since turned its attention to the condition of India’s schools.
School students, such as in Samuhi Bhatpurwa, are now doing something that is rare in India’s cultural traditions: questioning teachers and those in authority.
Coming close on the heels of the Gen Z protests, this new generation of protesters is being widely described as heralding a Gen Alpha movement.
What ails Indian schools
India operates one of the world’s largest school systems, teaching 247 million students in 1.5 million schools. About 70 percent of the schools are run by federal, state or local governments, the rest either by charities or private institutions.
The government’s official audit of schools in 2025-2026 reported improvements in access to education and suggested that the teacher-pupil ratio was improving — one teacher for every 24 students. School dropout rates are falling too, the data shows.
But the reality for many students and their parents is very different. Some schools operate in buildings that are also used to rear cattle.
“The children are demanding their rights. They want teachers, benches, school buildings, drinking water, electricity and toilets,” Bengaluru-based education rights activist, Nagasimha Rao, told Al Jazeera. “Unfortunately, for a long time, the basic infrastructure and manpower to run schools have been missing. It is the story of most government-run schools across the country.”
“Is it because poor children study in these schools?” asked Rao, referring to government-run schools, where the student body is predominantly composed of children from economically and socially marginalised communities.
In one of the first protests in the current wave, students of Sarvodaya Inter College in Uttar Pradesh came to their school on July 28 in their blue-and-white school uniforms and started protesting. The school, which has classes up to grade 12, lacks drinking water, electricity and even benches.
“No one can imagine how difficult it is for us to study in the school. There is no electricity, so no fans during the hot and humid summers. We don’t have a drinking water facility. Many students sit on the floor because we don’t have enough benches. So we decided to protest,” said class 12 student Manoj*.
Manoj’s friend and classmate, Neelam*, added that the students had been asking for basic facilities for a long time. “This time we decided to hold a formal protest with placards and sloganeering.”
Similar protests followed. On July 31 , students of Vaidyanath Vidyalaya in Parli in the western state of Maharashtra organised a demonstration against the shortage of faculty members. The school was established in 1941.
Gen Z supports Gen Alpha
On August 15 , when India celebrated its Independence Day, the CJP launched its grassroots initiative, ‘School Thik Karo (Fix The Schools).’
Ratna Singh, the CJP’s legal affairs head, told Al Jazeera that their movement fully backed the protests in schools across the country, seeking to improve the education system.
“During our Jantar Mantar protest in Delhi, we met many young children and their parents who had travelled from rural areas,” Singh said. “They spoke about the poor condition of schools, the shortage of teachers and potholed, untarred roads leading to schools, among other issues. It is also a natural progression of our (the CJP’s) movement to fix schools for a better future of our children.”
Several instances of violence were reported as CJP members visited schools in different parts of the country to check their conditions and speak to children.
Gaurav Bharti, a member of the CJP from Uttar Pradesh, alleged that “the police and local goons are threatening members of the CJP”.
“After I visited the primary school in Uttar Pradesh’s Karanpur Majra (a rural belt) on August 16 and exposed its poor conditions, the police force is after me,” he said. “The headmistress of the school has filed a police complaint against me. But we are not scared. We are demanding what is already mentioned in laws like the RTE Act.”
The Right to Education (RTE) Act, which came into effect in 2009, made education a fundamental right for children aged six to 14. It clearly defines infrastructural standards, including “all-weather buildings, water, sanitation and safety for children.” It also states that the teacher-student ratio should be at least 1:30.
But while the national average meets that bar, the government’s own data shows that India has 100,843 schools that have only a single teacher — across all grades. About 2.9 million children are enrolled in those schools. Conversely, India also has 5,663 ‘ghost schools’ — institutions with no enrolment.
Substandard food provided in India’s massive school lunch programme — known as the midday meal scheme — has often been another cause of protests.
In Bihar’s Simuara village on July 28 , around 50 students walked 4km to meet a senior bureaucrat to protest against the quality of the midday meals they were being fed. The school does not have access to piped water, so raw ingredients are not cleaned before they are cooked. The students complained that the quality of rice, lentils and vegetables was substandard — vegetables, they said, were often almost rotten.
What India’s school system needs are systemic fixes that “involve providing equally good infrastructure everywhere; hiring and enabling teachers; incentivising families to send their children to school as well as holding them accountable for non-compliance,” said Chennai-based educationist and political scientist, Swarna Rajagopalan.
The school protests also portend a future political challenge for governments in power. More than 30 percent of India’s population is under the age of 18. Many of those joining school protests today will be of voting age in 2029, when India next holds its national elections.
“The children are our future. If they don’t get proper education in a conducive atmosphere, it would derail India’s growth. These children are tomorrow’s voters too,” Akash Sarkar, an education activist from the eastern state of West Bengal told Al Jazeera. “They will definitely vote keeping in mind the interest of the country’s education system.”
To Sujata Gowda, a student at Bangalore University in Bengaluru, the recent wave of protests — first among the Gen Z and now Gen Alpha — isn’t surprising: Students across the country, she said, felt abandoned by the system.
“This angst has been brewing for a long time. That is why even school children are protesting. Our schools, colleges and universities need to be revamped,” the 21-year old, who is pursuing postgraduate studies in mathematics, told Al Jazeera. “We need qualified teachers, examinations should be conducted fairly, infrastructure should be improved.
“For that the authorities must listen to students,” she added. “Otherwise, more protests are likely to take place across the country.”
*The names of school children have been changed.

Lithuanian intelligence currently sees no increased threat from Belarus, Deividas Matulionis, President Gitanas Nausėda’s chief national security adviser, said Thursday.
“I specifically made additional inquiries today, and our services have no such information. As of today, we do not see an increased threat from the Belarusian side,” Matulionis told LRT RADIO.
He said that while Russian military installations are present in Belarus, Lithuanian intelligence has not detected new manoeuvre units that would pose a direct threat to Lithuania, Latvia or Poland.
Matulionis’ comments followed warnings by Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, who was visiting Lithuania and said she had received information about new military infrastructure being built in Belarus, including near the border with Ukraine and along its borders with European Union countries.
Matulionis said Lithuanian intelligence was closely monitoring developments in Belarus. A significant buildup of Russian troops would be a clear signal requiring action at both the national and NATO levels, he said.
However, Lithuanian intelligence services currently cannot confirm Tsikhanouskaya’s warnings, he said.
According to Matulionis, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko is also not interested in becoming directly involved in Russia’s war against Ukraine and is seeking to improve relations with the West and the United States.
Matulionis said Lithuania should not restore political relations with Lukashenko’s government but should maintain communication channels with Minsk to help prevent a potential escalation during a crisis.
Following a meeting with Tsikhanouskaya, Seimas Speaker Juozas Olekas said Belarusian railways could potentially be used to transport Russian troops and weapons. He said Lithuanian authorities were monitoring and controlling infrastructure being built in Belarus.
Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas has said Moscow may be considering attacks on critical infrastructure in the Baltic region using Ukrainian drones as a way of testing NATO’s cohesion. He did not specify how concrete the plans were.
Lithuania has maintained a hostile approach toward Belarus since Lukashenko launched a crackdown on the opposition following the disputed 2020 presidential election. Vilnius has also advocated for European Union sanctions against Belarus.

“I can’t explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to god,” Amir Maharjan, brother to one of the rescued workers, told The Associated Press. He said the family was on its way to the hospital to see him.
At least 557 workers are missing from the Trishuli 3A hydropower project along the Trishuli River, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the tunnel, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal.
Nepal’s Communication Minister Bikram Timilsina said officials remain hopeful that more workers will be rescued.
“We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people,” Timilsina wrote on his Facebook page.

About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, according to local authorities.

Lihtsad uudised 4. septembril
"Lihtsad uudised," meaning easy or simple news, is for anyone who wants to improve their Estonian language skills. Listen and read a selection of this week's news stories below.
Ülle Madise soovib olla kõigi Eesti inimeste president
Kolmapäeval valis riigikogu Eesti presidendiks Ülle Madise. Ta ütles pärast tulemuse selgumist Tallinnas pressikonverentsil, et kõik erakonnad ja kandidaadid, kes on valitud riigikogusse, esindavad rahvast ning väärivad austust ja lugupidamist.

Kaitseminister Hanno Pevkur lahkub ametist
Eesti kaitseminister Hanno Pevkur Reformierakonnast teatas kolmapäeva õhtul, et astub ametist tagasi. Ta põhjendas oma sammu sellega, et võtab poliitilise vastutuse kaitsevaldkonnas avastatud segaduste eest.
Prokuratuur algatas teisipäeval kriminaalmenetluse, et uurida riigikontrolli nii tänavu kui ka eelmisel aastal tehtud etteheiteid kaitseministeeriumi töövaldkonnale. Riigikontrolli hinnangul valitseb Eesti riigikaitse raamatupidamises suur segadus.
Kolmapäeval kirjutas meedia, et Eesti soovis osta Ukrainale mürske ja maksis 70 miljonit eurot ettemaksu India ettevõtjatele, kes aga polnud väidetavalt varem ühtegi mürsku müünud.
Pevkur ütles, et tema selle lepingu üle läbirääkimisi ei pidanud ja kaitseminister ei pea detailidega tegelema. "Kaitseminister ei loe üle sokke ja padruneid," sõnas ta.
Eestis läks tänavu esimesse klassi 14 700 õpilast
Üle Eesti läheb tänavu 1. klassi ligi 14 700 õpilast ning kokku asub üldhariduskoolides õppima ca 160 000 õpilast. Haridusminister Kristina Kallas soovis õpilastele kooliaasta alguse puhul uudishimu ja natuke ulakust mõtlemises.
"Ärge leppige alati esimese vastusega," ütles minister. "Õpetajatele soovin loovust ja vastupidavust. Mõnikord sünnib ju kõige parem õppimine just siis, kui tund läheb natuke teises suunas, kui plaan ette nägi."
Kutseõppes asub tänavu üle Eesti õppima üle 26 000 õpilase. Üliõpilasi on sel aastal üle 47 000.
Läti põllumehed ootavad Eesti firma investeeringut
Kui Eesti ettevõte Agrone ostab Lätis kaks piimakombinaati, siis Läti tootjad ootavad, et sealsed farmerid hakkavad oma piima eest rohkem raha teenima.
Baltimaade piimaturg on ühine, sest piima müüakse sinna, kus on kasulikum. Ka naabrite juures valmistatud tooteid on kõikjal poes saada.
Et Eesti ettevõtte investeering saaks teoks, on tarvis veel heakskiitu nii Eesti kui ka Läti konkurentsiametilt.
Politsei ei lähe enam kukkunud eakale inimesele appi
Seni on kodus kukkunud eakaid püsti aitamas käinud politseinikud. Siseministeerium aga otsustas, et häirekeskus enam politseinikke appi saata ei tohi. See töö jääb nüüd kiirabi ja omavalitsuste sotsiaaltöötajate teha.
Kohalikud omavalitsused aga ei tööta ööpäevaringselt ja nende töötajatel ei ole sageli ametiautot, millega abivajaja juurde sõita.
Ka sotsiaalministeerium ei arva, et see uus kord on mõistlik. Viimase aasta jooksul on politsei pidanud aitama 600 kukkunud hädalist.

El Niño is already wreaking havoc around the world — and it's only getting started
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:10:15 UTC
15:10:15 KST

In brief
- While El Niño is expected to peak later this year, some countries are already struggling through extreme weather linked to the phenomenon.
- Parts of Central America are suffering severe drought, and in Indonesia, El Niño is exacerbating widespread wildfires.
The strengthening El Niño is already disrupting lives around the world, as the United Nations warns the "surging" climate pattern is raising the risk of months of heatwaves, floods, drought and extreme weather.
On Thursday, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said there was a likelihood of "nearly 100 per cent" that El Niño will persist through to February, noting that this was the first time that an El Niño update had been so unequivocal.
The WMO's secretary-general, Celeste Saulo, said the climate driver, which was officially declared underway in June, has already dealt a blow to communities worldwide.
"We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies," she said.
The phenomenon is expected to peak at very high intensity towards the end of the year — potentially at a record-breaking level — with lasting effects on the climate well into 2027 and the prospect of unprecedented global heat.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
UN secretary-general António Guterres warned that El Niño is "being supersized before our eyes" by climate change.
"The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up," Guterres said in response to the WMO update.
El Niño is associated with higher global temperatures and can bring drought and extreme heat to some regions while increasing rainfall and flood risks in others.
In Australia, El Niño typically increases the likelihood of hotter, drier conditions in the east and south-east, though its influence varies, and other climate factors also shape rainfall and temperatures.
Warmer-than-usual weather is expected across most of Australia through the spring.
Here's how El Niño is already affecting some parts of the world:
Southeast Asia
More than a million students are learning remotely this week as toxic wildfire haze blankets parts of Indonesia, with officials warning that efforts to extinguish the blazes are entering a critical phase.
"Our problems are not over. September is the peak of El Niño," Indonesia's forestry minister Raja Juli Antoni told reporters this week.
El Niño is driving hotter, drier conditions in the region, intensifying a dry season that has seen thousands of hectares burnt.
Almost 95,000 hectares were burnt in July alone.
Indonesian forest fire forensics expert Bambang Hero Saharjo told the BBC this year's El Niño-fuelled blazes could burn an area as large as 11 million hectares.
The haze has spread across parts of Southeast Asia, triggering health warnings and hospitalisations.
The health ministry in neighbouring Malaysia has reported rising cases of asthma and conjunctivitis nationwide as air quality worsens.
Six districts in the state of Sarawak recorded hazardous Air Pollutant Index (API) readings, including the state capital, Kuching, where the API hit 407.
Under national guidelines, levels above 300 are classed as hazardous, while readings beyond 500 could prompt consideration of a local emergency.
Local resident Ivana Mason said the conditions are affecting her health and preventing her from going outside.
"If I do, I can literally taste the smoke in my mouth," she said.
Latin America
Multiple Central and South American countries, some of which are particularly susceptible to El Niño's influences, are on high alert as they brace for impact.
Panama, Ecuador, Honduras, Colombia and El Salvador have declared emergencies in response to the El Niño episode, activating agencies to prepare for imminent risks.
More than 70,000 corn-farming households in Central America's Dry Corridor — a drought-prone region spanning parts of Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador — have reported devastating crop losses, according to a recent report by Oxfam.
Further south, Peru has declared a state of emergency in a third of its cities due to El Niño, warning that intense heat and rain could leave people without enough to eat.
Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, and parts of North, Central and South America are among the regions more consistently impacted by El Niño events, according to associate professor Andrea Taschetto, a climate researcher at the University of New South Wales.
"The last El Niño had a really big impact in the Amazon Basin, and that affects all the communities that are along the Amazon River," she told SBS News.
The river network is a vital transport route for the region, she noted, meaning low water levels can disrupt access to food, healthcare and other essential supplies.
The World Food Programme has warned that El Niño is a massive threat to food security for millions of people, with the largest impacts expected in parts of Central America.
Its modelling showed more than 16 million people could be affected in Latin America and the Caribbean, with an 81 per cent increase in food insecurity projected.
El Niño could also disrupt global trade.
Starting Friday, the Panama Canal, an important shipping route connecting the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans, will restrict the number of vessels that can transit for only the second time in its history.
It's a bid to conserve water amid drought that may last until next year.
Five per cent of global trade passes through the man-made canal, which relies on water from reservoirs including Lake Gatun to operate locks that raise and lower ships in the waterway.
South Asia
Sri Lanka is among the South Asian countries badly affected by weather disruptions this year, with some key farming districts recording rainfall deficits of 85 per cent to 100 per cent below long-term averages.
Soaring temperatures have left large swathes of Sri Lanka's north, east and southern regions parched, with small tanks, rivers and lakes that usually feed crops and provide drinking water drying out.
The Sri Lankan government has said the impact this year could be the worst in decades and that water levels at hundreds of such tanks in the country have dropped to about 10 per cent.
Sri Lanka's current dry conditions are forecast to give way to heavy rains from late September until December, but those rains are expected to be followed by a prolonged drought early next year.
The government has set up a ministerial panel to deal with the fallout from what its environment minister has said would be the island's "worst" El Niño.

hissy cooling jacket pairs CO₂ cartridges with technical apparel for extreme urban heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:05:30 UTC
15:05:30 KST

Hissy brings a cooling system into lightweight technical apparel
Hissy is a wearable cooling system developed for increasingly high urban temperatures. The garment uses a dedicated CO₂ cartridge in place of the heavy batteries and fan-based ventilation commonly found in portable cooling devices. Once the cartridge is docked, high-pressure liquid carbon dioxide vaporizes within the system, absorbing surrounding heat and producing a cooling airflow of approximately -30°C.
The concept responds to the limitations of conventional cooling technologies in extreme heat. As global temperatures rise and summer outdoor activities become increasingly affected by heat, portable fans become less effective at temperatures above 35°C. Battery-powered cooling devices also become heavier and less efficient, while exposure to high temperatures can further affect battery performance and safety. Hissy addresses these constraints through a lightweight garment-based system that integrates the cooling hardware directly into the apparel.
The garment is organized around an internal tubular Air Path that distributes cooling through the body of the garment. Its pattern and construction are determined by the route of this internal system, with the fabric cut and sewn to accommodate the tubing. The Air Path follows an ergonomic spiral based on the natural curves of the body, helping prevent bending or kinking that could obstruct the high-pressure cooling spray. Micro-perforations along the Air Path direct the airflow toward the body’s major heat-generating areas. Their dimensions and distribution were established through thermal mapping and heat-distribution experiments, allowing the cooling pressure to remain consistent from the hardware connector through to the end of the tube. This localized distribution avoids dispersing airflow indiscriminately while supporting controlled thermal comfort.
Hissy system extends from cooling apparel To lifestyle products
The CO₂ cartridge is integrated into the sleeve through a magnetic docking structure. Instead of screw threads, the system uses magnetic attraction to draw the cartridge into position, where locking protrusions engage with the internal hardware. The connection prevents vertical extraction and keeps the cartridge secured against the recoil generated by the high-pressure cooling spray. Removal follows the same magnetic mechanism. A slight rotation switches the poles of the internal dual-magnetized structure to repulsion. A groove within the hardware guides the cartridge through the required release angle, allowing the empty cartridge to be removed with a simple twist.
Additional details address the garment’s use during outdoor activity. An internal strap and external sleeve zipper secure the hardware according to the wearer’s wrist size and limit movement during use. A dedicated chest pocket provides storage for spare cartridges, keeping replacements accessible while maintaining the garment’s integrated appearance. The cooling system designed by Dongheon Kang, Minseo Jung, Yuha Ko, Juhyeon Jeon, and Woohi Park for Samsung Design Membershipalso incorporates a circular approach to CO₂ use. The carbon dioxide is captured from industrial processes that would otherwise release it into the atmosphere and repurposed as the cooling medium. After use, the cartridges are collected, inspected, refilled, and recirculated. The system is designed to keep both the products and the CO₂ resource in circulation without adding net carbon to the atmosphere.
Hissy’s apparel features a function-driven design, cut and sewn to mirror the optimal path of the cooling airflow
Hissy is conceived as a broader cooling platform beyond the initial garment. Its proposed expansion is structured across three phases. The first extends the CO₂ cooling technology to other wearable formats, including footwear, to distribute thermal management across the body. The second applies the system to lifestyle products such as outdoor can coolers for keeping food and beverages cold. The third moves into industrial applications, positioning the technology as a B2B thermal-management system for machines operating in high-temperature outdoor environments, including delivery robots and drones.
Through this approach, Hissy combines wearable design, airflow engineering, material construction, magnetic interaction, and CO₂ recirculation into a cooling system intended to operate across personal, lifestyle, and industrial applications.

Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:04:06 UTC
15:04:06 KST

Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain
Scientists have revealed that the human brain’s earliest stem cells use both nutrients and physical signals to decide what kinds of brain cells to build.
- Date:
- September 4, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Los Angeles Health Sciences
- Summary:
- UCLA researchers have discovered two powerful influences that help guide how the human brain forms before birth. Radial glia, stem cells responsible for producing much of the cerebral cortex, change their behavior depending on how they process glucose and on physical contact with signals arriving from the thalamus. Those signals can alter which types of neurons are produced, including upper-layer neurons that are especially prominent in humans.
- Share:
Before birth, the human brain is assembled through an enormous series of cellular choices. At the center of this process are radial glia, a special type of stem cell that helps create many of the features that distinguish the human brain.
These cells produce large numbers of the neurons and support cells that make up the cerebral cortex, the brain region involved in thought, memory, and language. Radial glia are also believed to contribute to the unusually large expansion of the human cortex compared with that of other species. Although most disappear before birth, similar cells can later appear again in brain cancers for reasons scientists still do not fully understand.
"Radial glia are the coolest cells that have ever existed," said Aparna Bhaduri, an assistant professor of biological chemistry at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA. "They're really key to making us human. But they're also at the center of many neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders, as well as cancer -- so understanding how they make their decisions is one way to start understanding how those conditions arise."
Two new studies published in Cell and Science now provide a closer look at how radial glia make those developmental choices. Bhaduri and her colleagues found that the cells respond to two very different kinds of information: the way they process nutrients and direct physical signals from another part of the developing brain. Together, these findings offer new insight into how the human cortex produces its remarkable variety of cell types.
Metabolism helps direct brain stem cells
In the Cell study, researchers built a detailed map of metabolism in the developing human cortex. The project was a collaboration between Bhaduri's lab and Heather Christofk's lab and was led by co-first authors Jessenya Mil and Jose Soto.
To create the atlas, the team analyzed donated human tissue along with brain organoids grown from stem cells. Their results pointed to an unexpected conclusion: metabolism does not simply support brain development in the background. It can actively influence which kinds of cells are produced.
The researchers found that radial glia depend heavily on the pentose phosphate pathway, a metabolic process that uses glucose to make materials needed by cells that are dividing rapidly.
When the scientists lowered the amount of available glucose or interfered with this pathway, the stem cells changed what they produced. They began generating more inhibitory neurons and other cell types that normally appear later in development.
"What was surprising is that metabolism isn't just a passive thing that happens in the background," said Bhaduri, a member of both the UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center and the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center. "It can really control how stem cells make decisions."
The results could help scientists investigate how maternal nutrition, metabolic disorders, and other environmental influences affect the developing brain. The metabolic atlas also provides one of the most detailed resources yet for researchers studying metabolism during human brain development.
A signal arrives early from the thalamus
The second study, published in Science and led by first author Claudia Nguyen, examined a completely different source of developmental information. This time, the researchers focused on signals coming from the thalamus, a structure deep inside the brain that helps relay information throughout the nervous system.
Scientists have known for years that neurons in the thalamus send long projections toward the cortex. These wire-like fibers eventually form connections with specific cortical neurons. However, anatomical studies have shown that in humans, the projections reach the cortex long before those final connections are established.
That raised an important question: Why do the fibers arrive so early?
Using human stem cell-derived brain "assembloids," the UCLA researchers found part of the answer. The thalamic projections physically touch radial glia while the brain is still developing.
That contact changed the behavior of the stem cells. It caused them to produce more excitatory neurons, the primary signal-carrying neurons in the cortex. The effect was especially strong for upper-layer neurons, which are particularly expanded in the human brain.
"We already knew that these projections influence how the cortex develops," Bhaduri said. "What we specifically found is that this influence comes through an actual physical connection between the projections and the radial glia -- a point of contact that just hasn't been identified before, and one that very likely does not exist in rodents."
A gene linked to autism enters the picture
The researchers connected this physical interaction to NRXN1, a gene already known for helping neurons form connections with one another. Mutations in NRXN1 have previously been associated with autism spectrum disorder.
To investigate its role, the team created assembloids from patient-derived cells carrying an NRXN1 mutation. In these models, the altered thalamic signals behaved differently from signals made by unaffected cells.
Those changes shifted the balance between the number of stem cells and the neurons they generated. The result offers researchers a possible way to study how disturbances early in brain development could influence the formation of the cortex.
The developing brain is in constant communication
Although the two studies focused on very different mechanisms, they point toward the same broader idea. One examined metabolism, while the other explored neural connections, yet both showed that radial glia do not make their decisions in isolation. Their behavior is continuously shaped by signals from the environment around them.
The studies also demonstrate how dramatically organoid technology has changed the study of human brain development. About a decade ago, scientists had few practical ways to directly investigate how uniquely human neural stem cells behave.
Today, brain organoids and related models allow researchers to recreate important features of human brain development in the laboratory. These systems also make it possible to test questions that cannot be addressed through animal models alone.
Bhaduri hopes the findings will encourage scientists to view metabolism and physical cellular connections as active drivers of development rather than as background processes.
"Ultimately, these studies give us a glimpse under the hood of how these cells make decisions," she said. "Understanding those decisions is a first step toward understanding normal brain development, disease vulnerability and, potentially, how similar stem-cell programs operate in brain cancer."
This research was supported by the National Institutes of Health, the National Science Foundation, the Brain & Behavior Research Foundation, the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, the Rose Hills Foundation, the Esther A. & Joseph Klingenstein Fund, the Simons Foundation, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, the NIH BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network, the International Foundation for Ethical Research, the UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center's Stem Cell Research Training Program, and the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center and UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center Ablon Scholars Program.
Story Source:

Journal Reference:
- Jessenya Mil, Jose A. Soto, Abigail S. Krall, Julia Peloggia, Sara Frigui, Olivia S. Fong, Laila Sathe, Nedas Matulionis, Francesca Day, Linsey Stiles, Katrina P. Montales, Daria J. Azizad, Carlos E. Gonzalez, Elisa Fazzari, Matthew X. Li, Patricia R. Nano, Antoni A. Martija, Cesar A. Perez-Ramirez, Claudia V. Nguyen, Brittney Wick, Weihong Ge, Ryan L. Kan, Madeline G. Andrews, Maximilian Haeussler, Michael F. Wells, Heather R. Christofk, Aparna Bhaduri. Metabolic atlas of early human cortex reveals glycolytic remodeling and pentose phosphate pathway control of cell fate transitions. Cell, 2026; DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.07.023

“There is no such thing as a ‘sense of humor’ in the Criminal Code”: Russian stand-up comedians on surviving war and censorship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:03:55 UTC
15:03:55 KST

Russian stand-up comedy has changed dramatically over the past four and a half years of full-scale war. In early 2026, a Russian court sentenced comedian Artemy Ostanin to five years and nine months in prison for a joke about a legless Jesus. Within the stand-up community, the case was seen as a warning: anything said onstage can lead to very real trouble. Venues now ask performers in advance to keep their shows “apolitical,” while comedians themselves remove potentially risky material from acts or hide it behind hints and innuendo. Some comedians left Russia during the mobilization but later returned after finding that they could not afford to remain in exile. The Insider spoke to stand-up comedians who live and perform in Russia. They described what can be joked about today, how fear and self-censorship have changed the scene, and why even audiences are no longer always interested in political humor.
- 1.“Relax. I’ll go to prison, and you’ll be fine.” Stand-up comedian Viktor P.
- 2.“The audience has no idea how many jokes never make it to them.” Stand-up comedian Mikhail Z.
- 3.“Professional comedians are already consulting lawyers.” Stand-up comedian Alexei B.
- 4.“It’s making everyone a little paranoid.” Stand-up comedian Pavel V.
“Relax. I’ll go to prison, and you’ll be fine.” Stand-up comedian Viktor P.
Recently, I hosted a show at a popular bar in central Moscow. The organizers immediately asked us not to do anything political. There used to be times when someone would shout “Russia!” or start singing the national anthem or “Mother Earth” — none of that is allowed now, either.
And this is a bar in central Moscow, where young, modern people go — as modern as people can be these days. There is undoubtedly a demand for something political. You can give a little wink here and there. The kind of wink Ivan Urgant used to give — that’s about as far as you can go now.
For example, at one point my partner says, “I can’t talk about this.” And I say, “The only things we can talk about here are this or apples. Nothing else.” The audience understands that we’re talking about the party, and there’s an immediate, strong reaction. So you flash something for half a second — and that’s it.
There is an internal censorship among bar owners, comedians themselves, and stand-up club owners. The case of Artemy [Ostanin] shows how quickly things can escalate. Even if you didn’t mean anything by it, even if you hardly said anything at all, it’s still better to keep that in mind.
My audience is pretty modern and understands everything. But you still think: someone might record it, send it to someone, and then some activist could pick it up and make a big deal out of it.
I don’t think I’m important enough for anyone to want to put me in prison. But the news scares me — stories about completely unknown people being jailed for something, sometimes just for a repost. And you don’t always even understand what exactly the person did. It’s the same with performing onstage: you think not only about what you said, but also about how it might spread. Like with Nurlan Saburov: someone records something, and then it starts taking on a life of its own, separate from you. So you just become more careful.
The story of Artemy Ostanin, of course, shocked and deeply affected many of my friends and the stand-up community as a whole. When the whole avalanche was just beginning, many people told him to leave. But he treated what was happening as some kind of joke. Then he and his girlfriend tried to leave through Belarus, and they were eventually detained.
In the past, when something happened to comedians, the community reacted differently. Take Idrak Mirzalizade or Sasha Dolgopolov, for example. I clearly remember that when Idrak was having problems, we could end a show by saying, “Idrak is innocent,” or “Idrak should be free.” And we weren’t the only ones doing it. But when it happened to Artemy, nobody spoke out because they were scared. After that, venues became especially insistent: nothing about the “special military operation,” nothing about the war.
But, again, there is still a demand for it. And whenever I feel I can, I try to give a little wink. Sometimes, on the contrary, I take the position that everything is fine. For example, I see that people in the audience have understood, and I say, “America is complete garbage.” Everyone knows it’s post-irony. But technically, those are the words I said. As far as I know, the Criminal Code has no concept of a “sense of humor.”
Sometimes, though, the audience gets tense when political subjects come up. They’ve come to relax, to hear awkward stories about sex or the subway. I even say from time to time, “Relax. I’ll go to prison. You’ll be fine.” I’m not a political comedian. What matters to me is that people have fun.
Once, after a show, a couple of guys came up to me. They said, “That was great, we really loved it. Can we take a photo with you now and send it to a friend? He’s serving at the front right now.” What am I supposed to say to them? Of course, sure. I don’t want to get into a confrontation with them. I don’t want to try to change anyone’s mind or get into a political argument at a stand-up show. I don’t see myself as someone who can do that, and I don’t think it’s my job anyway. At the same time, I’ve been to protests. I was detained. I later emigrated, but I came back. You need money to live in exile, and I’m not a wealthy person.
There are, of course, comedians who describe their stand-up as political. Some joke about sanctions and liberals, perform in Donetsk, and so on. There’s one comedian, for example, who likes to call Vladimir Vladimirovich [Putin] “Uncle Vova” onstage and say, “I’ve got some political material.”
I keep an eye on comedians who have left, but at this point it’s really a matter of taste. I like what Idrak Mirzalizade does, and I like the club they run in Poland. I hardly watch Denis Chuzhoy, for example. Sometimes I feel that some comedians abroad lean too heavily into this “holier-than-thou” attitude. I accept that the problem may be with me. Maybe I just don’t want to admit that I’m also part of what’s happening because I’m still here. They chose to leave, and I didn’t. Well, I did, but then I came back. And when people tell me all this from abroad, sometimes I just don’t find it funny.
Sometimes I feel that some comedians abroad lean too heavily into this “holier-than-thou” attitude
I don’t watch comedians who joke about people who left or about emigration. I don’t even want to make myself angry over this propaganda. I have enough anxiety of my own. I don’t have the energy to sit around hating someone. I have to think about how I’m going to pay the rent.
These days I keep thinking about Ivan Urgant. His first appearance after Evening Urgant was canceled was a broadcast with Ayaz Shabutdinov. Ivan was talking to him about his business and creative work, and they were doing a presentation. The presentation had some blue-and-yellow charts. Ivan said, “Interesting choice of colors by whoever made this presentation.” Or there would be a shot of Dmitry Nazarov — and we know where he stands. Just very subtle things like that. But who finds that funny? I don’t know. It’s not really something for a mass audience anymore.
Do I feel hopeless? No. Probably because I simply don’t want to. I try to stay positive. I didn’t choose the time I was born into. And I still want to be happy. But I guess I’ve stopped expecting hot water to be a given. I’m just trying not to lose heart.
Of course, everything that’s happening gets me down. Sometimes I feel completely drained because I don’t know what else I can do or say. Maybe the only thing I can do is help the audience let off a little steam when I go onstage.
Yes, I don’t have the money to emigrate. But I actually like living in Russia. I’d like to be able to live here and travel at the same time. But I don’t feel like, “That’s it, I can’t make a joke about this subject onstage anymore — what a nightmare, my life is over.” I have no idea what will happen next. Maybe a year from now I’ll look back and think, “Wow, remember when we talked with that journalist? Those were the good old days. Things are nothing like that now!” Or maybe it’ll be the other way around.
“The audience has no idea how many jokes never make it to them.” Stand-up comedian Mikhail Z.
I perform at various venues around the city, and everything there is very chaste. Before a show, the organizer reads through my material and cuts anything that isn’t allowed. I had a pretty innocent joke about women who provide paid call-out services — caregivers. They told me, “Rephrase it so there’s no hint of prostitution.” But how am I supposed to rephrase it? In the end, I said, “A woman with an elevated level of social responsibility.”
Before a show, the organizer reads through my material and cuts anything that isn’t allowed
You can’t joke about VPNs. Crude jokes are off-limits, too — although it’s not clear what counts as crude. I had a joke: “My eyesight is so bad, I vomit farther than I can see.” They even banned the word “vomit.” So someone sits there reading through the material, marking things in red: cut this, absolutely not.
The organizer is about 25, but I understand why he does it: he’s simply afraid. Everything could be checked, someone could come along and jot something down in a notebook, and then there could be trouble. After all the cases of people being detained or punished for things they’ve said at concerts or on air, everyone is now playing it safe.
In fact, it’s even worse than ordinary censorship. Nobody directly orders the organizers to cut a joke about a caregiver or the word “vomit.” Instead, people try to anticipate what they could theoretically be punished for and ban even more — just to be on the safe side.
I don’t perform in clubs, although things are a little easier there. My audience is pretty academic, though: they sit politely, nobody drinks. So I’m grateful for everything. Of course, it’s frustrating when half your material gets cut. But as long as I can still perform, that’s something. Especially since the audience laughs — even if they have no idea how many jokes never made it to them.
“Professional comedians are already consulting lawyers.” Stand-up comedian Alexei B.
I suppose I should start by saying that in March of this year, stand-up comedian Artemy Ostanin was sentenced to prison. And that, of course, sent shockwaves through the stand-up community because it was the first high-profile case of its kind.
Before that, in September of last year, Dima Gavrilov was sentenced to 13 days in jail. At the time [of his alleged offense], he was living either in Armenia or Georgia, and during a performance he said something about the phrase “Russian pigs go home” — he said he liked that they were written there because they made him feel at home. He had a whole monologue about Russophobia, and that ultimately led to him being prosecuted.
But he asked us not to get involved in the case in any way or draw attention to it. He said he would deal with it himself with his lawyer and didn’t want to attract even more public attention. And, in fact, things turned out more or less fine and he was released.
Before Artemy was detained, I even messaged him to ask how things were going and whether he needed any help. He replied that everything was fine and that he would get out of it without a scratch. He didn’t.
A lot of comedians simply don’t know that laws like these exist. After what happened to Ostanin, though, they started getting nervous. Some have sent me their scripts and jokes and asked, “Do you think this could get me prosecuted under this law?” It’s pretty sad, because there’s no real legal awareness among the public.
Sometimes I listen to a monologue and think, Guys, you really can’t do that. And the person simply doesn’t understand that if he jokingly draws a Hitler mustache, sketches a swastika, or makes an ambiguous gesture, that could already be enough to trigger a prosecution. You explain it to him, and he looks at you as if to say, “Are you joking or are you serious?”
It seems to me that changes to the law like these simply don’t generate much public attention. They’re in the news, of course. People have been detained under these laws for years. But many simply don’t pay attention. There’s also this feeling that, “It definitely won’t happen to me. I’m not doing anything like that.” And then one day they could come knocking with a search warrant.
There are several factors at play. First, people are unaware of the law. Second, there’s a sense that things aren’t really that bad, that liberal media outlets are exaggerating it all and stoking panic. It’s like living under a dome: this hasn’t affected me so far, so it won’t affect me in the future, either.
We have a big chat for comedians with almost 3,000 people. Basically anyone who wants to perform can join, not just professional comedians. And after what happened to Artemy, there was a huge discussion there. But time passes, and everything quiets down again. I’ve been going to open mics lately, and I’m hearing jokes about Jesus, Hitler, terrorism, and 9/11 all over again. Almost nobody touches the “special military operation.” But the other subjects are coming back.
I’ve been going to open mics lately, and I’m hearing jokes about Jesus, Hitler, terrorism and 9/11 all over again
A novice comedian comes onstage and says, “I’m going to tell this joke now!” Sometimes it’s pure luck that nobody who matters happens to hear him. People regularly say some pretty controversial things from the stage. Sometimes the whole room even falls a little quiet and gets wary — okay, what’s he going to say next?
I joke a lot about the place where I was born and raised, the post-Soviet space, unrecognized territories, and all that. And I’ve noticed that people always get a little tense when those subjects come up. They’re waiting to see what I’ll say and what position I’ll take — whether I’m for or against. In other words, people want to establish my position first and only then follow me further into the subject.
And if I sense the audience isn’t ready, I usually steer things elsewhere. Because there’s also a sense that it isn’t safe. For example, people have started showing up at our shows whom we privately take to be employees of the “E Center.” They’re hilariously bad at disguising themselves. It’s like a cartoon where a bumbling supervillain’s sidekick is practically announcing, “Boss, I’ve hidden the bomb perfectly.” Someone shows up in plain clothes, but the jeans and the fanny pack… They just don’t fit the atmosphere. That obviously affects how you behave onstage.
I’ve had situations where I was finishing a joke and realized halfway through that it might not be safe.
When you’re writing material, you’re not sitting there with the Criminal Code in front of you. Then you go onstage, deliver the joke, and suddenly think: Okay, could that fall under some law? I’ve even said directly to the audience, “Come on, laugh a little louder, so that if anything happens, I won’t be the only one being taken to a pretrial detention center.”
If I’m performing with other comedians, I try to arrive at the very beginning of the show and listen to the host interact with the audience so I can get a sense of who’s in the room that night. For example, the host asks a man where he works, and he says he’d rather not say. We immediately suspect he works in the security services. And you subconsciously start going through your material in your head.
I know which of my jokes come close to the line. Some I cut; others I simply don’t dare tell. Sometimes I deliberately restructure my set. If I feel I’ve ventured into sensitive social territory and the audience reacts worse than usual, I quickly switch to safer subjects. I feel this constant juggling of topics because I’m a fairly anxious person and I keep a close eye on the news.
Professional comedians I know are already consulting lawyers: they send them their material and revise their jokes with the legal risks in mind. But a beginner who has simply come along to try stand-up may have no idea that he’s running afoul of some law. Especially since some of the wording is extremely vague — “insulting the feelings of believers,” and so on. At this point, you don’t even know what might be considered offensive, or to whom.
There’s a comedian who is writing material about marriage. Even he consults lawyers. There’s now this whole discourse around traditional values, family, and “traditional foundations.” He’s simply joking about not understanding the institution of marriage. We talk about love, about the higher feelings between two people, and then those two people go on Gosuslugi and click a button. It’s a completely everyday joke. But even here, he thinks: "Is this really safe?" Because you just don’t know anymore what might become a problem, or when.
Women tend to talk more about the battle of the sexes, sexism, and relationships. And sometimes that gives them a relatively safe way to talk about the war in general. For example, a woman comes onstage and says, “There seem to be fewer men around. I’m on dating apps, and it’s getting harder to meet anyone.”
Technically, she hasn’t said anything political at all. But everyone understands why there might be fewer men. It’s a form of Aesopian language. The comedian may not have intended any political message, but the audience reads one into it.
Feminist themes are complicated, too. At the same time, there’s now a major women’s stand-up scene, or fem-stand-up. There are women-only open mics. At one point, it even felt as though women’s stand-up had become stronger than men’s. It was as if the girls had really embraced that girl power.
Even if someone in the audience shouts something at a woman, she’s still in a stronger position. She’s onstage. She has the spotlights on her. She’s holding the device that amplifies her voice — a microphone. If some heckler shouts something, she can easily outplay him.
As for comedians who have left, I don’t think there’s any widespread resentment toward them within the Russian stand-up scene. Almost everyone has a friend who lives abroad. Everyone understands how hard it is to live in a foreign country — without your native language, your friends, your home, the culture you’re used to, and even the basic things of everyday life.
You can go to a place where there is freedom of speech and self-expression, but when that means abandoning everything you’ve built here — your work, your connections, your audience, your home — many people choose to stay.
When one side of the scales holds freedom of speech and the other means abandoning everything you’ve built, many people choose to stay
I currently live and work in Moscow. And for me, choosing between leaving behind everything I’ve built here and having the freedom to say everything that’s been weighing on me isn’t so simple. Just two years ago, I swore I would never set foot in another country. Now I realize that if things become too uncomfortable for me, I’ll leave. Of course, it’s frightening to think that I’d have to start my career almost from scratch. I’ve built relationships with organizers here, earned their trust, and developed my own audience.
I started thinking about emigration this year primarily because of something very personal: I started thinking about having a family and children. And at some point, I asked myself: "do I want my children to grow up in this country?" The answer was no longer clear-cut.
I’d say I still choose Russia about 90% of the time. But that 10% of doubt is there. It has to do, among other things, with my political views and with how I feel about what’s happening around me. The war has also started to feel physically closer. There are more reports of drone attacks and of things happening in Moscow and other regions. Every day you read the news: something is happening in Kursk, Belgorod, the Urals, the North.
You come across economic forecasts and new laws, and you inevitably start wondering how much longer this can go on. You ask yourself: "am I ready to get used to this new normal?" And, more importantly, "am I ready for my children to grow up accustomed to it?"
When my friends and I talk about politics, we generally understand each other. We’re mostly centrists; we don’t like radicalism, and we’re against the war. At the same time, we understand that there’s a vast political system in which different people make money and make decisions.
I watch Varlamov, Katz, various news sources, Sobchak, and others, and somehow piece together a reality I can live in. Then I visit my parents in another country and see that they watch all kinds of different channels: Russian, Ukrainian, and local.
I start watching all of it with them. You turn on Russian television, and some of the things I see there are physically hard for me to watch. Then you switch to Ukrainian news, sometimes in Ukrainian, and see what they’re saying there. Then you watch international news.
After trips like that, I usually return to Russia feeling more liberal, because I’ve had a chance to look at it from the outside, even if only a little. My parents lived through an armed conflict themselves in the 1990s. My father took part in it. They understand very well that war is horrible. But they also understand something else: these kinds of decisions aren’t made by ordinary people. Not by the public. They’re made by people at the top who have the power to make them. And everyone else is then left to find a way to live with the consequences.
“It’s making everyone a little paranoid.” Stand-up comedian Pavel V.
There’s a children’s show on STS Kids, one of the few TV programs featuring stand-up. The kids perform themselves, and everything is geared toward a young audience. Some of the participants are already 14 or 15, and those limits are starting to feel restrictive. They want to joke about teenage subjects, about things that are actually bothering them. But they perform alongside nine-year-olds for whom those topics are still taboo. And because it all airs on a children’s channel, there are pretty strict limits on what they can talk about.
At the same time, teenagers are quite happy to make political jokes among themselves. While they’re still young, they can get away with a lot because nobody takes them seriously. But once they turn 18 and start saying the same things into a microphone, the consequences can be very different.
Some of them understand this, while others aren’t thinking about it at all yet. They’re kids; they don’t think that far ahead: "Will I still be doing this in the future? Where will I be five years from now?" I started performing at around their age, when I was about 14. And if you compare what it was like then with what’s happening now, a huge amount has changed.
Even in early 2022, you could still say certain things onstage. People just made sure nothing was recorded and that no video got out. Now that thought barely even occurs to anyone. Self-censorship has changed dramatically. And it’s not just the comedians — the audience has changed too. If you suddenly start saying something like that out loud, it makes everyone a little paranoid. It’s as if one thought immediately hangs in the air: “This isn’t being recorded, is it?”
I remember that feeling well, when someone would still try to slip in a little joke or hint. People in the audience would literally sit up straight. Not necessarily because they disagreed, but because they were struck by the fact that someone had just said it out loud from the stage at a public event. It was as if everyone immediately thought: “If anything happens, I wasn’t laughing.” It’s not outright terror, more a constant sense of tension. There’s already too much of that around us as it is.
A lot of comedians have also reconsidered why they go onstage in the first place. Sometimes a beginner wants to make a statement, to say something important. But an experienced comedian understands that your primary job is to entertain people, make them laugh, and give them a good time. And some subjects are now such that people are more likely to tense up than to laugh.
Some topics have become off-limits not because anyone has officially handed you a list, but because people are intimidated. The atmosphere has changed. And I don’t sense much of a demand for political humor anymore. It seems to me that a large share of those who had a strong appetite for it have left. What remains are mostly people to whom it wasn’t that important to begin with. And, frankly, people are simply scared now. Sometimes you want to add a comparison to an everyday joke, then realize that it vaguely touches on politics — and that’s it. Better not.
Some topics have simply become off-limits, not because anyone has officially handed you a list, but because people are intimidated
Overall, there’s been more everyday comedy: observations about relationships, family, and things everyone can relate to. It’s safe. But you still don’t feel free. Probably because there are simply too many things you can’t talk about.
Of course I’ve thought about emigrating. In fact, I did leave. When the mobilization was announced, I was one of those Russians who left. And I got a taste of what it was like to have freedom in my material. At some point, the mere possibility of discussing something openly with people really hits you. You think, “Wow, so you can actually just say this out loud.” My situation is also somewhat complicated because, in a way, I’m avoiding military service. So even unnecessary interactions at the border are frightening.
Here, by contrast, there are things you simply don’t discuss publicly. In that sense, I really like what’s happening in Poland, for example. And it makes me sad that even just traveling there is quite difficult for me now. In general, it’s become harder for Russians to travel anywhere. But I find the Polish comedy scene fascinating because several languages are mixed together at once.
I lived in Armenia and spent time in Georgia and Uzbekistan. The industry is smaller in Uzbekistan. In Armenia, a stand-up club can operate in two languages, and both Armenians and Russians attend shows in either language. Everyone makes an effort to understand one another. Poland is even more interesting: there are Poles, Ukrainians, Belarusians, and Russians. A single stand-up club can host shows in three languages. That’s really cool.
In Russia, there are some pretty strange things happening around the English language these days. I performed at an English-language open mic in Moscow. The organizers are foreigners — British and American. And they were trying to figure out how to label an English-language open mic in Russian so that people searching for an event in English would still understand what they were going to. A foreigner living in Moscow who wants to attend an English-language event first has to see the event listing in Russian. It’s pretty strange.
In general, there’s this sense of a kind of legalized lawlessness in the air. There are brief moments when you think, “Oh, maybe things are going to get a little freer?” During the whole Yabloko episode, for example, there were literally a couple of weeks when it felt like, “Wait, what? Are we a liberal society again?”
One comedian had a joke about presidential experience. The idea was that if you’re an ordinary professional and you’ve gained a lot of experience at one job, you can take that experience to another job. It’s considered an advantage. But if you’ve been president of Russia for many years, you can’t take that presidential experience and get a job as president somewhere else. There’s no criticism in the joke. Nothing at all. It’s simply a name used for comparison. But the comedian says “Putin,” and the audience immediately goes, “Mmm.” Like Voldemort: a name that’s better left unspoken.
“Putin” is like Voldemort: a name that’s better left unspoken
The story of Artemy Ostanin has had a profound impact on everyone, of course. It’s horrifying, but also revealing. And what I find important is that people are waiting for Ostanin. That’s probably the best thing about the whole situation. He wasn’t some superstar comedian with a huge audience. By the standards of the broader comedy world, he was practically a nobody. And yet people haven’t forgotten him. So much has happened since then that any other news story could easily have been pushed out of people’s minds by the next one. But this story is still there.
Of course, there are stupid comedians, idiotic comedians, and fucking assholes who think it’s his own fault: “He shouldn’t have touched those subjects in the first place.” No. It’s not his fault. What the fuck? They simply took what he said, interpreted it in a certain way, and that was it. It doesn’t even matter that much whether the joke itself was good. You can listen to it a hundred times and say, “Well, it’s not the funniest joke in the world.” But destroying people over their words is horrifying.
And this case also made something else very clear: if you still want to talk about things like that, you now have to do it much more subtly. In terms of censorship, we’ve come very close to the Soviet satirists. If you want to say something, you have to speak in Aesopian language. You can’t simply state the point outright.
If you have a joke like that, people have to get it from the hint. You can only hint at it. If you want to talk about something, you have to really contort yourself. You can’t just say something about Putin or the authorities directly anymore. It has to be all half-hints.
As for pro-government, or what you might call "Z-humor," it certainly exists. There are venues where this kind of comedy is performed. Some projects even feature military personnel doing stand-up. There are comedians who joke about people who have left, about other countries, and so on. But I don’t think it’s becoming a genuinely popular genre. I simply try not to perform at those kinds of venues, so I don’t encounter much of it in my circle. And I don’t think audiences are particularly interested in it, either.
People are already tired of all this. Politics is more likely to trigger people than make them laugh. They go to stand-up to switch off. I can easily imagine someone living on the outskirts of Moscow. At night, he hears several drones being shot down. In the morning, he goes to work. He works all day. In the evening, he decides to go to a stand-up show in the city center, just to take his mind off things for a while. And then you start talking to him from the stage about drones. He still has to go home afterward — back to the place where those drones are. Why the hell would he want that?
It also seems to me that demand for stand-up itself has declined somewhat. Maybe people simply have less money. A ticket costing 1,000 or 2,000 rubles is already a significant expense for some. It’s entertainment, after all, and the price of everything has gone up. Even television stand-up projects, from what I can see, have started buying less material. Maybe that’s because viewership has fallen. And if demand is down, why buy something people aren’t watching?
Still, I want to believe this isn’t forever. I just want to be fucking blown away one day when I suddenly discover: “Wait, we can do this now?” Because I know exactly what that feeling will be like. I already experienced that high when I was living in Yerevan. You suddenly realize you can actually just talk about this subject — not in a whisper, not in hints, not checking whether someone is filming you on their phone. You can just say it. And I really want to feel that way here one day.

Volkswagen to cut 100,000 jobs in biggest ever industry shake-up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:03:07 UTC
15:03:07 KST

German car giant Volkswagen said that management and unions had agreed to cut a further 50,000 jobs by the end of the decade, bringing total job losses to 100,000.
Volkswagen is about to shed one in seven of its workers.
The German car giant said on Thursday that management and unions had agreed to cut a further 50,000 jobs by the end of the decade, on top of 50,000 already planned, bringing total losses to 100,000.
"It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities," the 10-brand group said in a statement.
The firm had approved a plan involving "the reduction of around 50,000 jobs" on top of another 50,000 already agreed, it added.
Hit by US tariffs, patchy demand for electric cars and, above all, fierce competition in and from China, Europe's largest carmaker is in trouble.
The group, which apart from its namesake brand also includes Audi and Porsche, had already agreed to cut about 50,000 jobs worldwide.
The total 100,000 cuts will be the largest restructuring ever carried out in the global automotive industry, amounting to about 15% of the carmaker's staff worldwide.
The cuts eclipse the auto industry's previous record-holders. General Motors cut 74,000 jobs and closed 21 plants in 1991 as it lost ground to Japanese rivals, and cut a further 47,000 jobs globally in 2009 during its financial crisis restructuring.
Ford cut 35,000 jobs and closed five plants in 2002, then targeted tens of thousands more under its "Way Forward" plan later that decade. Volkswagen's 100,000 is now the largest total on record.
Volkswagen further said that management and unions agreed the future of four German plants — in Hannover, Emden, Zwickau and Neckarsulm — could not be assured into the 2030s.
Their closure would mark the first time Volkswagen has shuttered full-scale factories in its home country.
The adoption of the plans by Volkswagen's supervisory board, made up of both labour and shareholder representatives, marks progress in delicate negotiations between the two sides.
"The supervisory board has unanimously approved the executive board's future plan presented today," CEO Oliver Blume said. "This is a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group."
Alongside its namesake marque, the group's stable spans Škoda, SEAT and Cupra at the mass-market end, Audi, Bentley, Lamborghini and Ducati at the premium and luxury end, and Porsche as a standalone sports brand.
