Video: Heavy rain overwhelms Pärnu sewer system, causes street flooding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:03:00 UTC
15:03:00 KST

Video: Emergency situation declared in Pärnu after heavy rain floods streets
A crisis situation has been declared in Pärnu after record rainfall — described as the rain of the century — caused widespread flooding, overwhelmed sewers and forced school closures.
The Pärnu city government wrote around 8:30 a.m. that the very large amount of rain that has fallen in the last few hours has placed a heavy burden on the sewage system and that the system is operating at full capacity.
"Unfortunately, both stormwater drainage and sewerage services have been disrupted, and in many places roads are difficult to pass due to water accumulation," the city noted.
The city government is asking motorists to be careful and avoid flooded roads. The city and service providers are working to resolve the situation.
"The situation is really difficult," the city's post reads.
The Weather Service reported that on Friday morning, more than 80 mm of rain had been measured in Pärnu and its surrounding areas in some places.
Meteorologist Kairo Kiitsak reported that as of 9:20 a.m., an exceptionally large amount of rain had fallen in Pärnu and its surrounding areas. Rainfall totals exceeded 100 mm, and in some places passed the 120 mm mark.
Heavy rainfall will continue during the day, especially in southwestern, central and eastern Estonia.
Rääma school sent the children home
Pärnu Rääma School announced on Friday morning that there will be no classes at the school due to heavy rain.
"The sewage system and toilets are not working and the lowest floor is covered in water," said Elmo Joa, principal of the Rääma school, adding that the children are being sent home.
Joa told ERR that they are currently waiting for a pump to remove the water from the basement floor.
"We're all doing well now. The children were coming to school. A lot of the younger ones who came with their parents were able to go back at the door because rubber boots would be suitable as a change of shoes. So they went back home nicely. They were very sad because it was raining outside and it wasn't raining inside. It was exciting here," said Joa.
Deputy mayor: We are declaring an emergency
Pärnu Deputy Mayor Sander Kilk said in a comment to ERR that after the crisis committee met, the city decided to declare a state of emergency.
"Since this water probably won't go away for several hours, there could be damage to property. Another thing we have a problem with are the sewer hatches that have come loose. The sewers can't handle this water, so they are dangerous if people drive cars, bicycles, or walk there," said Kilk.
According to Kilk, this is the first time that such a large flood caused by rainwater has occurred in Pärnu. It also became clear that the city was not prepared for such a crisis situation.
"Right now, the first goal is to resolve today's situation calmly and then we'll look ahead. It turned out that no previous city government has compiled a crisis manual, so to speak. We will definitely do that, and not just in the event of a small crisis, but also in all other possible cases. However, a staff has been put together, including department heads who are currently dealing with it, and we ourselves," said Kilk.
According to the deputy mayor, we currently have to wait for the rainfall to decrease or stop. Then we can start pumping water out of people's basements. In addition, the Pärnu Rescue Association is helping.
The Rescue Board has activated the regional headquarters and is implementing the flood emergency plan activities, supporting the local government. To the Board's knowledge, no lives are in danger.
Water entered the barrier at Pärnu Hospital
Tõnno Sikk, field manager of the Western Rescue Center, said on Vikerraadio's "Uudis+" program that it has been a very busy time for rescue resources.
"We have visited various sites, and there have been reports from private individuals where water has penetrated the basement. We have had to prioritize the events and have provided assistance to both Pärnu Hospital and some elementary schools. We are currently mapping the situation to identify the sites that need our help most urgently," said Sikk.
Water entered one of the locks at Pärnu Hospital, but the situation was brought under control in cooperation with the hospital.
"We also visited Rääma Primary School, where water threatened to flood the server room. We installed barriers there, and volunteer resources also helped ensure that the school did not have to close its doors for an extended period of time," said Sikk.
Professor: This could be called the rain of the century
According to Ottar Tamm, a junior professor at the Estonian University of Life Sciences, measurements have shown that intense rainfall is occurring more and more frequently and there is no reason to believe that this will be different in the future.
"In one hour, 33 millimeters of rain fell in Pärnu, which statistically occurs about once every seven years. In two hours, a total of 56 millimeters fell, which happens once every 22 years, and in six hours, once every 77 years. These are absolute values, but there is a lot of margin, so it can be completely freely called the rain of the century," said Tamm.
While citizens often demand that after every major flood, the municipality should build thicker sewer pipes and dig wider drainage ditches, hydrological scientists do not consider this a good solution.
"We need to do something on the ground to retain this rainwater. This involves nature-based rainwater solutions, where we delay the water. In the case of Pärnu, we are primarily talking about delay, not impregnation - we consciously keep the water in the places where we want it. If we don't keep it there, the water chooses its own flow path and inevitably the lowest place is often the basement," explained Tamm.
According to the researcher, Tallinn has worked hard and addressed the problem, compiling stormwater models and assessing where water collects and where problems arise. Tartu and elsewhere in Estonia have not seen any progress on Tamm.
"Today is a very good example of how we will not get anywhere by continuing as we have been, because there will be more and more such situations in the future. We must be prepared for this, or else society will have to accept that we will start to drown more - this is also actually a solution, but it just needs to be acknowledged," said Tamm.
Several tunnels closed in the Pärnu region
Due to heavy rainfall, the section of Audru Road under the Audru viaduct at km 0.5 is currently closed in Pärnu, as are the pedestrian tunnels under Ehitajate Road in the city of Pärnu, which have remained underwater.
The road maintenance officer and the pump station maintenance officer are inspecting the condition of the tunnels. The necessary traffic signs have been placed on site and the pump station technician is checking the condition of the pumps.
All the tunnel pumps have been operating at full capacity since early Friday morning, but the amount of rainwater has been exceptionally high, and therefore it will take time to pump out the water from the tunnels and dry them.
The rain has started to subside and the situation is expected to return to normal by the evening. The tunnels will remain closed until it is safe to use them again.
In addition to Pärnu, flooding may also occur in other regions. According to the Environment Agency, rainfall will continue in Pärnu County and move across to Virumaa in Järva County.
Editor's note: This piece was updated to include the declaration of an emergency situation in Pärnu, activation of the Rescue Board's regional headquarters, water entering Pärnu Hospital, the "rain of the century" assessment, and the closure of tunnels due to flooding.

Fancy cars and hanging with mum, the paradox of Aussie's EPL teen dream

Fancy cars and hanging with mum, the paradox of Lucas Herrington's EPL teen dream
Lucas Herrington has gone to number one with a bullet in 2026, at a speed so dizzying it would leave many teenagers' heads spinning.
Turning 19 this weekend, he is fresh off a breakthrough World Cup, has a multi-million-dollar contract in the best football league in the world, and has fans fawning over him.
But true to his persona on the pitch, the central defender is calm, level-headed and capable of tackling any challenge.
"My parents have always instilled that factor of humility in my life and having that humbleness to stay grounded and just to keep working hard," he told Australian media on a call from Hull.
"I'm always trying to get better. So I think it's always having that positive mindset that I've still got a lot of things to work on. And I'm not the finished product."
Herrington made his bolt-from-the-blue Socceroos debut in March, which turned into a maiden World Cup appearance a few months later.
His impressive efforts in North America captured interest from some of the biggest clubs in the world including Barcelona and Liverpool.
But he settled on Hull City, newly promoted in the English Premier League, and a five-year deal for a transfer fee reportedly worth $33 million with add-ons, to become the most expensive Australian player ever.
Alessandro Circati recently joined that rich list with his transfer from Parma to Benfica.
The money is astronomical for an Australian footballer, and despite his down-to-earth nature, even Herrington was lured in by the EPL stereotype of fancy, fast cars.
"It's a nice car park. I do have a car right now; it's nice. I'm enjoying it," he laughed, almost sheepishly.
But when he speaks about his off-field highlights in his few weeks in England, the teenager goes back to keeping it real.
"Mum's here at the moment. She leaves soon, so I've just been exploring around with her," he said.
"So that's been really nice, some great quality time with her."
Advice from a legend
Herrington made his debut for the Tigers off the bench in their upset win over Manchester United.
"It was only a week and a couple of days from when I landed to that game against Man United," he said.
"Great moment for the city and for me personally, with my mum and my agent in the stands, it was a super proud moment for me.
"And it was a great match, very grateful for the opportunity to be there."
He was again used as a substitute in a win over Coventry, while he started the EFL Cup penalty shootout win against Stoke.
A strong show of confidence for the youngster, who is the only Australian in England's top flight.
"It's probably the best league in the world. So to be here at 18 is super special," he said.
"I've always wanted to play in the Premier League, so I'm very grateful for the opportunity from the coaching staff and the club to do so. And I've loved my first three or so weeks here.
"It's a league with the best players in the world, so to be up against them every week is really special and a great challenge for me as a young defender.
"It's just about trying to learn as much as possible from the older boys in the team and just try and take every game as a lesson."
And don't mistake his modesty for meekness; he knows he belongs.
A message reinforced by former Sweden international Zlatan Ibrahimović, who publicly supported Herrington after missing a penalty in the Socceroos' World Cup round of 32 shootout loss to Egypt.
“This is just the beginning of your career," Ibrahimović said on Fox Sports USA's post-game analysis.
"You stepping up there, you show a lot of courage. Not everybody would do that. My friend, you're the best. Don't listen to the rest. Listen, Herrington, if you want to reach out, I'm here."
Ibrahimović made good on his promise and ended up calling the Queensland product himself.
"He just said, really don't fear anyone. I'm here for a reason, so just go enjoy," Herrington said.
Dreams do come true
Herrington's meteoric rise means he has not yet played for Australia in his home state.
Something the former Roar product hopes to do in the Socceroos' friendlies against Brazil later this month, in Townsville and Brisbane.
"It'd be a dream come true to play for the Socceroos in Brisbane," he said.
"Something that I've always wanted to do, and to play in front of hopefully a packed-out Suncorp would be a dream, and in front of my family and friends would be awesome."
And he is happy to be a role model for others.
"Just trying to be an inspiration for all the young Australians that there is really a pathway to the Premier League," he said.
"I think a lot of young footballers in Australia like me wake up at all hours in the morning to watch the Premier League.
"So hopefully I can make them proud, make Australia proud.
"Just to keep working hard, enjoy the process, and to have big dreams because dreams do come true."

UK has not done enough to prepare for shocks to food supplies, says watchdog
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:00:02 UTC
15:00:02 KST

The climate crisis, disease and cyber-attacks pose growing risks to the UK’s food supplies and the government needs to act to make the system more resilient, according to the public spending watchdog.
The National Audit Office (NAO) is urging the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) to work more closely with households, communities and businesses to ensure the flow of crucial food into the country can withstand supply shocks that are becoming increasingly common and severe.
Its latest report found Defra – the department responsible for security of food supply – had taken some steps to better prepare for future shocks, but said it had not done enough in recent years to get citizens and industry to plan for possible emergencies.
Britain relies on overseas imports for more than a third of its food, most of it entering through four ports – Dover, Felixstowe, Southampton and London Gateway – making supplies particularly vulnerable to potential disruption.
The NAO’s report comes after months of warnings about the resilience of the UK’s food supply chain from experts who have told households to build up a stockpile of long-life items they could rely on in an emergency. Britons are less prepared for potential future catastrophic events than citizens of several other European countries, according to government research.
The supply chain has already come under pressure during the Covid-19 pandemic and after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, although businesses including the nation’s largest supermarkets managed to keep goods flowing, in most cases without the need for significant government assistance.
However, Defra is less confident about the private sector’s ability to withstand future shocks, such as extreme weather events, without greater government intervention.
Food industry businesses praised Defra’s engagement with them during the pandemic, but told the NAO it had communicated with them less frequently since. The report said the companies had limited input into the government’s plans for reacting to supply disruption, which could mean officials created proposals that would not work in practice.
Gareth Davies, the NAO’s head, said: “Recent disruptions have shown the resilience of the UK’s food supply chain, but risks are increasing in likelihood and severity.
“Defra should learn from approaches taken in other countries, and strengthen preparedness for emergencies by testing plans with local government and industry.”
The government has designated food as one of 13 critical national infrastructure sectors it considers essential for the proper functioning of the country.
However, food industry representatives have said that does not go far enough and have called on ministers to add the UK’s cold stores and food transport hubs to the critical list, which would ensure their power supplies would be maintained in the event of widespread outages.
The NAO report comes just a few months after the trade body for cold storage and logistics, the Cold Chain Federation, accused the government of “complacency” over national food storage and urged ministers to make potential disruption to the UK’s food system an “immediate national priority”.
The last national exercise testing Defra’s preparedness for catastrophic events that would severely disrupt the availability of food took place in 2023, but did not include most supply chain businesses, the NAO found.
In addition, local resilience forums indicated they lacked clarity from Defra on what would be expected from them in the event of disruption.

Save the Children aid for 1.5 million in need wiped out by Iran war oil shock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:00:02 UTC
15:00:02 KST

The charity Save the Children has said the oil price shock unleashed by Donald Trump’s war on Iran is forcing it to “spend more to reach fewer children”.
The NGO analysed the increased costs of transport, fuel, food and medical supplies as a result of the Middle East conflict.
It calculated that the extra burden of delivering aid had already been $13m (£10m), which could instead have allowed it to reach an additional 1.5 million children.
Willem Zuidema, Save the Children’s global supply chain director, said: “The conflict in the Middle East is not only putting children at risk in the region but also globally, because every spike in fuel prices drives up the cost of every truck, every shipment, every box of supplies we deliver around the world. We are being forced to spend more to reach fewer children.”
Developing countries have tended to be hit hardest by the oil shock, which the International Energy Agency has called the largest disruption to supplies in history. Many governments have introduced restrictions on energy use.
Save the Children operates in about 110 countries, with a particular focus on safeguarding children’s rights. Its health and nutrition programmes reached more than 30 million children last year, including in hard-to-reach countries such as Afghanistan.
The charity said the additional costs of delivering aid were equivalent to 47 health clinics in Afghanistan operating for six months, or five 30-bed hospitals in Somalia operating for a year.
Before the conflict, the oil price was expected to be about $60 a barrel during 2026. After the US administration went to war with Iran, prompting Tehran to choke supplies though the strait of Hormuz, it surged above $100 a barrel.
Prices declined after the US-Iran ceasefire in the summer but have jumped back above $90 in recent days as hostilities have resumed. Recent US rhetoric about increasing economic sanctions on Iran has raised fears the conflict could continue indefinitely.
With the strait of Hormuz also an important conduit for fertiliser, the crisis has increased the prices of other commodities including food.
Zuidema said Save the Children had been working to source alternative supplies and transport routes in an attempt to keep costs under control.
“Despite the extreme challenges and rising costs, our teams are working around the clock to find alternative and cost-effective ways to deliver essential supplies and ensure we reach children where it is needed the most,” he said.
The higher price of providing aid is coinciding with declining global aid budgets. The Trump administration has gutted USAID, the country’s development agency, and the UK is among the other countries reducing spending.
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, which gathers authoritative data, found that global aid spending plunged by 23% in real terms last year.
Save the Children has previously criticised the UK government’s deep cuts to the overseas aid budget, with Moazzam Malik, its director, calling them a “tragedy”.
Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, who oversees aid spending, has been urged by charities and some Labour backbenchers to set out a path to fulfilling Gordon Brown’s promise to spend 0.7% of national income on aid.
Save the Children was set up in 1919 by two sisters, Eglantyne Jebb and Dorothy Buxton, who were horrified by the impact of a post-first world war export blockade on children in Berlin and Vienna.

‘It feels like Italy with the volume turned down’: readers’ favourite (smaller) city breaks in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:00:02 UTC
15:00:02 KST

Renaissance art without the crowds in Italy
Ferrara in Emilia-Romagna won me over precisely because it feels like Italy with the volume turned down. I stayed in a small family-run hotel near Via delle Volte, where mornings began with quiet cobbled streets and the smell of fresh pastries. The Palazzo dei Diamanti was almost empty when I visited, giving me space to enjoy its Renaissance art without crowds. Evenings meant cycling past terracotta walls to tiny trattorias serving pumpkin cappellacci, a traditional pasta dish. It’s a city that lets you slow down, breathe and enjoy its beauty.
John
One of Germany’s greenest cities
Next to flashy Munich or cool Berlin, Hanover in northern Germany has a reputation of being boring. It is totally undeserved: there are world-class museums, such as the modern art gallery Sprengel, one of the best-preserved baroque gardens in Europe – the Great Garden at Herrenhausen – impressive Victorian era architecture, 640 hectares (1,680 acres) of city forest (the Eilenriede, nearly double the size of New York’s Central Park) and a large artificial lake just south of the centre that you can travel on with a bus ticket (or hire a boat). Explore the city and its surroundings on more than 600 miles of cycle paths, find independent shops in the well-heeled art nouveau district of List or the multicultural Linden, and relax in a deck chair on Ballhofplatz with tea and cake at the Teestübchen.
Ulrike
The Algarve’s city of crafts
Bursting with Portuguese charm, Loulé is 10 miles inland from Faro, capital of the Algarve. The small city has a rich history of preserving traditional crafts, supported by Loulé Criativo, a network of community-driven artisans that keeps alive and celebrates the identity of Loulé and the Algarve. It includes the House of Weaving (Casa da Empreita) and the Watchmakers (Oficina do Relojoeiro) and Stringed Instrument Workshop (Oficina de Cordofones). In these vibrant spaces – where visitors can interact with artisans – the city’s heritage is preserved and passed down through generations. 
Sue
Unesco sites in northern France
Arras, 35 minutes on the train from Lille, has two Unesco world heritage sites: the belfry of the Hotel de Ville and the Vauban Citadel. Exploring the Boves, a 10th-century network of tunnels which played roles in the first and second world wars, is an amazing experience. Above are two magnificent large squares in the Flemish style with a wide variety of alfresco cafes, restaurants and indie shops. Arras also holds one of the biggest Christmas markets north of Paris, noted for its amazing range of international gourmet foods.
Bryan Boese
Artistry and cake in Sweden’s beautiful south
Malmö is easily accessible (being connected by bridge to Copenhagen) and very walkable. We enjoyed the free Malmö Konsthall arts centre with contemporary exhibitions and also the skateboard artistry in the square outside. The Western Harbour contains architectural gems, such as the twisted skyscraper Turning Turso, restaurants and swimming piers in a former industrial area. The cafe Hollandia offered classic Swedish cakes and a lovely atmosphere. The Disgusting Food Museum next door was an interesting cultural experience showing food considered to be delicacies in some countries, not so much in others. A sign shows the number of people who have thrown up (visit Hollandia first)!
Elisabeth
Brilliant beach and seafood in Sardinia
If you can tear yourself away from Poetto – surely one of the prettiest city beaches in Europe – you’ll find a lot more to love in Cagliari, capital of Sardinia. The huge indoor produce market is a riot of glistening seafood, local pecorino and sweet, nutty Sardinian treats. The town centre strides uphill from the port, with the elegant bulwark of Bastione St Remy delineating the ancient Castello district and serving up epic rooftop and coastal views. We missed the renowned archaeological museum, but that just gives us the perfect excuse to go back. Cagliari’s affordable seafood was a definite highlight, and Trattoria Lillicu’s chargrilled bream and calamari is another tempting reason to hurry back. 
Martha
Stained glass wonder in north-west Spain
In León, colours grab your attention and take away words. León cathedral completely wrongfooted me. This city seems to be under the British tourist radar. I thought I’d already seen stained glass that was worthy of heaven – this was another level. Coupled with this was how visitors were reacting. Everyone was using the free audio guide. No one was just marching round and ticking off the sights. People were learning and savouring the experience. The humble ninth-century San Isidoro church, one of the most important romanesque buildings in Spain, is a refreshing contrast. 
Deborah
Norway’s art nouveau gem
Ålesund is one of Norway’s most beautiful stops on an already spectacular western coast, despite having been devastated by fire in 1904. We reached the small, rebuilt art nouveau city via the breathtaking winding roads of the Trollstigen (the “Troll’s Path”) and had our first sighting from the top of the panoramic Aksla mountain viewpoint. Exactly 418 steps lead down to the historic centre where museums, cafes, restaurants and shops cluster around the Brosundet Canal in renovated warehouses and ornate buildings. Kayaking, a rib boat ride or a trip to the stunning Geirangerfjord? We couldn’t choose so did them all!
Teresa Stansby
The French city with a bit of everything
I spent five days in Saint-Malo this August. It has everything: a beautiful walled city with lots of history, a variety of beaches offering shifts in light and character throughout the day, a modernist tidal pool with a high diving platform. The city has so much pride, and the art inspired by its famous landmarks make for great souvenirs. My favourite thing, though? The wonderful cider at La Passage (on Instagram) with my sister. And despite the heat everywhere else, the temperature never got above 25C.
Sophie Amos
Winning tip: a watery Dutch master of a city
Leiden starts badly. The walk from the station is grim. Scruffy bars and vape shops. And then, suddenly, this watery Dutch gem reveals itself. Canals shoot off from a boat-filled basin, each one lined with grand brick mansions tapering to elegant finials under the sort of blue lowland skies that typify every good (and bad) Flemish painting. Dig deeper into its narrow traffic-free courtyards and squares with cafes spilling out light and chatter, much as they did when Rembrandt trudged to the school that still stands here, just round the corner from his first tutor’s studio. He’d find it mostly unchanged if he walked back. At Christmas, an ice rink spreads across the main canal, and the smell of warm wine, cloves and crepes hovers over the market stalls.
Bill Jones

====================================================================================================

Revealed: how companies ‘secretly’ use billions of litres of public water in drought-hit England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Less than 1% of businesses in England use more water than the daily needs of 10 million people, as millions of households face hosepipe bans and three-quarters of the country is in drought.
Businesses across England use 2.6bn litres a day from the public water supply, which includes potable and non-potable water provided by water companies. In total, businesses account for about 30% of public supply use, with two-thirds of their consumption in water-stressed areas, according to Mosl, the organisation that operates England’s business water market.
Tracking industrial water use appears difficult. Regulators say they are frustrated by a lack of data and “commercial secrecy”, and the water sector says it is prevented from planning effectively for growth industries.
The biggest users of the public water supply include oil refineries, chemical plants and paper mills, and some face no requirement to cut their consumption.
Mosl’s map of business water supply points, ranked by volume used, showed the site of ExxonMobil’s Esso refinery at Fawley, Southampton, as the largest user of public water supply. However, the site includes a number of other operators that also use the water, including waste, gas, chemicals and energy companies.
Mosl cited the refinery’s water use in written evidence to a House of Lords committee as an example of “the high volume of water wastage in industry that is not disincentivised by government or the regulatory framework”.
Mosl did not name the refinery but described its location, which was also visible on its map of supply points.
ExxonMobil disputed Mosl’s figures, saying its water use was commercially confidential. Mosl said it planned to ask the committee to redact parts of its evidence. During reporting, Mosl also removed a report and its supply point map from its website.
The refinery said the “vast majority” of the water it used came from the Solent strait for cooling, while “industrial water” was used for processes that could not easily be reduced without shutting down operating units. Potable water accounted for less than 1% of total consumption, it said.
Apart from refineries, other major users of the public water supply include paper mills and companies in the chemicals and soft drinks industries. But the overall picture of business water use is incomplete. One in 10 businesses are not metered, meaning their use is not measured or reported. Of those that are metered, only 11% have smart meters.
Despite Mosl collecting data on water taken from the public supply, it is not free to share all of it, even with government departments, according to Mosl’s chief executive, Sarah McMath.
McMath told the House of Lords committee that when the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) or the Environment Agency requested data, Mosl had to negotiate a bespoke agreement to share it.
Mosl was working with the water regulator, Ofwat, to change this, she said, so that data would be shared when it would benefit “the environment or society”.
A lack of data is already affecting national water planning. Gaps in local authority growth plans, combined with what the Environment Agency and Ofwat describe as “commercial secrecy, especially in the energy sector”, mean plans are often based on assumptions.
The Environment Agency and Ofwat are calling for mandatory reporting of current and projected water use across all sectors to improve water security.
A spokesperson for Mosl said: “Our data highlights both the opportunities and regulatory barriers to incentivising businesses to use less water. Rather than focusing on individual users – many of whom are actively seeking to reduce their water demand – we should focus on creating the right conditions to invest in water efficiency and increase water reuse where it is safe and practical.”
Water resources planning assumes business water consumption will fall by 9% by 2038 and 15% by 2050.
But the trade body Water UK argues the assumption is unrealistic as demand grows from new homes, as datacentres, hydrogen production and other developments. It wants water companies to be able to plan for projected demand rather than government reduction targets.
Companies are not required to report all their water use, and for some, the more water they use, the cheaper each unit becomes.
One operator told Mosl that a single UK datacentre uses 219m litres a year. It also has a tankered-water supply on standby if its mains connection fails, as well as its own borehole as a backup.
Businesses can also take water directly from rivers, lakes, aquifers and the sea via abstraction . This is regulated separately by the Environment Agency.
Some abstraction is invisible. Anyone can take up to 20,000 litres a day from a stream, borehole or spring without a licence or reporting it. The gap covers an estimated 850,000 people and organisations across England, mostly on farms and in rural areas.
Richard Benwell, the chief executive of the NGO coalition Wildlife and Countryside Link, said: “It’s surely an injustice that petrochemical and fossil fuel companies most responsible for the climate crisis are also draining … water supplies and drawing more water from our parched environment.
The water campaigner Feargal Sharkey said: “Yet again, regulatory ineptitude is allowed to triumph over the needs of people and the environment. While water supplies run dry, corporate bank accounts are flooded with the proceeds of corporate greed.”
Defra said the government was taking “decisive action to secure water supplies”, including planning to build nine reservoirs and investing in infrastructure.
A Water UK spokesperson said: “Supplies are increasingly at risk because England’s official forecasts for how much water the country needs rely on flawed assumptions. The water needed by fast-growing datacentres is explicitly excluded from the forecasts.
“At the same time, lower water bills have been prioritised over building a resilient system, meaning in some places water companies only have 2% of water spare to deal with increased demand.”
The Environment Agency said abstraction licences had strict conditions and were reviewed regularly, and that it was working towards the 9% reduction in business water use from the public supply.
Meanwhile, England’s water companies are losing about 2.2bn litres of water a day through leaking pipes.

Anti-national forces harming India's unity will face consequences: Adityanath
NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Friday warned that anti-national and anti-social forces seeking to spread hatred or undermine India's unity would face consequences, invoking Lord Krishna's message on the occasion of Janmashtami.Addressing a gathering in Mathura, the birthplace of Lord Krishna, on the second day of his visit, Adityanath emphasised that His teachings and message remained equally relevant today.
"Wherever the forces of goodness exist, they will be protected under all circumstances. But wherever anti-national and anti-social forces raise their heads, create hatred in society or attempt to harm India's unity, integrity and faith, Lord Krishna had already said 5,000 years ago what their fate would be," PTI quoted the chief minister as saying.Yogi Adityanath also cited the Bhagavad Gita's teaching, "Paritranaya sadhunam, vinashaya cha dushkritam" (for the protection of the righteous and destruction of evil), stressing that it continued to guide society.The chief minister highlighted the Braj region's role in preserving its religious heritage and the memories of Lord Krishna despite repeated invasions and attempts by various groups to impose their faith on India.
"Many invasions took place and many people tried to impose their faith on India, but no one could erase the Sanatan faith," Yogi Adityanath said."Those who dared to erase Sanatan faith themselves disappeared into the dust, but the memories of Shri Krishna and Radha Rani, not only in Braj but across India, continue to inspire us today and provide an encouraging environment for future generations," he added.The chief minister welcomed devotees arriving in Mathura for Janmashtami and extended his greetings to the people of Uttar Pradesh on the festival marking the birth of Lord Krishna.Yogi Adityanath has been in Mathura since Thursday for Janmashtami celebrations and has been attending programmes ahead of the festival.

Interview: Customer-oriented approach vital in AI-driven economy, says Sberbank CFO
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:58:59 CST
14:58:59 KST

by Xinhua writers Vladislava Chugueva, Zhang Chaoqun
MOSCOW, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Only companies that prioritize their customers' interests will survive and thrive amid the fundamental changes artificial intelligence (AI) has brought to the global economy, Sberbank Deputy Chairman and CFO Taras Skvortsov has said.
Over one billion people worldwide still lack access to formal bank accounts, and AI can effectively lower banks' service thresholds to reach these underserved groups, Skvortsov told Xinhua ahead of the ongoing Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.
As Russia's largest bank, Sberbank plays a leading role in the country's AI research and application, translating its advances in AI into more accessible everyday services for customers, he said.
In Russia, social tax deductions for education, fitness and medical expenses have long been underused because of cumbersome procedures. Sberbank has simplified the process with one-click processing, allowing customers to have the bank apply for deductions on their behalf.
"Within the framework of our human-centric strategy, we asked ourselves whether we could streamline the entire process for users, allowing them to simply tick a box to authorize Sberbank to apply for tax deductions on their behalf," Skvortsov said, noting that the bank expects the service to attract 60 million to 70 million users annually.
The bank itself is also among the biggest beneficiaries of AI, he noted, saying that the technology is transforming the traditional financial cycle of data collection, reporting, analysis and decision-making by generating analysis and actionable solutions as soon as data is acquired.
Sberbank has stepped up AI investment, Skvortsov said, spending about 100 billion rubles (1.15 billion U.S. dollars) on AI research and development in 2024 and planning to invest 350 billion rubles by 2026, with a focus on its GigaChat model and applications in personalized financial services, credit risk assessment and operational cost reduction.
Earlier this year, Sberbank unveiled Russia's first optical computing processor for AI applications, designed to speed up AI model training and deployment while improving energy efficiency, helping address rising power demands from AI data centers, he added.
In an era of global economic uncertainty, institutional resilience hinges on adaptability and a human-centric philosophy, Skvortsov said. "We believe that in a decade, only enterprises embracing this people-oriented mindset will survive and thrive."
"Companies that fail to prioritize user interests will gradually lose competitiveness and fade from the market," he said. ■

2026-09-04

14:58:44 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Japan's household spending dropped 3.6 percent in inflation-adjusted real terms in July from a year earlier, the eighth straight monthly decline, government data showed Friday.
The reading marked the steepest fall since a 6.3 percent slide in January 2024, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications said.
Households of two or more people spent an average of 301,245 yen (around 1,926 U.S. dollars) in the reporting month.
By category, food and beverage spending declined 1.3 percent as inflation weighed on purchases, while cooler weather than the previous year also curbed beverage demand.
Consumers gravitated toward cheaper prepared food, a shift a ministry official described as a "trend towards tighter spending."
Outlays for energy and water bills tumbled 9.2 percent, a drop an official attributed largely to reduced air-conditioning use amid lower temperatures than the same month last year.
The household spending data serves as a key indicator of private consumption, which accounts for more than half of Japan's gross domestic product.
The average monthly income of salaried households of at least two individuals fell by a real 3.8 percent to 689,476 yen, according to the ministry. ■

New Zealand records 3rd-warmest winter on record
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:58:33 CST
14:58:33 KST

WELLINGTON, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand recorded its third-warmest winter on record in 2026, with a nationwide average temperature of 9.7 degrees Celsius, Earth Sciences New Zealand said Friday.
The temperature was 1.1 degrees Celsius above the 1991-2020 winter average, making it the third-warmest winter since the country's seven-station temperature series began in 1909, the agency said in a statement.
Exceptional warmth in June and a relatively warm winter throughout the South Island were the dominant features of the country's overall seasonal temperature, while temperatures were near average in parts of Northland, Auckland, Waikato, eastern Bay of Plenty and Gisborne on the North Island, it said.
Winter rainfall was above or well above normal in Southland, Otago, southern and inland Canterbury and the West Coast on the South Island, while large parts of the North Island recorded below-normal rainfall, the agency said.
Impactful heavy rainfall from July 5 to July 9 affected eastern parts of the country, with three local states of emergency declared, it noted.
The highest winter temperature was 26 degrees Celsius on June 20 at Bromley in Christchurch, the South Island's largest city. It was the country's second-highest winter temperature on record. The lowest was minus 13.5 degrees Celsius at Lake Tekapo on July 12.
El Niño conditions in the tropical Pacific strengthened considerably from mid-winter onward, the agency said, adding that sea surface temperatures around New Zealand were mostly near or above average, with marine heatwave conditions experienced around much of the South Island and Tasman Sea during July and August.
Scientists said El Niño typically brings stronger, more frequent southwesterly to northwesterly winds, resulting in drier conditions in eastern and northern areas of both islands and wetter conditions in the western and lower South Island. ■

2 trapped Nepal workers rescued from buried tunnel 9 days after floods

2 trapped Nepal workers rescued from buried tunnel 9 days after devastating floods, and more voices heard
Kathmandu, Nepal — Rescuers in Nepal pulled two hydropower workers from a tunnel Friday as emergency teams raced to find more survivors, spurred on by the dramatic rescues more than a week after the devastating flash floods that killed more than 1,200 people.
CBS News' Ramy Inocencio said there was hope more survivors could emerge from the tunnel — possibly dozens more — as rescuers heard voices coming from deep inside the structure that the was covered by mud and filled with flood water during last week's catastrophe.
The two men were rescued from the Trishuli 3A tunnel nine days after floods, likely caused by a glacier collapse, devastated towns and swept away villages in Nepal.
Nepalese lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane posted about the second rescue on his Facebook page shortly after army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet confirmed the first trapped worker's rescue.
Nepal Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told Inocencio in a text message that he was "thrilled" about the two rescues and "hoping to see more survivors." He said it was unclear how many survivors might still be inside the tunnel, but with voices heard, he said the clock was ticking to find and rescue everyone still alive.
Rescuers first heard voices from inside the tunnel Friday morning, enabling them to locate the two men, Neupane said.
Local television news channels showed images of the first rescued worker, covered in mud, being carried from the site on a rescuer's shoulder. Officials said both men were in stable condition and were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu.
Mechanical foreman Sanjay Shah said "thank you" when he was pulled out, but he was then advised not to speak due to his weakened condition, Inocencio reported.
Amir Maharjan, brother of the other rescued worker, mechanical supervisor Kabir Maharjan, told The Associated Press he "can't explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to God." He said the family were on their way to the hospital to see him.
"We couldn't properly eat or drink for 10 days," Kabir Maharjan's wife, Hirashova, told CBS News partner network BBC News. "We were very scared. Now we are all happy. We are even crying."
At least 557 workers from the Trishuli 3A hydropower project along the Trishuli River remain missing, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the main tunnel, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal.
A Nepali energy adviser told Inocencio it was not just a tunnel that goes into the ground next to the Trishuli River, but a system of rooms and chambers that snake up and down, where the workers are apparently stuck.
The adviser also told Inocencio the trapped workers were some of the smartest engineers in Nepal, and they probably have been trying to figure their own way out, and how to get oxygen so they don't run out of air — the biggest risk.
At least 1,287 people were killed in the floods and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to the country's disaster management agency. China, as of late Wednesday, said 21 people were killed and 541 were missing on the Tibet side of the border.
About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, according to local authorities.
Prabesh Subedi contributed to this report.

Air India Phuket-Delhi incident: All 3 hydraulic systems failed; pilot tested positive for psychoactive substance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
05:57:23 UTC
14:57:23 KST

The hydraulic failure itself, the more immediate cause of the injuries onboard, unfolded within a five-second window. VT-EXO, an eight-year-old A320neo carrying 145 people, had just been cleared to climb from FL340 to FL360 after entering Kolkata Flight Information Region.
MUMBAI: The preliminary investigation into the August 4 Air India Phuket-Delhi accident has found that the aircraft's three hydraulic systems, green, blue and yellow, lost pressure within seconds while the A320 was cruising at 36,000 feet, triggering an autopilot disengagement, stall warning and an altitude upset. Alongside the technical findings, the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) has recommended that the DGCA take action against the Pilot-in-Command, who tested non-negative for psychoactive substance use following the flight."The confirmation of use of psycho-active substance is a serious concern, and AAIB recommends appropriate actions by DGCA on priority," the report said. The interim safety recommendation asked the regulator to "take appropriate actions as deemed fit to prevent abuse of psycho-active substance." Post-flight, both pilots underwent a breath analyser test, which came back satisfactory. But the subsequent psychoactive substance detection test returned a non-negative result for the PIC, a finding confirmed by a follow-up laboratory blood test. The co-pilot tested negative on both counts.The hydraulic failure itself, the more immediate cause of the injuries onboard, unfolded within a five-second window.
VT-EXO, an eight-year-old A320neo carrying 145 people, had just been cleared to climb from FL340 to FL360 after entering Kolkata Flight Information Region. At 04:02:43 UTC, the flight control system "detected loss of green hydraulic system." Four seconds later, the flight control (F/CTL) system detected loss of Blue and Yellow hydraulic systems. With all three systems compromised simultaneously, the autopilot disengaged, a continuous repetitive chime sounded, and the stall warning triggered for two seconds. The aircraft "encountered altitude upset," gaining 372 feet before falling 292 feet from its assigned level, the report said.The co-pilot, who was Pilot Flying, responded first to the upset before the captain took over the controls. Recovery was swift. "At around 04:02:52 UTC, the Blue hydraulic system was recovered, and a few seconds later, the Yellow hydraulic and the Green hydraulic systems were also recovered," the report said. It restored normal flight control surfaces within seconds of the failure.But with seatbelt signs off during cruise, the sudden upset threw passengers and crew around the cabin. Twenty-four people, including four cabin crew, needed medical attention on landing; four were hospitalised with serious injuries. The cabin damage was extensive: cracked ceiling panels across multiple rows, dislodged overhead bins, a broken emergency exit handle, a lavatory commode "uprooted from its original location," and a bent crew seat. Despite the injuries, the flight crew chose not to divert, opting instead to continue to Delhi while requesting medical priority from ATC. The aircraft landed safely on runway 11L at 05:30 UTC, around ninety minutes after the failure.Investigators have already flagged one detail for closer scrutiny: the aircraft was dispatched from Phuket under an active Minimum Equipment List item for the Power Transfer Unit, invoked a week earlier on July 28. The PTU serves as an auxiliary hydraulic source shared between the green and yellow systems, and its status at the time of the failure is expected to be a focus of the ongoing probe. Flight recorder data has been downloaded and is under analysis, and a technical team from Airbus and France's BEA inspected the aircraft in Delhi in mid-August, after which hydraulic components and fluid samples were removed for further testing.“The Airbus A320 aircraft has three hydraulic systems. They are identified as the green, blue and yellow systems. Together they supply hydraulic power at 3000 psi (206 bar) to the main power users. Services which are not used during flight are isolated from the main supply. Hydraulic fluid cannot be transferred from one system to another. Each system has its own hydraulic reservoir,” the report said, explaining the hydraulics on the aircraft.
On the green system, the normal source of pressure is the Engine Driven Pump (EDP) located on the left engine and, as an auxiliary source, the Power Transfer Unit (PTU). On the blue system, the normal source of pressure is the electrical pump (E-Pump) and, as an auxiliary source, the Ram Air Turbine (RAT). On the yellow system, the normal source of pressure is the EDP located on the right engine and as auxiliary sources the PTU and the electric pump (E-Pump). “Each hydraulic system pressurisation information is available for the aircraft systems through one pressure transmitter (numerical value of the pressure), two pressure switches (discrete value indicating if there is a loss of pressure). Relevant Hydraulic components were removed from the aircraft for further analysis,” the report said. The PTU is an auxiliary pressure supply for either the green or yellow systems without transfer of fluid between the two systems. It operates automatically if there is a delta pressure of 500 psi between the green/yellow or yellow/green hydraulic systems, it addedThe said report is preliminary, and a detailed technical investigation is still underway.

airBaltic agrees on financing of up to 257 million euros – interest rate set at 25% per year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
05:57:05 UTC
14:57:05 KST

Latvia’s national airline airBaltic has agreed with certain existing bondholders and third-party financing providers on the terms of bridge financing of up to 257 million euros, the airline said.
The financing is intended to strengthen the company’s liquidity and provide the financial resources needed to implement its new business plan.
The planned financing still requires approval from airBaltic’s bondholders and shareholders.
A bondholders’ meeting to consider the proposal has been convened for 11 September.
The airline explained that, subject to the necessary approvals and other conditions being met, 180 million euros is expected to become available shortly after bondholder consent is obtained, while a further 77 million euros will become available once additional conditions have been fulfilled.
The bridge financing is expected to be raised through the issuance of new bonds maturing on 26 February 2027. The interest rate has been set at 25% per year.
According to airBaltic’s stock exchange announcement, the transaction provides for the issuance of new higher-ranking “super senior” bonds of up to approximately 257 million euros. The financing would be provided by London-based investment management company Polus Capital Management and Israel-registered investment firm Klirmark Capital 4. Existing bondholders, including the Latvian state, will also have an opportunity to participate in the new issue on a pro-rata basis.
airBaltic Supervisory Board Chairman Andrejs Martinovs told LETA that the investors are prepared to provide bridge financing of up to 257 million euros, while all existing bondholders will also have the opportunity to participate in proportion to their current bond holdings.
“It is not a mandatory requirement, but an opportunity available to bondholders. This also applies to the Latvian state,” Martinovs stressed.
The financing is intended to refinance existing liabilities related to aircraft and engines, as well as cover ongoing expenses, including repair, maintenance and airport fees.
Commenting on the interest rate, Martinovs said it was the best financing airBaltic could currently obtain, as short-term bridge financing instruments of this kind are more expensive than other forms of financing. He stressed that airBaltic’s calculations and implementation of its business plan envisage that the company will be able to service such interest rates.
In its stock exchange announcement, airBaltic reiterated that its flight schedule will continue as planned throughout the implementation of the interim financing and review process, with no disruption expected for passengers.
The airline said the financing providers have committed to making the full amount of the planned financing available, subject to the necessary approvals and fulfilment of the other transaction conditions. All existing airBaltic bondholders will also have the opportunity to participate in providing the financing.
airBaltic stressed that the planned bridge financing does not depend on financial participation by the Latvian state. However, as an existing airBaltic bondholder, the state may, under recently adopted legislation, choose to participate in the financing proportionally to its bond holdings.
The planned financing forms part of broader measures aimed at strengthening airBaltic’s financial position and implementing its new business plan.
airBaltic CEO Erno Hildén said the planned financing would provide the liquidity needed for the airline’s next stage of development. He stressed that the revised business plan includes targeted measures to strengthen the company’s financial position and create a more efficient and financially self-sufficient airline, while the bridge financing would provide the time and resources needed to implement those measures without disrupting the planned flight schedule.
As previously reported, airBaltic’s Supervisory Board has approved a business plan that envisages raising 225 million euros in interim financing to improve liquidity, using the existing collateral pool securing the 2029 senior bonds.
In the longer term, the plan provides for the company’s recapitalisation through up to 225 million euros in new debt and 100 million euros in new equity. Part of the existing 2029 bonds would be converted into equity, while the remainder would be replaced with new, smaller debt of up to 125 million euros.
The business plan also envisages airBaltic operating 36 Airbus A220-300 aircraft by the end of 2026, compared with 54 aircraft currently, with the fleet gradually increasing to around 40 aircraft by 2031.
On 25 August, Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs promulgated the airBaltic Financial Stabilisation Measures Law, which had been adopted by the Saeima under an urgent procedure on 20 August.
The law authorises the government to potentially participate in the purchase of airBaltic bridge-financing bonds for up to 30 million euros, alongside private investors and on identical terms. The Cabinet may take a separate decision on purchasing the bonds if necessary.
The law also allows claims arising from the state loan and bonds already held by the state to be converted into airBaltic equity. This means that state-owned bonds worth 50 million euros and the remaining loan of more than 18 million euros may be converted into shares in the airline.
On 25 August, the government also approved extending the repayment deadline for the remaining 18 million euros of the state loan until 30 December this year.
airBaltic bondholders have also approved the capitalisation of the airline’s two nearest interest payments, as well as several other measures giving the company additional flexibility in implementing its revised business plan.
Interest payments due on 14 August and 14 November will be added to the principal amount of the bonds rather than paid in cash. Bondholders also approved a temporary waiver of minimum liquidity requirements until November 2026.
Last year, airBaltic Group’s revenue increased by 4.2% compared with 2024 to 779.344 million euros. The group recorded losses of 44.337 million euros, 2.7 times lower than in 2024. The airline carried a total of 5.2 million passengers in 2025, up 1% from the previous year.
German flag carrier Lufthansa became an airBaltic shareholder last summer. The Latvian state currently owns 88.37% of airBaltic, Lufthansa holds 10%, Danish businessman Lars Thuesen’s Aircraft Leasing 1 owns 1.62%, and other shareholders hold the remaining 0.01%. The company’s share capital amounts to 41.819 million euros.
Given its 2025 financial results and market conditions, airBaltic has suspended its potential initial public offering and does not currently consider an IPO a potential source of capital in 2026, according to the airline’s annual report.

What's next?
Luai will captain the Tigers in his final game for the club on Sunday against the Panthers. He will join the Eels in 2027 on a one-year deal before PNG's inaugural NRL season in 2028.
Benji Marshall insists Jarome Luai is entitled to spend his downtime as he pleases, dismissing "irrelevant" criticism of the Wests Tigers star's recent trip to PNG.
When Luai asked to change his flight out of Townsville following last week's loss to North Queensland, Marshall was unaware his star player would be travelling to his future home country to attend a golf tournament.
The trip came only days after Pepsi unveiled Luai as a brand ambassador ahead of his arrival at the Chiefs for their first NRL season in 2028.
Luai's trip to Port Moresby, and the first of what is likely to be many promotional opportunities with PNG brands, come while he remains on a seven-figure salary with the Tigers.

The five-eighth will also join Parramatta on a one-year deal before his first pre-season with the Chiefs, which begins in more than a year.

Marshall still believed Luai's signing was a success for the Tigers, who face top-two side Penrith in their last game of the season.
"There's no regrets from our side about bringing him here whatsoever because he did the job we needed him to," he said.
"I'm sure a lot of people probably have their opinions about what he hasn't done here, but all I've seen are the things he has done here and the impact he has had on the club.
"I'm sure he would admit himself that he would have liked to have contributed more on field performance-wise but all in all, he'll leave here having had an impact on our club."

This virus has evolved. Australia doesn't have a new vaccine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
05:55:36 UTC
14:55:36 KST

IN BRIEF
- Pfizer's latest COVID vaccine targets the XFG subvariant, but it has not yet been registered for use in Australia.
- Experts say Australia's vaccine update process could be streamlined as new COVID variants continue to emerge.
Australians can't yet access a COVID-19 vaccine tailored for new variants, highlighting how Australia's system tends to lag behind, as a major manufacturer confirms it has no plans to push into Australia's market.
Pfizer and BioNTech's latest COVID-19 vaccine, adapted to target the XFG subvariant, has been approved in the United States for the 2026-27 season, following international guidance to more closely match vaccines with contemporary circulating variants.
Australia does not yet have that formulation registered.
But experts say the lag is not necessarily cause for alarm, with Australia continuing to monitor circulating variants and having access to relatively recent updated vaccines.
Pfizer and BioNTech's LP.8.1-adapted COVID-19 vaccine was registered on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods in late 2025 and became available in Australia in December.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Moderna's LP.8.1 formulation has also been registered in Australia.
Australia has updated vaccines — just not the latest formulation
The issue is therefore less about Australia going without updated COVID-19 vaccines, and more about how quickly newer formulations can be made available as the virus continues to evolve.
Professor Paul Griffin, an infectious diseases physician and clinical microbiologist, said Australia tended to lag behind some countries in updating COVID-19 vaccines.
"I think it's just some of the way we're managing those updates just means it's not quite happening as streamlined a way as we might like," he said.
"We know that some countries are able to do that a bit more quickly."
Griffin said countries with more established frameworks could update vaccines closer to real time.
"We tend to lag behind a little bit," he said.
While he said faster access would be preferable, he also stressed the importance of continuing to update vaccines as the virus changes.
Several reasons for the delay
But Sarah McGuinness, a senior research fellow at Monash University, told SBS News there was no single explanation for why a new formulation might become available overseas before it does in Australia.
She said one factor is the decisions vaccine manufacturers make about which countries to seek regulatory approval in, and when, with vaccine sponsors responsible for deciding whether to seek regulatory approval in different countries.
McGuinness also said Australia is a relatively small market compared with areas such as the US and Europe, meaning new formulations are not always brought here first.
Peter Markey, a GP and public health physician who chairs the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners' public health special interest group, said Australian authorities were continuing to monitor the virus internationally.
He said governments, researchers and the World Health Organization would be watching circulating strains and sub-strains and "looking out for vaccines to match them".
There is also an established international process for determining which variants vaccines should target.
Pfizer and BioNTech say their latest XFG-adapted vaccine follows guidance to more closely match contemporary circulating variants.
Along with Pfizer-BioNTech's XFG-adapted vaccine, updated vaccines from Moderna and Novavax-Sanofi have been approved in the US for the 2026-27 season.
AstraZeneca has confirmed to SBS News that it has no plans to release a COVID-19 vaccine for the 2026-27 season.
It withdrew its vaccine from the global market in 2024, and it hadn't been available in Australia since 2023.
What does the lag mean for Australians?
For Australians, the emergence of newer formulations overseas does not mean the vaccines currently available are ineffective.
The challenge is keeping vaccine formulations aligned with a virus that continues to evolve.
Pfizer confirmed to SBS News that its LP.8.1-adapted vaccine is registered in Australia and available to people aged six months and older.
The company has not provided a timeframe for when its newer XFG-adapted vaccine could be submitted for Australian registration.
Griffin said Australia could nevertheless look for ways to streamline the updating process.
"I think that's just where we need to consider a really streamlined way of getting those updated vaccines here and available in Australia as quickly as possible," he said.
For now, experts say Australia's vaccine system is continuing to monitor the changing virus, while manufacturers decide which updated formulations to bring to the Australian market.

Fraud victims often trust scammers instead of the police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
05:55:00 UTC
14:55:00 KST

Fraud victims often trust scammers instead of the police
Scam victims increasingly hang up on real police officers, convinced they're speaking to fraudsters, says Valmar Viitak, head of the Northern Prefecture's serious‑crimes unit.
Viitak said there have also been situations where a relative notices suspicious behavior and alerts the police that the victim plans to meet a stranger to hand over money.
"Officers responding to the call try to convince the person that it's a scam, but the victim either completely denies what's happening or continues to believe they are carrying out tasks assigned to them as part of a secret police operation," Viitak said. Sometimes the victim calls a police patrol to have them verify the investigators who arrived on the scene.
In some cases, the victim asks the officer for a so‑called code word that scammers have previously agreed upon with them. The fraudster explains that the code word helps confirm that the victim is speaking to the 'right' people and that anyone who doesn't know it must not be trusted.
"If the responding officer cannot say the code word, the victim takes it as confirmation that the officer is not real," Viitak said.
These incidents are linked to the rise in scam calls in recent years. Fraudsters create the impression through multiple calls that the victim has fallen prey to a scam and must follow instructions to save their money. The victim is told they are part of a secret police operation and are helping catch criminals.
Scammers insist that the victim must not tell anyone, claiming it could hinder the investigation and lead to punishment. "In the final stage of the scheme, the victim is asked to hand over their cash, bank cards and documents to a courier or place them in a parcel locker for 'inspection'," Viitak explained.
Home and car go up for sale
In particularly severe cases, victims have sold their homes or cars and handed the proceeds to scammers. This manipulation can last days or weeks, during which fraudsters try to build a trusting relationship, show interest in the victim's daily life and give the impression that they care about their well‑being. Their goal is to make the victim feel that the person on the phone is trustworthy and trying to help.
"When someone has been under the scammers' influence for a long time, it's usually not enough for a police officer to show their badge or say it's a scam," Viitak said. Victims are often sincerely convinced they are doing the right thing. It can take a long time and a lot of explanation to persuade them otherwise.
Swedbank's head of customer services, Ede Raagmets, said there have been cases where a bank employee contacts a client, but the person suspects the caller might be a scammer. She noted that such cases have increased slightly compared to previous years.
"A typical situation is that the bank employee introduces themselves at the start of the call, and the client asks how they can verify the call is really from the bank," Raagmets said. She explained that clients have several ways to check whether the caller is genuinely from Swedbank.
For example, the client can end the call and dial Swedbank's customer support number themselves to ask whether the bank tried to contact them. The bank can also send a secure message to the client's online banking account. It is also important to remember that bank employees never ask for PIN codes or request that they be entered anywhere during a phone call.
Some days bring ten scam attempts
Omniva's communications manager, Agne Teder, said scam schemes occasionally reappear using Omniva's name. "Some days we don't receive any such inquiries, other days there may be ten," she said. It depends on the scammers' activity and which schemes are currently circulating.
Questions related to scams also reach Omniva's customer service and increase its workload, as people want to verify whether a message, email or call truly came from Omniva.
Calls from unfamiliar numbers should be approached with caution, and if the caller's story raises suspicion or fear, the call should be ended. Clear warning signs include pressure to act quickly, instructions not to tell family members, or requests to confirm something with PIN codes or hand over money.
The police do not involve people in secret operations and never ask anyone over the phone to identify themselves using Smart‑ID or Mobile‑ID. Scammers try to isolate victims from the outside world to make them easier to manipulate.
If you fall victim to fraud, you should first call your bank, block your cards and ask for transfers to be stopped. Then file a criminal report with the police and include all available evidence to help determine the scope of the incident.

Russian Conscripts Increasingly Blocked From Leaving Country Amid Mobilization Fears

2026-09-04

14:53:25 KST

Russian conscripts are increasingly being stopped at the border as authorities tighten restrictions on leaving the country, with the latest cases fueling fears that Moscow may be preparing for another mobilization.
Between Aug. 18 and 31, Russia’s human rights project “Idite Lesom” (Get Lost) received reports from 73 conscripts who tried to leave the country. Fifty managed to cross the border, while 23 were denied exit. In several cases, the travel bans appeared only during border checks.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
One conscript who had lived in Indonesia for years returned to Russia for a two-week visit but was unable to leave again. His registry record showed a travel ban.
Another was stopped at a Moscow airport despite saying he had never received a draft notice. He learned about the restriction only when he reached border control.
In another case, a conscript checked the electronic registry before a Moscow-Yerevan flight and found no restrictions. Border officers nevertheless told him he was barred from leaving. Minutes later, the ban appeared in the registry.
A conscript from Novosibirsk discovered he had received a draft notice only after being stopped at the airport. Although the military enlistment office later canceled the restriction, border guards stopped him again two days later because the ban remained in their system.
Still, not every conscript is being blocked.
One man with a draft notice for a medical examination and a valid deferment was able to fly to Yerevan because no travel ban was listed. Others successfully left Russia despite having paper draft notices. One conscript even crossed into Kazakhstan despite his registry showing a travel ban and other restrictions.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 3, 2026
Belarus is also becoming a less reliable route out. Of 11 conscripts who contacted “Idite Lesom” after attempting to leave through Belarus, four succeeded and seven were stopped.
Putin denies new mobilization plans
The tightening restrictions come as speculation grows that the Kremlin could announce another mobilization following September’s State Duma elections.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly dismissed such reports, most recently calling them an “information attack” aimed at disrupting the elections.
“There is no scenario today that would require mobilization,” Putin said Thursday at the Eastern Economic Forum. He described the reports as a planned information operation.
A day earlier, Putin called reports of a possible post-election mobilization “nonsense” and again rejected the possibility of a new mass call-up.
Putin has insisted that Russia does not need another mobilization, claiming that Russians continue to join the military voluntarily by signing contracts with the Defense Ministry.
He also claimed Russia has “no problems” recruiting troops for the war against Ukraine, while alleging that Ukraine’s armed forces are losing 8,000 to 12,000 personnel each month. He provided no evidence for the figure.
Despite the Kremlin’s repeated denials, speculation about a new mobilization has intensified since the summer.
Russian pro-war Z-channels reported in July that a potential forced call-up could involve as many as 1.2 million people. Western intelligence agencies have separately assessed that Russia is preparing military infrastructure to receive and equip additional recruits.
The Institute for the Study of War has also reported signs of preparations for a potential new mobilization. Western intelligence officials and several European officials who spoke to The Washington Post have not ruled one out, citing Russia’s heavy battlefield losses.
The Center for Strategic and International Studies estimates that Russian forces have suffered at least 1.4 million casualties in Ukraine, including severely wounded troops who cannot return to service.
Russia tightens the exit
Russia’s electronic draft system has already been used to restrict travel. After the electronic draft-notice registry was fully launched in March, Russians began reporting that failure to appear at military enlistment offices could trigger bans on leaving the country.
Authorities have also tightened coordination with Belarus. In April, a St. Petersburg conscript was stopped while attempting to leave Russia through Belarus, prompting the Movement of Conscientious Objectors to warn that border authorities in the two countries may have begun exchanging data from their military registration systems.
Meanwhile, Russians appear to be rushing to leave through other routes.
Amid the mobilization rumors, traffic through the Upper Lars border crossing between Russia and Georgia surged to record levels.
From Aug. 15 to 18, more than 19,000–20,000 people crossed the border each day, according to Russia’s Federal Customs Service – significantly more than during comparable periods in previous years.

At its meeting on September 3, the Kyiv City Council voted with 67 votes in favor of the draft resolution "On stabilizing the financial position of the Kyivmiskbud Holding Company by increasing the authorized capital," the company’s press service reported.
The document provides for consent to increase the company’s authorized capital by issuing additional shares in the amount of up to UAH 3 billion, while maintaining the shareholder’s stake in the Kyiv City Community, which owns 99.87% of the holding’s shares. The amount was calculated in accordance with the company’s Financial Plan for 2026-2028.
"Today marks a significant step in support of Kyivmiskbud and a clear signal to investors: the community and the city are on their side. The previous capital increase allowed us to resume work at 11 sites, and this year we are preparing to commission six residential complexes, complete with utility networks. Raising additional funds will ensure the continuity of construction in 2027-2028 and enable the company to fulfill its main obligation—to complete all facilities and hand over the keys to people, including military personnel and war veterans," noted Yuriy Tykhonovych, Acting Chairman of the Board of PJSC HC Kyivmiskbud.
According to Tykhonovych, after the appropriate funds are transferred to the 2027 city budget for the purchase of additional shares, Kyivmiskbud will receive an effective financial instrument to ensure stable operations during 2027-2028.
Kyivmiskbud’s construction portfolio currently includes 24 residential complexes at various stages of completion, including projects accepted for completion from Ukrbud Corporation in accordance with Cabinet of Ministers Order No. 772-r.
Tykhonovych also added that the decision to recapitalize Kyivmiskbud will not only reduce social tensions among thousands of investor families and restore confidence in the primary real estate market, but will also have a powerful multiplier effect on the capital’s entire economy.
Kyivmiskbud Holding Company was created in 1994 based on the assets of the state municipal construction corporation Kyivmiskbud by consolidating controlling stakes in 28 enterprises and other assets into its authorized capital. It comprises 40 joint-stock companies in which the company holds shares, as well as six subsidiaries and 51 associate enterprises. On October 31, 2024, the Kyiv City Council voted to increase Kyivmiskbud’s capital by UAH 2.6 billion through the issue and repurchase of additional shares. On June 23, 2025, the company’s shareholders supported a resolution to increase its authorized capital by UAH 2.6 billion through the issue of additional common registered shares. The company received this additional capital in December 2025. The Kyiv City Council acted as the sole participant in the share placement.
According to the National Securities and Stock Market Commission, the Kyiv City Council is the primary shareholder of Kyivmiskbud Holding Company.

“We will be asking for that money, though somewhat belatedly!”

Launched last year, the scheme allows them to pay for US-made weapons and ammunition supplied to Kiev. Moscow has maintained that additional Western weapons will not change the outcome of the conflict, arguing that they will only prolong the fighting.
Trump’s latest remarks came as he pushed back against reports that the conflict with Iran has severely depleted ammunition stocks, saying the US is ramping up production and currently keeping newly produced munitions for its own forces rather than selling them abroad.
The administration has also portrayed the Ukraine conflict as imposing a broader economic cost on the US. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this week that Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, coupled with the Iran war, contributed to an “energy shock” pushing up prices in the US.
