ASIC probing hundreds of audit complaints at big four accounting firms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
05:01:51 UTC
14:01:51 KST

ASIC reveals hundreds of complaints about alleged audit misconduct by big four accounting firms
The corporate regulator has been told by the big four accounting firms — KPMG, PwC, EY and Deloitte — that there have been 551 complaints about alleged audit misconduct.
In the wake of whistleblower revelations that confidential board papers from Lendlease were used to support bids for major audit tenders for Westpac and Dexus, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) is investigating the big four and asking them about internal whistleblower complaints.
The watchdog told a federal parliamentary hearing in Sydney today that it was looking at whistleblower complaints to the big four accounting firms dating from July 1, 2023.
ASIC's executive director of enforcement and compliance, Chris Savundra, told the hearing that, so far, 551 complaints had been made.
ASIC chair Sarah Court then clarified that "just to be clear … this includes whether the firms have received complaints relating to misconduct by registered company auditors, such as the misuse or sharing of confidential information".
"So that's what we have asked for," she said.
"And then we have used our compulsory information gathering powers in relation to obtaining that material."
She said the regulator was looking at "each of these complaints and ascertaining whether there is more work for ASIC to do in relation to investigations or enforcement action or activity in relation to particular issues".
"I don't want to suggest that there's, you know, 550 serious whistleblower issues," she said.
"We don't know and there's a lot of work for us, clearly, to be looking through those complaints, getting more information as we need it."
Senator Barbara Pocock asked if that 551 figure was "spread evenly across the four firms, 125-odd or over 100 in each of the four?"
Ms Court then suggested that the hearing go off-camera so ASIC could give the committee looking into the audit leaks scandal further information.
Senator questions whether KPMG 'turned over a new leaf'
Senator Pocock has also called on ASIC to broaden the period in which it investigates whistleblower complaints within the big four, noting that only going back over a three-year period does not capture historical complaints.
KPMG has argued that certain documents relating to the audit leaks scandal should not be released publicly because they are the subject of legal professional privilege.
Senator Pocock told the hearing that the KPMG leadership had consistently argued they had "turned over a new leaf" and alluded to the firm needing to be transparent.
"This committee has spent hours listening to the leadership of KPMG, [CEO John] Mr Sams and [chairman Michael] Obeid telling us that they've turned over a new leaf, that they are a new leadership, 'there is new culture, trust us', and yet here we are," Senator Pocock said.
"I think my expectation, I won't speak for everyone on this side of the table, but my expectation is that the performance of a new leadership requires delivery of outcomes.
"There is a clear message, certainly for me, that they'll be back talking to us again if they don't deliver what they say they're doing culturally."
In December 2021, another KPMG whistleblower wrote to ASIC about separate claims that the firm may have breached the corporations law.
In an email to ASIC in June, the whistleblower detailed how ASIC rejected their earlier attempt at making a disclosure, and it was their view that the regulator had to be "dragged kicking and screaming" to investigate alleged misconduct at KPMG.
ASIC began its investigation this year only after the allegations of the audit leaks whistleblower were aired by Senator Deborah O'Neill under parliamentary privilege.
While the federal government reviews laws protecting whistleblowers, Senator Pocock asked ASIC whether whistleblowers needed interim measures that might make them more willing to make disclosures about alleged misconduct.
Ms Court said she would have to reflect on that, but there needs to be "urgent clarity" about whether disclosures made to ASIC by whistleblowers are protected.
Did KPMG make 'false or misleading' statements?
ASIC also told Friday's hearing in a submission it was investigating documents KPMG had lodged with the regulator to determine if they contained false or misleading statements.
"ASIC is separately investigating alleged false or misleading statements in KPMG's 2025 Transparency Report, which was lodged with ASIC under the Corporations Act," ASIC said in the submission to Friday's hearing.
"Initial inquiries are focused on the basis for statements made in that report, including the statement that there were no whistleblower complaints related to audit quality."
Aside from commencing "surveillance of the Big Four accounting firms, to examine internal complaints received by those firms about their audit practices", ASIC was also now "conducting an assessment of the corporate entities in the KPMG corporate group to identify any director conduct that may require further regulatory consideration".
Ms Court has told previous hearings that the regulator was limited in investigating partnerships but on Friday said: "We are looking carefully at the various KPMG-related corporate entities because, as you say, the Corporations Act obligations would then apply in relation to those corporations."
Earlier in Friday's hearing, ASIC announced it was investigating whether superannuation trustee Diversa inappropriately charged fees to victims of the First Guardian collapse. Diversa ran the platforms that allowed thousands of investors to pump money into First Guardian.
ASIC has previously said about $300 million was invested into First Guardian from 2020 to 2024 through superannuation funds for which Diversa was trustee. The regulator is suing Diversa over alleged due diligence failures, but Diversa is fighting the legal action.

Budva travel guide: How Montenegro's dazzling riviera town is winning over Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
05:00:34 UTC
14:00:34 KST

Budva’s medieval old town, its beaches, nightlife and sites such as Sveti Stefan are turning Montenegro’s coast into a rising Adriatic destination, but the tourism boom is already revealing the challenges the country will have to confront.
There is something both disconcerting and fascinating about the road trip to Budva in the height of summer.
On one side lies the Adriatic, surprisingly calm, blue and bright. On the other, almost clinging to the shoreline, rise Montenegro’s mountains. Between them runs a road that in July and August seems unable to cope with the sheer number of cars, buses and tourists heading to one of the destinations that is most rapidly gaining prominence in this part of Europe.
Budva is one of the clearest examples of that transformation. The city combines a walled medieval old town with beaches, hotels, restaurants, terraces and a vibrant nightlife.
During the summer months its streets fill with tourists and, when the sun goes down, much of the seafront promenade takes on a different personality.
Music, bars, packed terraces and groups of young people roaming the city until the early hours create an atmosphere that, for a Spanish traveller of a certain generation, may feel surprisingly familiar.
Here it feels like the holidays never end: music spilling out of venues, crammed terraces, restaurants, clubs, families strolling along the seafront and young people intent on stretching the night out.
This is the other face of Montenegro, in contrast with the calmer image projected by its mountains, bays and small coastal villages.
And yet just a few minutes’ walk are enough to enter a completely different setting. The heart of Budva is still its Stari Grad, the old town. Behind its walls lies a maze of narrow stone streets, small squares, churches, restaurants and shops that speaks of the long history of a place considered one of the oldest settlements on the Adriatic.
Exploring it at sunset reveals the duality that probably explains much of Budva’s tourist success: you can spend the morning on the beach, wander a medieval town in the afternoon and end the day having dinner or a drink in a resort that in summer hardly seems to sleep.
Major hotel chains move in
The boom in Budva and Montenegro’s coast has not gone unnoticed by the big international hotel chains. Among them is Spanish group Iberostar, which has strengthened its presence in a country keen to establish itself as one of the Adriatic’s up-and-coming tourist destinations.
The company currently operates four properties in Montenegro, two of them in Budva, a significant presence in a market that is still small compared with other major Mediterranean destinations but increasingly attractive for international tourism.
One of the clearest examples of this bet is the Iberostar Waves Slavija 5*, 1.5 kilometres from Budva’s old town. From its rooftop, home to an infinity pool and the Rooftop Bar, you get sweeping views over the city, the Adriatic and the mountains that frame this stretch of coastline.
But Iberostar’s presence matters beyond any single hotel. The establishment of a Spanish chain with four properties in the country is also a sign of the transformation that Montenegro is undergoing as an emerging tourist destination in Europe.
The coast is rapidly evolving towards a more international hotel offering, especially around Budva, while trying to preserve precisely what sets it apart from other Mediterranean destinations: the extraordinary proximity between the Adriatic, historic towns and a mountainous landscape that begins almost where the sea ends.
Sveti Stefan: From fishing village to tourist icon
Just a few kilometres from Budva lies one of Montenegro’s most recognisable images.
Sveti Stefan is a small historic settlement built on an islet linked to the mainland by a narrow isthmus. Its outline of stone houses and reddish roofs, surrounded by the waters of the Adriatic, has become one of the country’s great postcard views.
What for centuries was a small community tied to fishing underwent a profound transformation from the mid-20th century onwards to become an exclusive tourist enclave and one of Montenegro’s international symbols. The views from the coast and nearby viewpoints offer one of the most spectacular scenes on the Adriatic.
Here too you find the contrast that accompanies travellers along much of their journey through Montenegro: the almost motionless sea set against an extraordinarily rugged, mountainous coastline.
A paradise caught in summer traffic
Driving that coastline also reveals one of the main problems created by Montenegro’s rapid tourism growth. In summer, getting around by road can be unbearably slow.
The coastal road carries an enormous volume of traffic and jams are common. Journeys that look short on the map can take much longer in July and August.
For those arriving by air, Budva has an important advantage: Tivat airport is just a stone’s throw away, offering an easy gateway for holidaymakers heading to this part of Montenegro’s coast.
Another challenge Montenegro faces as tourism grows strongly is entry into the country via the border with Croatia. On average, travellers crossing it by road take around two hours to get through in the height of the summer season.
It is hardly the best calling card for a country that aims to integrate ever more closely with Europe and that receives a large proportion of its visitors via the roads that connect it with its neighbours.
Montenegro is one of the most advanced candidate countries in the negotiations to join the European Union. Its future accession could also transform the experience of those travelling by road through this part of the Balkans.
For a relatively small territory that is increasingly dependent on tourism, easing border bottlenecks and improving infrastructure will be essential if it wants to absorb a growing number of visitors without undermining the traveller’s experience.
All the signs suggest those visitors will keep coming. Montenegro brings together many of the ingredients that have turned other Mediterranean destinations into tourism powerhouses: beaches, climate, heritage, gastronomy and a spectacular coastline concentrated into relatively few kilometres.
On top of that it offers a landscape hard to find elsewhere in the Mediterranean, where the sea and high mountains seem to be constantly competing for the same space.
Budva is probably the most intense expression of all this. It can feel noisy, crowded and chaotic in the peak summer weeks. Its traffic tests your patience and its nightlife is a long way from the image of peaceful retreat that some travellers might associate with Montenegro.
But that is precisely where part of its character lies. Budva is a medieval town on the Adriatic that turns into a major holiday resort when summer arrives. There is something of a Balkan Riviera about it and, at times, something of that Spanish Mediterranean of the 1990s when the nights seemed endless.
Today, the arrival of international hotel groups such as Iberostar shows just how far Montenegro is entering a new tourism phase. Between sea and mountains, between medieval walls and music-filled venues, Montenegro is now seeking its place among Europe’s major holiday destinations. And Budva seems determined to be at the forefront.

How ‘solar bonds’ could cut your energy bills without upfront installation costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
05:00:07 UTC
14:00:07 KST

A solar bonds scheme could absorb the financial impact of rooftop solar, while keeping your energy bill savings. Here’s how.
Interest in rooftop solar has surged in recent months, as Europeans scramble to protect themselves from the spiralling costs of fossil fuels.
According to an EU-wide analysis published in the Nature Energy journal, rooftop solar photovoltaics (solar PV) could supply around 40 per cent of Europe’s electricity by 2050. However, only around 10 per cent of Europe’s building rooftops are currently equipped with PV.
Governments across the continent are trying to bolster uptake by offering generous subsidies or financial perks. For example, in Ireland homeowners can receive grants of up to €1,800 through the country’s sustainable energy scheme – while public grants in Hungary can cover up to two-thirds of solar panel costs for homeowners providing they meet specific requirements.
Many other countries such as Germany and the Netherlands have implemented benefits such as 0 per cent VAT on solar panel sales and installation to make the switch more affordable. However, heavy upfront installation costs remain a huge barrier – particularly among low-income households.
But, could ‘solar bonds’ be the magic solution?
How much do solar panels cost and how long does it take to see a return?
The cost of installing solar panels can vary significantly, as there are many factors that can affect the pricing.
According to solar firm LOGI, a single family home in Europe typically needs between 6 and 15 kWp of solar power, depending on household size, heat pump use and electric car charging, which costs anything from €7,000 to €30,000. In the UK, a typical 4.5 kWp system is about £7,600 (€8,831).
While solar panels can save homeowners hundreds of euros on their energy bills every year, it can take time before you will see a return on your investment. Again, this can vary depending on multiple factors – including how much you have electrified your home, whether you work from home, and what type of tariff you are on.
Many experts, including the UK’s Energy Savings Trust, say it could take a typical home at least 10 years to recoup the costs of installing panels. It also requires hefty capital for installation, which in itself can cost up to £10,000 (€11,621). For many homeowners, this means taking out a loan subject to interest.
The need for ‘solar bonds’
This is why Dr Donal Brown, a senior researcher in energy policy and political economy at the Environmental Change Institute (ECI) is calling for government-backed finance to make rooftop solar more affordable.
Published by the Common Wealth thinktank, the report, titled A Right to the Sun, proposes a universal Solar Bond scheme under which all households with a suitable roof would be eligible to access solar panels without credit checks or other eligibility requirements that are usually associated with conventional loans.
This cost would be repaid over a 25-year period through household energy bills, with the finance attached to the property rather than the homeowner. This means if you move out, the loan and finance stays with the property, so the panels and their remaining repayments would be passed onto the next occupier.
The report found that such a scheme could save households at least £83 (€96) a year (or almost double with a battery) even when the cost of finance repayments are taken into account.
“Delivering this programme would also provide an opportunity to create jobs and improve livelihoods in communities across the UK,” the report says.
“A healthy market for rooftop solar installations already exists, with the Solar Trade Association estimating more than 42,000 new jobs could be created by an expanded rollout by 2030.”

Helen Goh’s recipe for brown butter apple and blackberry bars | The sweet spot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
05:00:02 UTC
14:00:02 KST

September is always a wistful time for me. Summer has all but slipped away, the days are noticeably shorter and the children are heading back to school. But there is comfort, too, in settling back into familiar routines. These bars, with their buttery oat crust, soft fruit filling and crisp, golden topping, are just the sort of thing to have waiting for whenever everyone drifts home. I like to use a mixture of apples – some that soften and collapse into the filling, others that hold their shape – to give the bars a little more texture and interest.
Brown butter apple and blackberry bars
These will keep for up to three days in an airtight container, and also freeze well, wrapped individually for convenience.
Prep 10 min
 Cook 1 hr 20 min
 Makes 12 bars
For the crumb base and topping
  250g unsalted butter, plus extra for greasing
  1 tsp anise seeds (optional)
220g plain flour
  95g rolled oats
80g oat flour, or blitz rolled oats until finely ground
150g light brown sugar
  ½ tsp fine sea salt
For the fruit filling
750g apples (5-6 medium apples), peeled, cored and cut into 1cm dice (about 600g net weight)
80g caster sugar
  Finely grated zest of 1 unwaxed lemon
  3 tbsp lemon juice
  Seeds from ½ vanilla bean pod, or ½ tsp vanilla bean paste
1 bay leaf
  1 cinnamon stick
1 pinch fine sea salt
  1½ tbsp cornflour
  300g blackberries
Grease and line a 20cm x 30cm baking tin with greaseproof paper, leaving enough overhang to help lift out the bars later. Put the butter in a medium saucepan on a medium heat and cook, swirling the pan occasionally, for about five minutes, until it smells nutty and the milk solids turn a deep golden brown. Take off the heat, stir in the anise seeds, if using, then leave to cool for five minutes.
Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Meanwhile, mix the plain flour, rolled oats, oat flour, brown sugar and salt in a large bowl. Pour over the browned butter, including all the toasted milk solids, and mix until evenly moistened. The mixture should resemble damp sand and hold together when squeezed.
Reserve about 350g of the crumb mix for the topping, then tip the rest into the lined tin, pressing firmly into an even layer ; use the base of a measuring cup or back of a spoon. This will help the bars hold together neatly when slicing. Bake for 18 minutes, until lightly golden around the edges.
While the base is in the oven, make the filling. Putu the diced apples, sugar, lemon zest and juice, vanilla, bay, cinnamon and salt in a large, deep frying pan on medium-high heat and cook, stirring occasionally, for five minutes, until the apples have softened slightly but still hold their shape.
Mix the cornflour with a tablespoon of water to make a smooth slurry, then stir into the apples. Cook for 30 seconds, until the juices thicken, then gently fold in the blackberries, just long enough for some to soften and colour the apples, while leaving plenty still whole. Discard the bay leaf and cinnamon stick.
Spread the fruit evenly over the baked base, then squeeze handfuls of the reserved crumb into irregular clusters and scatter over the fruit. A few gaps are nice so the fruit can peek through. Bake for 40-45 minutes, until the topping is deeply golden and the fruit juices are bubbling around the edges. Leave to cool completely in the tin before slicing into bars.

‘Capitalism is dying’: in Luton, these former car workers have a moral tale for our times | Aditya Chakrabortty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
05:00:01 UTC
14:00:01 KST

After everything, why would anyone still back Nigel Farage? In some of the comments below my piece last week about Reform UK, I spot the usual answers: Farage’s supporters are dim, racist, deplorable. Yet away from Westminster and the news cycle, Reform voters are being manufactured – not with headlines or crypto funds but through the failure of institutions they once trusted to protect them. To see what I mean, leave SW1 and go 40 miles up the road, to Luton.
In a deserted hotel bar, five men are reminiscing about how their world ended. Their minds are on a Friday afternoon in March last year, as the place where they had worked for two or three decades apiece, making friends and even meeting future wives, is about to shut for good.
Vauxhall came to Luton not long after the death of Queen Victoria; it helped build the town and gave it an economy and an identity. At its peak in 1971, the company directly employed 37,000 staff in Britain, mostly in Luton. Now it is leaving. On this afternoon, these men and so many of their soon-to-be ex-workmates are crowded around the assembly line. As the last white van comes off, they clap and cheer with pride for what they had been part of. Some cry. “It’s as if you had lost someone in your family,” remembers Paul Geary, whose ties with this place are four generations deep.
“It’s such a chunk of your life,” says Gerald Shalvey, who gave the company 34 years of his. Later, he walks back out on to the line and surveys the site where until this afternoon 1,600 people had worked. For the first time ever, the machinery is still and he hears nothing but silence: “an industrial graveyard”. Then he wonders what comes next, for him, his mates and his town.
For the hard right and far right alike, Luton is a contemporary hell. The star of countless memes and YouTube films, it spells migrants, Muslims and growing poverty. For some key players, the connection is personal. Luton boy Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as Tommy Robinson, has talked of how his stepfather worked at Vauxhall. Andrew Tate grew up in what he calls “the worst area of the worst town” (actually, the same estate as Geary). They lived through Luton’s long decline; then they monetised it.
The ex-Vauxhall workers talking to me are nothing to do with the rightward exploitation. But since their factory’s closure, they have seen fellow union members switch in droves from voting for Keir Starmer in 2024 to backing Farage. It’s not just Labour; their disgust is at a society they feel has let them and their families go under. A similar process is at work in other “industrial graveyards” from Grangemouth to Port Talbot and across the west.
In the east German province of Saxony-Anhalt, the far right looks set this weekend to win governing power for the first time in decades. Its current state premier, Sven Schulze, knows why: “We’ve seen how quickly we can lose our jobs, how quickly a company can disappear. That’s the experience east Germans have had, and it’s far deeper than west Germans think.”
There isn’t the space here to look closely at how Vauxhall left Luton, but the final episode comes in three parts. First, the then boss of the company’s owner, Stellantis, visits the plant early in 2023 and tells staff they need to halve manufacturing costs to compete with employees in Turkey. Whether Luton lives or dies is in their hands, he says, ending: “Good luck”. (These events were recalled by several employees and were not disputed by Stellantis.) Workers and managers collaborate and through a lot of sacrifice almost halve costs. It makes no odds: late in 2024, Stellantis announces it will close a plant that is profitable. Only Ellesmere Port will be kept open.
“Corporate greed,” say the trade unionists, who make counter-proposal after counter-proposal, to no avail. Some Unite members grumble to me about their leaders not fighting hard enough, and cite among examples a key meeting with the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, which the Unite head, Sharon Graham, did not attend but sent an aide. (When I checked this with Unite’s press office, it replied with lawyers’ letters and a statement saying Graham had “a pre-arranged meeting” but that she had negotiated directly with both Starmer and Reynolds on a government package of support to keep Luton open.)
Labour ministers make clear they will “support” Stellantis financially and otherwise to stay at Luton. But in dealing with this multinational carmaker, a G7 government does not have much more sway than a shop-floor steward. At the start of 2025, a frustrated Reynolds writes to a Luton MP that “despite these repeated offers from my department, Stellantis have been unwilling to engage in any discussions”. Then comes that Friday afternoon in March. As their factory closes for ever, workers are given a commemorative brochure and a medal made of scrap metal.
Now see this from a Luton worker’s point of view. The company to whom you’ve given half your life has first castigated you for not being as cheap as your Turkish counterparts, then upped and left. The union to whom you pay your subs wasn’t able to stop it going. Also impotent was the Labour government you voted for – again. Luton lost its car plant under Tony Blair, it lost its van plant under Starmer. Now you’re out of work, and – in the case of Mohammed Hussain, sitting next to me – you’ve just bought a house with a hefty mortgage. More than a year later, he’s still out of work.
Throughout our conversation, one man has barely spoken. Malik Mahmood cleaned at Vauxhall for 26 years; only now do his words come, in fits and starts.
“One year I struggled for work.” He went for so many jobs – “50? 60? Fucking loads” – but this honest man with a quarter-century of loyal service found no takers. The big black mark, he thought, was age: Mahmood is deep into his 60s. After months of burning through his Vauxhall payout, he took jobseeker’s allowance, walking through the town to sign on, getting £84 a week and an inquisition from jobcentre staff. He mimics them – “What you did? Have you found a job?” His face is etched with years of hard work and worry.
A few months ago, Unite published an internal report on the lessons from the closure of Vauxhall Luton. It’s a rare document, not least because trade unions like to celebrate victories rather than dwell on defeats, and this is its first mention anywhere in the press. At its heart is a survey of ex-Vauxhall workers and the finding that, a year after closure, like Mahmood and Hussain, 30% were still unemployed. At the same time, the report found, those ex-workers switched their politics. Less than 10% backed Labour as of this spring; more than 50% supported Farage.
In June, Mahmood finally landed a position in one of the new warehouses out of town. Now he depends on a mate to give him a lift into work, and his pay today is £1,000 a month lower than it was 18 months ago. This is typical of other Vauxhall survivors, the Unite report shows: even the winners have lost out. Getting laid off in a cost of living crisis is expensive, and the men here today rely on family members for help, and cut back on heating and groceries.
In the late 1960s, a group of sociologists visited then booming Luton, interviewing workers at Vauxhall and elsewhere for a renowned series of books, titled The Affluent Worker. Its central question was: when the working classes get middle-class salaries and mod cons, what happens to their class identity? Sixty years later, Britain is running the experiment in reverse, driving working-class families into deprivation and smashing up their communities. The results are not yet in, but they look bad.
The closure of Vauxhall Luton leaves a “vacuum”, says Geary: economically, socially and politically. “These were solid jobs with pensions and you were getting good money. You could get qualifications, a mortgage. What are the kids going to train at school to be? All on social media?” That vacuum, he says, is where the hard right and far right step in.
None of them set much store by Andy Burnham’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain. The workers have gone, and so have their skills. The economic models these guys discuss now are Donald Trump’s protectionism and Beijing’s historic public investment. European social democracy doesn’t rate a mention. “The system of capitalism is dying because people are seeing it’s not worked,” says Gary Reay.
We end by doing the photos, walking along the road that was once all Vauxhall. To get from one end of the site to the other was once a 15-minute walk filled with noise and people. Now the only sound is planes screaming away to holiday destinations. Shalvey points out the large Vauxhall badge still hanging from a brick wall. “What a waste,” he says. “What an idiotic waste of potential.”
- 
  Aditya Chakrabortty is a Guardian columnist

Europe weighs solutions to curtail Russia’s growing hybrid warfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
05:00:01 UTC
14:00:01 KST

Russia’s suspected sabotage campaign across Europe appears to be gathering pace again, confronting governments with a problem they have struggled to solve since the start of the war in Ukraine: how to impose a meaningful cost on Moscow for attacks that remain deliberately below the threshold of conventional war.
Over the past month alone, an explosives-laden drone was discovered next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport, Poland has faced suspected acts of sabotage, and a string of unexplained explosions and fires have hit defence facilities supplying Ukraine across Europe.
The attacks, aimed at sowing chaos and undermining support for Ukraine, vary widely in their ambition and sophistication, but share a common feature: they are often difficult to trace conclusively back to Moscow.
That ambiguity is built into the way the operations are organised. Russian intelligence services have shifted away from relying primarily on professional operatives dispatched across Europe. Instead, suspected saboteurs are increasingly recruited remotely, including through Telegram channels, and paid in cryptocurrency to carry out individual tasks – allowing the Russian intelligence officers directing them to remain safely at home.
The pattern was evident in Denmark this week, where authorities warned that Moscow was recruiting Danish citizens to carry out sabotage against defence companies with ties to Ukraine.
But the growing scale of the attacks, and the speed with which European governments are now prepared to point the finger at Moscow, suggest the mood may be changing.
When an incendiary parcel burst into flames at DHL’s Leipzig hub in July 2024, it took about nine months before German investigators reported a concrete link to the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency.
This time, Berlin moved far faster. Within days of the second incident at Leipzig airport, German officials publicly blamed Moscow – a sign both of growing confidence in identifying Russian operations and diminishing patience with what officials see as an increasingly brazen campaign of sabotage.
Yet while Berlin has become quicker to point the finger at Moscow, its punishment for now has followed a more cautious path.
Germany’s response to the failed Leipzig drone attack appeared calibrated to keep tensions in check, underscoring the harder question of what Europe can actually do beyond sanctions and diplomatic expulsions without risking a direct military confrontation.
Berlin announced the closure of a Russian cultural centre and a Russian consulate, prompting Moscow to shut down the already gutted Goethe-Institut – a measured retaliation rather than a real escalation.
Europe’s room for retaliation is also constrained by the powers given to its intelligence agencies. Unlike the CIA, many European services are primarily tasked with collecting intelligence and have far less latitude to conduct covert operations abroad. That leaves governments with relatively few tools between diplomatic and economic punishment on one end of the spectrum and overt military action on the other. To counter the shortcoming, several EU states, including the Netherlands, have recently put forward bills that would greatly expand the surveillance powers of the country’s intelligence agencies
One area where Europe can point to more tangible action is its growing willingness to detain vessels linked to Russia’s shadow fleet. On Wednesday, Norwegian authorities seized a Russian vessel in the Arctic archipelago of Svalbard at Ukraine’s request.
But critics argue that such measures are still not enough to deter Moscow.
“Every time we do nothing, we invite Putin to continue,” said one EU lawmaker, speaking on condition of anonymity.
That argument has been made most forcefully by Poland and the Baltic states, which have consistently pushed their western European allies to take a harder line against Moscow.
“Hybrid war is not just a nuisance on the internet,” the Polish foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, said on Thursday. “Hybrid war means assassination squads, it means arsonists, it means blowing up moving trains, like in Poland, it means breaches of airspace with drones and cruise missiles.”
“We need to convince Putin that such actions are not for free,” he added.
At the same time, Sikorski also appeared to acknowledge, somewhat jokingly, the limits of Europe’s existing toolkit. Recalling Poland’s response to previous suspected Russian operations, he said: “Every time Russia committed arson or tried to blow up a moving train … I closed one Russian consulate, but I ran out of consulates to close.”
Jakub Krupa contributed reporting

LRT English Newsletter – September 4, 2026.
Another potential corruption scandal erupted earlier this week after it became clear that a member of Lithuania’s Central Election Commission, Laura Matjošaitytė, had failed to disclose her links to the Nemunas Dawn party. She later got a job through a posting at a ministry run by the party. She denies all wrongdoing.
TELTONIKA SCANDAL
Questions surrounding Lithuania’s Teltonika goods in Belarus and Russia were rekindled after information surfaced – again – of its high-tech products entering the two countries. Teltonika maintains no wrongdoing and criticised the media investigation for allegedly failing to include its position and ignoring its proposals to cooperate in tracing the paper trail.
VILNIUS MUNICIPALITY SCANDAL
Vilnius Municipality reversed its decision to cook the rules to prevent workers’ representatives from being part of the managing boards of municipal companies. The earlier decision, backed by the Conservatives’ leadership, came under sustained criticism. Seemingly, it worked. Vilnius authorities denied any wrongdoing.
NO PLANS
You must have heard the saying – don’t believe it until Russia denies it. So now Moscow is denying it has any plans to attack the Baltic states, even reminding people that the Soviet Union had recognised the independence of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania.
BELARUS JAIL
A Lithuanian tour organiser was detained on the border after crossing into Belarus and sentenced over “extremism”. Again, Lithuania’s authorities reminded people not to travel to Belarus because exactly that can happen.
NO AIR
Despite repeated assurances from Lithuanian officials, airBaltic is halving next summer season’s flight routes from Lithuania amid the company's financial woes. Here’s a breakdown of what’s changing for travellers to and from Lithuania (as the country gears up to host the rotating EU presidency next year – not great).
Also, Lithuania’s tender for a subsidised London route has fallen apart. Poland’s LOT ran the London City–Vilnius flights until the scheme expired. Now, Lithuania sought to connect its capital with one of the main London airports for business-focused flights. The search would continue, the authorities said.
WOEING BEIJING
Lithuania is still moving slowly to restore diplomatic ties with Beijing, with one populist politician now seemingly eager to step into the breach. Ignas Vėgėlė, a former presidential hopeful who rose to prominence during his Covid-era campaigning, previously established a group in the parliament aimed at normalising China relations (he is also one of the Lithuanian MPs backing the normalisation of relations with the Minsk regime). The Seimas rejected funding for his trip to Brussels to meet with a Chinese rep, with Vėgėlė saying he will do it out of his own pocket.
And it’s not just Vėgėlė who proposed renewing contacts with Minsk. Now, the Seimas speaker, a social democrat, also said Vilnius should pursue dialogue – while also strengthening sanctions. Recall, there was much ado about the socdem’s approach to Belarus.
MIGRATION UPDATE
Eager to improve Lithuanian language proficiency among migrants, vocational training will now be offered only in Lithuanian (or bilingual). Find more details in the article here.
Now, the visible uptick in migration in Lithuania’s main cities is driving political rhetoric and economic reckoning. Namely, should Lithuania reconsider its current quota system? This year’s limit of 24,700 workers was exhausted in July, with business reps calling for a higher ceiling. Opponents, like the interior minister, say businesses should better utilise the existing labour force in Lithuania.

– Is Lithuania’s military responding to the changing nature of warfare?
– An open-air art gallery in Kaunas faces destruction amid renovation push.

How will bond market turbulence affect UK consumer finances?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Home loans are vulnerable to uncertainty in the financial markets. Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHome loans are vulnerable to uncertainty in the financial markets. Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesExplainerHow will bond market turmoil affect your mortgage, pension and savings in UK?Sell-off raises concerns of higher borrowing costs for households. Here’s what it could meanThe bond market sell-off has sparked fresh fears of higher borrowing costs for UK households. We look at what the turmoil in financial markets could mean for your mortgage, pension and savings.Cost and choice of home loans Experts think that the pricing on new fixed-rate mortgages could start rising again as a result of the bond market turbulence. That is because lenders get funding for home loans from the money markets.Fixed mortgage rates are largely influenced by “swap rates” rather than the Bank of England base rate. These wholesale rates can react rapidly to changing inflation expectations and financial market uncertainty.The spike in UK government borrowing costs has caused swap rates to jump sharply over the past week.On Thursday, Coventry Building Society was the first notable player to move, warning brokers of its intention to hike fixed-rate deals for new and existing borrowers from Monday. Other lenders are expected to reprice their mortgages in the coming days.This is Groundhog Day for borrowers, many of whom will feel as if they have been down this road before. But so far, the reaction from lenders has not been on the same scale as in the wake of the Liz Truss government’s disastrous mini budget in 2022, or even this spring, when the outbreak of war in the Middle East caused an economic storm.But Rachel Springall, a finance expert at the data provider Moneyfacts, says the jump in swap rates does “not bode well for borrowers, as lenders use swap rates as a key influence to reprice their fixed-rate mortgages”.With the majority of existing mortgage holders on a fixed-rate product, the current situation is a bigger deal if you need to remortgage soon or are trying to buy your first home. On Thursday, the average rate on a new two-year fixed-rate mortgage stood at 5.59%, while the typical rate on a five-year deal was 5.63%. In April these rates were at 5.9% and 5.78% respectively.David Stirling, an independent financial adviser at Belfast-based Mint Wealth, said: “Coventry won’t be the last, as lenders watch each other like hawks, and once one has repriced, the rest follow within a week purely to avoid being the cheapest rate on the market and getting swamped with applications they can’t fund at that price. “My advice to anyone looking to remortgage or purchase right now is simple: lock in your offer of a rate now.”PensionsIf you are aged under 50 and are saving into a pension, it is unlikely any of your money will be in bonds. It is instead probably going into stock market-based investments, and any short-term fall in the FTSE (it actually rose on Thursday after falling back earlier in the week) could be good news as you will get more shares for your money.If you are retired, you may have investments in government bonds (gilts) for the income they provide. These investors do not need to worry about changing prices and yields as they will still get the fixed cash payment – called a coupon – as expected. But the current turmoil is potentially a bigger worry for workers approaching retirement.It is very common for more of members’ pension pots to be moved into gilts as their retirement date gets nearer. If this is the case, and it is now time to sell those gilts, the investor could get less than they bargained for.“If you are closer to retirement, it’s worth reviewing what you are invested in, especially if you’re in a ‘lifestyling’ strategy that moves you out of equities into bonds the closer you get to retirement,” said Helen Morrissey, head of retirement analysis at the investment platform Hargreaves Lansdown.For younger workers with perhaps several decades to go until retirement, keep calm and carry on is not a bad message. You will be invested in a pension for a long time and will experience several periods of market turbulence, says Morrissey. “Taking kneejerk actions, such as changing investments or stopping contributions, can potentially make things worse by locking in losses.”Bear in mind that higher gilt yields should result in lower annuity prices, so anyone planning to trade in their pension for an annuity may not be worse off. (An annuity is a product that converts an individual’s pension pot into a regular, guaranteed income for the rest of their life).Annuity rates are usually closely linked to 15-year gilt yields, which have this week hit 28-year highs.Andrew King, pension technical specialist at Evelyn Partners, says a healthy 65-year-old buying a single-life level annuity with a five-year guarantee can now secure just over £8,000 of income with £100,000 in pension savings, compared with well below £5,000 a decade ago.Savings The most important thing for savings rates is the Bank of England base rate and where the markets expect it to be in the future.The money markets expect the Bank of England to leave interest rates on hold at 3.75% at its next policy decision on 17 September. However, the City expects one rate rise before the end of the year, and two more hikes in 2027.At the moment, the top-paying easy-access savings accounts pay about 4.5% interest or thereabouts.Sarah Coles, head of personal finance at the investment platform AJ Bell, says the current market gyrations tend to be good news for savings deals as banks usually react by increasing their interest rates. “This particularly affects fixed rate accounts, so we tend to see them move first and fastest.”“The market is already impressively competitive at the moment, so the reaction may not be particularly dramatic. However, the movements in gilt yields have actually pushed the best five-year fixed [savings] rate over 5%, and we are likely to keep seeing rates nudge up from here.”Explore more on these topicsBondsMortgagesPensionsSavings ratesInvestmentsSavingsexplainersShareReuse this content

Graham's Russia sanctions bill may not pass until US midterm elections, says Bloomberg
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04

Graham's Russia sanctions bill may not pass until US midterm elections, says Bloomberg
A Russia sanctions bill, which passed the Senate by an overwhelming majority just last month, is facing growing resistance in the US House of Representatives and is likely to be blocked at least until the November elections.
Source: Bloomberg, as cited by European Pravda
Details: The bill, authored by the late Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, a staunch supporter of Ukraine, would grant Trump authority to impose 100% tariffs on the five largest importers of Russian oil and natural gas, as well as on five countries that help Russia circumvent energy sanctions. China, India and Türkiye are the largest buyers of Russian petroleum products.
Some supporters of Ukraine in Washington have been pressing for the bill to pass as a way to demonstrate US support for Kyiv. However, it is unclear whether Trump would actually use the powers the bill would grant him, particularly with regard to China.
The overwhelming Senate vote in favour of the sanctions bill, 86 to 11, reflected the senators' desire to honour Graham's memory following his sudden death in July. The House of Representatives has taken a more cautious approach to the proposal.
On Thursday 3 September, House Speaker Mike Johnson said he doubts that the sanctions bill could be put to a vote before the 3 November congressional midterm elections. He said this was partly because lawmakers are scheduled to spend only a handful of working days in Washington over the next two months.
Johnson said senior Democrats on the Foreign Affairs and Ways and Means committees oppose the measure, pointing to broader difficulties in securing Democratic support. He added that there are also isolated "pockets" of concern among House Republicans.
"We all believe in sanctioning Russia, but you have to have the right formula if you are passing a bill. We're trying to work through that and make sure we can get a product that can get across the line," he told reporters on Thursday.
House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast said the bill is being evaluated, among other things, for its potential impact on petrol prices. Mast, a Republican from Florida, said that if the bill forces India and other buyers of Russian oil to turn to oil markets in other countries, it could drive prices higher.
"That is part of what's being evaluated right now," he said.
Petrol prices have spiked amid the war with Iran and are widely seen as a threat to the Republican majority in Congress ahead of the November midterm elections. The bill would also extend long-standing sanctions on Iran.
Meanwhile, Democrats are concerned that Trump could use the bill as a new legal basis to impose sweeping tariffs, as his existing tariffs are currently being challenged in court.
Johnson would need broad Democratic support if he were to try to pass the bill under the House's expedited procedure, which requires a two-thirds majority.
Growing concern among both Democratic and Republican lawmakers represents a victory for retailers and the influential business alliance US Chamber of Commerce, which have fuelled fears that the measure would provide the Trump administration with a new legal basis for imposing sweeping tariffs.
Background:
- Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, a co-author of the Russia sanctions bill, had previously expressed hope that it would receive final approval in September 2026.
- On 7 August, the US Senate voted 86 in favour of the Russia sanctions bill, co-authored by Graham and Blumenthal. The legislation provides for "punitive" tariffs on countries importing Russian energy resources.
- Earlier, the Senate disclosed details of the updated version of the bill.

Türkiye backs Syria chemical weapons cleanup, warns over Israeli strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
04:57:56 UTC
13:57:56 KST

Türkiye has backed Syria’s efforts to eliminate its remaining chemical weapons while warning that Israeli strikes on suspected sites could endanger civilians and destroy evidence needed to establish accountability.
Speaking at a U.N. Security Council meeting on Sept. 3, Türkiye’s permanent representative to the United Nations, Ahmet Yıldız, described the chemical weapons issue as one of the gravest legacies of the Assad era.
Syria’s willingness to work closely with the international community offered “genuine cause for optimism,” he said.
Yıldız said lasting progress would require practical, gradual and coordinated cooperation with Syrian authorities that took conditions on the ground into account.
He welcomed the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons’ July decision to restore Syria’s rights and privileges, which had been suspended since 2021, as well as agreements covering the verification of chemical weapons facilities.
Yıldız also welcomed the deployment of an OPCW team to Syria to oversee the destruction of Category 3 chemical weapons and said Türkiye awaited its report.
Years of concealment by the former government had complicated efforts to identify, secure and prepare chemical materials for destruction, he said.
Yıldız said Israeli strikes on suspected chemical weapons-related sites had made the task more difficult. Such attacks risked releasing hazardous materials, harming civilians and destroying evidence related to past chemical weapons attacks, he added.
Türkiye would continue helping Syria strengthen its technical and logistical capacity in line with OPCW standards, Yıldız said, adding that the shared goal should be “a Syria that is permanently free of chemical weapons.”

What's next?
Rowbottom and the Swans will kick off their finals campaign in the qualifying final against the Brisbane Lions at the SCG from 3:15pm AEST on Saturday. ABC Sport will live blog the match.
Sydney's James Rowbottom says he must "separate the person from the problem" in trying to support suspended teammate Nick Blakey amid a club crisis and finals campaign.
Blakey is one of five Swans players stood down for the remainder of the season for breaching the club's behavioural standards in a post-AFL match hotel party in August.
Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice have also been suspended from Sydney's finals campaign.
As the club mulls a call on the group's playing future, Blakey is reportedly searching for a trade following a deterioration in his relationship with the Swans.
Swans midfielder Rowbottom says he has only spoken to close mate Blakey about his welfare.
"I haven't spoken to Nick about any sort of details [about a trade]," Rowbottom said today.
"It's been a challenging period for him, and I'm just sort of reaching out as a friend.
"Living with him is another layer to the situation, and so I've reached out as a friend but, no, we haven't spoken about any of those sort of specifics.
"You've got to sort of separate the person from the problem when you live with someone, to try and offer support.
"I've been trying to do that."
The player suspensions are separate to a police investigation into sexual assault allegations and the events at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel after Sydney's round 23 game against Essendon on August 16.
No charges have been laid and there is no suggestion of any wrongdoing on the part of the five suspended players.
Rowbottom would not be drawn when asked if he was open to the five players returning to the club before the end of the season.
The group won't be at the SCG for the club's qualifying final against Brisbane on Saturday, but have individually spoken to teammates in the lead-up to the clash.
"It's a lot more complex than what I think or believe," Rowbottom said.
"The club is working through that with them and the relevant party. Honestly, it's above my pay grade."
Heeney and Warner's absence has meant Rowbottom has taken on the bulk of the midfield work with Errol Gulden and Jai Serong.
Rowbottom had returned to the side for the round 24 clash against North Melbourne after missing two weeks with a broken hand.
"For me, personally, I just do what the team needs and I have done that for the last eight years or so," the 25-year-old said.
"My role has been ever-changing this year. I've played a lot of half-forward, a lot of midfield, a bit of wing.
"Football's ever-changing, and I'm happy to take it as it comes."

Last summer in Estonia was warmer than usual
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
04:55:00 UTC
13:55:00 KST

Last summer in Estonia was warmer than usual
According to the Environment Agency, the average air temperature last summer was 16.8 degrees Celsius.
With August, the meteorological summer came to an end. Frequent rainfall made it wetter than usual, and sunshine was in shorter supply.
However, the summer was slightly warmer than average. The mean 24‑hour air temperature reached 16.8 degrees.
The hottest day was June 29 in Valga, when temperatures climbed to 29.7 degrees. The coldest was June 2 in Kuusiku, where the nighttime minimum dropped to 3.8 degrees. July was the warmest month of the summer.
Only one short heatwave was recorded, and that occurred in southern Estonia. The summer's only tropical night took place in July in southwestern Estonia.
--
Editor: Johanna Alvin, Argo Ideon

Ankara has long been criticizing the EU for losing its impartiality over the Cyprus question after admitting Greek Cyprus into the EU, although it rejected a U.N. referendum to permanently resolve the division of the island.
Türkiye launched the 1974 Peace Operation following a coup backed by the military junta in Greece that sought to unite Cyprus with Greece. Ankara carried out the operation to restore constitutional order and protect the Turkish Cypriot community after years of intercommunal violence. Following the partition of the island, the Turkish Cypriot side is recognized solely by Ankara.

The Sterlitamak Petrochemical Plant reportedly came under attack, Russian Telegram media channels reported. The facility produces aviation fuel and other materials used by Russia’s defense industry and has been targeted by Ukrainian drones several times previously.
Bashkortostan authorities acknowledged a drone attack on Sterlitamak’s industrial zone but did not immediately identify the facility struck.

Sterlitamak has repeatedly come under Ukrainian long-range drone attack. Ukrainian drones struck the city’s petrochemical plant in November 2025 and again in April 2026, targeting a facility that supplies aviation fuel and other materials to Russia’s military-industrial complex. Most recently, drones also attacked Sterlitamak’s industrial zone on Aug. 27.
The Sterlitamak Petrochemical Plant began operating in 1963 in the Soviet Union and is owned by Russian chemical holding Ruschem, formerly called Russian Hydrogen.
Ukraine's tactic of striking oil and gas processing plants in Russia have forced some facilities to reduce or halt production, contributing to shortages of fuel for citizens and military operations, and cutting off a major source of funding for Russia’s continued aggression.

Türkiye posts three export records in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
04:53:07 UTC
13:53:07 KST

Türkiye recorded three new export highs in August, with monthly shipments reaching $23.47 billion, eight-month exports rising to $185.01 billion and the rolling 12-month total climbing to $280.3 billion.
Exports increased 8.1 percent from a year earlier in August, while the January-August total was up 4 percent, Trade Minister Ömer Bolat said on Sept. 3.
Imports, however, grew faster than exports. They rose 10.5 percent year-on-year to $28.71 billion in August, widening the monthly trade deficit by 22.3 percent to $5.24 billion.
In the first eight months, imports increased 5.3 percent to $250.79 billion, while the trade deficit grew 9.3 percent to $65.79 billion.
Bolat said exports had maintained their momentum despite weaker global conditions. Türkiye needs an additional $1.7 billion in annualized exports to meet its 2026 goods export target of $282 billion, he added.
Automotive exports rose 2.3 percent to $2.8 billion in August, while chemicals exports increased 3.4 percent to $2.7 billion. Mining exports climbed 24.4 percent to $650.5 million and ship and yacht exports advanced 22.9 percent to $100.5 million.
Defense and aerospace exports fell 38.7 percent year-on-year to $511.4 million in August, although their eight-month total remained 16.2 percent higher at $6.3 billion.
The United States accounted for the largest increase in exports during the first eight months, with shipments rising by $1.2 billion. Exports to the European Union grew 1.8 percent to $78.1 billion, while exports to Gulf countries declined 7.2 percent to $18.7 billion.
Turkish Exporters Assembly head Mustafa Gültepe said jewelry, electrical and electronics products, and ferrous and nonferrous metals made the largest contributions to August’s increase.
Gültepe welcomed recent revisions to employment support and a 250 billion Turkish Lira financing package for manufacturers but said exporters needed further measures to regain competitiveness.
“We are awaiting the new foreign-currency conversion support arrangements to be announced in October,” he said.

Nepal foreign minister denies 'compensation' claim
Nepal foreign minister Shisir Khanal on Friday clarified that his statement regarding financial compensation from countries, including India, following last week's catastrophic flash floods was from the perspective of climate change and its impact in his country.Also Read | 'Not charity': Nepal seeks compensation from major industrial emitters for deadly flood"Neither I nor anyone in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs or Government of Nepal has claimed or asked for compensation from India or any other country, including China or the United States," Khanal told ANI. "Our call has been for the global community to look at this disaster from the perspective of climate change and the impact it's having in Nepal."His clarification came after Nepal launched a diplomatic push to seek compensation from "major greenhouse gas emitters." Khanal had told local media that although the Himalayan nation contributes "virtually negligible" greenhouse gas emissions, it is bearing a "disproportionate share" of the consequences of climate change."We are paying the ultimate price for a global crisis we did not create... This is not a matter of charity; it is a matter of legal and moral liability," he told Kantipur TV, excerpts of which were published by The Kathmandu Post.
Meanwhile, the death toll from the Rasuwa floods had risen to 1,259 as of 7 pm Thursday, according to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).
'Nepal, India, and China face similar climate risks'
Khanal further stressed that Nepal, India and China share the Himalayan ecosystem and face common climate risks, calling for greater regional preparedness and international support."I've also mentioned that all three countries — China, India, and Nepal face and share similar environmental ecosystems. We are all impacted by climate change in the Himalayas as well. Our call is for all these three countries to come together to be better prepared," he added, urging the global community to recognise the broader impact of rising temperatures and climate change on vulnerable communities.
He also thanked India for its swift humanitarian assistance and underscored the need for regional cooperation.India was among the first countries to assist Nepal, sending emergency rescue equipment, modular bridge components, dewatering pumps, medical supplies and other relief materials. Its first relief aircraft arrived on August 26 with 10 tonnes of supplies, followed by 37.5 tonnes on August 27 and another 10-tonne consignment. A fifth aircraft later carried an 11-member rescue team, specialised equipment and 5.5 tonnes of essential medicines.According to Khanal, India had remained in close contact with Kathmandu and was ready to provide further assistance as needed."In this disaster context, right after the disaster, we began to receive communication from Indian officials and they have provided all kinds of support and they have said they are standing ready to provide any support that the government of Nepal needs. We've been communicating as need arises and the government of India has fully supported our initiative. So in the future also, as new requirements come up, we communicate and they stand ready to provide support," the minister said.

Trump administration to break ground on 250-foot Washington arch despite legal challenges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
04:46:25 UTC
13:46:25 KST

The Trump administration on Thursday announced plans to break ground on a 250-foot (76-meter) arch in Washington, despite legal challenges and the lack of final approval from a government planning authority.
The arch is part of Trump's broader effort to leave his architectural mark on America's capital city, with projects including a new White House ballroom, renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and redevelopment of a golf course in East Potomac Park.
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said on X/Twitter that excavation work on the Great Triumphal Arch and Military Observation Deck would start "over the next two-week period."
With a design evoking Paris' Arc de Triomphe, the monument would rise near the Arlington National Cemetery, a military burial ground, which supporters say would honor the sacrifice of American veterans.
But opponents say the arch would destroy the cemetery's carefully designed historic sight line between Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House. Although Congress approved building a memorial at the site more than 100 years ago, congressional Democrats say current congressional approval is legally required.
Lawsuit seeks to halt project, argues congressional approval required
A lawsuit seeking to halt the project also argues that Trump needs congressional approval.
The case is pending before US District Judge Tanya Chutkan, who in an April hearing sharply questioned Trump's authority to build the monument. The plaintiffs withdrew a request for a preliminary injunction after the government agreed to provide 14 days' notice before starting construction.
The project also has yet to receive final approval from the National Capital Planning Commission, which is considering whether to grant an exception to the 130-foot (40-meter) building height limit that applies to most of Washington.
The Trump administration has argued the limit should not apply to the arch.

Smoking raises death risk by 55% in people with diabetes, global experts call for active quit treatment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
04:43:34 UTC
13:43:34 KST

A meta-analysis of 48 studies involving 1.13 million people found a 55% higher risk of death, while another study of about 130,000 people with diabetes found 48% higher overall mortality and 36% higher cardiovascular mortality among smokers.
NEW DELHI: Smoking increased the risk of death from any cause by 55% among people with diabetes, according to evidence reviewed in a new international consensus that calls for smoking cessation to be treated as an essential part of type 2 diabetes care. The experts say patients who smoke should be offered medicines, intensive behavioural counselling and regular follow-up instead of being given a one-time “quit smoking” warning.The recommendations, published in Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice, are the first dedicated international consensus on smoking cessation specifically for people with type 2 diabetes. They were developed by 35 experts from 13 countries, including Indian diabetes specialist Dr Anoop Misra.
The consensus recommends varenicline as the first-line medicine where available, with nicotine replacement therapy or bupropion as alternatives when varenicline is unavailable or unsuitable. Medicines should be combined with structured, intensive behavioural support and repeated contact rather than brief counselling alone.The stronger approach reflects the added risk smoking poses in diabetes. A meta-analysis of 48 studies involving 1.13 million people found a 55% higher risk of death, while another study of about 130,000 people with diabetes found 48% higher overall mortality and 36% higher cardiovascular mortality among smokers.
Doctors should review patients within two weeks of quitting and again at four weeks, checking blood sugar, weight, blood pressure and medicines, as quitting can alter drug metabolism and sometimes require dose adjustments.Weight gain, a common concern, should not deter quitting. In a US cohort of 10,809 people with type 2 diabetes, median weight gain within six years of quitting was 3.2 kg. Long-term quitters had lower all-cause mortality than continuing smokers regardless of weight gain, with mortality hazard ratios of 0.69, 0.57 and 0.51 for no gain, up to 5 kg and more than 5 kg gain, respectively.Smoking is also linked to kidney damage in diabetes, with higher risks of albuminuria and diabetic nephropathy. A Japanese study of 2,490 people with type 2 diabetes found insulin resistance rose with cigarettes smoked per day and fell with time after quitting.
Quitting, however, can be difficult. Some patients may not recognise the link between smoking and diabetes complications, while others fear weight gain or use cigarettes to cope with stress and anxiety. The experts recommend personalised quit strategies and relapse prevention.The consensus also highlights gaps in diabetes care, where smoking cessation often remains limited to brief advice. It calls for routine smoking assessment, active treatment, metabolic monitoring and relapse prevention as part of diabetes care.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

====================================================================================================

Japan’s FOIP 3.0: Is Pragmatism That Delivers Resilience Enough?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
04:43:00 UTC
13:43:00 KST

When Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae visited Vietnam in early May this year, she presented an “evolved version” of the Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP), a key plank in Japanese foreign policy, which is being called FOIP 3.0. The “Updated FOIP” specifies as priority areas “Building economic infrastructure for the age of AI and data,” “Co-creation of economic growth opportunities through public-private collaboration and rule sharing,” and “Enhancing cooperation in the field of security to ensure regional peace and stability,” each with its own items for concrete cooperation.
The FOIP was first proposed by the late Prime Minister Abe Shinzo in a speech in Nairobi in 2016. The keyword for FOIP 1.0 was “connectivity,” reflecting the fact that it was launched in the middle of a major shift in the power balance triggered by the rise of China.
International division has only deepened since, following the outbreak of the Russo-Ukrainian war, and with the rise of the Global South, international politics have become more complex still. It was in response to this that then Prime Minister Kishida Fumio proposed the New Plan for a FOIP, or FOIP 2.0, in 2023, along with the keyword “inclusiveness.”
Building on this foundation, the keyword for FOIP 3.0 as proposed by the Takaichi administration is “resilience.” With any improvement of relations with China unlikely in the near time, and with the United States pursuing an exceedingly unpredictable foreign policy under Trump, Japan faces what might be called a double risk. It needs to deepen cooperation with Indo-Pacific countries to mitigate those risks and ensure autonomy and resilience. The new FOIP is thus heavily shaped by the imperative to revitalize the Japanese economy and strengthen economic security through cooperation with the Global South, including the ASEAN countries.
The idea of connecting Japanese growth strategy, economic security, and Global South strategy has been clear enough since the Kishida administration. That administration adopted the New Policy toward Enhanced Cooperation with Global South Countries in June 2024. It also implemented institutional schemes to strengthen cooperation with the Global South, such as launching the Global South Future-Oriented Co-Creation Project and Official Security Assistance (OSA) as well as reforming the Official Development Assistance (ODA). The Asia Zero Emission Community (AZEC) is another scheme launched under that administration. However, whereas FOIP 2.0 emphasized Japan’s ideal international order and its commitment to that order, FOIP 3.0 does not define an order as explicitly; instead it pushes a pragmatism that more clearly emphasizes economic renewal and the restoration of Japan’s vitality.
The three priority areas specified in the FOIP 3.0 each list their own spheres for concrete cooperation. They are the 17 strategic fields identified by the Council for Japan’s Growth Strategy established under the Takaichi administration, areas in particular where Japan wants to promote development, with special emphasis being placed on AI and semiconductors, digital server security, and information and communications, quantum technology, and other fields that are relevant to digital hegemony.
What the times may call for is precisely this kind of pragmatism: an emphasis on revitalizing the Japanese economy and strengthening economic security in the name of “resilience.” Resilience has become an equally important theme for the ASEAN countries as they navigate what one might call the “geoeconomic turn.” Confronted with Trump tariffs, the energy supply disruptions from the Strait of Hormuz crisis, and related pressures, they have become increasingly interested in cooperation to mitigate geoeconomic risks. Key to surviving this uncertainty will be each ASEAN country’s ability to connect its national interests and resilience to broader cooperation across the region. Through FOIP, Japan aims not only to cooperate with individual ASEAN countries but to support ASEAN’s collective efforts to build resilience, contributing to risk mitigation across the region.
Japan can no longer rely on overwhelming economic power and technological advantage as the basis for cooperation with ASEAN countries and other parts of the Global South. There are limits to cooperation built solely on the pragmatism of shared gains. For Japan to earn the trust of ASEAN countries and others in the Global South, it must also clearly demonstrate its commitment to a rules-based international order capable of constraining the arbitrary actions of major powers. Japan is advancing concrete initiatives, but it must also clearly articulate the worldview behind FOIP — the kind of order it is trying to build — in light of today’s upheavals.

US drone tariffs go into effect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
04:36:41 UTC
13:36:41 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – US drone tariffs on imported drones and key components took effect on Thursday, CNA reported.
The White House said the policy aims to reduce dependence on Chinese supply chains and boost domestic production. President Donald Trump signed the executive order on Aug. 13 after an investigation by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick claimed that foreign producers of drones and components threatened national security.
The US has imposed tariffs up to 100% on larger drones with capabilities deemed particularly sensitive, including those weighing over 25 kg with thermal imaging capabilities, as well as their docking stations and key components. Smaller drones that do not pose security risks will face a 25% tariff, while less-sensitive drone components will be taxed on Feb. 9, 2027.
Drones and components from Taiwan, the European Union, Japan, Liechtenstein, South Korea, and Switzerland face a 15% tariff. Drones from the UK received a lower 10% tariff.
The policy targets Chinese manufacturers like DJI, which controls more than 70% of the global drone market. The US has blacklisted DJI since 2022 for ties to the People's Liberation Army.

Cabinet proposes NT$145.7 billion in additional Taiwan defense spending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
04:36:41 UTC
13:36:41 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Cabinet on Thursday approved NT$145.7 billion (US$4.64 billion) in additional defense spending for 2026, including funding for missile systems and uncrewed vehicles excluded from a special defense procurement law.
The Cabinet approved a record NT$607.6 billion in supplemental spending for the 2026 central government budget, per Rti. The defense allocation includes NT$4.1 billion for personnel, NT$8.2 billion for operations, and NT$133.4 billion for military investment.
The personnel funding includes NT$2.5 billion to expand military recruitment and NT$1.6 billion to increase allowances for combat units and eligible personnel. The operating budget includes NT$7.3 billion for ammunition and NT$900 million for the Taiwan Tactical Network integration project.
The military investment portion includes NT$13 billion for seven projects, NT$55.9 billion for three types of drones, and NT$64.5 billion for two classified projects, Rti reported. The package also includes funding for the Integrated Battle Command System, Chien Kung missiles, and uncrewed vehicles covered by the recently passed unmanned vehicle law.
Cabinet Spokesperson Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) directed that the systems be included because national defense could not wait for the legislative process, according to Rti. The Legislative Yuan previously approved a scaled-back version of the special defense procurement law that excluded the unmanned systems and other domestically developed weapons.
Lee said the government would review the legislation and its implementation after receiving it Wednesday. She said the supplemental budget was intended to make up for delays in military buildup.
Department of Strategic Planning Director Lieutenant General Huang Wen-chi (黃文啓) said the special defense budget was originally NT$1.25 trillion and covered 23 items, per CNA. Because the full amount was not approved, the 13 items for domestic production, commercial purchases, and Taiwan-US joint development were included in the supplemental budget.
Huang said the supplemental budget was proposed primarily based on the military buildup schedule, as uncrewed vehicle units began forming last year and all units were in place as of January. The military plans to procure 40,000 coastal attack drones, 600 coastal reconnaissance drones, and 100 small one-way unmanned surface vessels in 2027, per Storm Media.
