VLADIVOSTOK, September 3. /TASS/. Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsiya) will interact with the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) on maintaining the safety of commercial flights, head of the agency Dmitry Yadrov told reporters, adding that there have been no official contacts so far.
"If there was such a request, it must be considered by the ICAO Council, after which a decision may be taken to notify ICAO member states of the information contained in the request. We will surely talk with the International Civil Aviation Organization," he said on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF).
Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency has not received any requests so far, Yadrov noted. "We have seen an ICAO commentary on that matter. However, there have been no official contacts so far. Obviously, we will also work on that issue with the Russian Foreign Ministry for them to join the matter as well," he said.
ICAO does not have the authority to close airspace over Russia, the agency’s head explained. "They can only make recommendations," he said.
Earlier, ICAO said in response to a request from TASS that the global risk of weapons being used against passenger aircraft was rising, adding that states should take more active measures to protect civil aviation from threats associated with armed conflicts. The organization considers it essential to share intelligence promptly regarding potential threats to aircraft and to conduct more thorough risk assessments for flights within national airspace. ICAO is also updating its recommendations on flight safety over and near conflict zones and is urging countries to make firmer commitments to protect civil aircraft.
Earlier, Russian President Vladimir Putin commented on Vladimir Zelensky’s "warning" to airlines regarding the danger of flying over Russia, saying that Moscow would find means to respond if the Kiev regime’s threats against civil aviation are carried out. Threats against civil aviation amount to an act of state terrorism, he stressed, adding that one does not negotiate with terrorists. In turn, Russian Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin said that the ministry found solutions to ensure the safety of civil aviation and would not tolerate threats.
The Eastern Economic Forum is taking place on September 1-4 in Vladivostok on the campus of the Far Eastern Federal University. The main theme of this year’s EEF is "The Far East: Development for the Benefit of People." The event is organized by the Roscongress Foundation with the support of the Russian government. MOSCOW, September 3. /TASS/. As part of a comprehensive upgrade, Russia’s Zanoza-10 FPV drone has been equipped with artificial intelligence for automatic target acquisition, the manufacturer, Zanoza Drones, told TASS.

23:43:54 KST

More than 18 Houthis have been killed and others wounded or captured as Yemeni government forces repelled an attack and launched a counteroffensive west of Taiz, the army’s media centre said.
The Houthis attacked army positions in the Maqbanah Mountains, attempting to infiltrate areas including Al-Ahtoub, Al-Tuwair, Al-Kadha and Jabal Ghabari, according to the statement on Thursday.
Yemeni forces thwarted the infiltration attempts before launching a counterattack against Houthi positions, backed by concentrated artillery fire targeting their positions and gatherings.
Drones shot down as fighting intensifies
The army said more than 18 Houthis were killed, while others were wounded and several were captured. It added that the bodies of some Houthi members remained in the areas where clashes took place.
Army air defences also shot down three Houthi drones attempting to target military positions, while several Houthi vehicles were destroyed, killing those aboard, according to the statement.
Yemen’s official television broadcast footage showed Houthi prisoners captured during the fighting on Taiz’s western fronts, but did not give a number.
Renewed clashes challenge fragile lull
The escalation followed reports that Houthis had targeted areas in Taiz and Hudaida provinces with 14 ballistic missiles and drone attacks, according to the Yemeni army.
Yemen has experienced a relative lull since April 2022 in a conflict that began nearly 12 years ago, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and other areas in 2014.
Fighting has intensified again in recent weeks in provinces including Marib, Al-Jawf, Al-Dhalea and Taiz.
The renewed violence comes as Yemen continues to face severe humanitarian and economic crises. A Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government supports government forces, while Iran is accused of supporting the Houthis.
The Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia in July.

New EU border system triggers hours-long queues at Brussels Airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:40:56 UTC
23:40:56 KST

Non-European travellers arriving at Brussels Airport faced waiting times of up to three hours at border control during peak morning hours on Thursday due to the rollout of the EU's new Entry/Exit System (EES) and a seasonal surge in returning holidaymakers.
Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens confirmed the delays to Dutch-language public broadcaster VRT, noting that non-European passengers experienced three-hour queues upon arrival. By contrast, European citizens using automated passport-control gates experienced shorter wait times, generally between 30 and 60 minutes.
The delays stem largely from the implementation of the EES, a digital border-management system that electronically registers non-European nationals entering and leaving the Schengen Area.
The system replaces physical passport stamps with biometric checks, including fingerprints and facial scans.
"The registration requires more steps and time per passenger. As a result, waiting times build up rapidly during busy periods," Franssens said.
Although the Belgian government deployed additional Aviation Police personnel ahead of the summer season to staff all available control booths, the airport reported that the extra workforce has proven insufficient during high-volume periods.

Lives on hold: Young Iranians watch their futures slip away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:40:11 UTC
23:40:11 KST

Share & more
The past six months of bombs, geopolitical tensions and the looming threat of a wider conflict have created a suffocating sense of uncertainty for many Iranians. And it’s not just about the airstrikes. Young people say the period since the US and Israel first struck their country in late February has been one of anxiety-inducing limbo, with their futures put on hold indefinitely.
The New Humanitarian spoke to five young Iranians in the capital, who shared what it feels like to be trapped, watching their best years slip away. From cancelled weddings and crushing unemployment to never-ending news updates and the vanishing of simple pleasures, their stories offer a window into what it is like to live through a war that has taken away their ability to plan for tomorrow.
In Tehran and across the country, fresh US and Iranian strikes this week were a stark reminder that, after half a year of bombing and a war of words between the US and Iran, ceasefire talks remain stalled. The Strait of Hormuz remains largely shut, while the core issues driving the conflict remain unresolved.
Iranian citizens have been left bracing for hostilities to resume at any moment. In the 40 days after the US and Israel launched attacks in late February, more than 3,500 people – including hundreds of civilians – were killed, according to the Iranian government.
While Iran’s economy has struggled for years amid sanctions, US economic pressure and the war have compounded the pain. Iranian officials have put the economic damage from the war at more than $270 billion, though the figure is a preliminary estimate. Inflation reached nearly 88% year-over-year in July with the rial hitting a record low on 2 September, while sweeping corporate budget cuts have triggered mass layoffs; more than a million people in a country of 87 million are believed to have lost their jobs.
Even when the skies over Tehran are quiet, the five young people whose words are featured here – Ziba, Nima, Fatema, Sima, and Amir Ali* – say the agony has shifted beyond the bombing itself. What weighs most heavily now is the paralysis of not knowing what comes next.
Names have been changed due to security concerns, and words have been translated, condensed, and edited for clarity.
Ziba, 27, watched her wedding plans fell apart
“Every major milestone in my life has been frozen”
My morning routine now begins before my feet even touch the floor. The very first thing I do when I wake up is grab my phone and open my main news channels. I have to scroll through everything posted overnight. The news cycle here changes by the minute. You might go to bed reading that a diplomatic agreement is imminent, only to wake up and find out that infrastructure was bombed while you were sleeping. I have to know exactly what reality I am waking up into.
The initial shock we felt when this first started has morphed into something else, but there are still moments that completely rattle me. It’s terrifying when I go outside and see massive lines of people panic-buying fuel at the petrol stations. I look at them and think, “What will happen to the city if they strike tomorrow?”
My nights are consumed by a different kind of anxiety. A few months ago, I didn't even know what [the live online flight tracker] Flightradar was. Now, before I can attempt to sleep, I am on the app monitoring the airspace over the Middle East. I check to see if civilian planes are still flying over Iran, or if flights are still landing in Israel. If I see commercial planes in the sky, I tell myself it's safe enough to close my eyes.
Even our family group chats offer no escape; they are a constant stream of terrifying rumours. Someone will forward a fake message claiming a nuclear strike is coming tonight, alongside advice to hoard food or buy power generators.
To cope with the overwhelming dread, I downloaded half a dozen mindless puzzle games on my phone. But the stress gave me such severe insomnia that I used to wake up multiple times a night just to check the news. Now, I have to take sleeping pills. When the anxiety becomes too heavy, I put on a podcast and play the puzzle games for hours, waiting for the medication to finally make my eyes heavy enough to sleep.
Every major milestone in my life has been frozen. My fiancé and I got engaged exactly 40 days before this recent wave of conflict began. We were deep into planning the wedding, but it completely fell apart. How can you book a venue, buy a wedding dress, or put down deposits when you don’t know if a war will break out tomorrow? We have stopped all planning and will probably just move into our apartment quietly without a celebration. It breaks my heart because I had to let what was supposed to be one of the best nights of my life go.
Even my smallest daily joys have vanished. I used to be obsessed with online shopping and skincare routines. I haven't bought anything in months. I am literally scraping the last drops out of my old makeup containers. Every time I think about restocking, I stop myself. I need to hoard every rial in case the economy collapses and I get laid off. And honestly, what is the point of a skincare routine if a war breaks out?
When I hang out with my friends, the panic has been replaced by a heavy numbness. Six months ago, we took every threat seriously. Now, if someone reads a headline out loud about an impending attack or a peace talk, we just laugh. We have become completely desensitised. Underneath that numbness is a profound grief. The prime years of our youth — the years we should be growing and experiencing life — are being destroyed by the egos of global powers who do not care about regular people.
Nima, 21, fears his attempt to leave Iran has set him back
“The sheer terror of being completely left behind”
For the past two years, my life has been defined by a single, obsessive goal: to emigrate from Iran by the time I turn 21. I took a massive risk and dropped out of university to make this happen. I work in video production and editing now, and every decision I’ve made since leaving school – every late night staring at editing deadlines, every rial I’ve desperately managed to save, every expensive language class I’ve paid for – has been dedicated to preparing for a visa interview at the French embassy and securing a way out. But since the conflict escalated last year, and with this endless, agonising cycle of ceasefires and new threats, my carefully constructed roadmap has been thrown into absolute chaos.
The uncertainty we are living through isn't just an abstract political talking point on the news; it is a solid brick wall standing between me and my future. I am supposed to be finalising my paperwork right now, but I wake up every morning paralysed by questions I cannot answer. If I am finally ready for my visa interview next month, will the foreign embassies in Tehran even be open? Are they quietly evacuating their diplomatic staff right now? Will any country even issue visas to young Iranians right now, or are we considered too high-risk? You just don’t know, and that not-knowing is suffocating.
The uncertainty we are living through isn't just an abstract political talking point on the news; it is a solid brick wall standing between me and my future.
Beyond the geopolitical anxieties, there is the grinding financial exhaustion of trying to survive here. Every single day, just staying afloat becomes harder. The economic fluctuations are tied to the military news cycle. You walk into a local shop and suddenly a pack of cigarettes is exponentially more expensive because of a headline about a potential strike; tomorrow the tension might ease and the price drops slightly, only to shoot up again the next day. We live completely at the mercy of breaking news alerts.
My absolute deepest fear is the very real possibility of losing on both fronts. I sacrificed my university degree for this emigration dream. I held back from fully committing to long-term career progression in the local video industry because I was saving all my energy and resources for a life abroad.
If this state of violent limbo drags on, what happens to me? I won't have my degree, I won't have advanced my career here, and I won't have successfully emigrated either. It’s the sheer terror of being completely left behind, stuck in a void. That is the heaviest burden I carry right now: the creeping realisation that while I wait for the world to decide our fate, my youth is just slipping through my fingers.
Fatemeh, 26, is being squeezed by inflation, job losses, and rising rents
“Watching the prices skyrocket day by day has been terrifying”
The first direct hit I took when the conflict escalated was deeply personal. My partner and I used to work together, but as the economic panic set in, our company began downsizing, and he was laid off. Almost overnight, we were forced into a long-distance relationship. The emotional toll of losing that daily proximity, combined with the crushing stress of his sudden unemployment, put a massive strain on both of us. But that was only the beginning.
Then came the hyperinflation. Watching the prices skyrocket day by day has been terrifying. To give a specific example: During the height of the tension, I wanted to buy a pair of sneakers that cost around four million tomans ($20). Before I could save enough, the price shot up to nearly seven million.
Food prices have increased by 100%. I’ve had to completely eliminate things from my grocery basket that I used to buy without a second thought. Something as simple as a tub of ice cream or snacks? I don’t even walk down those aisles in the supermarket anymore. I just can't justify the cost.
But the absolute hardest blow has been the threat to my basic security: my housing. The inflation resulting from these cycles of war and peace has forced everyone into survival mode. I am working much more now than I was before the conflict just to stay afloat. My roommate realised that staying in a fixed-salary job like she had was financial suicide, so she decided to pivot to doing skincare and facials because service prices and wages inflate and shift alongside the economy.
We live in central Tehran, in a neighbourhood filled with students and bookstores. It’s not the right demographic for premium beauty services. So she decided to move to west Tehran, to a neighbourhood where people have more disposable income. Her plan is to rent a one-bedroom apartment and convert half of it into a skincare studio.
Her decision left me completely stranded. The relentless inflation has wiped out my ability to save anything. I am left hovering between the earth and the sky. I don't have enough money for a new deposit. If I want to find a place of my own, I will have to drown myself in loans and borrow from everyone I know. Even then, my monthly rent will increase by 100%.
The scariest part is the logic behind my roommate's move. From the outside, taking such a massive financial risk in this unstable economy seems insane. But she firmly believes that if she doesn't make this leap this year, she will never be able to do it. The future looks so overwhelmingly dark and unpredictable that her mentality is literally now or never. She is convinced things are going to get so much worse that soon, even taking a risk will be impossible.
Sina, 20, lost the job he hoped would lift his family out of poverty
“A relentless exercise in overthinking”
I come from a lower-income, working-class family. My father is a labourer who has done gruelling physical work his entire life just to feed the family. For a brief moment, I truly thought I was going to be the one to break our family's cycle of poverty.
I had worked hard and managed to land a great, professional job. It was my golden ticket to pull myself up, build a real career, and finally change my social standing. But when the threat of war escalated and the economic shock hit, budget cuts followed immediately. I was one of the first people laid off, and my entire trajectory collapsed.
For the past five or six months, my existence has been reduced to desperately searching for work. I have sent out between 150 and 200 résumés. I’ve gone to countless interviews, but the answer is always the same. Because of the geopolitical situation and the shrinking economy, companies aren't hiring; they are completely frozen or downsizing.
Waking up every day as an unemployed 20-year-old in Tehran is a relentless exercise in overthinking. You wake up with nothing to do but obsess over what is going to happen next. Will prices go up again? You set a goal to save money to buy something basic, and by the time you reach that amount, the item has become drastically more expensive.
But the absolute hardest part is the sheer humiliation and guilt of losing my financial independence. I try to strip my expenses down to the bare minimum so I don't run out of the little money I have left. But sometimes, when I hit absolute zero, I have to ask my father for cash just to get by. At 20, with the pride of a young guy who thought he had finally made it and was supposed to start helping his family, it is a crushing feeling. Having to ask a tired, aging labourer for money just so you can buy a coffee? It completely destroys your dignity. I look at how hard he works, and the guilt eats me alive.
My biggest fear for the next year is that the inflation will spiral so far out of control that we won't be able to afford breathing. The most normal routines from a year ago are now impossible luxuries. Going out for dinner or to a cafe is something you can maybe do once every 10 days now; if you did it every night, your entire month's salary would vanish in two weeks.
People ask if I am afraid of a war breaking out. Honestly, no. I am not afraid of things coming to a head and our fate finally being decided. What genuinely terrifies me is this endless, paralysing limbo where my youth is wasted, and I am dragged right back to the bottom.
Amir Ali, 26, has seen his ambitions shrink after losing his job
“My only strategy is to do absolutely nothing”
At first, I told myself I wasn't bothered by the sound of missiles or the endless talk of war. But slowly it crept into my psyche and took over everything. My baseline level of stress has skyrocketed. I find myself becoming aggressive, snapping at things that used to be completely normal. There is this constant, heavy feeling that my basic safety is under threat.
But honestly, the hardest part isn’t the threat of war itself; it’s the absolute uncertainty. It’s the sheer paralysis of not knowing. You wake up in the morning and ask yourself, “What will happen today?” You check your phone and the news says things are calming down. Half an hour later, a new headline breaks, warning that everything is about to get worse. That relentless whiplash strips the life out of you because it makes it impossible to make a single long-term decision.
“The hardest part isn’t the threat of war itself; it’s the absolute uncertainty.”
The most immediate blow I took from the conflict was to my livelihood. I lost my main job and the steady income I relied on. That single event derailed every plan I had for the future. I had been diligently saving money for months just to upgrade my car. I wasn’t going to buy something luxurious, just a normal step forward. But with the economic shock and my lost wages, that plan evaporated. I couldn't pull the trigger.
Now, just changing my car feels like the absolute ceiling of my ambitions. Buying a house? That is a total pipe dream. Unless you have some miraculous exception, no one can buy property here on a normal salary anymore. Even the thought of getting married has been completely taken off the table. The inflation is so aggressive and the costs are so astronomical that you just give up. I genuinely don't know what to do anymore.
People ask if I have ideas to start a business or invest if things ever quieten down. The truth is, our economic environment is so deeply unhealthy and unpredictable that starting a business feels like walking into a trap.
In this climate, my only strategy is to do absolutely nothing – just freeze, keep my head down, and try to protect the little I have. You can't get a bank loan, because how can you commit to monthly repayments when you don't know if you'll have a job next week? That shadow hangs over every daily routine. I am terrified of being laid off again because no position is secure. And the saddest part is that it’s not just me. Look at anyone in my friendship circle. We are all deeply exhausted, trapped in this exact same limbo, totally clueless about what to do with our lives.
This journalist who authored this piece writes under a pseudonym due to security concerns.

Two new British support ships named at Appledore
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:38:46 BST
23:38:46 KST

The second and third ships in the Royal Fleet Auxiliary’s new Fleet Solid Support programme will be named RFA Reliant and RFA Resourceful, with the names revealed as the keel was laid for first-of-class RFA Resurgent at Appledore in North Devon, the Royal Navy has said.
The three ships are being built to provide ammunition, stores and other supplies to Royal Navy vessels at sea, including the UK’s aircraft carriers. Sections of the vessels are being constructed at Navantia facilities in Appledore and Cadiz, as well as in Belfast, before being transported to Harland & Wolff’s Belfast facility for final integration.
Commodore Sam Shattock, head of the Royal Fleet Auxiliary, announced the names of the remaining two ships during the keel-laying ceremony for RFA Resurgent, which took place on Merchant Navy Day.
He said: “Today represents the moment when vision becomes reality, when plans and drawings come to life, effectively becoming the ship’s birthday.”
On the name of the first vessel, he added: “RFA Resurgent’s name speaks of renewal, resilience and the ability recover stronger from challenge.”
“Those qualities are reflected not only in the ship itself, but also in the people who will design, build, support and ultimately sail her.”
As part of the keel-laying ceremony, a coin was welded to the keel of RFA Resurgent by a Navantia UK apprentice, continuing a shipbuilding tradition marking the formal start of construction.
Each Fleet Solid Support ship will have a core RFA crew of 101, with accommodation for a further 80 personnel when required. Those additional personnel could include teams operating helicopters and boats or carrying out other specialist roles.
The vessels are intended to replenish Royal Navy ships with munitions, supplies and provisions while at sea. The Royal Navy says they will also be able to support wider operational activity, including counter-piracy and counter-terrorism missions and operations alongside allied forces.
The design also includes energy-efficient technologies intended to reduce power consumption. The ships are being built with the ability to use low-carbon, non-fossil fuels and future sustainable energy sources, with the Royal Navy saying the design is intended to allow the vessels to achieve Carbon Zero status by the end of their planned 30-year operational lives.
RFA Resurgent revives a name previously carried by a merchant vessel converted into a fleet replenishment ship in 1957. That ship remained in service until 1979 and supported a Joint Services scientific expedition to the Indian Ocean in 1975.
The name RFA Reliant has previously been used by three vessels, including stores and air stores support ships and a helicopter support ship. The most recent Reliant was a merchant vessel taken into naval service in 1983 and used during the multinational deployment to Lebanon in 1984, including during evacuation operations. She was sold in 1986 after being replaced in the helicopter support role by RFA Argus.
RFA Resourceful is a new name for the RFA, selected to follow the adjective-based naming convention of the class. The Royal Fleet Auxiliary previously operated an armament stores ship named RFA Resource, which served between 1966 and 1997 and received battle honours for the Falklands and Kuwait.
The Fleet Solid Support programme is also intended to support investment in UK shipyards, apprenticeships, skilled employment and domestic supply chains, while combining work in Britain with construction and expertise from Navantia’s Spanish facilities.

Scottish Government moves to strengthen defence industry
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
15:33:11 BST
23:33:11 KST

The Scottish Government is developing a new Defence Industrial Growth Programme intended to increase the economic benefit Scotland receives from defence, with ministers pointing to security pressures, high-value employment and the need to strengthen long-term industrial resilience.
The commitment appears in the Programme for Government, which says ministers will “establish a responsible defence industrial growth programme to maximise the economic benefits to Scotland from increased UK and allied defence spending.”
A Scottish Government spokesperson told the UK Defence Journal: “Scotland is well placed to seize the opportunity of increased UK defence spending with a highly skilled workforce, world-class universities and internationally recognised manufacturing. The conflict in Ukraine is a reminder of the increasingly complex and immediate threats we face, underlining the importance of maintaining a strong and resilient defence capability.
“Our aerospace, defence, security and space sectors contribute around £3.7 billion to the economy and support approximately 37,000 jobs. We can maximise the economic benefits of these sectors through a responsible approach while supporting innovation, skills development and building long-term economic resilience.
“The Cabinet Secretary for Economy will meet with representatives from across the sector to discuss how the Defence Industrial Growth Programme can maximise the economic benefits arising from increased UK and allied defence spending, supporting economic growth, high-value jobs and national resilience. Further details of the Programme will be announced in due course.”
Defence procurement remains reserved to the UK Government, but the Scottish Government and Parliament control a number of areas which affect the industrial base, including skills, economic development, business support, research and innovation.
Scotland already hosts substantial parts of the UK defence industry. BAE Systems is building Type 26 anti-submarine warfare frigates on the Clyde, while Babcock is constructing Type 31 frigates at Rosyth. The wider sector also includes radar, optronics, aerospace, underwater systems, engineering and other defence supply-chain activity.
SNP Westminster leader Dave Doogan said the programme would operate against a wider backdrop of pressure on defence spending and procurement.
Doogan told me: “There is an awkward truth at the centre of Andy Burnham’s new government which is that his new chancellor appears unable to provide the quantum to invest in defence that he, as Defence Secretary, resigned in protest over. This matters across the defence industrial complex and that includes here in Scotland. When a government is self-evidently unable to fund its own defence obligations it does not inspire the private investment in people or capital that our sector requires.
Confidence in Scottish defence product in our allies has never been higher across all domains and the MOD must capitalise on this with base load orders placed in good time and in full rather than piecemeal treasury drip feeding. Mr Burnham says Westminster isn’t working and he wants to change things, he could start by injecting some much needed pace and ambition into defence procurement.”
Former SNP defence spokesman Stewart McDonald also welcomed the announcement and highlighted the powers already available to the Scottish Government and Parliament in areas surrounding defence industry.
McDonald told me: “This is a welcome and, in some ways, overdue announcement from the Scottish Government. It’s welcome because it’s the pursuit of our own domestic security interests and that of our allies and partners, but also in terms of our domestic economic interest. Defence may be reserved but the Scottish Government and Parliament have considerable powers that can ensure Scotland’s defence sector is operating at full pace – particularly around skills, R&D, public finance and innovation.
“The key is to ensure the defence programme is agile, inclusive of key strategic partners and wastes no time in getting to work. I’m looking forward to seeing how it pans out.”
The Scottish Government has not yet set out the level of funding attached to the programme or the specific forms of support that will be offered. Ministers say the Cabinet Secretary for Economy will meet representatives from across the sector before further details are announced.

Ukraine lags behind Russia in AI tech application for drones — Zelensky’s adviser

23:31:05 KST

MOSCOW, September 4. /TASS/. Ukraine has so far only created prototypes of technical solutions for applying AI technologies to drones, while in Russia these solutions have already entered mass production, Sergey Beskrestnov, a freelance adviser to Vladimir Zelensky and an expert in communications and unmanned systems, said.
"The Russians have overtaken us in the technology of applying neural networks directly on board unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). <...> We have similar applications. But for the Russians, this is a mass-produced solution that has long been used on a large scale across the entire front. <...> At this pace, they can increase this application to thousands, even tens of thousands of UAVs. We don’t have that. There are prototypes demonstrating that such technologies can work for us. But we don’t have an UAV that we could produce in the tens of thousands," he said in an interview with the Ukrainian IT industry news portal Dou. He noted that this solution enables the recognition of visual objects and targets using AI, which makes the drone autonomous and independent of an operator.
Another area where Ukrainian developers are also losing the technological race to Russia is jet-powered UAVs. According to Beskrestnov, Ukraine currently lacks effective interceptors against this type of drone. "We have at least four types of jet-powered interceptors, but they are in the final stages of testing and evaluation under combat conditions. It’s too early to talk about mass-producing them by the millions--we’re still in the final testing phase," the expert said. He noted that, for now, aircraft must be deployed to take down jet-powered UAVs flying at altitudes of 4-5 kilometers.
Beskreznov said that the problem arose during the development phase, when Ukrainian manufacturers did not expect Russian UAVs to be capable of reaching such high speeds. "We need a much faster interceptor, and that requires a design change--a new challenge for manufacturers," he explained.
Earlier, Pavel Palisa, deputy head of Zelensky’s office in charge of military issues, acknowledged that the interceptor drones currently at the disposal of the Ukrainian armed forces cannot effectively counter Russian jet-powered drones. According to him, Ukrainian developers are "exploring options," but the problem has not yet been resolved.

Housing costs push Vilnius buyers toward regions – but prices rise there, too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:27:00 UTC
23:27:00 KST

Residents priced out of the Vilnius housing market are increasingly looking to regional cities, but finding affordable homes there is becoming more difficult as prices rise.
In Panevėžys, Lithuania’s fifth city in the north of the country, the supply of newly built apartments remains limited, while prices are increasingly approaching those in the capital. Experts say the high cost of land is one factor pushing up prices for new housing.
A four-bedroom apartment in a building constructed in 1981 is currently listed for 125,000 euros. The apartment, which is being sold with only a few pieces of furniture, requires renovation. Realtor Adrian Orlov of Hausitus said the building’s brick construction makes it attractive to buyers because the apartments can be more easily remodelled.
The same apartment would have cost about 25% less last year. Housing prices have risen across much of Lithuania this year, with Panevėžys recording one of the fastest increases among the country’s major cities.
Demand is particularly strong for newly built homes.
“Now that people have seen how expensive older apartments have become, demand for new construction has started,” said Vaidas Šukys, head of Hausitus. “But the prices are really like those in Vilnius.”
Some newly built apartments in Panevėžys are listed at about 4,000 euros per square metre. A two-room apartment with only partial finishing can therefore cost about 220,000 euros.
Romualdas Paulauskas, head of the Panevėžys office of Ober-Haus, said developers are planning premium housing in the city centre, with partially finished apartments and upgraded common areas.
Despite rising prices, real estate experts say more young families are returning to Panevėžys from larger cities after being priced out of their local markets.
Žygimantas Mauricas, chief economist at Luminor, said the trend could continue as housing costs reshape where people choose to live.
“This is an economically active city and we will probably see a pattern similar to that in many Western European countries, where a growing share of locals are leaving the great cities, particularly Vilnius, for smaller towns and other regions,” he said.
The cost of land is one reason new housing is becoming more expensive, experts said. Municipalities could help by making land available more cheaply or leasing it for projects aimed at providing affordable housing, said Arvydas Valius, head of Hanner, one of the country’s biggest developers.
Despite higher prices, demand has not weakened. Panevėžys recorded 6% more registered housing transactions in the second quarter of this year than during the same period last year.

JUBA, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- The World Food Program (WFP) warned Friday that funding shortfalls will cut off food assistance for 400,000 South Sudanese refugees and internally displaced persons (IDPs) following September distributions.
The WFP said it is working with the United Nations (UN) High Commissioner for Refugees and the International Organization for Migration to coordinate with the South Sudanese government and inform affected refugees and IDPs about upcoming cuts to assistance.
The UN agency warned that the impending aid cuts come at the peak of the rainy season, a critical period when food is scarce, market prices spike, and flooded and degraded roads severely hamper humanitarian deliveries.
The WFP said it requires 280 million U.S. dollars to scale up humanitarian assistance in South Sudan through January 2027, where millions of people continue to suffer from acute food and nutrition insecurity.
The funding will enable the agency to maintain critical nutrition services as severe budget shortfalls force sweeping reductions in assistance across South Sudan.
Without sustained support, the WFP warned that vulnerable women and children face a heightened risk of severe malnutrition and life-threatening health complications. ■

PHNOM PENH, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- The second meeting of the China-Cambodia public-private sector dialogue mechanism was held in Phnom Penh on Thursday.
The meeting was attended by Cambodian Deputy Prime Minister and First Vice Chairman of the Council for the Development of Cambodia Sun Chanthol, Chinese Ambassador to Cambodia Wang Wenbin, and more than 70 officials from over 20 Cambodian ministries and representatives from over 70 Chinese-funded enterprises.

He stated that both sides should continue to make good use of the China-Cambodia public-private sector dialogue mechanism, accurately address corporate needs, actively promote the implementation of outcomes, and translate the consensus reached at the meeting into tangible results.
The China-Cambodia public-private sector dialogue mechanism meeting is held every six months. It is co-hosted by the Chinese Embassy in Cambodia and the Council for the Development of Cambodia, and organized by the Chinese Chamber of Commerce in Cambodia. ■

China to implement revised regulation on power accident response, investigation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
22:44:55 CST
23:44:55 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- China will implement a revised regulation on emergency response to and investigation and handling of electric power safety accidents, as the country works to strengthen safety governance amid rapid renewable energy development and the construction of a new power system.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang has signed a State Council decree promulgating the regulation, which will take effect on Jan. 1, 2027.
The regulation, consisting of 38 articles, requires power companies and users to strengthen the screening of potential accident hazards, adjusts criteria for classifying power accidents by taking into account factors including grid scale and structural changes and the grid-related performance of power generation equipment, and clarifies the safety responsibilities of entities connected to the power grid other than power companies and users.
Power companies should formulate emergency rescue plans and conduct regular drills, according to the regulation. It also calls for improved procedures in accident investigations, requiring investigation teams to notify supervisory authorities and invite them to participate in the investigation.
China has continued to strengthen power safety governance in recent years. During the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), both the number of power-related workplace accidents involving casualties and the number of fatalities declined compared with the previous five-year period.
As the country promotes a green and low-carbon transition in the energy sector and accelerates building a new power system, the power sector is also facing new situations and challenges.
In July, the National Energy Administration issued an action plan for power safety production during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), calling for a shift toward preventive risk management and solid efforts to prevent and defuse major systemic safety risks.
Notably, the plan calls for strengthened safety management of new-energy power generation, with improved safety standards for key scenarios including offshore wind power and new-energy bases in desert. The application of artificial intelligence in smart safety equipment will be encouraged, and the research into AI large model-based technologies for power safety management will also be promoted. ■

Military reception for war criminal Mladic draws EU condemnation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:58:50 UTC
22:58:50 KST

The body of convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic was returned to Serbia with military honors on Sept. 3, drawing condemnation from European officials and renewed scrutiny of Belgrade’s handling of his funeral.
Mladic’s coffin was flown from the Netherlands aboard a Serbian government aircraft, accompanied by his son and Justice Minister Nenad Vujic.
Draped in the flags of Serbia and Bosnia’s Serb-led Republika Srpska entity, it was carried from the aircraft by Serbian soldiers and taken under police escort to a military hospital in Belgrade for an autopsy.
Small groups of supporters gathered along the route, lighting flares and displaying banners.
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot condemned the honors, calling them “shameful and disrespectful” to Mladic’s victims and their families.
“I condemn that act in the strongest terms,” Prevot wrote on X, adding that it was taking Serbia further from the European Union’s fundamental values and ran counter to expectations of an EU candidate country.
EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos postponed a planned visit to Serbia, saying the glorification surrounding Mladic’s death was incompatible with the values underpinning the country’s EU path.
Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic also warned that a state funeral would amount to Serbia closing its own door to the bloc.
Funeral arrangements have remained politically sensitive.
Vujic said last week that Mladic would receive all military and state honors “to which he is entitled.”
President Aleksandar Vucic later said no final decision had been made and that the arrangements rested with Mladic’s family.
His burial is expected to take place in Belgrade on Sept. 7.
Mladic died on Aug. 27 at the age of 84 while serving a life sentence at a United Nations detention facility in The Hague.
The wartime commander of the Bosnian Serb army was convicted in 2017 of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. The charges included his role in the 1995 Srebrenica genocide, in which more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed, and the siege of Sarajevo.
Mladic was arrested in Serbia in May 2011 after nearly 16 years in hiding. His convictions and life sentence were upheld on appeal in June 2021

Europe’s biggest carmaker to shed 100,000 jobs in historic overhaul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
14:37:45 UTC
23:37:45 KST

Europe’s biggest carmaker to shed 100,000 jobs in historic overhaul
German car giant Volkswagen is set to shed around 100,000 jobs worldwide after management and unions agreed to cut a further 50,000 positions by the end of the decade, the company has said. The reductions would amount to roughly one in seven of its global workforce.
Volkswagen, like much of German industry, is facing a severe financial and operational crisis, having watched profit margins collapse. CEO Oliver Blume has cited the loss of Russian energy as a key factor, along with increased competition from China.
The scale of the restructuring marks a dramatic retreat for a company long regarded as a symbol of German industrial strength. Volkswagen already had around 50,000 job cuts underway at its namesake brand, Audi, Porsche, and software subsidiary CARIAD, mostly through voluntary departures and early retirement. The latest plan effectively doubles that figure.
If carried out in full, the loss of around 100,000 positions would be the largest workforce reduction ever undertaken by a global automaker. Volkswagen employs roughly 650,000 people worldwide.
The cuts go far beyond payroll. Volkswagen has acknowledged that its European factories have capacity to build more than 500,000 vehicles a year beyond current demand, while the future of plants in Hanover, Emden, Zwickau, and Neckarsulm is uncertain once their existing model programs end between 2031 and 2034. No competitive replacement models have yet been secured for the four sites.
The company is also shrinking its ambitions elsewhere. Its model range is set to be cut by as much as half, while investment and research spending for 2027-2031 has been capped at €135 billion ($157 billion). Volkswagen is restructuring around annual sales of roughly 9 million vehicles and is targeting a 9% operating margin by 2030.
Hit by US tariffs and patchy demand for electric cars, Europe’s largest carmaker is struggling on several fronts. The crisis has been compounded at home by soaring energy costs since Berlin abandoned cheap Russian pipeline gas following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, increasingly relying on costlier LNG imports, including supplies from the US.
Russian presidential investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev has linked Germany’s industrial decline directly to its break with Russian energy. “No Russian gas – no German industry,” he wrote on Friday, commenting on plans by steel giant ArcelorMittal to shut major operations in Duisburg, affecting around 550 of the site’s 800 workers.
The energy shock has eroded a competitive advantage that underpinned German manufacturing for decades. The country subsequently suffered two consecutive years of economic contraction followed by sluggish growth, with manufacturers cutting production, investment, and jobs.
At the same time, Volkswagen has been losing ground in China, once its most important market, to domestic rivals such as BYD and Geely. Chinese automakers have also expanded rapidly in Europe, putting additional pressure on Volkswagen as it struggles to make its electric vehicles competitive on price and cost.
Volkswagen has steadily scaled back production at home. Last December, it ended vehicle production at its Dresden plant – the first time in the company’s nine-decade history that it had stopped carmaking at a German factory. BASF, Bosch, Continental, and other major German manufacturers have also closed or downsized facilities in recent years.
